0.title: Luke: The Gospel of the Saviour of the World
0.overview:
Luke is the longest book in the New Testament. It is also, in the judgment of many, the most beautiful — a Gospel written by a physician who was also a literary artist, a historian who was also a theologian, a Gentile who understood the Jewish roots of everything he was describing better than most of his contemporaries. When Luke sets out to write an orderly account of the things that have been accomplished among us, he produces something that is at once a careful historical document, a theological masterpiece, and a pastoral letter addressed to a world hungry for good news.

The author never names himself, but the ancient tradition is unanimous: this is Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), the companion of Paul (2 Timothy 4:11; Philemon 24), the man who stayed with Paul when everyone else had left. He was almost certainly a Gentile — the only Gentile author in the New Testament — and this shapes everything he writes. He sees in Jesus the fulfilment not just of Israel's hopes but of the deepest longings of the whole human race. His Gospel is addressed to Theophilus, probably a Roman official of some standing, and through him to the entire Gentile world. Luke wants the world to know that what happened in Judea was not a local religious event. It was the turning point of all of history.

Luke writes in two volumes: the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. Together they tell the story of what Jesus began to do (the Gospel) and what he continued to do through his Spirit in the church (Acts). The Gospel ends where Acts begins — with the ascension and the promise of the Spirit. This two-volume structure matters for reading Luke: his Gospel is not a self-contained biography but the first act of a larger drama, the story of how the good news of the kingdom moved from a manger in Bethlehem to the centre of the Roman world. The Gospel is movement toward Jerusalem; Acts is movement from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Luke's great themes are the themes of the kingdom come in unexpected ways. He gives more space than any other evangelist to women, to the poor, to Samaritans, to Gentiles, to tax collectors and sinners — the people whom polite religious society had written off as beyond the reach of God's grace. He is the Gospel of the outsider welcomed in. He records more miracles than any other Gospel. He shows Jesus praying at every major turning point of his ministry. He is the Gospel of the Holy Spirit, who appears from the first chapter to the last. And above all, he is the Gospel of joy — the word appears more times in Luke than in any other Gospel — because at the centre of everything is the announcement that the Saviour has come, and his name is Jesus.

1.title: The Announcement of the King
1.overview:
Chapter 1 of Luke is one of the most carefully constructed passages in all of Scripture. Before a single miracle is performed, before a single sermon is preached, before Jesus has spoken a word in public — Luke gives us seven scenes of annunciation, visitation, and praise that set the theological coordinates for everything that follows. He is telling us, from the very first verse, what kind of Gospel this is going to be: historically grounded, theologically rich, and written to produce the certainty of faith in a world that desperately needs it.

The chapter opens with a prologue that is unlike anything else in the New Testament — a formal literary preface, modelled on the prefaces of great Hellenistic historians like Thucydides and Josephus, establishing Luke's credentials as a careful historian and his purpose as a pastoral one. He has investigated everything carefully; he writes in orderly sequence; his goal is that Theophilus may have certainty about the things he has been taught. This is not mythology. This is history — specific, datable, verifiable history — and Luke wants his reader to know it.

From the prologue, the chapter moves into a world saturated with Old Testament atmosphere. Zechariah and Elizabeth are introduced in language that echoes Abraham and Sarah; the angel Gabriel appears as he did to Daniel; Mary's Magnificat is the New Testament's Psalter. Luke is making the claim that the long story of Israel — the story of promise and longing and waiting — has reached its culmination. The God who made promises in Eden, who called Abraham, who spoke through the prophets, is now fulfilling everything he said. The silence of four hundred years is over. The angel's voice breaks into a world that thought God had gone quiet, and nothing will ever be the same.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The prologue of Luke is the only place in any of the four Gospels where the author steps out from behind the narrative and speaks in his own voice. What he says in four verses establishes the whole intellectual and pastoral framework of what follows. He is writing history — but history in the service of faith. He has predecessors; he has done his own research; he has a named recipient; and he has a stated goal.

The word in v. 1 for what the many compiled is diēgēsis, a narrative that leads a reader through events from end to end. The “orderly” of v. 3 is a different word, kathexēs, meaning in sequence, each thing in its proper place. That need not mean a rigid diary order; Luke sometimes gathers material by theme rather than by date. What he promises is an account with a shape you can follow and trust.

The “many” who had already attempted this were not writing fraudulently, and Luke names their work without a sneer. But he has something to add: his own careful investigation, traced back to the source, from the eyewitnesses themselves. The word in v. 2 is autoptes — those who saw with their own eyes — and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Luke's history is not rumour at several removes. It is testimony from the people who were there.

Theophilus is greeted as “most excellent,” a formal Roman honorific used of senior officials (cf. Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25). He may be a patron who funded the research, an official investigating the Christian movement, or a recent convert who needs the foundations confirmed. The goal Luke states in v. 4 is asphaleia — the firm ground that comes of knowing that what you believe is true. For Luke, faith is grounded in history or it is not Christian faith at all.

Which raises the question a thoughtful reader feels at once: if Luke sifted sources like any careful historian, in what sense is this God's word rather than Luke's book? Scripture's answer is that it is both. The same Spirit who fills Elizabeth and Zechariah in this chapter was at work in the physician who went looking for people who had been there — guiding the questions, the witnesses, the material kept and the order set (cf. 2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:21). God did not bypass Luke's mind; he used it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The prologue's insistence on eyewitness testimony and careful investigation is the New Testament's answer to every form of Christianity that treats the historical details of the gospel as negotiable. Luke does not begin with timeless spiritual principles. He begins with what happened. The things accomplished among us are events — specific, dateable, observable events — and his first act as a historian is to establish their factual grounding.

This rules out from the start any reading of the Gospel as mythology, allegory or spiritual symbol. The incarnation, the miracles, the death, the resurrection: these are things that took place, in a named reign, in a known country, in front of people who could be questioned about them.

The goal of certainty (asphaleia) is the pastoral heart of the prologue. Luke is not writing to entertain, nor primarily to persuade the uncommitted. He is writing to confirm the faith of someone already taught the Christian story who needs to know that what he has been taught is true. That is the function of historically grounded preaching in every generation — not to introduce people to a religious experience but to settle them in a historical faith.
verseByVerse.examples:
The prologue models what responsible handling of the gospel looks like for any teacher or preacher: go back to the sources, investigate carefully, present the findings in order, and do it all in the service of the hearer's certainty. The person in the pew wrestling with doubt does not need vague spiritual reassurance. He needs the kind of careful, ordered account Luke is about to provide.

The best pastoral response to doubt is rarely “just trust.” It is nearer to “let me show you why trust is reasonable” — which is precisely what the next twenty-four chapters do.

And asphaleia is a gift the gospel gives to those who receive it on its own terms: not the brittle certainty of someone who has never been challenged, but the settled certainty of someone who has looked at the evidence and found it solid. Theophilus is meant to close this Gospel knowing not only that Jesus is Lord but why that claim can be trusted — and equipped to give the reason to anybody who asks.

verseByVerse.quote: Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke does not open with a vision, a genealogy, or a voice from heaven. He opens with paperwork. Picture the desk: several accounts of Jesus already written out and stacked in front of him, a list of names of people who were there, and a Gentile physician with a stylus, checking one against the other. That is where the third Gospel begins — not in a trance, but in an inquiry.

The word for what the many produced is diēgēsis, a narrative: not a scrapbook of sayings but an account that carries a reader from one end of the events to the other. And Luke says these are things that have been accomplished — brought to completion, filled full. He is not describing incidents that merely happened. He is describing promises that landed.

His sources are named with a precision worth slowing down for. They are autoptai — from autos (self) and a root meaning to see: those who saw it with their own eyes. The word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and it belonged to the vocabulary of Greek historical writing. Luke is claiming exactly what a historian claims. These same men are hypēretai tou logou, servants of the word: they did not only witness it, they have spent their lives handing it on.

Which raises the question a thoughtful reader feels at once. If Luke interviewed people and sifted documents like any careful researcher, in what sense is this God's word rather than Luke's book? Scripture's answer is that it is both, and that the one does not crowd out the other. The same Spirit who fills Elizabeth and Zechariah later in this chapter was at work in the physician who went looking for people who had been there — guiding the questions he asked, the witnesses he found, the material he kept, the order he set it in (cf. 2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:21). God did not bypass Luke's mind. He used it. The research is not a crack in the doctrine of inspiration; it is how, in this case, inspiration went about its work.

Notice also what Luke does not do. He does not attack the others who have written. He calls their work an undertaking, mentions it without a sneer, and gets on with his own. A man forging a religion suppresses the rival accounts. A man reporting an event welcomes them, because more witnesses make a case stronger, not weaker.

The Christian faith is the only religion in the world whose founding documents invite the reader to go and check them. It rests on things done in daylight, in front of people whose names were known and who could be visited and asked. Luke is about to tell a story with an angel in it. He begins by saying where he got it.

verseByVerse.quote: it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Luke steps forward in the first person, and every phrase is a claim he means to be held to.

Having followed all things closely is one word in Greek, parēkolouthēkoti — to follow alongside, to trace a matter back along its course. And for some time past is stronger than it sounds: anōthen, from the top, from the source. He has not skimmed. He has walked up the stream to the spring.

An orderly account is kathexēs — in sequence, one thing after another in its proper place. The word is worth a moment, because readers sometimes trip over it when they lay Luke beside Matthew and Mark and find the same episodes in a different order. Luke is not promising a diary timed to the day. He is promising an account with a shape that can be followed: material grouped so that the sense of it comes through, as when he sets the rejection at Nazareth at the head of the ministry because it is the doorway into everything after it. Orderly does not mean chronological to the hour. It means nothing has been thrown in at random, and where he puts a thing can be trusted.

Most excellent is kratistos, the formal address for a man of rank; Luke uses it of Governor Felix and Governor Festus in his second volume (Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25). Theophilus is very likely a real man of standing, possibly the patron funding the work. His name means “lover of God,” or “loved by God,” which has led some to read it as a stand-in for any Christian reader. Both can be true at once and the Gospel loses nothing either way: Luke wrote to a particular person, and that person's name happens to describe everyone who will ever read the book.

Something in that dedication is worth keeping. Luke could have addressed the longest book in the New Testament to the church at large and made a monument of it. He addressed it to one man who needed it, by name, with his title spelled out. The largest works of God usually have a particular person's name written at the top of them.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the purpose of the whole book, stated in one line — and it is not what a modern reader expects.

The word is asphaleia. It is built from a (not) and sphallō (to trip, to make to stumble): literally, un-trippability. Greek writers used it of a bolted door, of a prisoner held securely, of ground that will not give way underfoot. Luke did not write so that Theophilus would feel warmer about Jesus. He wrote so that when Theophilus put his weight down, the floor would hold.

And notice who this is for. The things you have been taught is katēchēthēs, the word behind our “catechism.” Theophilus is not an enquirer being evangelised. He has already been instructed. He already believes. And Luke thinks he needs a book anyway. That single observation cuts across a habit of mind common in the church, which treats evidence and argument as entry-level material a believer graduates from. The longest book in the New Testament, with its shepherds and its Magnificat and its prodigal son, was written for a Christian's certainty.

Here is a test worth running. Take the thing you would say you believe most firmly about Christ, and ask: how do I know that? If the honest answer is “because I have always been told so,” that is not nothing — most of what any of us knows arrived that way. But it is precisely the position Theophilus was in, and God thought it worth a whole Gospel to move him past it. A faith never examined is not necessarily a false faith. It is an untested one, and everything gets tested eventually.

There is comfort on the other side of that too. Some readers are frightened of examining what they believe because they suspect it will not survive the examination. Luke's answer is to hand over the evidence himself. He is not nervous. A man who had assembled a beautiful legend would not begin by telling you he checked it against the people who were there (cf. John 20:31; 1 Pet. 3:15).

Certainty, in this book, is not a temperament. It is not the confidence of someone who has never had a doubt. It is the settledness of a man who went and looked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–25 — Birth of John the Baptist Foretold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
With v. 5 Luke moves from the historian's prologue to the historian's narrative, and the contrast could hardly be sharper. From a formal Hellenistic preface he plunges into a world saturated with the Old Testament. Zechariah is a priest; Elizabeth is a daughter of Aaron; and they are described in language almost identical to the description of Abraham and Sarah — both righteous, both blameless, and she barren.

A reader steeped in the Hebrew Scriptures recognises the pattern at once. God is about to do something only God can do. He did it with Sarah, with Rebekah, with Rachel, with Hannah. Now he does it a last time, because the child born of this barren womb will prepare the way for the one who needs no human preparation to be born.

The setting of the announcement is itself a sermon. Zechariah is at work, in his division's fortnight, chosen by lot for the incense offering — the one duty most priests never received and no priest received twice (vv. 8-10). The whole multitude is praying outside at the hour of incense. God breaks four hundred years of silence not at a moment of revival but in the middle of an ordinary rota.

The appearance of Gabriel is the first angelic announcement in Scripture since the book of Daniel, and the detail is deliberate. Daniel received angelic revelation about the end of the exile and the coming of an Anointed One; Gabriel's reappearance signals that what Daniel waited for is arriving.

The announcement about John is a mosaic of Old Testament promise: the name John (“the LORD is gracious”), the prohibition on wine and strong drink (echoing the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6 and the birth of Samson), the filling with the Spirit from the womb (echoing Jer. 1:5 and Isa. 49:1), and the ministry in the spirit and power of Elijah (fulfilling Mal. 4:5-6). Every detail is a fulfilment of something Israel had been promised and had been waiting for.

Zechariah's response is entirely understandable and entirely insufficient. He asks how he can know — and then supplies his evidence, which is his age. He is asking for proof while the proof stands in front of him. The muteness that follows is as much mercy as discipline: nine months in which he can speak nothing except what God has spoken, and a limit written into the sentence (“until the day that these things take place”).

The chapter does not hurry past what that cost him publicly. The crowd waiting outside expected the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 and did not receive it; a man came out of the Holy Place making signs, and there was no benediction that day (vv. 21-23). And he stayed to the end of his rota, serving out the fortnight in silence.

Elizabeth's response, by contrast, is hidden joy. Her first recorded words are not about the child but about God: the Lord has done this for me, and he has looked on me to take away my reproach among people. She understands what Zechariah will need months to grasp — that this is grace, and grace needs no explanation.
verseByVerse.theology:
The barrenness of Elizabeth, like that of Sarah and Hannah before her, is the Old Testament's persistent symbol of human inability and divine sufficiency. The child of promise is always the child who could not have been born by human power alone. That is not incidental; it is the pattern of grace. God works precisely where human capacity has run out.

The child born to a barren womb, the nation born out of an enslaved people, the Messiah born of a virgin — the pattern holds in every case, and the point is the same in every case: salvation is of the LORD, and not of man.

Gabriel's description of John's ministry — that he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah — identifies John as the fulfilment of Malachi 4:5-6, the last prophecy of the Old Testament. Israel's canonical story ends with the promise of Elijah. It begins again here, with his arrival.

And the four hundred years of silence end not with a king or an army but with a priest's speechless vision in the temple. God's timing is consistently unexpected, and his entry points are consistently the last places power would have chosen.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's request for a sign is the response of a man whose theology was correct and whose faith, in the moment, was smaller than his knowledge. He knew the God who opens barren wombs. He had read the stories and offered the prayers. But when the answer stood in front of him he asked for evidence.

The gap between what we confess and what we trust in the moment is one of the most honest things the Bible shows about the life of faith. And Gabriel's response is not contempt but the gift of silence: a season of enforced dependence on what God has said rather than on what Zechariah can say.

Elizabeth's instinct to remain in seclusion for five months (v. 24) is the instinct of someone who knows that a gift this size needs to be received before it is announced. A soul that has received extraordinary grace sometimes needs to be quiet with it before it can speak of it.

The rush to publicise every experience of God's goodness can short-circuit the deeper work the grace was given to do. Elizabeth sits with the miracle, lets it form her, and waits.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The polished Greek of the prologue stops, and the sentence that follows could have come straight out of the book of Judges. In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest… Luke has just proved he can write like a Greek historian. Now he writes like the Old Testament, because that is the world the story is walking back into.

The date is fixed and checkable. Herod the Great died in 4 BC: a client king under Rome, an Idumean by descent rather than a son of David, a builder of extraordinary ambition, and a man who murdered his own wife and three of his sons. That is the throne Israel had. Luke names it in his first narrative sentence so that nobody mistakes what kind of night it was when the light came.

Zechariah belongs to the division of Abijah, the eighth of the twenty-four priestly courses David had organised (1 Chr. 24:10). By this period there were far more priests than the temple could use; each division served two weeks a year, and within a division the daily duties were assigned by lot. Elizabeth is a daughter of Aaron as well — priestly on both sides, which was considered a particular honour. His name means “the LORD has remembered.” Hers means “my God is an oath.” Between them the two names say what the chapter is about.

Then comes the description that ought to stop an attentive reader: both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord. Blameless? Luke has read the same Scriptures that say there is none righteous, no, not one (cf. Ps. 14:3; Rom. 3:10-12). He is not contradicting them. This is covenant language — the same verdict given of Noah and of Job. It is not a claim that they never sinned. It is a claim that when they sinned they brought the sacrifice God had appointed, and that there was nothing in their lives a neighbour could point at and say there is where they let God down.

Blameless is not sinless. It is the description of a life with nothing hidden in it — and it is one of the kindest words in the Bible, because it is a standard an ordinary believer can actually be held to.

Which is what makes the next verse hurt. Luke has spent two verses establishing that this couple did everything right. He is about to say what it got them.

verseByVerse.quote: But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But. One word, and the whole picture inverts.

Stage it properly. They are old now. There is a room in that house that was going to be for a child and has been used for storage for thirty years. There were the early years of quiet confidence, when everyone assumed it was only a matter of time. Then the years of remedies and of prayers with a shape to them, specific and hopeful. Then the year — and every couple who has walked this road can name it — when they stopped saying when and started saying if, and then stopped saying anything at all. Elizabeth has attended the births of every woman in that village. She has held other people's babies for forty years and handed them back.

And add what our world does not add. In first-century Judea childlessness was not merely a private grief; it was a public verdict. Children were the visible mark of God's favour (Ps. 127:3-5), so a barren woman walked through the market under a rumour: that God had looked at her and turned away. Elizabeth's own word for it, when the reproach is finally lifted, is oneidos — disgrace, the thing people say about you (v. 25). She has been a sentence in other people's conversations for four decades.

Luke sets her deliberately in a line. Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, the unnamed wife of Manoah — the Old Testament keeps returning to the same closed door, and it is never an accident of the plot. The child who matters most in Scripture is always the child who could not have come by ordinary means. That is not God being difficult. It is God making sure that when the child arrives, nobody can mistake where he came from.

But this has to be said carefully, because a childless reader is holding this page. Elizabeth conceived. Hannah conceived. Sarah conceived. And thousands of women just as righteous, who prayed just as long, did not — and their stories are not in the Bible because their stories are the ordinary ones. It would be a cruelty to read this verse as a pattern with your name in it: hold on faithfully and the answer will come. Some of the most God-fearing people who ever lived went to their graves without the thing they had asked for every day of their lives.

What the verse does say is this. The silence of God is not the absence of God. Luke has just recorded that these two were righteous before God, which means that whatever the barrenness was, it was not a verdict, and it was not a punishment. The village had read the evidence and got the sentence exactly backwards.

That is worth sitting with, because it is the thing a suffering believer most needs and least believes: the circumstance is not the verdict. And the reason for their waiting was not in them at all. It was that the forerunner of the Messiah could not be born until the Messiah was six months away. They did not know that. They could not have known it. For forty years the reason for their sorrow was a reason that had not happened yet.

That is not a formula for anyone else's grief, and it does not promise anybody a Gabriel. It does say that a delay can have its cause stored so far ahead of a person that no amount of praying will bring it into view — and that a God who can hold a plan steady through four hundred years of prophetic silence can be trusted with the twenty you have been waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Follow the odds for a moment, because they matter.

There were, on the usual estimates, thousands upon thousands of priests in Israel and exactly one incense altar. Each of the twenty-four divisions served two weeks in the year, and within a division the day's duties were drawn by lot. Burning the incense was the summit of them all: to pass through into the Holy Place alone and stand at the golden altar in front of the veil, with the Most Holy Place on the other side of it. The custom was that a man who had once been chosen was taken out of the draw, so that as many as possible might have the day. Which meant most priests never received it, and a man who did received it once.

This was Zechariah's once. An old man, at the end of a lifetime of faithful and unremarkable service, drew the lot for the greatest moment his office could ever give him. And Luke says he was chosen by lot — which is to say, by what everybody in that courtyard would have called chance. Proverbs had already given the true account of what happens when the lot is thrown: it is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov. 16:33).

Meanwhile, outside, the whole multitude is praying. Incense went up at the morning and the evening sacrifice, and the rising smoke was a picture of what the people were doing in the courtyard: let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Ps. 141:2; cf. Rev. 8:3-4). So here is the scene at the moment God breaks four hundred years of silence — a crowd in a courtyard praying, and one old man alone in the smoke, doing what his fathers had done, on the settled understanding that this is what you do and God does not answer out loud any more.

It is worth noticing where God chose to interrupt. Not at a revival meeting. Not in a season of unusual spiritual intensity. At the appointed duty, taken in its turn, by a man whose name had come out of a container. Zechariah went to work that morning knowing it was the biggest day of his career and having no idea it was the biggest day in four centuries.

The routine is not the opposite of the encounter. In this chapter it is the address.

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was not looking for this. He was in the middle of a fixed liturgy, in a room he had never stood in before, and when he raised his eyes somebody was there.

Standing on the right side of the altar of incense — the place of favour, and the detail says the visitor was not passing through. He was waiting. Zechariah had been chosen by lot that morning. The messenger had been at that altar by appointment.

And Zechariah is terrified. Fear fell upon him: the verb is the one used of something dropping onto a man from above. This needs saying plainly, because the angels of popular imagination are decorative — soft-featured, faintly apologetic, harmless. Every angel in Scripture who appears to a human being has to open by saying do not be afraid, and they say it because it is necessary. Isaiah came apart at the seams (Isa. 6:5). Daniel's strength drained out of him and he fell on his face (Dan. 10:8-9). John, who had leaned on Jesus's chest at supper, fell at the feet of the glorified Christ as though dead (Rev. 1:17). These are not nervous men.

The reason is not that angels are hostile. It is that a creature made of dust and carrying a conscience cannot meet the unfallen without discovering what he is. Fear here is not a failure of faith. It is accurate perception arriving all at once.

And there is something almost unbearable about where it happens. Zechariah has spent his life inside the machinery of holiness — the courses, the lots, the incense, the washings, the curtain — every part of it designed to manage the distance between a holy God and a people who could not survive him unmediated. He has handled the equipment for fifty years. Now the thing the equipment was for has walked into the room.

Readers sometimes ask whether this still happens — whether angels appear now. Scripture does not slam the door: some have entertained angels unawares (Heb. 13:2), and they are sent out to serve those who will inherit salvation (Heb. 1:14). But notice the shape of every appearance in the Bible. Nobody summons one. Nobody has a method. They arrive on God's errand, say what they were sent to say, and go. And notice what they are for. Not to be looked at, but to carry a message. From the moment Gabriel opens his mouth, he is no longer the interesting thing in the room.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to him, 'Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard.

Stop at that sentence, because it raises a question the text never answers directly and every reader asks. Which prayer? Zechariah is an old man. His wife is long past childbearing. Whatever he had once prayed about a son, he had almost certainly stopped praying years ago; nobody keeps asking for a thing when the door has visibly shut. So the announcement lands on a man who is no longer asking.

Two answers are possible, and both are true. The first is that the prayers of twenty and thirty and forty years ago were heard when they were prayed. The Greek is a passive — your prayer was heard — and God's hearing is not the same event as his granting. The request went in. The file was never closed. The answer was scheduled for a date that had nothing to do with Zechariah's biology and everything to do with a second child six months behind this one.

The second is quieter and probably nearer. He is standing at the incense altar, and the incense is the prayer of the nation. The priest at that altar prayed for Israel: for the redemption of Jerusalem, for the coming of the Lord to his temple, for the end of the silence. That is the prayer on his lips when Gabriel arrives. And the answer he is handed is a son — because the son is how the nation gets its answer. He prayed for the redemption of Israel and was told to go home to his wife.

Both readings say the same thing about God, and it is not a small thing. He does not lose requests. And when he answers, he frequently answers on a scale that makes the original request look like a rough draft.

Now the harder half, because somebody reading this has a prayer that has gone twenty years without a word. Notice exactly what Gabriel says and does not say. He does not say your prayer has been granted. He says it has been heard. Those are different, and Scripture will not let us collapse them: Paul asked three times and was told no, and the no was itself the answer (2 Cor. 12:8-9). What this verse forbids is the conclusion the silence keeps pressing — that the request never arrived, that it fell into a room with nobody in it. It arrived. It was heard. It has been heard every single time. God has never once not been listening. He has often not yet been speaking.

And there is a mercy in the delay that is easy to miss. Had Elizabeth conceived at thirty, the child would have been a comfort to his parents and nothing more. Because she conceived at seventy, the child was a sign to a nation. Those decades of grief were not wasted; they were the setting the jewel had to be cut for. That is not offered as an explanation of anybody else's waiting — most waiting gets no explanation this side of the grave. It is offered as evidence that the category exists.

Then the name, and God chooses it, not the father: you shall call his name John. In Hebrew, Yohanan — the LORD has been gracious. A couple who had been told by everyone around them for forty years that God had withheld his favour were instructed to name their son God has shown favour, and to say it out loud at every meal for the rest of their lives.

verseByVerse.quote: And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gabriel gives the child's greatness a very exact location. He will be great before the Lord. Not great in Jerusalem, not great in the estimate of the crowds who will pour out to hear him, and certainly not great by the measures Herod was using nine miles away. John will die in a cell on the whim of a girl dancing at a birthday party, and the sentence still stands. Greatness before the Lord is not measured at the end by anything visible.

The joy is not private either. Elizabeth's neighbours will rejoice at the birth (v. 58), but Gabriel says many will, and he is looking well past the village. A childless couple's sorrow was a household matter. This child's arrival is a public event.

He must not drink wine or strong drink is the language of the Nazirite vow (Num. 6:1-4), which also lay on Samson from the womb (Judg. 13:4-5). But there is a difference, and it is the whole point. A Nazirite took the vow himself; a parent could dedicate a child, as Hannah did with Samuel. John neither takes it nor is given it by Zechariah. God imposes it before the boy exists. The consecration is not the family's offering to God. It is God's claim staked on a child not yet conceived.

Because this is here, it should be said that Luke does not make abstinence the higher path — and Luke himself is the one who blocks that road. A few chapters on, Jesus says that John came neither eating bread nor drinking wine and they called him demon-possessed, and the Son of Man came eating and drinking and they called him a glutton and a drunkard (7:33-34). The same Gospel that gives John's austerity gives Christ at a wedding where the wine ran out. John's abstinence is a uniform, not a law. It marks him as the wilderness prophet, the man standing outside the system and calling the system to repent. A believer who abstains is free to. A believer who does not is not a lesser Christian. And anyone using this verse to grade another man's holiness should read on four verses and notice who the abstainer's Master turned out to be.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb. Jeremiah was known and consecrated before he was formed (Jer. 1:5); the Servant was called from the womb (Isa. 49:1). Luke means John's equipping for his office rather than a doctrine of infant conversion, and it will become visible in six verses' time when the child moves at the sound of Mary's voice.

But the direction of it is unmistakable, and it is the direction grace always runs. Before John could believe, or refuse, or understand, or want anything at all, God had already begun. Nobody in this story gets to God first.

verseByVerse.quote: And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gabriel now says what the child is for, and nearly every phrase is a quotation. Israel had not heard a prophetic word for four hundred years, and the last words in the last book of their Scriptures were these: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers (Mal. 4:5-6). The Old Testament closes mid-sentence, waiting. Gabriel picks the sentence up.

Notice the direction of the turning: he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. Not to a programme, a party, or a temple. To God himself. That is what repentance is, and it is why John's preaching will sound so much ruder than religion usually does.

Keep Gabriel's exact wording in mind, because a reader with an open Bible will hit a puzzle here. When the priests came out and asked John point-blank, Are you Elijah?, he answered flatly, I am not (John 1:21). Yet Jesus said of that same man, he is Elijah who is to come (Matt. 11:14). They are not contradicting each other; they are answering two different questions. John denies what his questioners meant — that he was the Tishbite himself, returned in person from heaven. Jesus affirms what Malachi meant: that the promised forerunner had come at last, in the spirit and power of Elijah, exactly as Gabriel says here. The prophecy was never that a man would come back. It was that a ministry would come again — the same blunt voice, the same rough clothing, the same summons to a nation to turn round before the LORD arrives.

And do not hurry past the domestic clause, because it is the strangest item on the list. God announces the greatest turning point in the history of the world, and among the first effects named is that fathers will turn towards their children. That is not decoration. Where a nation goes cold towards God, the first place the cold shows is the kitchen table; and where God returns, the first place the thaw shows is the same table.

A man who has not spoken properly to his son in eleven years and has a hundred good reasons why; a daughter who long ago wrote her father off and has the paperwork to justify it — Malachi says the coming of the LORD reaches into that, and Gabriel says it has started. Revival that leaves a family exactly as it was is not the revival Malachi promised.

Then the last phrase, which has been the job description of every servant of God since: to make ready for the Lord a people prepared. John is not the destination. Everything about him — the desert, the voice, the diet, the crowds — exists to get a people ready for somebody else. He is the road, not the city.

verseByVerse.quote: And Zechariah said to the angel, 'How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.

Every reader stops here, and the question is always the same. Why is Zechariah struck dumb for asking, when Mary asks what looks like the same question sixteen verses later and is answered kindly? Gideon laid out a fleece twice and God went along with it (Judg. 6:36-40). Abraham asked how am I to know? in almost these words and was given a covenant ceremony instead of a rebuke (Gen. 15:8). If God is patient with them, why not with this man?

The answer is not in the question. It is in the sentence that follows it.

Mary asks how will this be, since I am a virgin? — a question about mechanism, asked by somebody who has already accepted that it is going to happen. Zechariah asks how he can know, and then supplies his evidence: for I am an old man. That little for is the whole difference. He is not asking Gabriel to explain; he is explaining to Gabriel. He has weighed the announcement against what he knows about ageing bodies, and the announcement has lost. Gabriel's own diagnosis two verses later says precisely this and nothing else: because you did not believe my words.

There is something almost unbearable about the timing. He is standing in the Holy Place. An angel is in front of him. The incense is still rising. Every external condition for faith that a human being could possibly ask for is in place — and the man's mind goes to his age.

Which is the reason this verse frightens people, so let it be said plainly. Does God strike down those who doubt? No. Read what the Bible actually contains. The psalmists shout at God for whole psalms, and the shouting is in the Scriptures. Job argues for thirty chapters and is vindicated over his tidier friends. A father cries I believe; help my unbelief and gets his son back the same hour (Mark 9:24). Thomas demands to put his hand in the wound and is offered the wound (John 20:27). God is not brittle. He has never once been rattled by an honest question.

What happened to Zechariah is not the punishment of doubt. It is the granting of a request. He asked for a sign — and he got one, and it was himself. He wanted evidence he could hold. God gave him nine months of it, attached to his own face. It is one of the oldest mercies in Scripture that God so often gives us exactly what we asked for, in the form we would never have chosen.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered him, 'I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God. He does not argue biology with the old priest. He gives his name and his post, and that is the whole of the rebuttal.

The name should have gone off in Zechariah's head like a bell. Only two angels are named anywhere in Scripture, and the last time this one appeared he came to a man in exile with a message about how long the waiting would be: seventy weeks are decreed for your people, and at the end of them an Anointed One (Dan. 8:16; 9:21-24). Gabriel is the angel of the countdown. A priest steeped in Daniel is being told by the very messenger who set the clock that the clock has run out — and he asks him for a sign.

I stand in the presence of God is a courtier's phrase, and it carries the authority behind the message. Gabriel does not speak for himself. He has been sent, and the words he brings have just come out of the throne room. To weigh them against a doctor's estimate is not caution. It is a category error.

Then the sign, and it is heavier than Zechariah expected: silence, until the day these things take place.

It is easy to read that as punishment and stop there, but look at what it does to him. Zechariah is a priest, and a priest's work runs on words — the blessing, the recitation, the teaching, the pronouncing. He is stripped of the one faculty his whole office depends on, and left with nothing to do but turn over what Gabriel said. Nine months is exactly the length of time it takes to watch a promise you refused to believe come true in front of you, slowly, day by day, in your own house. And he will not be able to say a word about it to anybody. He will have to believe it in private first.

There is a limit written into the sentence, too: until the day that these things take place. The discipline has an end date, and the end date is the fulfilment. God does not put him in the dark and leave him there. He puts him in the dark until the light he refused to believe in comes into the room.

Which will be fulfilled in their time. Gabriel is entirely untroubled. The word will be fulfilled — not because Zechariah eventually came round, but because God said it. The promises of God do not draw their strength from the faith of the person who hears them. Which is precisely why they can be leaned on by people whose faith is thin (cf. 2 Tim. 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke takes the camera outside for three verses, and it is one of the small perfect touches in his Gospel.

The crowd is waiting, and they have begun to look at one another. The incense offering did not take long, and a priest who lingered in the Holy Place was a worrying sight — the whole architecture of the place rested on the assumption that a sinful man in a holy room might not come out again. They are wondering at his delay.

And when he does come out, he cannot do the one thing they are standing there for. The priest who had burned the incense came out to pronounce the blessing over the people: the Aaronic blessing, some of the oldest words in Israel's worship. The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace (Num. 6:24-26). Zechariah opens his mouth and nothing comes out.

Consider what that congregation took home. The blessing was not pronounced. The service ended wrong. A man came out of the Holy Place gesturing with his hands like somebody who had seen something, and there was no benediction in Jerusalem that day.

Israel had waited four hundred years for God to speak, and on the day he finally did, the man appointed to bless them was struck dumb — because the LORD was about to make his face shine upon them in a way no formula could carry. The blessing was not cancelled. It was on its way in person.

Then the detail that quietly does the most work: when his time of service was ended, he went to his home. He stayed. He finished the fortnight. He served out the rest of his rota in silence, doing everything that did not require a voice, with the greatest news in four centuries locked inside him and no way of telling a soul.

There is a whole doctrine of faithfulness in that sentence. Obedience is largely what a person keeps doing after the moment of glory has passed and he is back on the roster with nothing to show for it.

verseByVerse.quote: After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, 'Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elizabeth conceives, and then does the last thing anyone would expect. She disappears for five months.

Luke does not say why, and readers have guessed for centuries. The likeliest reading is the simplest. She is an old woman in a small village where everyone has known for forty years that she cannot have children. A pregnancy at her age would first be doubted, then discussed, then examined by every neighbour with an opinion. She waits until the thing is past argument — until the God who did it is the only possible explanation — and only then lets herself be seen.

There is wisdom in that worth borrowing. Not every mercy needs announcing the day it arrives. Some works of God are still soft when they happen, and putting them straight in front of a crowd that will handle them roughly can damage them. Elizabeth sits with hers for five months, alone with God, before she gives it to anybody else. The instinct to publish everything immediately is not faith. Very often it is only noise.

Then she speaks, and what comes out is pure theology. Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me. Not “we have had wonderful news.” Not a word about herself. The Lord did it; the Lord looked. And the verb is the one used when God saw the affliction of his people in Egypt and came down to do something about it (Exod. 3:7-8). It is not casual noticing. It is the look that ends in action.

And notice what she says was taken away. Not the barrenness — the reproach. Oneidos: the disgrace, the thing people said. That is the wound she reports, and it tells you where the injury actually lay. She had lost the child she never had. She had also lost forty years of standing in a room: every wedding she attended, every festival, every conversation that changed direction as she came in.

What God took away that morning was not only a medical condition. It was a sentence a whole village had passed on her, and which she had heard them pass.

She had lived under other people's verdict for four decades. It turned out that the only verdict ever actually recorded about her was the one in verse 6, and it had read righteous before God the whole time.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Six months after the annunciation to Zechariah, Gabriel is sent again — this time not to a priest in the temple but to a young woman in Galilee. The contrast is everything Luke is about. The gospel does not move from centre to periphery, from the established to the marginal, from the important to the overlooked. It moves the other way.

The temple in Jerusalem is where Gabriel went first; a village in Galilee, to a girl betrothed to a builder, is where he goes next. Nazareth was small and undistinguished — so undistinguished that Nathanael would later ask whether anything good could come out of it (John 1:46). The answer, it turns out, is everything.

Gabriel's greeting is without precedent in Jewish literature. Nobody else in the Bible is greeted this way. Mary is “favoured” — kecharitōmenē, the perfect passive participle of charitoō: one who has been, and remains, the recipient of grace. The word shares its root with charis, grace. She is the graced one, the one on whom divine favour has freely fallen.

Roman Catholic theology has developed from this greeting the doctrines of Mary's immaculate conception and sinlessness; the Reformed reading takes the word as referring to God's gracious choice of Mary for this specific task rather than to any inherent quality in her. The distinction matters, and Mary settles it herself at v. 47 when she calls God her Saviour. In Luke's account the wonder is never Mary's worthiness. It is God's freedom.

The announcement of Jesus's birth is the most theologically dense passage in the chapter. Gabriel says four things: he will be great; he will be called Son of the Most High; the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father; he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.

These claims are simultaneously royal and divine. The throne of David identifies him as the Messiah of Israel's hope; the title Son of the Most High and the endless kingdom move beyond anything a merely human king could claim. Gabriel is announcing the fulfilment of 2 Samuel 7:12-16 and the inauguration of the kingdom of Daniel 7:14. The Messiah Israel expected and the Son of God the disciples would confess are one and the same person.

Mary's question is entirely different in character from Zechariah's request for a sign. She does not doubt; she asks for clarification. The mechanism puzzles her, not the possibility. And Gabriel's answer is the most direct statement of the incarnation in the Synoptic Gospels: the Holy Spirit will come upon her, the power of the Most High will overshadow her, and the child will be called holy, the Son of God.

The language of overshadowing (episkiazō) echoes the cloud of divine presence that covered the tabernacle (Exod. 40:35) — the presence of God taking up residence. Mary is the new tabernacle, the place where God chooses to dwell. And her response, “Let it be to me according to your word,” is the finest answer to divine grace in the New Testament. Not resignation. Not reluctant compliance. Surrender that is also worship.
verseByVerse.theology:
The title “Son of the Most High” places Jesus in direct relationship to the God of Israel's covenant. In Daniel 7:18-27 it is the saints of the Most High who receive the kingdom; here the kingdom is given to the Son of the Most High himself. Gabriel is announcing not merely that Jesus will be the greatest of Israel's kings but that he is the figure Daniel saw receiving dominion, glory, and a kingdom that will not be destroyed.

The Davidic covenant and the everlasting kingdom of Daniel meet in this child — and a thousand years of promise, apparently stalled since the exile, resume in a single sentence spoken in a village house.

The Holy Spirit's role in the conception is the New Testament's clearest statement that the incarnation is a divine act and not a human achievement. Mary supplies the humanity; the Spirit supplies the initiative that makes this birth unlike every other.

The result is not a demigod — a being partly divine and partly human — but a fully human being who is at the same time the eternal Son of God. This is what the church has confessed from the beginning: two natures, one person, without confusion or mixture. Gabriel does not explain the mechanics of the mystery. He announces the reality.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary's “Let it be to me according to your word” is the model response to a divine call that exceeds comprehension. She does not understand how this will happen. She does not know what it will cost. She cannot see Simeon's sword or the hill called Golgotha. She says yes to a future she cannot see, on the strength of the word of a God she trusts.

That is what faith is — not the confident feeling that everything will be easy, but the willingness to place yourself in the hands of the One who has spoken.

The contrast between Gabriel's errand to the temple in Jerusalem and his errand to a house in Nazareth is Luke's first great declaration that the gospel is for everyone. The most important conversation in human history took place not in a palace or a sanctuary but in the home of an ordinary girl in a town nobody thought much of.

God's greatest gifts consistently arrive through the most unlikely channels — which means no person, no place and no circumstance is too small or too obscure to be the site of divine grace.

verseByVerse.quote: In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six months later Gabriel is sent again, and Luke means the reader to feel the drop.

The first annunciation was in Jerusalem, in the temple, in the Holy Place, at the hour of prayer, to an ordained priest of the line of Aaron in the middle of the liturgy. The second is in a village in Galilee, in a house, to a girl with no title, no office and no lineage worth recording. Same angel, same errand, opposite ends of the world.

Nazareth is not mentioned once in the Old Testament, nor in Josephus, nor in the rabbinic lists of Galilean towns. Archaeology suggests a settlement of a few hundred people, farming and quarrying, on a ridge off the main road. Nathanael's famous question — Can anything good come out of Nazareth? (John 1:46) — is less snobbery than bewilderment. It is the sound a man makes on being told the Messiah comes from a place he has to think for a moment to locate.

She is a parthenos, a virgin, and she is betrothed. Betrothal in that culture was not an engagement in the modern sense. It was legally binding from the day it was made: the couple were called husband and wife, unfaithfulness counted as adultery, and it took a certificate of divorce to end it. It usually lasted about a year, during which the woman remained in her father's house. So Mary is legally bound to Joseph and still living at home — which is exactly the condition in which a pregnancy is a catastrophe.

Luke's whole Gospel is in this contrast, and he will go on making it: shepherds before scholars, a Samaritan before a priest, a tax collector before a Pharisee, a dying thief before the men who arranged the cross. God's gifts do not come in at the front door. They arrive round the back, through people nobody thought to ask.

One note for the reader tracking the promise. Of the house of David attaches, in the Greek, to Joseph — and Joseph is not going to be this child's father. How the son of Mary comes to hold David's throne is a real question, and Luke will take it up properly when he sets out the genealogy in chapter 3. For now it is enough to see that God has been steering towards this house for a thousand years, and that the heir of David is a builder in a town of four hundred people who does not yet know what he is about to be told.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to her and said, 'Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!' But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greetings, O favoured one, the Lord is with you!

Nobody else in the Bible is greeted like this. The word is kecharitōmenē, and it repays taking apart, because a great deal has been built on it. Its root is charis — grace. Its form is a perfect passive participle, which in Greek means: something was done to her, and the result of it stands. Not “gracious one,” as though describing her character. Not “full of grace” in the sense of a vessel with grace to hand out; that is the Latin gratia plena, and it carried the word further than the Greek will go. The plainest English is: you who have been graced. Somebody else is the actor here. Mary is the one it happened to.

From this greeting the Roman Catholic Church has developed a great deal — that Mary was preserved from original sin at her own conception, that she remained sinless, that she may be prayed to as a channel of grace. Protestants should say what they can say warmly before they say what they cannot. Mary is the most highly favoured woman who ever lived; the Reformers said so without embarrassment, and Calvin refused to let anyone speak lightly of her.

But the word here says the opposite of what it is asked to prove. Grace, by definition, is not owed and not earned; a perfect passive participle formed from charis tells you that Mary received something — which is exactly what a woman needing nothing could not do. And she will settle it herself in nineteen verses, in a song, with the Spirit on her: my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour (v. 47). Only the drowning have any use for a lifeboat.

Then notice what troubles her, because Luke is careful about it. She is not frightened of the angel. She is greatly troubled at the saying, and she tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be — the verb is one of reasoning a thing through. Gabriel has not yet mentioned a child. All he has said is that she is graced and that God is with her, and she is turning the sentence over, working out what on earth it could mean. This is not a passive girl. The first thing Luke tells us about her mind is that it went to work.

And here is the sentence worth holding on to, because favoured is one of the most misread words in the Christian vocabulary. It did not mean an easy life was coming. Being the favoured one of God bought Mary a pregnancy nobody would believe, a fiancé who nearly divorced her, a birth among animals, a refugee run into Egypt with a killer behind her, a son whose neighbours tried to throw him off a cliff, and an old man in the temple telling her that a sword would go through her own soul.

God's favour is not a promise of comfort. It is a promise of God — which is a far better thing to be given, and a far heavier thing to carry.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to her, 'Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favour with God. Gabriel now explains the greeting he opened with, and the explanation is not about Mary at all. She has found favour. It is the phrase used of Noah in a world God had already decided to flood: Noah found favour in the eyes of the LORD (Gen. 6:8). Nobody manufactures that. A man does not find what he produced himself.

Then the announcement, and it comes in the plainest words imaginable: you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus.

Jesus is the Greek form of Yeshua, a shortened Joshua — the LORD saves. It was a common enough name; there are several in Josephus. Luke does not pause to translate it, though Matthew does when the angel speaks to Joseph: you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21). But the name is already the whole sermon, and it is worth hearing what it does not say. The child is not called the LORD reigns, or the LORD comes, or the LORD judges — all of which would have been true. He is called the LORD saves. And the naming is done before he is conceived, which means the rescue was decided before the rescuer had a body.

Notice too how ordinary the mechanics are. She will conceive; she will carry; she will bear. There is no suggestion that the pregnancy will be shortened, or painless, or visibly supernatural to anybody watching. The eternal Son enters the world through nine months of nausea, backache and swollen ankles in a house with a dirt floor. God did not arrange a dignified entrance. He arranged a real one.

And this is the hinge on which the whole Bible turns. From the promise in Eden that a woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head, through the covenant sworn to Abraham, through the throne promised to David, through every prophet who said a virgin shall conceive and unto us a child is born — the entire weight of it comes down on one sentence spoken in a back room in Galilee.

The Word by whom the world was made is going to be knitted together inside a girl. He who holds the stars in their courses will have to be carried. He who feeds every living thing will need to be fed. Heaven's answer to a ruined world was not a decree issued from a safe distance but a Son, sent, named before conception, called the LORD saves because that is what he came to do — and there has never yet been a soul who came to him for it and was turned away.

verseByVerse.quote: He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four claims, and they climb.

He will be great — with no qualifier attached. Of John, Gabriel had said “great before the Lord” (v. 15); the measuring rod was named because John needed one. Here there is no measuring rod, because there is nothing to measure him against.

He will be called the Son of the Most High. In biblical usage “called” frequently means “shown to be” — the title is not conferred so much as recognised. Israel's kings were spoken of as God's sons by adoption at their coronation (Ps. 2:7; 2 Sam. 7:14). This one is the Son before anybody crowns him.

The Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David. This is the promise of 2 Samuel 7:12-16, made a thousand years earlier and unfulfilled ever since: a son of David whose kingdom would be established for ever. The last real Davidic king had been dragged off to Babylon six centuries before. The throne had stood empty so long that an Idumean client of Rome was sitting in the palace. Gabriel says the promise is not dead. It was waiting for the right heir.

And of his kingdom there will be no end. Here the language stops being merely royal. Daniel had watched one like a son of man come to the Ancient of Days and receive a dominion that shall not pass away (Dan. 7:13-14); Isaiah had promised a child whose government would increase without end (Isa. 9:6-7). No merely human king ever gets that sentence, for the plain reason that human kings die.

A reader will fairly ask whether this has happened. Jesus never sat on a throne in Jerusalem. Israel is not restored as a kingdom. The house of Jacob is not visibly ruled by David's son. Sincere Christians answer this differently, and both answers love the same Bible and read it with the same seriousness.

Many — including teachers a reader may know and value, MacArthur and Ryrie and Walvoord among them — hold that the promise is literal and still ahead: Christ will reign in Jerusalem over a restored Israel, and Gabriel's words will be fulfilled as plainly as they were spoken. Others, in the Reformed tradition, hold that the reign began at the resurrection, when God seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority (Eph. 1:20-21) — and point out that Peter said as much at Pentecost: God swore to David that he would set one of his descendants on his throne, and this Jesus God raised up (Acts 2:30-32).

Both readings agree on everything Gabriel actually says here: that the throne is his, that the kingdom is real, and that it has no end. Whatever else is still to come, no future is coming in which he is not King.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said to the angel, 'How will this be, since I am a virgin?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
How will this be, since I am a virgin?

Literally she says, since I do not know a man — the Hebrew idiom for sexual relations that runs right back to Genesis 4:1. And the tense matters: it is present, not past. She is not saying “I never have”; she is saying “that is not my situation.” She is betrothed, and betrothal was legally binding, so the obvious answer would have been: you will be married within the year, and this is how children ordinarily arrive. She does not give it. Something in Gabriel's behold, you will conceive has landed on her as immediate, and she has taken it that way.

Sixteen verses earlier a priest asked a question and lost his voice. Why is she answered warmly? The words look similar. The postures are opposite.

Zechariah asked how shall I know this? and then produced his evidence — for I am an old man — which is not a question but a rebuttal. Mary asks how will this be? and produces nothing at all. She raises no objection, offers no counter-argument, requests no proof. She has accepted that it will happen and wants to know how. The difference is not the intelligence of the question but the direction it faces. One is asking God to justify himself; the other is asking God to explain himself. God has never once refused the second.

That distinction is worth keeping, because honest believers regularly go quiet in prayer for fear of asking the wrong thing. There is no forbidden question in this chapter. What Gabriel meets with silence is not enquiry but the settled decision that God's word has already been weighed against the facts and found wanting. Ask anything. The line is only crossed when the asking has stopped being asking.

And there is something else in her question that ought to be said out loud, because it is easy to miss underneath the theology. She does not ask what will people say?

That question was coming, and it was going to cost her more than anyone else in this chapter. A betrothed girl visibly pregnant had, under the law, put herself within reach of stoning (Deut. 22:23-24); at best she faced a quiet divorce and a lifetime of whispering. It simply is not what she asks first. Her mind goes to God's method before it goes to her own reputation — and she has perhaps ten seconds in which to think.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered her, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gabriel does not explain the biology. He describes an action of God, in two lines of Hebrew-style parallelism, and then names the result.

The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. The second verb is episkiazō, and it is not a euphemism. It is temple language. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the cloud that settled on the tabernacle so that even Moses could not go in, because the glory of the LORD filled it (Exod. 40:35). It is the word for the cloud on the mountain of transfiguration (9:34). Wherever this verb appears, God is taking up residence. Mary is being told, in the only vocabulary Israel possessed for it, that she is about to become the place where God dwells.

A modern reader deserves the blunt question put plainly: did this happen, or is the virgin birth a legend the church draped over Jesus to dress up his importance? Two things need saying.

First, Luke means it literally. The word is parthenos, and Mary's own objection settles the sense: she is betrothed, and says she has not known a man. This is a claim about biology, made in a culture that knew perfectly well where babies come from. Second, it does not read like legend. The pagan tales sometimes offered as parallels — a god taking a mortal woman, a hero fathered by Zeus — are lurid couplings producing half-divine hybrids. This is their opposite: no union, no partner, a quiet overshadowing, and a wholly human child.

And nobody inventing a Messiah's origin would have invented this one, because it left Mary a betrothed girl visibly pregnant before her wedding. That is not a badge of honour but a scandal she would carry, and her son with her: years later men would sneer at him in public, we were not born of sexual immorality (John 8:41). Legends are built to impress. This account cost the family its reputation, and the Gospels record it soberly anyway, because it was true.

It matters, too — not as a conjuring trick to prove he was special, but because of who was being born. The one conceived here is not a new person who began in Nazareth. He is the eternal Son, and the virgin conception is how the eternal Son took a real human nature — born of woman, genuinely one of us (Gal. 4:4) — without simply becoming one more son of Adam, produced by ordinary generation and heir to Adam's ruined line. Truly human, truly from Mary; and truly the Son of God, his person originating not from the will of man but from the Most High. Take away the miracle and you do not have a simpler Christ. You have a different one.

Therefore the child to be born will be called holy — the Son of God. The Word by whom everything that exists was made became an embryo. The Son who had no beginning acquired a birthday. He who fills heaven and earth was, for a season, a few millimetres long, in the dark, under a girl's heart, in a village nobody had heard of. Angels stoop to look into this and cannot exhaust it, and no creature has ever measured the distance he came down.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. For nothing will be impossible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary asked for no sign, and God gives her one anyway. That is worth noticing: the man who demanded evidence got silence, and the girl who demanded nothing got a relative six months pregnant in the hill country. God is generous with confirmation to people who were not holding out for it.

Her who was called barren — Luke lets the village nickname be heard. That is what Elizabeth had been called for forty years, and Gabriel repeats it in the same breath as the news that it is finished.

Then the line that closes the announcement, and it is among the most quoted and most misused sentences in the Bible: For nothing will be impossible with God.

Read it in Greek and the sense sharpens considerably. What is translated nothing is literally no word — rhēma, a spoken word, a declared thing, an utterance. Gabriel is not making an open-ended claim about everything a human being can imagine. He is making a claim about what God has said: no word God speaks will fail to do what it was sent to do. And he is quoting, too. This is very nearly verbatim what the LORD said to Abraham when Sarah laughed behind the tent door (Gen. 18:14).

That distinction matters, and it matters most to the person most likely to need it. This verse gets written on cards and handed to families in hospital corridors, and it is heard as a promise that the outcome they are desperate for is available if only they can believe hard enough. Then the outcome does not come, and a grieving person concludes either that God let them down or that their faith was too small. Both conclusions are false, and the verse never said what they were told it said. It is not a blank cheque with the amount left for us to fill in. It is a signature under what God has already put in writing.

Which is better, not worse. A God who did anything anybody asked would be a God run by whoever prayed last, and the world would be ungovernable inside an hour. What is guaranteed here is stronger and steadier: not that everything is possible, but that nothing God has promised can fail. He said a barren woman would conceive, and she is in her sixth month. He said a virgin would bear a son, and the room is about to go quiet.

And if the request you are carrying is not among the things God has put in writing, that is not the end of the matter. Look hard at the list of things he has written down: that he will never leave you; that nothing in the whole of creation can separate you from his love; that he is working all things together for your good; that he will finish what he began in you; that he will raise your body out of the ground (John 6:40; Rom. 8:28, 38-39; Phil. 1:6; Heb. 13:5). Not one of those is negotiable, and not one of them depends on the strength of your grip.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said, 'Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.' And the angel departed from her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.

The word she uses of herself is doulē — the feminine of doulos, a bondservant, a slave. It is not modesty. It is a legal category, and it describes somebody with no right of refusal, whose time and body and future belong to another. Mary reaches for the strongest available word for belonging entirely to somebody else, and applies it to herself before she has been told anything more about what is coming.

Let it be to me is a single word, genoito, and its form in Greek is the mood of wishing — not a shrug of resignation but a reaching towards. She is not saying I suppose it must happen. She is saying let it happen.

Count what she agrees to in that half-second. She will be pregnant before her wedding, in a village of a few hundred people where everyone will do the arithmetic. Joseph will conclude she has betrayed him and will decide to divorce her; Matthew tells us his mind was made up before an angel changed it (Matt. 1:19-20). The law's provision for a betrothed girl found with another man is written down, and she will have read it (Deut. 22:23-24). Her explanation will be that an angel came. There is no version of this in which she is believed.

She says yes anyway. And the yes is given to a messenger who is about to leave — and the angel departed from her — after which there is nobody in that room but a girl and the God she has just handed her life to.

She is not being held up here as something the rest of us are expected to reproduce; nobody else will ever be asked this. But the shape of it is the shape of every real obedience. She is asked to say yes to a future she cannot see, on the strength of a word from a God she can trust. That is what faith always is. It is never the confident feeling that things will turn out comfortably. It is the decision to trust the character of the one who is speaking, at the precise moment when the content of what he has said has made everything harder.

There was another garden and another woman, and a word from outside asking to be believed. That one weighed God's word against the evidence in front of her — the fruit looked good, and the serpent had a point — and reached out her hand. This one weighs nothing and reaches for nothing, and simply says: let it be to me according to your word. The long ruin that began with a woman disbelieving God had begun to be undone by a woman believing him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Mary leaves for the hill country of Judah “with haste” — the word suggests urgency, even a kind of breathless joy. She has just received the most overwhelming news in history, and the angel has told her that her elderly relative is also pregnant. She goes at once, not to tell the story but to be with somebody who might understand it: someone else visited by grace in a way that makes no human sense.
