The moment Mary's greeting reaches Elizabeth, the child in Elizabeth's womb leaps. John recognises Jesus before either of them has been born. This is not sentimental detail; it is Luke's first testimony to what the Baptist's whole ministry will be. Jesus is the one who is coming, and John exists to point towards him. Even in the womb, before any conscious act of faith, John responds to the presence of the Lord.

The Holy Spirit fills Elizabeth in that moment and she speaks with prophetic clarity. Mary is blessed; the fruit of her womb is blessed; and Elizabeth marvels that “the mother of my Lord” should come to her. That exclamation is the first confession of Jesus's lordship in Luke's Gospel, and it comes from a woman who cannot know it by any natural means. The Spirit has revealed it.

The word kyrios on Elizabeth's lips is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the divine name itself. She is not saying “the mother of an important person.” She is saying “the mother of the one who is LORD.” The full theological weight of the title is present from the beginning.

And the section does not end with the confession. It ends with a beatitude, and the beatitude is about faith: “blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfilment of what was spoken to her from the Lord” (v. 45). Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, does not finally commend Mary's womb, her lineage or her purity. She commends her trust.

That is the section's real climax, and it sets Mary directly against Zechariah, who heard the same angel in the same six months and did not believe. Luke has framed his whole opening around a single question: the word of God has come — will it be received?
verseByVerse.theology:
John's leap at the sound of Mary's greeting is a pre-natal act of recognition that is also a pre-natal act of worship. The Reformed tradition reads this, alongside Jeremiah 1:5 and the Baptist's filling with the Spirit from the womb, as a sign that divine grace and knowledge precede human consciousness. The child does not decide to leap; the Spirit moves him.

This is the grace that goes before us — that calls and shapes and prepares before we are capable of any response. It is not an argument for conscious infant faith. It is a sign of the sovereign grace of God that precedes every human act.

Elizabeth's blessing of Mary — “blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” — applies the Old Testament's blessing language to the New Testament's supreme moment of grace. The construction is a Hebrew superlative: most blessed of women. Mary stands in the line of those through whom God has worked unexpected deliverance.

But she surpasses them all, because the one she carries is not a deliverer of Israel only but the Saviour of the world. And v. 45 keeps even that from becoming a cult of the mother: what the Spirit singles out in her is not her body but her believing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary goes to Elizabeth with haste — not to process her experience alone, not to work things out in private, but to be with somebody who can understand. The instinct is exactly right. The grace of God is not meant to be received and kept in isolation.

The community of the gospel is the community of those who have all, in one way or another, been visited by unexpected grace, and who find in each other's company the confirmation and the joy that private reflection cannot produce. An isolated believer is a believer at risk.

Elizabeth's question — “Why is this granted to me?” — is the question of someone who has not lost the astonishment grace produces. She has been told by an angel that she will bear a child; she is herself six months into an impossible pregnancy; and when she hears Mary's greeting her first response is wonder at the privilege of the moment.

The soul still capable of asking “why me?” in the face of God's gifts is a soul grace is still shaping. The moment we begin to feel we have earned the visit, something essential has been lost. And notice what is entirely absent from Elizabeth: any trace of comparison with the younger woman whose portion is plainly larger than her own.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In those days — immediately. Mary does not sit down to process. She packs.

Stage the journey, because it is not a stroll. From Nazareth to the hill country of Judah is somewhere between eighty and a hundred miles: four or five days of walking, through or around Samaria, over rough country, in the first weeks of a pregnancy, by a girl probably in her mid-teens. Luke does not say who went with her. He says she went with haste.

She is not going in order to break the news. Gabriel has already told her that Elizabeth knows something like it from the inside. She is going to be with the one other person on earth who will not think she has lost her mind.

That instinct is exactly right and deserves naming. Grace that has just landed on a person is heavy, and the first thing it looks for is somebody else who has been under the same weight. This is a good deal of what the church is for, and it is why an isolated believer is a believer at risk. Neither of these two women could have explained her situation to anybody else in Israel. Each of them could explain it to the other in a sentence.

Then the moment. Mary calls out a greeting at the door and, before Elizabeth has understood anything, the child inside her moves. The baby leaped in her womb. The verb skirtaō is the one the Greek Old Testament uses of hills skipping like rams (Ps. 114:4) and of the twins struggling inside Rebekah (Gen. 25:22).

And the order of Luke's sentence is precise and deliberate. The baby leaps first; then Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit. The mother's prophecy comes second. The first person in the New Testament to recognise Jesus Christ was a six-month-old unborn child who could not see, could not reason, and had no idea what he was doing.

Luke, who was a physician, chooses his word for that child carefully. He calls him brephos. It is the same word he uses of the newborn Jesus lying in the manger (2:12, 16), and the same word he uses of the infants people brought to Jesus to be touched (18:15). Unborn at six months, newborn in the straw, babe in arms — one word, three stages, no seam anywhere. Luke does not pause to argue the point. It is simply how he saw it, and how he wrote it.

John's entire ministry will consist of pointing away from himself towards somebody else. He began it before he was born, in the dark, at the sound of a voice — the first man to recognise the Lord, and he did it without a single thought in his head. Which is a fair picture of how anybody comes to recognise him.

verseByVerse.quote: and she exclaimed with a loud cry, 'Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elizabeth does not greet Mary. She shouts.

Luke's phrase is a loud cry, and the noun is used elsewhere of a battle shout and of the cry that goes up at the arrival of a bridegroom. This is not a decorous welcome at the door. An old woman has been ambushed by the Holy Spirit in her own hallway and comes out of it at the top of her voice.

Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. The construction is a Hebrew superlative: most blessed of women. And note the order — she blesses Mary, then moves immediately past her to the child, and never comes back. Every word after this is about him.

And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? This is the first confession of Jesus as Lord in Luke's Gospel, and it is made by a pregnant old woman in a village house about an embryo she cannot see. The word is kyrios, and on the lips of a daughter of Aaron steeped in the Greek Old Testament it is not a courtesy title. It is the word that stands in that Bible for the divine name itself. Elizabeth is not saying “the mother of somebody important.” She is saying that the child inside her young relative is the LORD.

Now look at who is speaking and to whom. Elizabeth is the elder by decades. She is the priest's wife, the daughter of Aaron, the one with the angelic visitation in her own household and a miracle six months advanced. Mary is a teenager from Galilee engaged to a builder. By every measure a human being naturally reaches for, the seniority runs one way — and Elizabeth's first instinct is to ask why she has been granted the privilege of the visit.

There is not a trace of comparison in her, and that is rarer than any miracle in this chapter. Two people are blessed at the same moment, unequally, and the one with the smaller share is the one who is delighted. Most of us can manage to be pleased for somebody else right up to the point where their gift is visibly larger than ours, and then something goes quiet inside. The Spirit filled Elizabeth, and what came out was joy at another woman's greater portion.

It is worth adding that her question — why is this granted to me? — belongs to a person who has not lost her astonishment. She has had an angel in the family and an impossible pregnancy of her own, and she is still amazed to be visited. Familiarity with grace is the occupational hazard of everyone who has known God a long time. The moment the visit stops being a surprise, something has begun to harden.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elizabeth explains what happened at the door, and then pronounces a beatitude — the first in Luke's Gospel, spoken by a woman, six months before Jesus is born.

The baby in my womb leaped for joy. She interprets her own child's movement, and she does it under the filling of the Spirit, so this is not a mother's fond guess. The word for joy, agalliasis, is the strongest one available: exultation, the gladness that cannot sit still. Gabriel had promised Zechariah joy and gladness at the boy's birth (v. 14). It has started early.

And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfilment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.

Read what Elizabeth actually commends. Not Mary's purity. Not her lineage. Not her womb — she has just blessed that, and now she moves to something else and gives it the emphatic final position. What the Holy Spirit singles out in the mother of the Lord is that she believed.

Set that beside Zechariah on the same page and the chapter's whole argument comes into focus. Two people receive an announcement from the same angel in the same six months. One does not believe, and is silenced. One believes, and is blessed. Luke is not moralising about temperament. He is showing, before Jesus has drawn breath, what this entire Gospel is going to be about: the word of God comes, and everything turns on whether it is received.

Luke will come back to this and make it explicit. Later a woman in a crowd calls out to Jesus, Blessed is the womb that bore you — the natural thing to say, and very close to what Elizabeth says here. And Jesus answers her: Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it (11:27-28). He is not disowning his mother. He is redirecting the blessing onto the thing his mother actually did — which is exactly what Elizabeth commends in this verse, and exactly what stands open to anybody reading this page.

And notice when she believed. Not once the pregnancy showed. Not after Joseph came round, or Simeon confirmed it, or the shepherds turned up with their story. Mary believed that there would be a fulfilment: future, unseen, unverified, and about to make her life extremely difficult.

Faith is not the conclusion reached once the evidence is safely in. It is trust extended across the gap while the evidence is still on its way. Everything else in the Christian life stands downstream of whether that gap can be crossed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–56 — Mary's Song of Praise: The Magnificat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Magnificat — named from the first word of its Latin translation, “My soul magnifies the Lord” — is the New Testament's greatest hymn and one of the most theologically rich passages in Scripture. It is modelled so closely on Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 2:1-10 that some have argued Luke originally assigned it to Elizabeth; but the text is clear, and the reasons for it belonging to Mary are overwhelming.

Mary is the New Testament's Hannah — the woman through whom God's greatest act of salvation is brought into the world. And like Hannah she responds not with private gratitude but with public theology: a proclamation of what God is like, what he has done, and what he always does.

The song falls into two movements. The first (vv. 46-50) is personal. Mary sings of what God has done for her: he has looked on the humble estate of his servant; he has done great things for her; his mercy extends to those who fear him. The second (vv. 51-55) is cosmic and historical: God has scattered the proud, brought down the mighty, exalted the humble, filled the hungry, sent the rich away empty, and helped his servant Israel.

Those verbs are past tense — the Greek aorist, expressing completed action — even though none of it has yet visibly happened. Mary sings in the prophetic past: what God is going to do in Jesus is so certain that she sings it as already accomplished. This is the faith that sees the invisible reality and speaks it before it is seen.

The theology of the Magnificat is the theology of the great reversal — the consistent pattern in which God works through what the world considers weak, low, foolish and despised, to accomplish what power and wisdom cannot. The proud are scattered; the mighty brought down; the humble exalted; the hungry filled; the rich sent away empty.

This is not a manifesto for violent revolution — every verb has God as its subject — but the testimony of a God whose ways are not our ways, who chooses the foolish things of the world to shame the wise (1 Cor. 1:27). Mary has understood it because she has lived it: she is herself the lowly servant God has honoured beyond imagining.

And the song ends where the story began, with Abraham (vv. 54-55) — the reversals are not God changing his policy but God keeping an old appointment. Then, with no transition at all, Luke notes that Mary stayed three months and went home (v. 56). She walked back to Nazareth visibly pregnant, to a fiancé who would decide to divorce her. The extraordinary is set down in the middle of the ordinary, and the ordinary is where it has to be carried.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Magnificat's use of the past tense for events that have not yet occurred — he has scattered the proud, he has brought down the mighty — is the linguistic form of prophetic certainty. The prophets of Israel consistently spoke of future events in the past tense when the certainty of God's word made the outcome as sure as if it had already happened.

Isaiah 53 does exactly this, narrating the Servant's suffering and vindication in the past tense centuries before either occurred. Mary's song places her in that prophetic line — not as one who has received a vision of the future but as one who has received the seed of the future in her own body and understands what it means.

The “humble estate” (tapeinōsis) of Mary is a condition of insignificance and social unimportance. God has looked upon it — epeblepsen, cast his eyes upon, deliberately noticed — not despite it but through it. This is the theology of election that runs from Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, and David the youngest over his brothers, to Galilee over Jerusalem and Mary over every princess in Israel.

God's choices consistently invert the world's criteria. The reason is not that the lowly are inherently virtuous. It is that the glory of a grace which chooses them cannot possibly be confused with a favour granted on the basis of merit.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Magnificat has been sung in Christian worship since the earliest centuries — in the evening prayer of the church, in the liturgies of East and West, in the hymns of the Reformation — and set to music by composers from Monteverdi to Bach. It is not merely a beautiful poem. It is the church joining Mary's song, declaring that the God who did great things for her is doing great things still.

Every Christian who sings it stands in the line of Mary's witness: scattering the proud, filling the hungry, keeping covenant with his people, is what he is still doing.

It is also among the most politically subversive texts in the New Testament — not because it calls for revolution but because it announces a King whose reign will outlast every human empire, whose justice will overturn every human injustice, and whose mercy will outlive every human cruelty. More than one government has banned its public recitation.

The church that sings this song is the community that knows how the story ends, and that knowledge shapes how it lives now: not grasping for power, not trusting in the mighty, not filling itself with the world's goods, but living in the pattern of the God who scatters the proud and exalts the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said, 'My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary answers Elizabeth's shout with a song, and it is not the song of a startled teenager. It is stitched out of the Psalms, Hannah's prayer, Isaiah, Genesis, Micah and Job — something like fifteen allusions in ten verses, most of them from the Greek Old Testament. This is what happens when a girl who has hidden Scripture in her heart is put under sudden pressure. What comes out is what was already in.

My soul magnifies the Lord. The verb is megalynei, to make great, to enlarge — which raises a fair question, since God cannot be made greater than he is. The answer lies in the two kinds of lens. A microscope takes something small and makes it appear larger than it is. A telescope takes something unimaginably vast and lets it appear nearer its true size. Worship is never the first of those. Mary is not inflating God. She is bringing him close enough to be seen as he actually is — and everything else in the picture, including her own alarming circumstances, takes its proper proportions the moment he does.

And my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour.

There is the sentence that settles the question raised at verse 28. A great deal of devotion has been built on Mary: that she was conceived without sin, that she remained sinless all her life, that she may be asked to carry our requests to her Son. And here, in the second line of her own song, with the Holy Spirit upon her, Mary calls God my Saviour. Not “the Saviour,” in general. Mine. A person who needs no rescue does not use that word, and never has.

Mary is not standing above the redeemed and looking down. She is standing inside them, singing. And this takes nothing away from her. It puts her exactly where she puts herself, and where she is most worth looking at: the first and best of a very long line of people who had nothing whatever to bring and were given everything.

Look at what she does with what she has been given. She does not examine herself. She does not narrate her feelings. Her soul goes out of itself and grows larger by looking at somebody else — and the one she looks at is not an idea but a rescuer with a name, who has been at this work since Eden, who has never yet abandoned a promise, and who at that moment was small enough to be carried under a girl's ribs and great enough to hold the heavens together. There is no danger of magnifying him too far. The whole of eternity will not be long enough to get him into proportion.

verseByVerse.quote: for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. The word is tapeinōsis — lowliness, low position, the state of counting for nothing. Mary is not describing her humility as a virtue. She is describing her social altitude, which was ground level. And the verb for what God did, epeblepsen, is the word for a deliberate turning of the head: the choosing to notice.

That is the whole logic of God's choosing right through the Bible, and it is worth pressing on for the reader who has spent a lifetime being passed over. Not the eldest son but the youngest. Not the impressive brothers but the boy left out in the field with the sheep. Not the capital but a village. Not the priest but the girl. Nobody in this chapter was chosen because a talent scout spotted them.

God looks in the direction nobody else is looking, and that is not a consolation prize for people who did not make the first team. It is his settled method, and Paul states it in so many words: he chose what is low and despised in the world, so that no human being might boast in his presence (1 Cor. 1:28-29).

For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.

This line deserves to be faced rather than hurried past. Protestants have often been so anxious about what has been built on Mary that they have quietly declined to obey a plain sentence of Scripture. Elizabeth has just called her blessed. Mary says it here with the Holy Spirit on her. A church that never calls Mary blessed is not being careful; it is disagreeing with the text. So call her blessed. She is the most favoured woman who ever lived.

Then notice what she immediately does with it. She gives the reason in the very next breath, and the reason is not herself: for he who is mighty has done great things for me. She is blessed because of what was done to her, not because of anything she can do for anybody else. That is the difference between honouring Mary and praying to her, and it is the difference between a mirror and a lamp. A mirror is not honoured by being stared at. It is honoured by being looked along, to the light it is turned towards.

And holy is his name. She has just said that the greatest thing which ever happened to a human being happened to her — and her sentence ends by getting out of the way.

verseByVerse.quote: And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse is the hinge of the song. Everything before it is about Mary; everything after it is about the world. And the joint between them is mercy.

His mercy is eleos, the Greek Old Testament's regular word for the Hebrew hesed: not pity felt at a distance but committed, covenanted loyalty — the love that has bound itself and will not walk away. It is the word used of a God who keeps steadfast love for thousands of generations (Exod. 34:6-7). Mary is saying that what has happened to her is not an exception. It is a sample.

For those who fear him. This deserves explaining plainly, because few phrases do more damage when they are misheard. The fear of the LORD is not being frightened of God. Every reader who has ever lain awake wondering whether God is waiting to catch him out should hear that clearly: that is not what the Bible means.

The fear of God is what a man feels standing at the foot of something vast — the awe that reorders him, that makes him careful, that puts everything else in the room into proportion. It is entirely compatible with running to him. In fact it is the only thing that makes running to him make sense, since a God small enough not to be feared would be a God too small to be worth reaching.

From generation to generation. A teenager is singing about grandchildren she will never meet. The covenant God does not deal with people in isolation; his mercy has a long reach down a family line, and the promise runs to children and to children's children (cf. Ps. 103:17; Acts 2:39).

That is worth taking hold of by anyone praying for a child or a grandchild who has walked away. The mercy that reached Mary in Nazareth had been travelling towards her since Abraham. It does not lose speed with distance, and it does not require the previous generation to have finished the job. Nothing in this verse guarantees a particular grandchild; it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. What it does say is what kind of God is being prayed to — one whose stated habit is to keep turning up in a family long after the people who first prayed for it are dead.

verseByVerse.quote: He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song turns outward, and the tense turns strange. He has scattered… he has brought down… he has exalted… he has filled… he has sent away. All past. All completed. And none of it has happened. Rome is at the height of its power. Herod is still in his palace. Nobody has been brought down from anything.

This is the prophetic past, and Hebrew prophecy uses it constantly: when God has spoken, the outcome is so certain that it can be reported as history. Isaiah described the Servant's suffering and vindication in the past tense seven centuries before a nail was driven (Isa. 53). Mary is doing the same thing, and she can do it for one reason — the thing that guarantees the reversal is already inside her. From where she is standing the war is over. What remains is the clearing up.

Is this a call to revolution? The Magnificat has been banned by more than one government, and it has been read as a manifesto by movements that arrived carrying rifles. Read the verbs. Every one of them has God as its subject. Mary is not summoning anybody to storm anything. She is describing what God does, what God has always done, and what he is about to do again — and the way he is doing it at this moment is by placing himself inside a poor girl in an occupied province. The overthrow is real, and it is total, and there is no army in it.

Then the line most readers would rather skip: the rich he has sent away empty. That is uncomfortable, because most people reading this are, by any measure the world has ever used, the rich. And it will not do to spiritualise it away into an attitude of the heart and move on, because Luke of all the evangelists refuses to let us. This is the Gospel that gives us the rich fool with his barns, the rich man and Lazarus, the ruler who went away sad, and Jesus saying it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye (12:16-21; 16:19-31; 18:22-25).

But notice the mechanism, because it is exact. The hungry are filled and the rich are sent away empty, and both go home with what they arrived with room for. Nobody is turned away at the door for owning things. They are sent away empty because they came full, and a full man cannot be filled. That is why money is so dangerous — not because God objects to it, but because it is the most efficient device ever invented for producing the sensation of not needing anything.

So here is a test that takes about a minute to run. Think of the last time something went badly wrong: a diagnosis, a bill, a phone call at an odd hour. What was the first thing reached for? For most of us the honest answer is a resource — savings, a contact, a plan. There is nothing wicked in any of that. But whatever gets reached for first is, in practice, the thing being trusted. And the reversal Mary is singing about is not chiefly about who owns what. It is about who, when the ground moves, still has anything left to stand on.

verseByVerse.quote: He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song ends where the story of salvation began.

He has helped his servant Israel. The verb is a word for taking hold of somebody in order to support them — the hand under the elbow of a man who is going down.

In remembrance of his mercy. When Scripture says that God remembers, it never means that something had slipped his mind. God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Gen. 8:1). God remembered his covenant, and heard the groaning in Egypt (Exod. 2:24). Remembering, in the Bible, is not recall. It is action taken on the basis of a commitment already made. It is a promise coming due.

As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever. That promise was made to a childless old man in Ur, in a world which had never heard of Israel, roughly two thousand years before this girl opened her mouth in a hill-country kitchen: in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed (Gen. 22:18). Two millennia of silence, exile, occupation, apostasy, restoration and more silence — and God had not moved an inch off the wording.

Notice what this does to the reversals she has just sung. They are not God changing his policy, or finally losing patience with the powerful. They are God keeping an old appointment. The scattering of the proud and the filling of the hungry is what covenant faithfulness looks like when it finally arrives in a world arranged the wrong way up.

Two thousand years is a long time to hold a sentence steady. Kingdoms rose and were levelled. The family that carried the promise sold one of its own sons into slavery, and worshipped a calf, and split in two, and went into exile, and came back smaller. The line thinned until it ran through a village carpenter and a girl nobody had heard of.

And not one syllable of what God said to Abraham was ever withdrawn, renegotiated, or quietly allowed to lapse. He had bound himself by an oath, to a man long dead, about descendants not yet born — and he kept it, because that is what he is like, and because there has never been a moment in the history of the world when it was safe to bet against his word.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three months, and then she walks home. Luke gives it half a sentence, and it is the half that carries the whole weight of what the yes at verse 38 actually cost.

Do the arithmetic. Elizabeth was in her sixth month when Mary arrived (v. 36); three months later she is at term. Whether Mary left just before the birth or stayed for it Luke does not say, and it is better not to guess. What is certain is where she went: back to Nazareth, along the same four or five days of road, now around three months pregnant — which is to say, beginning to show.

She had left Nazareth an unremarkable betrothed girl. She returns to a village of a few hundred people, all of whom know her, all of whom know Joseph, and every one of whom can count. She has no evidence of any kind. Her only account of herself is that an angel came into the room, and the one other person on earth who would believe it is now eighty miles behind her.

Matthew supplies what happened next, and it is not gentle: Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly (Matt. 1:19). That is the man's best instinct — he intends to be as kind as he can while ending the marriage. It took an angel in a dream to stop him. So Mary walked home to a fiancé who was going to conclude she had betrayed him, and to a village that was going to agree with him.

There is no record of God warning her about any of that in advance. Gabriel told her about the child, the kingdom, the Spirit and her relative. He said nothing about the whispering, or about the look on Joseph's face. She found out the way everybody finds out — by arriving.

Luke reports the whole thing in nine words and moves on, and that restraint is itself a kind of testimony. The mother of the Lord did not get an easier road on account of who she was carrying. She got the ordinary road, walked in the ordinary way, with heaven inside her and nobody able to tell.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 57–66 — The Birth of John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The birth of John is narrated with characteristic Lukan brevity — one verse for the birth itself, and then immediate attention to what matters most, which is the naming. In Jewish custom the name was given at circumcision on the eighth day, and was normally taken from the father's family. The community assumes the child will be called Zechariah.

Elizabeth insists that he will be called John. The community is astonished — there is nobody in the family by that name — and they turn to Zechariah himself. He calls for a writing tablet and writes: his name is John. And immediately his mouth is opened, his tongue is loosed, and he speaks.

The sequence is telling. Zechariah does not begin to speak until he has first obeyed. The muteness that fell at his unbelief is lifted not when he privately makes up his mind but when he publicly and irrevocably acts on the word Gabriel gave him. The name John was not Zechariah's choice; it was God's command (v. 13).

By writing it without qualification he is doing what Mary did in a different register: surrendering his own preference and his family's expectation to the word of God. And the moment he does, the word God gave him is restored to his own mouth.

A small detail in v. 62 fills out the whole nine months. The family made signs to him, which means he could not hear either; the word used of him in v. 22 (kōphos) covers deafness as well as muteness. He had been sealed inside his own head since the day at the altar, with nothing in there but Gabriel's sentence.

The neighbours and relatives are filled with fear, and they laid up all these things in their hearts — a phrase that will appear again of Mary after the shepherds' visit (2:19) and after the temple episode (2:51). Luke's Gospel is full of people who receive these events and hold them, turning them over, not fully understanding but refusing to let go.

That is the posture the gospel consistently produces: not an immediate confident grasp of everything, but the faithful keeping of what has been received, waiting for the understanding that comes in its own time.
verseByVerse.theology:
The crowd's question — what then will this child be, for the hand of the Lord was with him — is the question the rest of Luke-Acts will answer. John will be the voice crying in the wilderness, the preparer of the way, the greatest among those born of women (7:28).

He will baptise Jesus, proclaim the coming kingdom, confront Herod, and die in prison before Jesus's ministry reaches its climax. He is the last and greatest of the prophets, the hinge between the old covenant and the new. The hand of the LORD that the community perceives is the hand that has been shaping him for this purpose since before his birth.

The motif of a whole community sharing in the response to God's action — neighbours and relatives rejoicing, all who heard wondering, everyone laying these things up in their hearts — reflects Luke's consistent understanding that the gospel is not a private transaction between an individual and God. It is a public event that transforms communities.

The birth of John affects not only Zechariah and Elizabeth but the entire social network of their neighbourhood. The ripple of grace always extends further than the point of impact.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's obedience at the naming — writing “his name is John” without qualification, against the family's expectation — is the delayed obedience of a man whom nine months of silence have changed. He came into the temple a man of correct theology and insufficient trust. He emerges from the silence a man who writes the word of God on a tablet before he says a word of his own.

The discipline has done its work. The man who needed a sign is now content to be one — the father who names his child what God chose, regardless of what the neighbours think.

The fear that falls on the community is the biblical response to the nearness of the holy. This is not terror but the awe that the presence of God in human history always produces. They sense that something larger than ordinary life is moving through the birth of this child, and they are right.

The instinct to hold that sense carefully — to lay it up in the heart — is exactly the right response to grace that exceeds our comprehension. Not analysis, not immediate explanation, but faithful keeping: holding what has been received until it is better understood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the time came. Luke's phrase is literally that her time was fulfilled — the same family of words he has been using since verse 20 for a promise reaching its appointed date. Nine months earlier a mute priest came home from the temple with an announcement he could not make. The house has been silent ever since. Now there is a baby crying in it.

The neighbours and relatives hear, and Luke records their theology rather than their congratulations: the Lord had shown great mercy to her. That is eleos again, covenant kindness — the same word Mary has just sung twice and Zechariah will use twice more before the chapter ends. The village reads the birth correctly. They do not call it luck, and they do not call it a medical curiosity. They name the one who did it.

And they rejoiced with her. Hold that against verse 25. The reproach she named — the thing people said — has become the thing people celebrate. The same social circle that had carried a verdict about Elizabeth for forty years is now in her house, delighted. Nothing about her has changed. What changed is that God acted, and the whole neighbourhood's account of her changed with it.

There is a comfort here for anyone whose reputation has been fixed by a circumstance they never chose. The village's opinion of Elizabeth was never the truth about Elizabeth. It was the best guess of people who could only see the outside; it was wrong for forty years; and it was overturned in an afternoon.

That does not mean every unjust verdict is overturned in this life. Many are not, and it would be dishonest to promise otherwise. It does mean that no human assessment is final, and that the only verdict still standing at the end will be God's — which, in Elizabeth's case, had read righteous before him since verse 6, the entire time the village was talking.

Notice too that the joy is corporate. Gabriel had promised that many will rejoice at his birth (v. 14), and here is the first instalment: a house full of neighbours. God's gifts are never given to one household only. Grace lands on a person and spreads through everybody standing near them.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, but his mother answered, 'No; he shall be called John.' And they said to her, 'None of your relatives is called by this name.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day they come to circumcise the child, exactly as the covenant had required of Abraham and every generation since (Gen. 17:12; Lev. 12:3). John is brought into the covenant people by the sign God gave, on the day God set. It is worth noticing that the forerunner of the new covenant begins his life marked with the sign of the old one.

Naming took place at the circumcision, and the family's expectation was obvious enough that Luke says they would have called him Zechariah after his father. It was a proud thing to do: a first son, born to an old priest by a miracle, carrying his father's name and his father's office. Everyone in the room assumed it. In a sense they had already done it.

Then his mother answers, and the Greek is as flat as English can make it: No; he shall be called John.

That is a remarkable sentence, and not only for its firmness. Zechariah has been unable to speak for nine months. How does Elizabeth know the name? Either he wrote it out for her at some point during the silence, or she was told the same thing herself. Luke does not say, and it is better not to invent. What Luke does record is that when the moment came, the woman with no standing at all in that discussion contradicted her entire family, in public, on the strength of a word from God — and did not soften it. The no is unqualified.

The room's response is not theological. It is social. None of your relatives is called by this name. That is the whole argument. Not “the name is wrong” but “the name is not ours.” It is the oldest objection in religion and the least examined: we have never done it that way.

The pressure Elizabeth is under is very ordinary and very familiar. It is not persecution. Nobody is threatening her. It is a room full of people she loves and will still be living among next week, all of whom think she is making a mistake, and all of whom mean well. That is far harder to withstand than hostility, and it is the form most believers actually meet.

She had nothing to appeal to except what God had said. It was enough, and she held it for the whole length of the argument, alone, until somebody put a writing tablet into her husband's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, 'His name is John.' And they all wondered. And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a small detail that changes the picture of the whole nine months. They made signs to his father.

Signs — not questions. Zechariah's condition in verse 22 is described with the word kōphos, which in Greek covers both an inability to speak and an inability to hear; it is the word used of the deaf man in Mark 7:32. And the room's behaviour settles it, because nobody gestures at a man who can hear them.

So Zechariah had spent nine months not merely unable to speak but unable to hear. He could not hear his wife's voice. He could not hear the neighbours arguing about his son's name. He would not hear the child cry. He had asked for evidence, and God had sealed him inside his own head with nothing in there but the sentence Gabriel had spoken.

He asks for a writing tablet — a wooden board with a wax surface, the notepad of the ancient world — and writes five words. And the Greek is worth having exactly. Not he shall be called John, which is what Elizabeth said, but John is his name. Present tense. Zechariah is not casting a vote or proposing a compromise. He is reporting a fact settled nine months earlier in a room with an angel in it. The matter had never been open.

Now notice when his voice comes back. Not when he privately came round. Not in the sixth month, when the pregnancy became undeniable. Not at the birth. Immediately after he wrote the name. The silence lifted at the point of public, irreversible obedience — when he put in writing, in front of the whole family, at the cost of every expectation in the room, the word he had refused to believe.

And then the first sound out of a mouth God had held shut for nine months. Not an explanation. Not an apology to his wife, nor an account of what he had seen at the altar, nor a word about how hard it had been. He spoke, blessing God.

The man had had nine months to compose his first sentence, and when the seal came off, what came out was praise. Something had been done in that silence which could not have been done any other way — and the God who did it had shut his mouth in the first place for exactly this.

verseByVerse.quote: And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, 'What then will this child be?' For the hand of the Lord was with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The news travels, and Luke records the two things it produced.

First, fear. Fear came on all their neighbours — the same reaction that fell on Zechariah in the temple, now spread across a district. This is the proper human response to discovering that God is actually operating in the neighbourhood. Not excitement. Not curiosity. Fear.

It is a reaction Luke will record again and again across his two volumes: at the catch of fish (5:8-9), at the stilling of the storm (8:25), at the raising of the widow's son (7:16), and after Ananias and Sapphira, when great fear came upon the whole church (Acts 5:11). A God who can be discussed comfortably has usually not turned up yet.

Second, the treasuring. All who heard them laid them up in their hearts. This is one of Luke's signature phrases, and he will use it twice more of Mary — after the shepherds (2:19) and after the boy in the temple (2:51). It describes people who do not understand what they have seen, cannot explain it, and will not put it down. They store it.

That is a posture worth learning, because it is the one most needed and least practised. Something happens with God's fingerprints on it and no available explanation: a providence that cannot be coincidence; a prayer answered in a way that raises more questions than it settles; a suffering that will not resolve into a lesson. The two usual responses are to force a meaning onto it prematurely, or to shrug it off as nothing.

Luke's neighbours do neither. They carry it, unexplained, and wait. Some of what God does is only legible years later, and the people who can read it then are the ones who kept it.

What then will this child be? The question hangs over the hill country, unanswered, for thirty years. Luke will answer it, but not yet — and the last line of the section says the answer is not in doubt. For the hand of the Lord was with him. All through the Old Testament that phrase means one thing: God has taken hold of a life for a purpose of his own. Whatever the child turns out to be, it has already been decided.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Zechariah's song — called the Benedictus from its first word in Latin, “Blessed” — is the longest prophecy in Luke's first chapter and in many ways its theological climax. Where Mary's Magnificat looked back at what God has done throughout Israel's history, the Benedictus looks forward to what God is now doing through the two children, and across the whole sweep of the covenant from Abraham to this moment.

It is the song of an old priest who has spent nine months in silence, and who opens his mouth for the first time not with relief or apology or explanation but with praise and prophecy.

The song falls into two movements. The first (vv. 68-75) is about Jesus: the God of Israel has visited and redeemed his people, has raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David, and has fulfilled the oath he swore to Abraham, so that his people might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness all their days.

The second (vv. 76-79) is about John: the child will be called the prophet of the Most High, will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, and will give knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of sins, because of the tender mercy of God by which the sunrise will visit them from on high. The two movements map exactly onto the two births — the greater to Jesus, the preparatory to John.

Verse 77 is the interpretive key to the whole song, and it answers the objection a modern reader raises at v. 71. Rome was never overthrown; Jerusalem fell within seventy years. But the salvation Zechariah means is defined by Zechariah himself: knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins. The enemies in view are deeper than any empire.

The image of the sunrise from on high (anatolē) is among the most beautiful in Luke's Gospel. The word means both sunrise and, in the Greek Old Testament, the Branch of messianic prophecy (Jer. 23:5; Zech. 3:8; 6:12). Zechariah the priest knows his prophets, and the word he chooses reaches back through centuries of longing.

The Branch, the Sunrise — the one who gives light to those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, and who guides their feet into the way of peace. Nine months of silence have filled this man's mouth with something far better than anything he said before it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Benedictus is covenant theology at its most compact. Zechariah identifies the coming of Jesus as the fulfilment of three overlapping promises: the Davidic covenant (the horn of salvation in the house of David, vv. 69-70), the Abrahamic covenant (the oath sworn to Abraham, vv. 73-75), and the prophetic promise (the forerunner going before the Lord, vv. 76-77).

All three lines of God's covenant faithfulness converge in the two children born in this chapter. The God who made promises to Abraham two thousand years earlier is fulfilling them — not approximately, not symbolically, but specifically, in the births of two real children at a datable moment in history.

The purpose of that salvation is stated with remarkable precision in vv. 74-75: that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. Salvation is not merely rescue. It is freedom for a particular kind of life.

The one delivered from the enemy's hand is freed not for autonomous self-determination but for worship — for service before the face of God, in holiness and righteousness, without the crippling fear that guilt and condemnation produce. This is the goal of redemption: a people who serve God freely because they have been freely saved.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's first words after nine months of silence are praise and prophecy — not self-vindication, not explanation, not a word of reproach for the community that doubted him. The discipline of the long silence has produced a man who, when he opens his mouth, speaks entirely about God and about what God is doing.

That is the fruit of involuntary silence used well: what comes out at the end is not our own words. Preachers, teachers and parents forced into seasons of silence — made to listen rather than speak, to receive rather than give — often find that what finally emerges is purer and truer than anything they said before it.

The Benedictus ends with John: the child grew and became strong in spirit, and was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel. The wilderness is both his geographical home and his spiritual formation. He is being shaped in hiddenness for the public ministry that will announce the Coming One.

Every major figure in redemptive history has had a wilderness — Abraham, Moses, David, Elijah, Paul, and the Lord himself. The wilderness is not the failure of the plan. It is the formation of the messenger, and it cannot be hurried.

verseByVerse.quote: And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, 'Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nine months of silence, and now the Holy Spirit fills him — and the first thing the man does is prophesy. Not explain. Not describe what he saw. He preaches.

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel. The opening is a standard Jewish benediction; it is how the Psalms bless God (Ps. 41:13; 72:18; 106:48), and Zechariah the priest has said the words thousands of times. He has never once said them about this.

For he has visited and redeemed his people. Two verbs, and both are loaded.

Visited is epeskepsato, and it does not mean a social call. It is the word for God coming to see about his people with the intention of acting — the word used when God came down because he had seen the affliction in Egypt (Exod. 3:16; 4:31), the word for a shepherd looking over a flock, the word behind our “oversight.” When God visits, something happens.

Redeemed is lytrōsis: the buying back of a slave or a prisoner by the payment of a price. It is the word Israel used of the exodus, and the word underneath the whole system of firstborn redemption that Zechariah had administered his entire working life. He does not yet know what the price is going to be. He knows the transaction has begun.

And it is worth pausing on how long the room had been quiet. From Malachi to Gabriel is roughly four centuries. Four hundred years without a prophet. Empires came and went across that ground; the Maccabees fought and won and were corrupted; the temple was defiled, cleansed, and rebuilt in marble by a murderer — and through all of it heaven said nothing. Generations of faithful Israelites were born, said their prayers, and died without ever hearing a word. Zechariah himself had served a lifetime in a temple where God had not spoken in living memory.

And then, without warning, in the ordinary rotation of a village priest's fortnight — he came. He had not gone anywhere. He had not lost interest. He had not been waiting for Israel to improve, because Israel had not improved. The silence was never abandonment; it was an appointment being kept from the other end of it, on a date fixed before the world was made. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who visits and redeems, and who has never yet been late for anything.

verseByVerse.quote: and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us;
verseByVerse.commentary:
A horn of salvation. The image is an animal's horn — the ox, the wild bull — and throughout the Old Testament it stands for strength, and specifically for strength that acts. The LORD is my rock… my horn of salvation (Ps. 18:2). And there is one text Zechariah is almost certainly quoting: There I will make a horn to sprout for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed (Ps. 132:17). The rescue God has raised up is not an idea or a message. It is a power, and it is in David's house.

As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old. Zechariah's second point is that none of this is new. The salvation arriving in his own household is the one the prophets described for centuries, and he wants it on record that God has not improvised.

Then the line a careful reader will stumble over: that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us.

Rome was not overthrown. Israel was not liberated. Seventy years after this song Jerusalem was burned and the temple pulled down stone from stone. Was Zechariah wrong? He is speaking, Luke says, filled with the Holy Spirit — so the question is not a small one, and it deserves a straight answer.

Two things answer it, and the second is much the stronger.

The first is that Zechariah is not offering a political forecast in his own words. He is repeating the language of the covenant promises, and covenant language about enemies runs deeper than any particular empire. The enemies Scripture finally names are not Roman. They are sin, death, and the devil — and a Gospel that ends at an empty tomb has something to say about all three.

But the better answer comes from Zechariah himself, eight verses later. He is about to define the salvation he is singing about, in so many words: to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins (v. 77). That is his own gloss on his own prophecy. The rescue he means is not from an occupying army. It is from guilt. The old priest who had spent his life killing animals for other people's sins is announcing that the sins themselves are about to be dealt with.

Which is the deeper deliverance, and every man in that house would have said so if asked. Rome could take a man's property, his freedom and his life. It could not touch the thing that would still have been wrong with Israel on the morning after Rome fell.

verseByVerse.quote: to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah now reaches back past David to Abraham, and names the guarantee.

The oath that he swore to our father Abraham. There was only one occasion on which God swore an oath to Abraham, and it is the most terrible chapter in Genesis. It came on a mountain, after a knife had been raised over a bound boy and a hand had stopped it: By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD… I will surely bless you, and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed (Gen. 22:16-18). Hebrews notices what that means — having no one greater to swear by, God swore by himself (Heb. 6:13). The promise Zechariah is standing on is underwritten by God's own existence. It cannot fail without God failing.

And it is worth seeing what happened on that mountain and what did not. Abraham was spared his son. The ram was in the thicket, and the father walked down the hill with the boy beside him. When the promise sworn there finally came due, the Father who swore it climbed a hill outside Jerusalem with his own Son, and there was no ram, and he came down alone (cf. Rom. 8:32).

Then Zechariah states what the whole rescue is for, and this is the heart of the Benedictus: that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. Salvation is not merely being got out of something. It is being got out in order to be free for something, and the something is worship. The verb is latreuein, the word for priestly service, the temple word — and Zechariah, a priest, applies it to the whole people.

Without fear. Stay on that, because a great many believers serve God with a low, constant dread running underneath everything they do: dread of not having done enough, of a God who is quietly disappointed, of the sin that keeps coming back, of what will be said at the end. Such a person prays like an employee filing a report to a supervisor who is already unimpressed.

That is not the arrangement. Zechariah puts deliverance first and service second, and the order is not decorative. The fear has to be dealt with before the serving can begin — and God deals with it. He does not ask his people to manufacture the freedom themselves. Perfect love casts out fear, and fear has to do with punishment (1 John 4:18). The reverent awe of verse 50 stays, and deepens for ever. The cringe goes. A servant still trying to secure his position is not yet doing the work; he is auditioning for it.

All our days. Not on the good days. Not in the seasons when it is going well. All of them.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For nine verses Zechariah has sung about somebody else's son. Now he turns and looks at his own, eight days old, and speaks to him directly. These are the only recorded words Zechariah ever addressed to John.

And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High. Note the ranking — and note that a father is making it. Jesus is Son of the Most High (v. 32); John is prophet of the Most High. A prophet is a great thing to be; Jesus will say that among those born of women none is greater (7:28). It is not the same thing at all. Zechariah, holding his miracle baby on the day of his circumcision, tells him plainly that he is the servant of another. There is not a trace of ambition in the sentence.

For you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways. The line is Isaiah 40:3 and Malachi 3:1 laid together: prepare the way of the LORD. And notice the pronoun, because it is quietly enormous. In both prophets, the one whose way is being prepared is the LORD himself, the God of Israel, named by his covenant name. Zechariah applies it to the child in Mary's womb.

To give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins. Here is the Benedictus telling you what it has meant all along. Not the salvation of a nation from an army, but of a people from their sins. That is the standard by which every claim to be preaching the gospel can be measured, and it has not shifted in two thousand years.

And the word is knowledge. John's work is not to procure the forgiveness — he cannot — but to make it known, so that people understand what is on offer and who is offering it. Preaching does not create the salvation. It carries the news of it, and news is useless in a locked drawer.

It is worth asking what John's method of giving that knowledge actually was, since Luke tells us in chapter 3 and it is not what most people expect of a herald of good news. He told people the truth about themselves. You cannot hand a man the knowledge of forgiveness while he is convinced there is nothing to forgive. That is why the road to Bethlehem runs through repentance, and why a preacher who never troubles anybody has not prepared a way for anything.

verseByVerse.quote: because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the summit of the song, and the old priest reaches for an image rather than an argument.

The tender mercy of our God. The Greek is splanchna eleous — literally the bowels of mercy. Ancient people located the deepest feelings not in the heart but in the gut, and the word describes compassion felt physically, the kind that turns a man over inside. It is the word used of Jesus when he sees the widow of Nain walking behind her son's body out of the town gate (7:13). The reason given here for the whole plan of redemption is not God's justice, or his glory, or his sovereignty — all of which are true and none of which is named. It is that something in God moved.

Whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high. The word is anatolē, and it carries two meanings at once, both of which this priest knew. It is the ordinary word for the rising of the sun. It is also the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the Branch, the promised shoot from David's stump: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch (Jer. 23:5; cf. Zech. 3:8; 6:12). Zechariah — who shares his name with the prophet who used that word twice — picks the one word in the language that says dawn and David's heir in the same breath.

To give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death. The verb is the one to hold on to. Not those who walk in darkness. Not those who search in it. Those who sit. It is the posture of somebody who has stopped moving, because there is nowhere to go and no way of seeing the way there.

Anyone who has watched depression settle on a person, or sat with someone six weeks after the funeral when the visitors have stopped coming, or lain awake at four in the morning with a diagnosis, knows that position exactly. The Bible's picture of humanity apart from God is not a traveller who has taken a wrong turning. It is somebody who has sat down in the dark.

And the mercy of the image is in its mechanism. Nobody has ever helped the sun come up. There is no technique for it, no preparation, nothing whatever contributed by the people sitting in the valley. The light arrives from above, on its own schedule, whether or not anyone below is ready — and when it comes, the same people who could not find the path can suddenly see the whole country. That is what grace is. Not a lamp handed to a man so that he can go looking. A sunrise.

Four hundred years of night, and a world sitting in the shadow of death since a garden gate closed behind it. And then over the eastern rim, without a sound, without permission, without one hand raised anywhere to help it — the light. Not a torch, not a candle carried by a prophet, but the Dayspring himself, the Branch of David, the Sun of Righteousness rising with healing in his wings, to give light to people who had long since stopped looking for it and to set their feet, one by one, in the way of peace. He rose then. He has not set since.

verseByVerse.quote: And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verse, thirty years.

Luke has spent seventy-nine verses on nine months, and now he covers three decades in a sentence and moves on. Everything a biography would want — the boy's education, his father's teaching, when Zechariah and Elizabeth died and left him, how he came to be in the desert at all — is simply absent.

The child grew and became strong in spirit. Luke will use almost the same words of Jesus at 2:40. Something is being formed that will not be visible until it is needed.

And he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

The Judean wilderness is not sand. It is a wasteland of limestone ridges and dry gorges falling away towards the Dead Sea: brutally hot, almost waterless, and empty. That is where the son of a Jerusalem priest spent his twenties. He had a hereditary right to serve in the temple — the courses, the incense, the rota his own father had drawn the lot in. He never took it up. The greatest man born of women, by Christ's own reckoning, spent thirty of his thirty-odd years doing, so far as the record goes, nothing whatever.

That is a hard verse for anybody whose life currently feels like a waiting room: the years that count for nothing on any visible ledger, the training that has never been used, the gifts nobody has asked for, the long stretch in which a person is plainly being prepared for something that shows no sign of arriving.

Luke's one-line summary of thirty such years is worth having: they were not lost. Every element of what John eventually was came out of them. The plain speech that could not be bought, the total indifference to being liked, the ability to look a king in the face and tell him the truth about his marriage — none of that is learned in a city. It is what the desert does to a man, and it cannot be got any other way, or in any less time.

It has to be said as well that John did not know how long the wilderness would last. There was no calendar with the date circled. He was there until the day — and the day was in God's diary, not his. That is the real condition of the waiting: not knowing whether this is preparation, or simply what the rest of life is going to look like.

The desert years did end, of course, and when they did the whole country went out to hear him. But the sentence that mattered had been written long before any of that: the hand of the Lord was with him (v. 66) — and it was with him in the wilderness for thirty years, while nothing whatever appeared to be happening.

1.text: <sup>1</sup> Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, <sup>2</sup> just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us, <sup>3</sup> it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, <sup>4</sup> that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught. <sup>5</sup> In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. <sup>6</sup> And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord. <sup>7</sup> But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years. <sup>8</sup> Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, <sup>9</sup> according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. <sup>10</sup> And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense. <sup>11</sup> And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. <sup>12</sup> And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. <sup>13</sup> But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. <sup>14</sup> And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, <sup>15</sup> for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb. <sup>16</sup> And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, <sup>17</sup> and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.” <sup>18</sup> And Zechariah said to the angel, “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.” <sup>19</sup> And the angel answered him, “I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. <sup>20</sup> And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.” <sup>21</sup> And the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were wondering at his delay in the temple. <sup>22</sup> And when he came out, he was unable to speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the temple. And he kept making signs to them and remained mute. <sup>23</sup> And when his time of service was ended, he went to his home. <sup>24</sup> After these days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and for five months she kept herself hidden, saying, <sup>25</sup> “Thus the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my reproach among people.” <sup>26</sup> In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, <sup>27</sup> to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David. And the virgin's name was Mary. <sup>28</sup> And he came to her and said, “Greetings, O favored one, the Lord is with you!” <sup>29</sup> But she was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be. <sup>30</sup> And the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. <sup>31</sup> And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. <sup>32</sup> He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, <sup>33</sup> and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.” <sup>34</sup> And Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I am a virgin?” <sup>35</sup> And the angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God. <sup>36</sup> And behold, your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son, and this is the sixth month with her who was called barren. <sup>37</sup> For nothing will be impossible with God.” <sup>38</sup> And Mary said, “Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.” And the angel departed from her. <sup>39</sup> In those days Mary arose and went with haste into the hill country, to a town in Judah, <sup>40</sup> and she entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth. <sup>41</sup> And when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the baby leaped in her womb. And Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit, <sup>42</sup> and she exclaimed with a loud cry, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! <sup>43</sup> And why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? <sup>44</sup> For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy. <sup>45</sup> And blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord.” <sup>46</sup> And Mary said, “My soul magnifies the Lord, <sup>47</sup> and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, <sup>48</sup> for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; <sup>49</sup> for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. <sup>50</sup> And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation. <sup>51</sup> He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; <sup>52</sup> he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; <sup>53</sup> he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. <sup>54</sup> He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, <sup>55</sup> as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.” <sup>56</sup> And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home. <sup>57</sup> Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. <sup>58</sup> And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her. <sup>59</sup> And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, <sup>60</sup> but his mother answered, “No; he shall be called John.” <sup>61</sup> And they said to her, “None of your relatives is called by this name.” <sup>62</sup> And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. <sup>63</sup> And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” And they all wondered. <sup>64</sup> And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God. <sup>65</sup> And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, <sup>66</sup> and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, “What then will this child be?” For the hand of the Lord was with him. <sup>67</sup> And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, <sup>68</sup> “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people <sup>69</sup> and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, <sup>70</sup> as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, <sup>71</sup> that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us; <sup>72</sup> to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, <sup>73</sup> the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us <sup>74</sup> that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, <sup>75</sup> in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. <sup>76</sup> And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, <sup>77</sup> to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins, <sup>78</sup> because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high <sup>79</sup> to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.” <sup>80</sup> And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

2.title: The Birth of the King
2.overview:
Chapter 2 of Luke is the world's most familiar story — and precisely because of that familiarity, it is the story most easily received without being heard. We have heard the angels and the manger and the shepherds so many times that the shocking strangeness of the events has been smoothed away by repetition. Luke is a careful historian, and he intends these details to be astonishing: the Emperor of Rome issues a decree, and the decree unwittingly fulfils a prophecy he knows nothing about. The Son of God is born not in a palace but in the place where animals feed. Heaven's armies appear not to priests or rulers but to shepherds — the lowest of the low in first-century Jewish society. The incarnation is not a dignified event. It is a scandal.

The chapter moves through four scenes: the birth in Bethlehem (vv. 1–7), the angels and the shepherds (vv. 8–20), the presentation in the temple with Simeon and Anna (vv. 21–40), and the twelve-year-old Jesus in the temple (vv. 41–52). Together they establish three things about the child: he is born in the line of David and in fulfilment of Scripture; he is recognised by the Spirit-filled as the one Israel has been waiting for; and he understands himself, from the earliest age, as defined by a unique relationship with the Father that supersedes even the claims of family.

The presentation in the temple (vv. 21–40) is one of Luke's most theologically dense passages. In Simeon's song — the Nunc Dimittis — the scope of the child's significance is made explicit for the first time: he is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.” He is not merely the Messiah of Israel; he is the fulfilment of the universal promise of Isaiah (42:6; 49:6), the Servant who is to be the light of the nations. And the shadow of the cross falls even here: Simeon tells Mary that a sword will pierce her soul, that this child is set for the falling and rising of many, that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed. The manger casts the shadow of the cross from the very beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Birth of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The birth of Jesus is introduced by one of the most politically freighted sentences in the New Testament: “In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus.” Augustus was the most powerful man in the world — the man who had ended a century of Roman civil war and inaugurated the Pax Romana. He called himself divi filius, son of the deified Julius. The Roman world hailed him as saviour, as lord, as the bringer of peace and of good news.

Luke places that decree at the head of the story of the one who is the true Son of God, the true Saviour, the true Lord, the true bringer of peace and good news. The contrast is not accidental. Luke's Gospel is, among other things, a counter-narrative to the propaganda of Rome — and it never once raises its voice to say so.

Augustus's census serves God's purposes without Augustus knowing it. He orders a registration for taxation; God uses it to bring a Galilean couple to Bethlehem, where Micah had said the ruler of Israel would be born (Mic. 5:2). The most powerful man on earth is, unwittingly, the instrument for keeping a seven-hundred-year-old promise.

This is the biblical theology of providential history.
