There are seasons when a person who has known God for years cannot find him. Prayer goes flat. The Bible reads like a manual. Nothing has been consciously renounced, and nothing is there.

Notice what Mary and Joseph did. They did not press on to Nazareth hoping he would turn up. They went back to the last place they had him, and they kept looking until they found him. And notice where he turned out to be — not lost at all, not hiding, not withdrawn in displeasure. He was in his Father's house, exactly where he had always been, doing exactly what he had come to do, and it was they who had walked a day's journey in the wrong direction while assuming he was somewhere in the group.

That is very often the shape of it. The sense of absence is real and the distress is real. But the searching is a going back, not a going further on — back to the word, back to the place he said he would be, back to the last thing he actually said. He is not usually as far away as three days of walking would suggest.

verseByVerse.quote: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They find him sitting among the teachers.

The picture is not a boy lecturing the professors, which is how the story is often told and is not what Luke says. He is sitting among them — the posture of a student; listening to them; and asking them questions. That was exactly how rabbinic instruction worked: the teacher put a question, the pupils answered, the pupils asked in return, and understanding was reached by exchange. The boy is doing what a learner does, in the ordinary manner, in the appropriate place.

What is not ordinary is the effect. All who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers. He is holding his own with the finest theological minds in Israel, in the temple, at twelve.

These may well have been men whose names are still known — the Passover crowds were gone, and this is the season when the leading teachers sat in the temple courts and taught publicly. If so, some of them lived long enough to hear him again.

Two things deserve saying about this scene, and they pull in opposite directions until they are held together.

The first is that his understanding is genuinely remarkable, and Luke wants that noticed. The wisdom announced in verse 40 is now visible, and it is not a normal twelve-year-old's grasp of Scripture. Something is here that the teachers cannot account for.

The second is that he is learning. He listens; he asks. The eternal Son, who as God knows everything, is a boy in a real human mind that has to be taught — and he is being taught, by ordinary Jewish teachers, in the ordinary way, out of the Scriptures. The wisdom Luke reports is not information downloaded past his humanity. It is the wisdom of a boy who has been listening carefully to the word of God since he could speak, and has never once let any of it go.

Which is the most quietly encouraging thing in the paragraph. There is no shortcut here that we are not offered. The way the boy Jesus came to know the Scriptures is the way anybody comes to know them: by sitting where they are taught, listening to them, asking about them, and turning them over. He did it perfectly, and he did it by the ordinary means.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his parents saw him, they were astonished. And his mother said to him, 'Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.' And he said to them, 'Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.

That is not a serene woman. That is a mother at the end of three days, and Luke does not clean it up. The word for distress is a strong one — it is used of torment and anguish. She is not asking for information; she is asking the question every frightened parent asks the moment the fear turns to relief, which is how could you do this to us.

It is worth registering that Scripture lets her say it. The mother of the Lord speaks sharply to the Son of God, in the temple, in front of the teachers, and the Bible reports it without embarrassment and without correcting her tone. There is a whole permission in that for people who have been taught that honesty with God must first be made polite.

And then the first recorded words of Jesus in this Gospel — the first words of his that anybody wrote down — and they are a question answering a question.

Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?

The must is the hinge. The Greek is dei, divine necessity, and Luke will use it about forty times across his two volumes for the compulsion of God's plan: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22), must rise on the third day (24:7), the Scripture must be fulfilled (22:37). Here it appears for the first time, on the lips of a twelve-year-old, and everything that follows in Luke and Acts is the working out of it.

If your Bible reads about my Father's business rather than in my Father's house, nothing is wrong. The Greek says simply in the things of my Father, and will carry either sense; and the two are not rivals, since the house is where the business is done.

Now the question a careful reader is entitled to ask: did he sin? He is under the fifth commandment like every other Jewish boy, and he has just caused his parents three days of anguish. If he broke that commandment, the whole gospel comes apart, because a Saviour who needs saving cannot save anybody.

He did not, and the answer is in his own reply. He had not run away, and he had not been forbidden to stay. He had done nothing his parents told him not to do; he had assumed — and his words say he expected them to assume it too — that when the caravan left, everyone would know where the son of this family would be. His did you not know is not insolence. It is genuine surprise that after twelve years they had to be told.

And there is the gentlest possible correction inside it. Mary said your father and I. He answers by naming a different Father, and by locating himself in that Father's house. He is not disowning Joseph, whom he will go home and obey for another eighteen years. He is telling his mother, once, and then not again for a very long time, that there is a prior claim on him — and that she of all people had the means to know it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.

Luke could have left that out. It is not flattering to anybody, and a writer building a legend would have had the parents nod wisely and treasure the moment. Instead he records that the two people closest to Jesus on earth heard him explain himself and did not follow it.

Take the measure of what these two already knew. Mary had been visited by Gabriel and told this child would be called the Son of the Most High. She had sung a song about it. Joseph had been told in a dream who the boy was, and had taken his family to Egypt to keep him alive. They had heard shepherds, and Simeon, and Anna. If anyone on earth had the material to understand a sentence about the boy's Father, it was these two.

They did not understand it.

That is one of the most quietly liberating verses in the Gospel, and it should be said plainly for the reader who suspects that a real Christian ought to find all this clear by now. The mother of Jesus did not always know what her son meant. She had more evidence than any of us will ever have, and there were things he said that went straight past her.

Understanding, in Scripture, is not the entry fee for faith. It is one of the things faith is given, in instalments, over a long time, and usually later than we would like. Mary's response is not to demand that he explain himself again, and it is not to decide that the saying cannot have meant much. Luke tells us in the very next verse what she did with it, and it is the same thing she did at verse 19: she kept it.

There is a way of handling what we do not understand that quietly disposes of it — filing it under things that are probably not important, or that scholars disagree about, or that will make sense one day, and then never returning to it. And there is Mary's way, which is to put it somewhere safe and go on carrying it.

She was still carrying this one twenty years later, when she stood at the foot of a cross and it began, at last, to make sense.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them.

The boy who has just spoken of a Father greater than Joseph gets up, walks eighty miles home, and puts himself under the authority of a village builder and a poor woman for the next eighteen years. Luke's verb is continuous: he was being subject to them. Not a single act of compliance but a settled condition, sustained through his teens and into his manhood.

There is no contradiction between verse 49 and verse 51, and the pairing is the whole point. Being about his Father's business, for a twelve-year-old in Nazareth, meant obeying his mother. Anyone who has ever used a sense of higher calling as a reason for neglecting a plain nearer duty has the shape of this passage exactly backwards.

And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. The second time in this chapter, and the same verb (v. 19). She still does not understand it. She still will not let it go.

And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.

Sit with that phrase — increased in wisdom — because it is one of the sharpest windows in the New Testament onto who Jesus is, and a thoughtful reader is right to stop at it. How can the eternal Son, the one through whom all things were made and in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3), increase in wisdom? Did he not already know everything?

The answer is the mystery the church has confessed from the beginning: in the one person of the Son there are two whole natures, divine and human, and they are not blurred into a third thing. According to his divine nature he knew all things and never learned anything. According to his human nature he really was a boy in Nazareth who had to learn his letters, memorise the Scriptures, listen to the rabbis, and grow — mind and body together — as every child grows. The verse is not loose language. It is the exact truth about him. He did not merely appear to be a developing child; he was one.

This is the same reality met from the other side in his own confession that he did not know the day of his return (Mark 13:32): omniscient as God, genuinely limited as man, in the one undivided person.

And it matters for more than doctrine. It means the Lord his people follow was once twelve, and once seven, and once an infant who could not lift his own head; that he knows growing up from the inside, and what it is to learn slowly and not yet understand; and that the humanity he took up in order to save ours was the real thing, all the way down. He did not play at being human. He became it, and grew into it, and lived it out through eighteen unrecorded years in a hill town — so that at last a fully human life could be offered to the Father, from beginning to end, with nothing missing.

3.title: The Voice and the Son
3.overview:
Chapter 3 marks the formal beginning of the story Luke has been preparing for since chapter 1. Thirty years have passed in a single verse (2:52). Now the word of God comes to John in the wilderness, and the ministry of preparation begins. Luke anchors the moment in history with a precision unmatched anywhere in the Gospels: the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the governorship of Pontius Pilate, the tetrarchies of Herod and Philip and Lysanias, the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. Six named officials, layered like the rings of a tree, establishing exactly when the word of God broke in. Luke the historian is insisting: this happened. You can date it. You can place it. It is not legend.

John's ministry is introduced through Isaiah 40 — “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” — establishing that his role is not to be the destination but the signpost. He is the voice; another is the Word. His message is the message of the prophet: repent, be baptised, bear fruits worthy of repentance. The crowds who come to him receive not comfort but confrontation: “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?” John is the great deflater of religious presumption — the man who tells Israel that Abrahamic descent is not a sufficient credential before the coming Judge. The axe is at the root of the trees. The one who comes after him will separate the wheat from the chaff with an unquenchable fire.

The chapter ends with two moments of quiet immensity: the baptism of Jesus, where the Trinity is revealed in a form no theologian could have anticipated — the Son in the water, the Spirit as a dove, the Father's voice from heaven — and the genealogy, which traces Jesus's lineage back through David, through Abraham, through Adam, to God himself. Luke's genealogy runs in the opposite direction from Matthew's and reaches further back: not just to Abraham (the Father of Israel) but to Adam (the father of the human race). Jesus is not merely the King of the Jews; he is the son of Adam come to undo what Adam did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — John the Baptist Prepares the Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke opens the public ministry with a synchronism — a dating device borrowed from the great historians of the ancient world, who anchored their narratives in the reigns of known rulers. Six officials are named: Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate, Herod Antipas, Philip, Lysanias, and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas.

This is the world into which the word of God intrudes: Roman imperial power, Jewish client kings, and a compromised religious leadership. And the word comes to none of them. It comes to John, in the wilderness, the son of a village priest. The contrast is pointed. All the power of the world is irrelevant to God's timing; the word comes when God is ready, to whom God chooses, in the place power does not trouble to look.

The names are also checkable, and they have been checked. Lysanias of Abilene was long cited as proof of Luke's carelessness until an inscription from the reign of Tiberius turned up near Damascus honouring exactly that man in exactly that office.

John's message has three parts. First, a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins — a rite John did not invent, but radically reapplied. Jewish practice had a baptism for Gentile converts entering the covenant people; John baptised Jews, which said out loud that being born inside the covenant was not enough and that Israel itself needed converting. It was scandalous, and it was meant to be.

Second, a demolition of presumption: “Do not begin to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Ethnic heritage is no substitute for personal repentance, and the axe is already at the root.

Third, practical instruction to three specific groups who ask the same question — what shall we do? The crowds are told to share a spare tunic and their food. Tax collectors are told to collect no more than the authorised figure. Soldiers are told not to extort, not to lay false charges, and to be content with their pay. Notably, neither the tax collectors nor the soldiers are told to leave their work. Repentance in John's mouth has hands and feet, and all three answers land on money.

The climax is not John's own proclamation but his announcement of another: “He who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptise you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” The one who follows is not an improved John; he is of a different order altogether. And Luke calls the whole of this preaching — vipers, axe, unquenchable fire and all — good news (v. 18).

The section closes with Herod shutting John in prison for confronting him over his marriage to his brother's wife. The voice is silenced immediately before the Word begins to speak. The herald makes way for the King.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's declaration that God can raise up children to Abraham from stones is the most radical possible challenge to the theology of ethnic privilege. It disconnects the promise from the bloodline and reconnects it to faith and repentance.

This is not the abolition of the covenant with Abraham; it is the clarification of what that covenant always meant. Paul will develop the same argument in Galatians 3 and Romans 4: the true children of Abraham are those who share Abraham's faith, not merely his biology. John stands at the hinge of the covenants and announces what the new covenant will make explicit — the community of God is defined by repentance and faith, not by descent.

The baptism of the Holy Spirit and fire announces two aspects of the Coming One's work that belong together. The Spirit is the agent of new birth and renewal, the fulfilment of Ezekiel's new heart and Joel's outpouring. Fire is the agent of purification — the refiner's fire that burns away dross, and the thresher's fire that consumes chaff.

John does not separate these two; they are two sides of one coming. For those who receive him the fire purifies; for those who reject him it consumes. Everyone who meets Christ is touched by fire. The only question is which kind.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's instruction to the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers is one of the clearest demonstrations in the Gospels that repentance is not a feeling but a change of direction that shows. The crowd asks “what shall we do?” and the answer is not “attend synagogue more faithfully” or “pray more earnestly.” It is “share your tunic and your food.”

The tax collector's repentance looks like honest accounting; the soldier's looks like honest soldiering. Genuine repentance always takes the shape of the specific sin it is turning from — and in both those cases it meant staying in a compromised trade and doing it straight, at real financial cost, alongside colleagues who would not.

John's willingness to confront Herod Antipas over his adulterous marriage (v. 19) — knowing what it would cost him — is the model of prophetic courage before political power. He did not reserve his hard message for crowds who could do him no harm; he took it to the palace, where it was entirely unnecessary and entirely dangerous.

The man who tells the crowd hard truths and comfortable things to the powerful has not yet learned from John. And John's own end is worth facing honestly: he did everything he was sent to do, and finished in a cell. Faithfulness is not always repaid in this life.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six named rulers, in strict order of precedence — emperor, governor, tetrarchs, high priests — and then the sentence turns and the word of God goes past every one of them and lands on a man in a desert.

The structure is the argument. Luke is doing what the great historians of his world did, pinning his story to datable public figures; but he is also making a point about where God speaks. All the power in that list is irrelevant to God's timing. The word comes when God is ready, to whom God chooses, in the place power does not bother to look. It was always so — Moses at the back of the wilderness, Elijah at a brook, Amos among the sycamore figs. And it is worth noticing that God had a temple, a priesthood and a high priest in that list, and did not use them.

Then the phrase itself: the word of God came to John. That is Old Testament language, the standard formula for the call of a prophet — the word of the LORD came to Hosea, to Joel, to Jonah. Israel had not heard it in four hundred years, and it is being used again. Luke's readers would have felt the shock of it: the line of the prophets, which everybody assumed had closed, has just been reopened.

There is a second thing in that dense little roll of names, and it bears directly on whether any of this can be trusted.

One of the six was for a long time used to convict Luke of carelessness. He names Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene — but the only Lysanias the history books knew of was a king of Chalcis executed in 36 BC, some sixty years too early to be reigning here. Sceptics pointed to it as proof that Luke had muddled his facts.

Then the ground gave up its witness. An inscription found near Damascus, from the reign of Tiberius, honours Lysanias the tetrarch — a later Lysanias, holding exactly the office Luke assigns him, in exactly the period Luke places him. The evangelist was right, and his critics had been working from an incomplete list.

This is not an isolated rescue. Again and again where Luke can be checked against stone and inscription — the politarchs of Thessalonica, the proconsul of Cyprus, the first man of Malta — the detail once called a blunder has turned out to be precise. So when he says the word of God came in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, with these men in these offices, he has earned the right to be believed. He is not decorating a legend with borrowed dates. He is reporting something that happened, at a time that could have been marked on a Roman calendar.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John comes out of thirty years of silence with one message and one river.

A baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. Every word is loaded, and the first thing to get clear is the one most often misunderstood. Repentance is metanoia — a change of mind that turns into a change of direction. It is not primarily an emotion. A man can weep over his sin all night and repent of nothing; a man can turn round with a dry face and have repented completely. The test is not how sorry you felt but which way you are now facing.

One thing about this baptism would have struck his first hearers far harder than it strikes us. John did not invent the rite. Judaism already practised ritual immersion, and there was a baptism for converts — the washing by which a pagan entered the covenant people. The startling thing was not that John baptised. It was whom he baptised.

He stood in the Jordan and called Jews into the water. To ask a son of Abraham to be immersed like a Gentile convert was to say something scandalous out loud: that being born inside the covenant was not enough, that Israel itself needed converting. That is precisely why, four verses later, the crowd reaches for the credential it assumes will settle the matter — we have Abraham as our father — and why John knocks it away so hard. He had already answered it by the water he was standing in.

And the geography preaches too. The Jordan is where Israel came into the land under Joshua, out of forty years in the wilderness. John stands at that same river calling the nation to come out and start again — as if the whole history since had to be wound back and begun once more from the crossing.

Then Luke identifies him from the prophets: the voice of one crying in the wilderness. It is Isaiah 40, the chapter that opens Comfort, comfort my people — and the image behind it is a road gang. When a king travelled, men went ahead to make the road passable: filling holes, cutting through ridges, straightening the route so the royal party could come through.

That is what John is. Not the king. The road crew. And what he is levelling is not a highway in the desert but the ground in front of a nation's heart, so that when the King comes there is a way in.

verseByVerse.quote: Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke quotes two more verses of Isaiah 40 than Matthew and Mark do, and he does it for the sake of the last line.

First the road-building. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low. The picture is of a landscape being made passable — and it works in both directions at once, which is the point. Valleys come up. Mountains come down. The low places are raised and the high places are levelled, and the result is a road on which everybody is walking at the same height.

That is what the coming of Christ does to people, and it is worth being concrete about it. The person crushed flat by failure, by shame, by years of being nobody, is lifted; the person built up high on competence and reputation and being right is brought down. Both are uncomfortable. Both are necessary. Nobody arrives at Christ on the level they were standing on, and the ones who find it hardest are not usually the ones in the valley.

The crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways. The word for crooked is the word for twisted, bent out of true. Every honest person knows something in themselves answering to it — the thing that will not come straight, the habit of self-protection, the small dishonesty that has been there so long it feels structural. Isaiah says the road crew has been sent for that too.

And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.

Here is why Luke kept quoting. Matthew and Mark stop before this line; Luke, writing with the whole world in view, will not. All flesh — not all Israel. It is the universal note that has already sounded twice in this Gospel, in Simeon's arms (2:32) and in the angel's all the people (2:10), and it will keep sounding until Acts ends in Rome.

But read what it actually promises, because the sentence is sometimes stretched further than it goes. It does not say all flesh shall be saved. It says all flesh shall see the salvation of God. The salvation will be public, visible, put where nobody can claim it was hidden from them. That is a promise about the reach of the announcement, not about the response to it — and John spends the next three verses making brutally clear that seeing and receiving are not the same thing.

Still, hold what it does promise. There is no corner of the world too far off the road for this. Isaiah's highway runs through every landscape there is, and the salvation of God has been set where all flesh will see it.

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, 'You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
verseByVerse.commentary:
You brood of vipers!

Stop and take in who he is talking to. These are not his enemies. They are not the delegation from Jerusalem or the men who will later arrest him. Luke says it plainly: the crowds that came out to be baptized by him. These are the people who walked into the desert to repent, and this is how he greets them.

The insult is exact. A brood of vipers is a nest of snakes — and the picture behind it is one every farmer in that country knew. When stubble is burned off a field, the snakes come racing out ahead of the flames. John looks at a crowd streaming down to the river and says: I know what you look like. You look like the wildlife leaving a fire.

Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? The question is not a compliment on their foresight. It carries a sting — who told you that running for the water would be enough?

So why is he so hard on people who have come to do the right thing? Because he can see what they have come for. There is a way of pursuing religion which is entirely about damage limitation: getting into the water, getting the ritual done, getting the insurance in place, and changing nothing whatever. A man may be perfectly sincere in wanting to escape the consequences of his sin and have no interest at all in leaving it. John will not baptise that. The next verse is his terms.

Then the wrath to come, which a modern reader may find harder than the snakes. It needs saying plainly, because it is regularly caricatured. The wrath of God is not divine temper. It is not God losing control, or taking offence, or reacting badly. It is the settled, holy, entirely just opposition of God to everything that ruins what he has made.

And it is worth asking honestly what the alternative would be. A God who looked at cruelty and abuse and betrayal and felt nothing would not be a kinder God; he would be a moral vacancy. We do not admire that in people. We do not call a man good because he can watch a child harmed and remain unmoved. The wrath of God is the shadow cast by the love of God — it exists because he cares, infinitely, about what is being done to his world and to the people in it.

John announces it as coming, which means it is not here yet, which means there is time. That is the only reason a man stands by a river shouting at people instead of standing back and letting it arrive.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now John's terms, and there are two of them: bear the fruit, and drop the credential.

Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. The phrase is precise — fruits worthy of, fruits that match. He is not asking for a general improvement. He is saying that real repentance produces something visible and appropriate to the thing repented of, and in two verses' time he will give three worked examples so that nobody can pretend the demand was vague.

And notice the direction of the logic, because this is where an anxious believer can get badly hurt. Fruit is evidence of repentance; it is not the cause of it, and it is not what earns anything. A tree does not become an apple tree by producing apples. But the fruit is how you can tell.

Which is worth saying carefully to the reader who has just read that sentence and gone straight to their own barrenness. There is a kind of self-examination that is faithful and a kind that is corrosive, and the difference is where it looks for the answer. The corrosive kind stands under the tree counting, gets a number it does not like, and concludes it is not really a Christian. The faithful kind notices the shortage and goes back to the root. John's whole ministry was about turning people to God, and a man frightened by his own lack of fruit is a man in the exact condition John was preaching for.

And do not begin to say to yourselves, We have Abraham as our father. Luke's do not begin is almost affectionate: he can see the words forming. This was the answer everybody had ready. Descent from Abraham, circumcision, membership of the covenant people — the credential nobody had ever seriously questioned.

God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. He is probably pointing. The Jordan valley is full of stones, and the argument is devastating in its simplicity: the God who made Isaac out of a dead womb can make a son of Abraham out of a rock. There is nothing so unpromising that he cannot make it a child of the promise — which means that the family tree that seemed to guarantee everything guarantees nothing at all.

The modern versions of the credential are not hard to name. Christian parents. Baptism as an infant. Membership of a good church. Thirty years in the same pew. Every one of these is a genuine mercy, and not one of them is the thing itself. A man may be inside all of it and still have never once turned round.

Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Not the branches — the root. This is not pruning. And even now means the blade is already resting against the wood: not a threat about the distant future but a description of the present moment, with the axeman standing there.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds asked him, 'What then shall we do?' And he answered them, 'Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then shall we do?

It is the right question, and it is the one the preaching was for. Notice that they do not argue with him. Nobody points out that he has just called them snakes. The crowd hears that the axe is at the root and asks the only sensible thing a man can ask in that position.

And John's answer is the most surprising thing in the chapter. Here is the last of the prophets, the forerunner of the Messiah, standing in the wilderness with the crowds of Israel in front of him and the whole weight of the old covenant behind him, asked point-blank what repentance requires. He does not say: come to the temple. He does not say: fast, pray, keep the feasts, tithe, study. He says:

Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.

A tunic was the basic garment worn next to the skin. Most people had one; a person with two had a spare. So the instruction is not sell everything and it is not give until you are destitute. It is startlingly modest and startlingly concrete: if you have two and somebody near you has none, that is what the second one is for.

Which lands somewhere very specific for a modern reader, because the honest arithmetic is uncomfortable. Almost nobody reading this owns two tunics. We own thirty, in a wardrobe, several of which have not been worn in two years. And John's test is not what percentage we give away; it is whether the surplus is understood to be ours or understood to be for somebody.

That is the shift he is asking for, and it is a shift of ownership before it is a shift of behaviour. The person who thinks of the second coat as their property, from which generosity is an occasional deduction, will always give a little and feel good about it. The person who thinks of the second coat as already belonging to whoever has none will simply hand it over, and will not think of it as generosity at all.

Here is a test that takes a minute. Look at what is in the cupboard, the fridge, the account — and ask, of the part beyond what is actually needed: whose is that? The answer, said out loud, is usually more revealing than any amount of introspection about one's spiritual state.

Repentance, in the last prophet's definition, reaches the wardrobe before it reaches the vocabulary.

verseByVerse.quote: Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, 'Teacher, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Collect no more than you are authorized to do.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the tax collectors come down to the water, and it is worth understanding what that meant.

These were Jews working the Roman revenue system. The empire farmed out collection: a man bought the right to collect in a district, paid Rome its figure, and kept whatever else he could extract. The system did not merely permit extortion; it ran on it. So a tax collector was two things at once in the eyes of his neighbours — a collaborator with an occupying power, and a thief with legal protection. They were barred as witnesses, lumped in with prostitutes, and hated with a completeness that is hard to convey.

And they came out to be baptised. They call John Teacher, which is a courtesy the crowds did not bother with. And they ask the same question the crowd asked.

Now watch what John does not say.

He does not tell them to quit. This is one of the most remarkable moments in the chapter and it is regularly read past. Here is a profession soaked in injustice, tied to a pagan empire, despised by every godly person in Israel — and the prophet's instruction is not get out of it. It is collect no more than you are authorized to do.

Do the job. Do it honestly. Take the legal figure and not a denarius more.

That is a word many Christians need and few expect. There is a persistent instinct that real repentance ought to mean leaving — leaving the industry, the firm, the compromised environment — and that staying is a failure of nerve. Sometimes leaving is right, and Scripture knows of work that cannot be done honestly at all. But John's answer to a room full of men in a corrupt trade was to send them back into it clean.

Consider what that cost. A tax collector who takes only the authorised amount earns very little; the profit was in the margin. John is telling these men to accept a permanent drop in income in exchange for a clear conscience, and to go on working alongside colleagues who will not do the same and will do better out of it. That is far harder than resigning. Resigning is over in a day. This is every day.

And it is the shape of most Christian obedience. Not a dramatic exit, but the same desk, the same job, the same people, done straight — with less money and no applause, for years.

verseByVerse.quote: Soldiers also asked him, 'And we, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soldiers next, and their question has a small word in it that changes the tone: And we, what shall we do? There is something almost anxious in it. They have heard him answer the crowd and answer the tax collectors, and they want to know whether there is anything for men like them.

These are probably not Roman legionaries but troops in Herod's service, often used to back up the revenue men — the muscle standing behind the table. Which explains why John's instructions are the ones he gives.

Do not extort money from anyone by threats. The verb means to shake down, to intimidate. It is what happens when a man with a weapon stands near a man with a purse.

Or by false accusation. A soldier could report a man, and the report would be believed, and the man would pay to make it go away.

And be content with your wages.

Again, no instruction to leave the army. A pagan uniform, an occupying power's business, and John sends them back to the barracks — with three things to stop doing and one thing to start being.

That third instruction is the one that turns the other two into something more than rules, and it is worth staying on. John has diagnosed the root. Why does a soldier lean on people? Because his pay is poor and there is money to be had. Deal with the extortion by prohibition alone and you have a man permanently resentful, permanently tempted, obeying with clenched teeth. Deal with it by contentment and the temptation loses its handle.

Contentment is not the same as having enough. Paul learned it in prison and said so explicitly: he had learned to be content in plenty and in hunger, and the learning was the point (Phil. 4:11-13). It is not a temperament some people are born with. It is something acquired, slowly, by people who have found something they cannot lose and have begun to reckon everything else against it.

And notice that all three of John's answers — to the crowd, to the tax men, to the soldiers — are about money. The last prophet of the old covenant had one question in the desert about what repentance looks like, and three times he answered it at the wallet. Not because money is the worst of sins, but because it is the place where a man's actual convictions are recorded, in figures, whether or not he agrees with them.

verseByVerse.quote: As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all, saying, 'I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds have reached the point of asking the question out loud, or nearly out loud — all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ. It is not an unreasonable guess. He is the first prophetic voice in four hundred years; the whole country is going out to him; and Israel had been waiting a very long time.

Here is a man who could have had it. Not by seizing anything — merely by not correcting them. He needed only to be a little vague, to let the question hang, to accept what people were pressing on him.

John answered them all. He does not let it hang for a sentence.

What he says is not modesty; it is arithmetic. The strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. Unfastening a man's sandals and washing his feet was the lowest job in a household — a Jewish slave could not be required to do it, and it was left to Gentile servants and to the wife. John, whom Jesus would call the greatest man born of women, says he is not fit for the job the lowest servant is given. That is not a man with a poor self-image. That is a man who has seen accurately the difference between himself and the one coming.

I baptize you with water, but… he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.

The contrast is not between two grades of the same thing. Water is external; it can wash a man's skin and leave his heart untouched, and John knows it. What is coming is a drenching in God himself — the promise of Ezekiel, a new heart and a new spirit put inside a man (Ezek. 36:26-27), and of Joel, the Spirit poured out on all flesh (Joel 2:28-29). John can put a man under the water. Only one person can put the Spirit inside him.

A word to the reader who has been taught that baptism in the Spirit is a second, later experience to be sought after conversion, and who may have spent years anxious about whether they have had it. Sincere Christians differ here, and many who hold that view love Christ better than most of us.

But look at where the New Testament actually lands the phrase. Every time it appears, it points to what the Messiah does when he comes — and Peter, explaining Pentecost, applies it to what happened to Cornelius's household the moment they believed, saying God gave them the same gift as he gave to us when we believed (Acts 11:16-17). Paul says plainly that in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body (1 Cor. 12:13). Every Christian has it. That is not a reason to want less of the Spirit's work; it is the ground for asking for more of it, out of security rather than out of fear.

verseByVerse.quote: His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's last recorded image is a farmyard, and it is not a gentle one.

Picture the threshing floor: a flat area of packed earth or rock, usually on high ground to catch the wind. The cut grain has been trodden or beaten to break the husk from the kernel. Then a man takes a winnowing fork — a broad wooden shovel — and throws the whole mass into the air. The wind takes the light chaff and blows it aside; the heavy grain falls back onto the floor. The tool does not create the difference between wheat and chaff. It reveals it.

That is the picture, and every part of it is doing work.

His winnowing fork is in his hand. Already. Not fetched when needed — held.

To gather the wheat into his barn. This is the first thing named, and it should not be hurried past on the way to the fire. The purpose of a harvest is the grain. The whole operation exists for the barn.

But the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.

There is no way to soften that and no honest reason to try. Chaff was burned; it was worth nothing and it was got rid of. And the fire is unquenchable — a fire nobody can put out.

This is the doctrine of hell in a single image, and it comes from the mouth of the man Jesus called the greatest of the prophets — as it comes, more often and more plainly, from the mouth of Jesus himself. Christians have differed about the nature of the fire, some holding that the wicked are finally consumed rather than kept in conscious suffering. The mainstream of the church has not read it that way, and the words of Christ elsewhere are hard to bend in that direction. What is not in dispute among any who take the text seriously is the reality of the judgment and the finality of it.

And here is what must be said next, because it is what John says next. Two verses later Luke calls all of this good news.

How can it be? Because the alternative to a God who separates is a God who does not care what happens to his world — who lets the cruelty and the abuse and the lies go into the barn along with everything else, for ever. A universe with no final sorting is a universe where nothing is ever put right. The fire is terrible; a harvest with no fire in it would be a harvest with no justice in it.

And the winnower is announced before he arrives, by a man sent out ahead of him for that purpose, standing in a river, with the water still running. Nobody has to be chaff. That is why he is shouting.

verseByVerse.quote: So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence, and it does something to the whole chapter that a reader ought not to miss.

So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.

Go back over what has just been recorded. He called the congregation a nest of snakes. He told them the wrath of God was coming and asked who had tipped them off. He demolished the one credential they were all relying on. He said the axe was already against the root. He finished with a fire that cannot be put out.

Luke's verb for that is euangelizeto. He was evangelising them. He preached good news.

That single word settles an argument that never quite goes away. There is a persistent assumption that the hard parts of Christian preaching are the price of admission for the good parts — the unpleasant preliminaries a preacher gets through in order to arrive at the comfort. Luke does not see two things there. He sees one, and he calls all of it gospel.

And on reflection it is obvious. If the axe really is at the root, then a man who tells you so is not being harsh; he is being kind at some personal cost, and the man who assures you the tree is fine is not being kind at all. Nobody thanks a doctor for a cheerful manner about a tumour he has decided not to mention. The news is only good if it is true — and if it is true, then the warning is part of the goodness.

Many other exhortations, Luke adds. What we have of John's preaching is a summary; there were months of it, and Luke has given us the shape rather than the transcript.

It is also worth noticing who he preached it to: the people. Not a school of disciples, not an inner circle — the ordinary population of Judea, streaming out to a desert to be shouted at by a man in camel's hair, and going home changed. Whatever else John was, he was not an acquired taste.

He had one job, and he did it for about six months, and then it was over. The next two verses tell us how.

verseByVerse.quote: But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke closes John's story before Jesus's begins, and he does it in two verses with a great deal held back.

The facts underneath are these. Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, had visited his half-brother in Rome and come back with his brother's wife, Herodias — who was also his own niece. To marry her he put away his first wife, the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, an insult that would eventually cost him a war. And the law was explicit: You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife (Lev. 18:16; 20:21).

John told him so.

That is the whole of it, and it is worth pausing on how unnecessary it was. John's ministry was at the Jordan, among crowds who came to him. Nobody required him to address the tetrarch's marriage. He could have preached repentance to Judea for years without ever mentioning the palace, and he would have died an old man.

He went to the one man in the country who could have him killed, and told him the truth about his private life.

Luke's phrasing is careful: and for all the evil things that Herod had done. So it was not one sermon about one marriage. John kept at it, across the whole range of the man's conduct — and Mark tells us something Luke leaves out, that Herod used to listen to him gladly and was perplexed by him (Mark 6:20). There was a strange, doomed relationship there: a king who liked hearing the preacher who condemned him, and killed him anyway.

Then the sentence Luke ends on: added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison. Not a martyrdom scene. Not a speech. A door shut, and a summary clause, and the voice is gone from the story.

There is something here that has to be faced by anyone who thinks faithfulness is repaid in this life. John did exactly what he was sent to do. He did it without flinching, without ambition, without ever once diverting the crowd's admiration onto himself. And he finished in a cell in a desert fortress, and was executed at a birthday party because a girl danced well and her mother held a grudge.

Luke's placing is deliberate. The forerunner ends in prison on the page immediately before the one he announced steps into the river. The voice is silenced just as the Word begins to speak. But silencing the herald does not stop what the herald announced. Herod could shut the door on John. He could do nothing whatever about the man standing in the water at verse 21.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The baptism of Jesus is narrated with remarkable brevity in Luke — briefer even than in Mark. Luke does not linger on the event; the baptism itself is a participle, almost an aside. What he focuses on is what happens while Jesus is praying afterwards.

This is characteristic. Luke consistently shows Jesus at prayer at the great turning points of his ministry (3:21; 6:12; 9:18; 9:28; 11:1; 22:41). The baptism is not the centre of the scene; the prayer is. And what happens during it is the most explicit Trinitarian moment in the Synoptic Gospels: the Son in the water; the Spirit descending in bodily form like a dove; the Father's voice from heaven.

Why is Jesus baptised at all? John's baptism was for repentance and forgiveness, and Jesus has nothing to repent of. Matthew records John's protest and Jesus's answer: “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

He is baptised not because he needs what the water signifies but because he is identifying himself with the people he came to save. He enters the water of repentance as the representative of those who need to repent; he will enter the waters of death as the representative of those who deserve to die. The Jordan is the first public act of the substitution that ends at Golgotha.

The Father's voice weaves two Old Testament texts together. “You are my Son” is Psalm 2:7, the royal psalm of the Davidic king. “With you I am well pleased” is Isaiah 42:1, the opening of the first Servant Song. Jesus is simultaneously the royal Son of David and the suffering Servant of Isaiah — the King who will reign and the Servant who will be crushed. Both identities are laid on him at the outset, and the whole ministry is the working out of what it costs to be both at once.
verseByVerse.theology:
The descent of the Spirit “in bodily form, like a dove” is Luke's careful insistence that this was a visible, physical event — not a vision or an inward impression but something anyone standing on the bank could have seen.

The dove carries a layered background: the dove of Noah signalling that the judgment was over (Gen. 8:8-12); the dove of the poor person's offering (Lev. 5:7; and 2:24 in this Gospel); and, most significantly, the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Gen. 1:2), where the verb is used elsewhere of a bird brooding over its nest. The Spirit is over the water again. A new creation is beginning.

The Father's declaration comes before Jesus has performed a single public miracle, preached a single sermon, or won a single crowd. The pleasure of the Father in the Son is not contingent on performance; it is the expression of the love that existed between them before the foundation of the world (John 17:24).

That is the theological foundation of grace: the beloved Son is beloved before he does anything. And the Christian who is in Christ shares the status — not earned but given, not provisional but settled.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus praying at his baptism is the first instance of a pattern that runs through the whole Gospel. The implication is not that prayer is a mechanism that causes the Spirit to descend. It is that prayer is the posture of one who depends entirely on the Father rather than on his own resources.

The Son of God prays before every major act of his ministry — not because he lacks information or power, but because prayer is the expression of the relationship that defines him. The disciple who prays before decisions and transitions is not following a technique. He is following his Lord.

The Trinity is present at the Jordan in a way impossible to mistake and impossible to fully systematise. The three are distinct: the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends, the Father speaks. The three are simultaneously present, simultaneously active, simultaneously directed towards one redemptive event.

The doctrine of the Trinity is not a philosophical puzzle invented by later councils. It is the description of what happened at the Jordan. The church was simply trying to find words adequate to what the evangelists reported.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened.

Two details in that sentence are Luke's alone, and both are worth having.

The first is when all the people were baptized. Luke puts Jesus at the end of the queue, in among everybody else. He does not describe the baptism itself at all — the verb is a participle, almost an aside, and Luke moves straight past it. What interests him is not the ceremony but where Jesus was standing while it happened: in the same river, on the same day, with the same crowd, receiving the same sign.

Which raises the question the chapter has been building towards and Luke leaves the reader to ask. John was preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (v. 3). What is the one man in history with nothing to repent of doing in that water?

Matthew preserves the exchange Luke omits. John tries to stop him, and Jesus answers: Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness (Matt. 3:15). He is not there because he needs what the water means. He is there because he is taking his place among the people he came to save — standing in the sinners' queue, at the sinners' river, receiving the sinners' sign, on the first day of his public life.

It is the opening move of the great exchange, and it will be finished on a hill where he takes the sinners' death. Everything he did between those two points he did in that position: numbered with the transgressors, from the Jordan to the cross (Isa. 53:12).

The second detail is and was praying. No other Gospel says it. And it is the first appearance of something Luke will do all the way through: at every hinge of the story, he shows Jesus at prayer. Before choosing the Twelve, he prays all night (6:12). Before Peter's confession, he is praying alone (9:18). At the transfiguration, he goes up to pray (9:28). In Gethsemane (22:41). On the cross (23:34, 46).

Note what that means and what it does not. The prayer does not cause the heavens to open, as though it were a technique. It is the posture of a Son who does nothing out of his own resources. If the Son of God would not begin his ministry without praying, the question of whether prayer is a good use of time before a decision has been settled by somebody with far better reasons than ours to skip it.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavens open, and all three persons of the Godhead are present in one sentence.

The Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove. Luke is the only evangelist who adds in bodily form, and he adds it on purpose. This was not an inward impression or a private vision. Something happened in the air over the Jordan that could have been seen by anyone standing there.

Why a dove? The image has several roots and they run together. A dove came back to Noah over a drowned world with a leaf in its beak, and the judgment was over (Gen. 8:8-12). Doves were the offering of the poor — the two birds Mary had carried into the temple (2:24). And at the very beginning, the Spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters, a verb used elsewhere of a bird brooding over its nest (Gen. 1:2). The Spirit is over the water again. Something is being made new.

Then the voice. You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.

It is two Scriptures woven together, and the combination is the whole programme of the ministry that is about to start. You are my Son is Psalm 2:7 — the coronation psalm of the Davidic king, the one who is given the nations for his inheritance. With you I am well pleased is Isaiah 42:1 — the opening of the first Servant Song, about the one who will not break a bruised reed and who will be despised and crushed for the sins of others.

King and Servant. The throne and the cross, laid on him in a single sentence, before he has done anything at all.

And that last point is the one to hold. The Father speaks this over him before the first sermon, before the first healing, before a single disciple has been called. There is no ministry yet to be pleased with. The delight is not a wage paid for work completed; it is the settled love of the Father for the Son, older than the world (John 17:24).

Which is the ground under the feet of everybody who is in Christ. The verdict spoken over him at the Jordan is the verdict spoken over all who are joined to him — not earned, not provisional, not reviewed annually. You do not work in order to be loved. You are loved, and then you work.

Here is the Son, standing in the water where sinners stand, having taken their place before he has taken a step. Here is the Spirit, coming down on him as gently as a bird, to rest and not to depart. And here is the Father, breaking a four-hundred-year silence to say what he thinks of him. Everything the world was made for, and everything it was ruined for, is standing in one river on one morning — and heaven is entirely delighted with him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–38 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's genealogy is unlike Matthew's in three decisive ways: it runs backward, from Jesus to Adam rather than from Abraham to Jesus; it is placed after the baptism rather than before the birth narrative; and it extends past Abraham to Adam, and past Adam to God.

These are not inconsistencies but theological choices. Matthew writes for a Jewish readership and presents Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel's covenant story, beginning with Abraham. Luke writes with the world in view and presents Jesus as the answer to the human story, beginning at the Jordan — where his identity has just been declared by the Father — and tracing his lineage to the first man.

The genealogy also differs from Matthew's in many of the names between David and Joseph. Some hold that Luke traces the line through Mary; others that one evangelist follows legal succession and the other physical descent; others appeal to the complexities of levirate marriage. No solution is free of difficulty, and the church has lived with the two lists for two thousand years without resolving every detail.

What is clear is that the difference does work. Matthew's line runs through Solomon and the kings — the line that carries the legal right to the throne, and also the line under the curse pronounced on Jeconiah, that none of his offspring would prosper sitting on David's seat (Jer. 22:30). Luke's runs through Nathan, a son of David who never reigned and whose descendants never came under that word. The crown descends by one branch and the blood by another, and they meet in one child.

Most of the names between David and Joseph are otherwise unknown — thirty-five men of whom Scripture records nothing except that the line ran through their houses. Further back the list passes through Ruth the Moabite, through Perez the son of Tamar, through Abraham who twice lied about his wife. God ran the promise straight through a family history containing foreignness, deception and disgrace, and did not clean it up first.

The placement after the baptism gives the list its frame. The Father has just said “You are my Son”; the genealogy answers the question whose son, exactly? He is the son of Joseph as registered; the son of David, which is his royal credential; the son of Abraham, which is his covenantal one; the son of Adam, which is his human solidarity. And at the end of the list — the son of God.

He is the Son of God who has become the son of Adam, so that the sons of Adam might become the sons of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The genealogy ending in “son of Adam, son of God” is Luke's most compact statement of the theology of the incarnation. Jesus traces his human lineage to the first human, establishing the full solidarity of his humanity with every person who has ever lived.

He did not merely appear in human form. He entered the long human story at its most specific and particular point, with real ancestors and a real history — which is what Paul means by “born of woman, born under the law” (Gal. 4:4). Fully embedded in the situation he came to redeem.

The contrast between Adam and Jesus implicit here becomes explicit in Romans 5:12-21 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-49. Adam brought death; the second Adam brings life. Adam's disobedience constituted many sinners; the second Adam's obedience constitutes many righteous.

Luke's genealogy does not spell out that typology — that is Paul's work — but it establishes the premise on which the typology stands: Jesus is the son of Adam, which means Adam's story is part of his story, and his story is the answer to Adam's.
verseByVerse.examples:
The genealogy is one of the portions of Scripture readers habitually skip — a long list of unfamiliar names that looks like a necessary but uninspiring prelude. But it is the gospel in miniature. It announces that the salvation of the world came not through power or privilege but through the long, winding, sometimes scandalous history of real families making real choices.

Every name in the list is a person whose life contributed to the moment when the Son of God stood in the Jordan, and almost none of them had any idea of it. Providence is not abstract. It is as specific as a name — including the thirty-five names in this list about whom history has kept nothing else at all.

The final phrase, “the son of Adam, the son of God,” is the summary of everything the Gospel will demonstrate. Jesus is fully human and fully divine, and the two cannot be separated without destroying the gospel.

A Jesus who is only divine cannot save us, because he cannot represent us. A Jesus who is only human cannot save us, because he has no righteousness to give. The Jesus of Luke's genealogy — rooted in human history all the way back to Eden, and named by the Father as his Son — is the only Jesus who can do what needs doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age.

Luke gives the age with an about, which is exactly the sort of thing a careful historian says when he has not got the day. But thirty is not a random figure. It is the age at which a Levite entered the service of the sanctuary (Num. 4:3), the age at which Joseph stood before Pharaoh (Gen. 41:46), the age at which David began to reign (2 Sam. 5:4). Whatever else it signalled, it was the age at which a man in Israel was considered fit to be given a life's work.

Eighteen years of that life had gone by since the last thing Luke recorded, and not one line of them survives.

Then being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli — and the parenthesis is doing careful work. Luke has spent two chapters establishing that Joseph is not this child's father, and he will not now quietly contradict himself. As was supposed preserves the virgin conception while allowing the legal line to stand. Joseph's son by law, by household, by trade and by every register in Galilee; not by blood.

Now the difficulty any reader with two Gospels open will run straight into. Set Luke's list beside Matthew's, and from David onwards they do not match. Matthew comes down through Solomon and the kings of Judah; Luke comes down through Nathan, another of David's sons (2 Sam. 5:14), through names that appear nowhere in the royal chronicles. Matthew has roughly twenty-seven generations between David and Jesus; Luke has about forty-two. And most pointedly, Matthew calls Joseph the son of Jacob while Luke calls him the son of Heli.

Christians have answered this in three main ways. Some hold that Luke gives Mary's line, Joseph being reckoned son of Heli as his son-in-law — which fits Luke's careful as was supposed and his close interest in Mary through chapters 1 and 2, though it must be granted that Luke writes son of Heli and not father of Mary. Others appeal to levirate marriage, the law by which a man who died childless had offspring raised up to his name by his brother (Deut. 25:5-6), so that one man could carry a legal father and a biological father under two names. Others hold that Matthew traces the legal succession to the throne while Luke traces physical descent.

Each answer carries a difficulty, and it is better to say plainly that we cannot settle it from where we stand than to manufacture a certainty the evidence will not bear. Genealogies in that world were kept to make a point, not to satisfy a modern registrar, and these two evangelists are making different points.

What is worth seeing is that the difference does real work rather than real damage — and the next entries will show where.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven verses, thirty-five names, and almost none of them is known.

That is worth stating rather than skipping, because it is the most striking thing about this stretch of the list. From Joseph back to David, Luke names men who appear nowhere else in Scripture. Maath, Naggai, Esli, Josech, Joda, Elmadam, Cosam, Jorim, Melea, Menna — no stories, no deeds, no record of anything they said or did. Whoever they were, they lived and died and left nothing behind them except that the line ran through their houses.

Only two names in the whole stretch surface elsewhere. Zerubbabel and Shealtiel (v. 27) are the leaders of the return from Babylon, the men who laid the second temple's foundation. Everything either side of them is silence.

Then, at verse 31, the list arrives at Nathan, the son of David — and here is where the two genealogies do their different work.

Matthew's line runs from David through Solomon and the kings. That is the line that carries the legal right to the throne — and it is also the line that runs through Jeconiah, of whom the LORD said: Write this man down as childless… for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David (Jer. 22:30). A curse lies across the royal succession.

Luke's line runs from David through Nathan — a son who never reigned, whose descendants never sat on the throne, and who therefore never came under that word. Put the two lists together and something remarkable appears: the crown descends by one branch and the blood by another, and they meet in one child. Joseph gives him the legal title; the physical descent comes another way. Whatever remains unresolved among the names, the two lists agree on everything that matters.

And there is a quieter thing in these seven verses for anybody who feels that their life has not amounted to much. Thirty-five men whose only recorded achievement is that they existed, married, and had a son. History has kept nothing else about them. God kept their names.

They had no idea what they were part of. Not one of them lived to see the point of his own place in the list. They simply took their turn — and every one of them was necessary, and every one of them is written down in the book that will outlast every other book, because the Son of God came through their houses.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the names begin to be recognisable, and with them the whole familiar story comes back up through the list.

Jesse, Obed, Boaz. That is the last page of the book of Ruth, and it is worth remembering what stands behind it. Boaz married a Moabite widow — a foreigner, from a people the law had barred from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (Deut. 23:3). Their son was Obed, Obed's son was Jesse, and Jesse's son was David. The line of the Messiah runs directly through a woman who by birth had no right to be anywhere near it.

Nahshon was the chief of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness (Num. 1:7), the man who led out at the head of the column when Israel marched.

Perez, the son of Judah — and here the list goes somewhere most family trees would rather not. Perez was born of Tamar, Judah's widowed daughter-in-law, whom Judah failed to provide for and then took for a prostitute at a roadside without recognising her (Gen. 38). It is one of the ugliest chapters in Genesis. And that is where the line runs.

Then Jacob, Isaac, Abraham, and the whole of the patriarchal history in five words. Jacob the deceiver; Isaac the son who should never have been born; Abraham who twice passed his wife off as his sister to save his own skin, and who was given the promise anyway.

What that stretch of the genealogy says, and says without a single word of commentary, is that God brought his Son into the world through a family history containing deception, prostitution, foreignness, cowardice and long stretches of nothing at all.

He did not clean it up first. He did not route around the shameful parts. He ran the line of the promise straight through Tamar and Rahab's Jericho and Ruth's Moab and Judah's roadside, and then had it written down and read aloud in public for two thousand years.

There is a mercy in that which is easy to miss. A family history is one of the things people are least able to change and most often ashamed of. Luke is quietly reporting that the Saviour of the world has one too — and that God is not embarrassed by it, and did not require it to be respectable before he would work through it.

The promise given to Abraham, that in his offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed, has been travelling down this line for two thousand years by the time Luke writes it out. It never once depended on the quality of the people carrying it.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last four verses take the line back past Abraham, past the flood, past the whole history of Israel, to the first man — and then one step further.

Matthew's genealogy stops at Abraham, because Matthew is establishing that Jesus is Israel's Messiah. Luke keeps going, and the difference is the whole shape of his Gospel. He is writing for the world.

A note for the reader with a Bible open at Genesis, because there is a real puzzle here. Verse 36 has Cainan, the son of Arphaxad — and the Hebrew text of Genesis 11 has no such name; it runs Arphaxad, then Shelah. The name is present in the Greek Old Testament that Luke and his readers used. Some hold that the Greek preserves a name the Hebrew line dropped; others that a copyist's eye slipped, since a Cainan appears a few names later in the list. It cannot be settled from where we stand. What is worth knowing is that biblical genealogies regularly skip generations — Matthew does so openly — and were never intended to function as a complete census of everyone who lived.

The son of Noah — the whole human race narrowed to one boat. The son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch — the man who walked with God and was not, because God took him.

And then: the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

Luke has put the genealogy immediately after the baptism, and now the reason is plain. At verse 22 a voice from heaven said You are my beloved Son. At verse 38 the list arrives at the same title from the other end. The Son declared at the Jordan is traced back, through seventy-seven generations of ordinary and disgraceful and forgotten people, to the son of Adam — and past Adam, who had no father, to God.

He is the son of Adam. That is the point of every name in the list. He did not appear in human form as a visitor wearing the costume of our race; he entered the human story at its most specific and particular point, with real ancestors and a real history, all the way back to the beginning. What Adam ruined, he is now inside — as one of us, from the same stock, subject to the same conditions, related by blood to every person who has ever lived.

And he is the Son of God. Where the first Adam was made and failed, the second Adam has come and will not.

Two men stand at the head of the human race, and the list that runs between them is a catalogue of what the first one's failure cost. Every name is a man who was born and died. Every name is a link in a chain of dust returning to dust, stretching unbroken from a garden to a river in Judea — and at the end of it, standing in the water with the Spirit resting on him and his Father's voice still in the air, is the one who came to break it.

4.title: The Testing and the Anointing
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the chapter of beginnings and confrontations. It opens with the Spirit leading Jesus into the wilderness for forty days of testing — the place where Israel repeatedly failed, now entered by Israel's true representative who will not fail. It continues with the dramatic scene in the Nazareth synagogue where Jesus reads from Isaiah 61 and announces that the Scripture has been fulfilled in their hearing — only to be driven out of the town by the same people who had initially marvelled at him. And it concludes with a succession of healings and exorcisms in Capernaum that demonstrate in action what the Isaiah text announced in words: the kingdom of God has come.

The temptation narrative (vv. 1–13) is the interpretive key to the whole of Jesus's ministry. The devil offers Jesus three things — bread, power, and supernatural protection — and each offer is a shortcut around the path of obedience and suffering that leads to the cross. Jesus refuses each offer with the word of Scripture, demonstrating that the weapons of his warfare are not the weapons of power but the word of God and trust in the Father. The one who overcomes the devil in the wilderness will face him again, in various guises, throughout the ministry — and will face him definitively in the garden of Gethsemane and on the cross. The wilderness is not the final battle; it is the first.

The Nazareth sermon (vv. 14–30) is Luke's programmatic statement of Jesus's mission — the equivalent of the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew. Luke places it at the beginning of the public ministry as the manifesto of the kingdom: good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed, the year of the Lord's favour. The question the sermon raises — who is included in the “year of the Lord's favour”? — is answered by two Old Testament examples that the congregation finds intolerable: Elijah went not to an Israelite widow but to a Sidonian one; Elisha healed not an Israelite leper but a Syrian one. The good news of the kingdom is for the excluded, the foreigner, the unexpected. This is the gospel Luke has been writing toward since chapter 1 — and the congregation's response is homicidal rage.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temptation follows immediately on the baptism: the Spirit who descended at the Jordan now leads Jesus into the wilderness for forty days. The sequence is deliberate. The Father's declaration of sonship — “You are my beloved Son” — is at once followed by the devil's challenge to it: “If you are the Son of God…”

The wilderness is where the identity given at the baptism is tested, and where the question of what kind of Son Jesus will be is answered. Will he use divine power for his own relief? Will he take the world's kingdoms by the world's methods? Will he force the Father to prove his care? The answer each time is no — and the no is spoken not by supernatural force but with the word of Scripture.

The three assaults correspond to Israel's three great wilderness failures. Israel hungered and grumbled (Exod. 16); Jesus is tempted to turn stone into bread.
