Israel worshipped the golden calf (Exod. 32); Jesus is offered the kingdoms for an act of worship. Israel tested God at Massah (Exod. 17:1-7); Jesus is urged to throw himself from the temple. At every point where Israel failed, Jesus stands — and he does it by the means available to every Israelite: the word of God, believed and obeyed. All three of his answers come from Deuteronomy, the book Moses gave Israel before they entered the land.

The final offer is the subtlest, because it comes with chapter and verse. The devil quotes Psalm 91 — accurately, so far as it goes. But he stops the quotation at “to guard you” and omits the psalm's own qualifier, “in all your ways.” The promise covers the paths of obedience; it does not cover a stunt. The temptation is not to misread a promise but to use one as leverage — to demand that the Father demonstrate his care by preventing the consequences of a chosen folly.

Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 6:16 and the memory of Massah. The difference between trust and testing is the difference between resting in God's faithfulness and requiring him to prove it on our terms. The person who says “I will believe God loves me if he does this specific thing” is not trusting God. He is testing him.

The section ends with a phrase Luke intends to be remembered: the devil departed “until an opportune time.” The wilderness was the opening exchange, not the war.
verseByVerse.theology:
The temptation establishes Jesus as the second Adam as well as the true Israel. Adam was tempted in a garden of abundance and failed; Jesus is tempted in a wilderness of deprivation and stands. Adam's failure brought sin and death into the human story; Jesus's obedience begins the reversal.

This is the logic Paul unpacks in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15: what the first Adam lost, the second Adam wins back. And the victory is not won by raw divine force but by the very means God made available to Adam — the word of God, and the decision to trust it rather than the alternative on offer.

The devil's departure “until an opportune time” (v. 13) signals that the conflict continues through the ministry — in the demons, in the religious leaders, in the crowd's wish for a political king. The appointed opportunity is the passion: “Then Satan entered into Judas” (22:3); “this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (22:53).

And at the cross the wilderness temptations return almost verbatim — save yourself; come down; if you are the Son of God. What looks there like Satan's victory is the moment of his defeat, because the Son who refused every shortcut in the desert walked the full cost of obedience to its end.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's weapon against every temptation is Scripture — received, remembered, and spoken with precision. He does not argue philosophically, does not marshal feelings, and does not reach for resources unavailable to ordinary disciples. He quotes the word of God.

That is not a pastoral cliché but a pattern with hard practical consequences. The Christian who has stored up Scripture has the weapon Jesus used. The Christian who has neglected it is left to improvise arguments in the moment, which is not a fair fight.

The devil quotes Psalm 91 accurately, and with a clause removed. The most dangerous misuse of Scripture is never the obviously wrong use; it is the superficially plausible one — a true promise lifted out of its context and used to license what the context forbids. Every cult and every proof-texted disaster has this shape.

Which is the argument for knowing not merely verses but the shape of the whole book. A man who knows a hundred verses can be beaten by a hundred and one. A man who knows what God is doing across the whole of Scripture can recognise a true verse being turned against its own purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit who came down at the Jordan now leads him into a desert — not away from God but deeper into the Father's purpose. And Luke is precise about the direction of travel: he goes in full of the Holy Spirit, and he is led by the Spirit. The Spirit does not shield him from the testing. The Spirit conducts him into it.

Forty days. The number is not decorative. Israel was forty years in the wilderness and failed there repeatedly; Moses was forty days on the mountain; Elijah walked forty days to Horeb. Jesus goes where Israel went, on Israel's terms, and does what Israel could not do.

And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry. Luke, the physician, understates it. Forty days without food takes a body to the edge of what it can survive, and the last sentence is almost comic in its restraint. The attack comes at the point of maximum physical weakness, which is where such attacks generally come.

But a difficulty sits in the very first line, and a thoughtful reader should not step over it. The Spirit of God leads Jesus to a place of temptation — yet James says plainly, God tempts no one (Jas. 1:13). Does God then lead his own Son into temptation? And if he does, what are we asking when we pray lead us not into temptation?

The knot loosens once you see that one Greek word (peirasmos) covers two things English keeps apart. It can mean a test — a trial meant to prove and strengthen, the way God tested Abraham on the mountain (Gen. 22) and tested Israel forty years to know what was in their heart (Deut. 8:2). And it can mean a temptation — an enticement whose whole aim is to make a person fall. The two can occupy the very same moment while pulling in opposite directions.

That is exactly what happens here. From the Father's side this is a test: the Spirit leads the Son into the wilderness to prove and display an obedience the world would need to see. From the devil's side the identical event is a temptation: every word out of his mouth is designed to make Jesus fall. God ordains the testing; Satan supplies the enticing. They are not the same act, though they share the same forty days, and God never does the second.

So take both truths home. When God leads you into hard testing he is never trying to make you sin (Jas. 1:13); he is proving a faith he fully intends to carry through, and he has bound himself to provide the way out (1 Cor. 10:13). And lead us not into temptation is not the fear that God might tempt us. It is the prayer of people who know their own weakness and ask the Father to keep the test from ever becoming a fall — the very thing the sinless Son did not need, and we do.

One more thing, before the attack begins. Jesus was tempted. Really tempted, by a real enemy, at real cost. Which settles a question that torments sensitive believers: being tempted is not sinning. The pull itself is not the fall. If it were, the Lord who was tempted as we are, yet without sin (Heb. 4:15) could not be our Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: The devil said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.' And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.

Two things are being attacked at once, and it takes a moment to see both.

The first is obvious: hunger. He has not eaten for forty days. And there is nothing wrong with bread — he will make it for five thousand people before this Gospel is much older, and he will hand it to his friends on the last night of his life. The temptation is not to a bad thing. It is to a good thing, taken by the wrong hand at the wrong moment.

The second is buried in the first word. If you are the Son of God — and the Greek construction here does not mean supposing you were. It is closer to since you are. The devil is not questioning the title he heard announced over the Jordan forty days earlier. He is proposing that a Son with a Father like that ought not to be this hungry, and that if the Father is not going to do something about it, the Son should.

That is the shape of the thing, and it is worth naming because it is the shape it usually takes. Temptation rarely opens by suggesting that God does not exist. It opens by suggesting that God is not looking after you, and that you had better see to yourself.

It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone. He answers with Deuteronomy 8:3, and the context is the whole point. Moses is explaining to Israel why God let them go hungry in the desert and then fed them with manna: that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD. Israel was hungry, grumbled, and demanded. Jesus is hungrier, and quotes the lesson Israel refused to learn — in the same desert, about the same God.

Notice what he does not do. He does not argue. He does not analyse the temptation or explain why it is wrong. He answers from Scripture and stops. And the Scripture he uses is not obscure; it is a verse any Jewish boy would have learned, from a book any Jewish boy would have memorised. His weapon is one that was available to every person in Israel and is available now.

The practical shape of this is worth having plainly. There will be a moment — perhaps this week — when a real need meets a wrong way of meeting it: money that could be had by a small dishonesty, comfort that could be had from a bottle or a screen, affection that could be had from someone else's spouse. The need is genuine. The hunger is not sinful. What is being offered is a way of feeding yourself that does not go through the Father's hand — and the question underneath it is always the same one: is he actually going to look after you, or had you better see to it?

verseByVerse.quote: And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him, 'To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second assault changes altitude. The devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. Luke does not say how — no mountain is mentioned, and the phrase in a moment of time suggests something other than an ordinary view. Every empire, every capital, every throne, laid out in an instant.

Then the offer, and it comes with a claim attached: To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will.

Is he lying? It matters, because if that sentence is simply false the temptation has no force at all, and Jesus does not treat it as false. He disputes the price, not the ownership.

The New Testament will not let us dismiss the claim. Jesus himself calls Satan the ruler of this world, three times in John's Gospel (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11). Paul calls him the god of this world (2 Cor. 4:4). John writes that the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19). Something real is being described.

But look at the word he uses: it has been delivered to me. Handed over. By whom? Not seized, not created, not owned outright — held on licence, from someone who can revoke it. The devil is a usurper administering territory that was never his, on a lease he did not write and cannot extend. His claim is true and it is far smaller than it sounds.

And here is what makes this the subtlest of the three. What he offers is not something Jesus should not want. The kingdoms of the world are exactly what the Father has already promised him: Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession (Ps. 2:8). Every empire in that flash of vision is going to be his. The devil is offering him his own inheritance.

What is being offered is a shortcut. The nations, without Gethsemane. The crown, without the cross. Everything the Father promised, delivered this afternoon, at a price that looks small compared with what it would otherwise cost.

That is the form this temptation almost always takes, and it is worth being concrete. It is rarely a straightforward invitation to do evil. It is the right thing by a wrong route: the ministry built on a manipulated figure, the marriage entered by a compromise, the promotion by the quiet betrayal of a colleague, the reconciliation bought by pretending an offence never happened. In each case the goal is good. The road is the problem — and the road is what Jesus was sent to walk.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is written, You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.

Deuteronomy 6:13, and again the setting matters. Moses is warning Israel about what will happen when they enter the land and find themselves suddenly comfortable — cities they did not build, wells they did not dig, vineyards they did not plant. The danger is not persecution; it is prosperity. And the commandment given for that moment is the one Jesus reaches for now.

Notice what he does with the devil's claim. He does not dispute it. He does not argue about who owns the kingdoms or on what terms. He goes straight past the whole question to the one word that decides it: worship.

Because that was always what was on the table. The offer was not really about territory. Strip away the vision and the glory and what remains is a transaction — a moment of bowing, in exchange for everything. And the little word Jesus adds by quoting is the one that shuts the door: him only.

Worship is not divisible. It is not the sort of thing that can be given to one and then, on a separate occasion, to another. A man who worships two things worships neither; he simply has one master he admits to and one he obeys. Jesus will say it in so many words later in this Gospel: no servant can serve two masters (16:13).

And that is why this is the hinge of all three temptations. The first was about bread, the third will be about proof, but underneath every one of them is the same question: who is God here? Every temptation any human being has ever faced comes down to that, however small the surface of it looks. Behind the second glass, the unopened message, the figure adjusted on the form, is a very quiet transfer of allegiance — a moment in which something other than God is trusted to deliver what only God can give.

Which means the test is not usually taken in the moment of crisis. It is taken beforehand, in the settled question of what a person actually worships when nothing is happening. Jesus came into that wilderness with the answer already fixed, and the devil found nothing in him to negotiate with.

Here is a test that can be run without much difficulty. Not what do I say I believe? but: what is the thing whose loss would make life feel unlivable? Whatever answers that question is being worshipped, whether or not it has ever been called by that name.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third assault moves to Jerusalem, and it comes with a Bible verse.

The pinnacle of the temple was probably the south-eastern corner of the platform, where the ground falls away sharply into the Kidron valley — a drop the Jewish historian Josephus said made you dizzy to look down. Below, the courts would have been full. This is not a private test. It is a proposal for a public one.

And now the devil changes his weapon. Twice Jesus has answered it is written. Very well: for it is written. He quotes Psalm 91:11-12 — a real psalm, a genuine promise, about the protection God gives to the one who dwells in the shelter of the Most High. Nothing about the words is invented.

Except that something has been left out, and it is the clause that would have ended the conversation.

The psalm reads: For he will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways. The devil quotes it as far as to guard you — and stops. In all your ways is gone. And your ways is precisely the point of the promise: God guards his people in the paths they walk in obedience to him. Jumping off a building to see whether he will catch you is not one of your ways. It is not a way at all.

That is worth having as a permanent piece of equipment, because it is how Scripture is nearly always misused. Not by inventing a verse — anyone can check an invented verse. By quoting a true one with the qualifying clause removed, or the occasion changed, or the covenant context stripped off. Every cult, every ruinous proof-text, every disastrous decision made on the strength of a verse lifted out of its paragraph has this shape. The words were accurate. The sentence they came from was not consulted.

Which is the strongest argument there is for knowing not merely verses but the shape of the whole book. The man who knows a hundred verses can be beaten by a hundred and one. The man who knows what God is doing in Scripture as a whole can hear a true verse being used against its own purpose and say so.

And notice what the temptation actually is. Not to doubt the promise, but to use it — to manufacture a crisis that obliges God to act, and call the manufacturing faith. It is the most religious of the three, and the only one that comes with chapter and verse.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is said, You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.

Deuteronomy 6:16, and Moses finishes the sentence with the place-name that explains it: as you tested him at Massah. Massah is the incident in Exodus 17. Israel is thirsty in the desert; there is no water; and instead of asking, they quarrel and demand, and the question they put is recorded because it is the question underneath all such demands: Is the LORD among us or not?

That is what testing God is. It is not asking him for something — Scripture is full of people asking, urgently and repeatedly, and God never once objects. It is making his response the condition of believing him. It is setting up a situation in which he must act in a specified way or be found wanting, and then calling the arrangement faith.

The line between trust and testing is fine to look at and absolute in practice. Trust says: he is good, and I will do what he has told me to do, and leave the outcome with him. Testing says: I will construct a circumstance that forces his hand, and I will read the result as a verdict on whether he loves me.

It is worth being concrete, because most people who do this have no idea that is what they are doing. It is the bargain made silently at two in the morning — if this scan comes back clear, I will know he is with me. It is the decision taken with no wisdom and no counsel, on the grounds that God will surely honour boldness. It is the resignation handed in without a plan, filed under stepping out in faith. And it is the terrible weight that settles when the scan is not clear, because a verdict was attached to it that God never agreed to.

He does not owe us a demonstration. That is not coldness; it is the only arrangement under which a relationship is possible at all. A God who could be summoned by staging the right circumstance would not be God, and a faith that needed him summoned would not be faith.

And there is a mercy in Jesus's refusal that is easy to miss. He could have jumped. The angels would have come; the promise was real. He declined to make his Father prove himself — and the reason he declined is that he did not need proving. He had heard the voice at the Jordan. He knew whose Son he was in the wilderness, hungry, with nothing whatever to show for it.

A reader with Matthew open will notice that the temptations come in a different order there — bread, temple, kingdoms in Matthew; bread, kingdoms, temple here. Neither writer is mistaken, because neither claims a stopwatch account. Matthew joins his scenes with then and again; Luke strings his with and, the loosest connective in the language. Matthew, who will close on a mountain with all authority given to the Son, saves the kingdoms for last. Luke, whose whole Gospel leans towards one city — who began in the temple and will end there (24:53) — saves Jerusalem for last. The order is a signpost, not a clock.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.

Two clauses, and both matter.

Every temptation. The arsenal was emptied. Whatever else the devil had, he used it, and none of it worked. That is worth stating plainly, because the wilderness is sometimes read as a warm-up. It was not. It was everything he had, brought against a man weak with hunger and forty days alone, and it failed completely.

Then: until an opportune time. Luke's word is kairos — not merely a later date but a suitable one, the right moment. The enemy withdraws, and he withdraws to wait.

Luke means this as a signal, and he will pick it up again exactly where he intends. The next time Satan appears by name in this Gospel is at the Supper: Then Satan entered into Judas (22:3). And in the garden, when they come for him with torches, Jesus tells them what hour it is: this is your hour, and the power of darkness (22:53). The wilderness was the opening exchange. The opportune time was Gethsemane and the cross — and there the temptations came back in almost their original shapes. Save yourself. Come down from the cross. If you are the Son of God.

So the victory here is real, and it is not final. Which is a fact about the Christian life as well, and it needs saying to anyone who has been surprised by it.

There is a particular discouragement that belongs to the believer who genuinely settled something — who fought a thing through, prayed it through, thought it was dealt with — and then finds it standing in the doorway again eighteen months later, looking exactly as it did. The conclusion that suggests itself is that the earlier victory was not real, or that nothing has changed, or that this will simply go on for ever.

The verse says something different. The enemy left because he had been beaten; and he came back because he had been beaten and had not stopped. A returning temptation is not evidence that the last resistance was fraudulent. It is evidence that the war is longer than the battle.

And notice the timing he chose, both then and later. Not while Jesus was strong, but at the end of forty days without food. Not in the middle of the ministry, but on the last night, in the dark, when his friends were asleep. The opportune time is a real category, and it is generally the hour of exhaustion. Which is a good reason to be more careful, not less, when you are tired — and no reason at all to conclude, when it comes, that you have gone backwards.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus returns from the wilderness “in the power of the Spirit” — the forty days have not depleted him but concentrated the anointing. He teaches through Galilee and is praised by everyone. Then he comes to Nazareth, where he grew up, and on the Sabbath stands to read.

He is handed the scroll of Isaiah and finds the place: Isaiah 61:1-2. “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor.” He reads it, rolls up the scroll, hands it back, and sits down. Every eye in the room is on him. And he says: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

The passage is a Jubilee text — the year of the Lord's favour is the fiftieth year of Leviticus 25, when debts were cancelled, slaves freed, and lost land returned. Jesus announces that the true Jubilee has arrived. And he stops mid-sentence: Isaiah goes on to “the day of vengeance of our God,” and Jesus does not read it. The favour has come; the reckoning waits for a coming still ahead.

The congregation's first response is admiration — they marvel at his gracious words and say “Is not this Joseph's son?” It is simultaneously flattering and dismissive: impressed by the local boy, unprepared for the claim. Jesus reads the room and pre-empts the demand he can see forming: “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, 'Physician, heal yourself.' What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here also.”

Then he does the thing that turns admiration into fury. He tells two stories from their own Scriptures: Elijah sent past every widow in Israel to a pagan widow in Sidon (1 Kings 17), and Elisha cleansing a Syrian general while Israel's lepers went uncleansed (2 Kings 5). In both, the prophet bypasses Israel and the blessing lands on an outsider.

The congregation hears it perfectly. The year of the Lord's favour is not automatically theirs; they could be the ones passed over. It is a challenge to every form of religious privilege, and the response of privilege threatened is exactly what one would expect. They drive him out of town to the brow of the hill, intending to throw him off. He passes through the midst of them and goes away — because the hour, and the place, and the manner of his death are not theirs to choose.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Isaiah text Jesus reads is a Jubilee text, and the Jubilee was Israel's built-in rehearsal of release: the trumpet, the cancelled debt, the freed slave, the restored land. Jesus announces that the ultimate Jubilee has arrived — not an economic reset but a cosmic one. The debt of sin cancelled, the captivity to Satan ended, the blind given sight, the oppressed set free.

This is why he can say “today.” Not soon, not when conditions improve, but today, in your hearing — and the “today” does not depend on the congregation's response. It depends on who has just sat down.

The rage at the Elijah and Elisha stories is the rage of religious privilege challenged. They wanted a Messiah for Israel who would bless Israel and defeat Israel's enemies, not one who would take the blessing to the enemies themselves.

Every generation of the church faces the same temptation: to want Jesus for itself, to treat the gospel as the property of those who already have it, and to be offended when grace reaches people who had been written off. The Nazareth synagogue is the permanent warning against a Christianity that has lost the scandal of grace.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” is the most decisive today in Luke's Gospel — and this Gospel is full of them: “unto you is born this day a Saviour” (2:11); “today salvation has come to this house” (19:9); “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43).

The gospel in Luke is always a present-tense announcement, never merely past-tense history or future-tense hope. The Scripture fulfilled in Jesus is not fulfilled in some spiritual realm remote from the present moment; it is fulfilled now, here, in the hearing of particular people in a particular room.

Jesus walking through the crowd that means to kill him (v. 30) is the first of several moments in Luke where he moves through danger untouched — not because violence is ineffective but because his hour has not come. His death must be the death he chooses, on the terms the Father has set.

And the scene is a warning about familiarity. Nazareth had thirty years of information about Jesus and was the one town where he could do almost nothing. The people who received him in this Gospel were, almost without exception, those who met him with no prior file: a centurion, a Samaritan, a woman with a bad name, a tax collector, a dying criminal.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went into the wilderness full of the Holy Spirit (v. 1). He comes out in the power of the Spirit. Forty days of hunger and assault have not depleted him. Something has been concentrated.

That is worth registering, because the usual assumption about hard seasons is that they take something out of a person and the best that can be hoped for is recovery. Luke reports the opposite. The testing did not drain the anointing; it proved it, and a proved thing carries weight that an untested thing does not.

And a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. Luke compresses here. Between the wilderness and Nazareth there is a period of ministry he does not narrate — John's Gospel fills in some of it, with the wedding at Cana and the first visit to Jerusalem — and Luke simply notes that word was spreading.

This matters for reading what comes next, because Jesus will shortly refer to things he did at Capernaum that Luke has not yet described (v. 23). Luke told us at the outset that he was writing an orderly account (1:3), and that word means arranged in a followable sequence, not clocked to the day. He is about to place the Nazareth visit at the head of the ministry because of what it explains, not because it was necessarily first.

And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.

Hold that last phrase against what happens fifteen verses later, when the congregation of his own village tries to throw him off a cliff. Luke has set the two side by side deliberately. The universal early approval is real — and it is worth almost nothing, because it has not yet been tested by anything he actually came to say.

That is a pattern worth knowing. A ministry, a message, or a man can be widely admired right up to the first moment of genuine confrontation, and the admiration will tell you nothing about what is underneath it. The crowds that praised him in Galilee were the same kind of crowds that would shout in Jerusalem three years later, and the second shout was not a change of mind. It was the first one, finally tested.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day.

Stay on that phrase, because five words are doing a great deal of work. As was his custom. This was his habit. Week after week, for something close to thirty years, the Son of God walked to a small building in an unremarkable village and sat through the service.

Consider what was on offer there. A synagogue in Nazareth in the 20s meant a handful of families, the same faces, an attendant, a set of scrolls, prayers everyone knew by heart, and a teaching ministry that on any given week was probably very ordinary indeed. Whatever he received in that room, it was not instruction he needed. He had more of the Spirit than every teacher in Galilee combined, and he could have explained the Scriptures to any of them.

He went anyway. Every week. Including, on this particular Sabbath, to a congregation that would try to kill him before the morning was over.

That is a quiet rebuke to a very common piece of modern reasoning — that a person who is not being fed, or who finds the preaching thin, or who has outgrown the place, is thereby excused. Jesus had better grounds for that argument than anyone who has ever used it, and he did not use it.

And he stood up to read. The custom was to stand for the reading of Scripture and sit to teach. Any competent adult male could be invited to read, and the reading from the Prophets followed a reading from the Law.

And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place. Luke's verb suggests searching until he located it. Whether the passage was the appointed reading for that day or one he sought out, he handled the scroll like a man who knew where things were in it — which, given the eighteen unrecorded years, he did.

He was handed the book he had inspired, in the village he had grown up in, and he found the sentence about himself.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me.

Isaiah 61, and Luke has been building towards it since the Jordan. The Spirit descended at the baptism, led into the wilderness, brought him back in power — and now the man on whom the Spirit rests reads out the passage about the man on whom the Spirit rests. Anointed is the verb behind Messiah and Christ. He is reading his own job description aloud.

And it is a job description. Every clause names something the following chapters will contain.

Good news to the poor. Luke's Gospel will be full of them: shepherds, a woman with two coins, a beggar at a gate, a tax collector who could not lift his eyes. Liberty to the captives. Recovering of sight to the blind. To set at liberty those who are oppressed.

Are these literal or spiritual? The answer is that the question is badly put, and Luke will not let it be answered either way alone. Actual blind men receive actual sight in this Gospel; actual poor people are actually fed. And the same Gospel says that the deepest poverty is a man who has stored up goods for himself and is not rich towards God, and that the worst blindness is in people whose eyes work perfectly. Both are meant. A Christianity that spiritualises every one of these clauses has stopped doing what Jesus did; a Christianity that keeps them all material has stopped saying what he said.

To proclaim the year of the Lord's favour. This is not a figure of speech. It is the Jubilee of Leviticus 25 — the fiftieth year, when the trumpet sounded, debts were cancelled, slaves walked free, and land sold off in hard times went back to the family that had lost it. Israel's own calendar contained a rehearsal of release, and he stands up in a village synagogue and says the real one has arrived.

Then notice where he stops. Isaiah's sentence does not end where Jesus ends it. The prophet wrote: to proclaim the year of the LORD's favour, and the day of vengeance of our God (Isa. 61:2). Jesus reads the first half, rolls up the scroll, hands it back, and sits down — breaking off in the middle of a line.

That is not carelessness. It is the most eloquent silence in the Gospel. The favour has come today; the vengeance has not. He came the first time with the trumpet of release, and the day of reckoning waits for a coming still ahead.

Everything in between — every year the world has had since that morning in Nazareth, including this one — is the unrolled length of that unread half-sentence. The trumpet has sounded. The debts are cancelled. The prison doors are standing open and the year of favour has not closed, and the one who stopped reading mid-verse is the one holding it open.

verseByVerse.quote: And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down.

Luke slows the film down. Three ordinary actions, described one at a time, and then a silence: the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him.

Sitting was the posture for teaching. So the room knows a sermon is coming, and they are waiting for it — the local boy, back from wherever he has been, about to expound the great Servant passage. There will have been a rustle, and then nothing.

Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.

That is the sermon. There may have been more — Luke says he began to say — but this is the whole of it in one line, and there is nothing else like it. Prophets said thus says the LORD. Scribes said Rabbi so-and-so taught. This man reads a seven-hundred-year-old prophecy about a Spirit-anointed liberator and says: that is about me, and it is happening now, in this room, while you are listening.

There are only three possible responses to a sentence like that, and being impressed is not one of them. Either the man is deluded, or he is lying, or the year of the Lord's favour has just begun in a village of four hundred people. The one thing that cannot be done with it is to admire the delivery — which is precisely what the congregation is about to attempt.

Today. The word is sēmeron, and it is one of Luke's. Unto you is born this day a Saviour (2:11). Today salvation has come to this house (19:9). Today you will be with me in Paradise (23:43). Something in Luke's Gospel refuses to let salvation be filed under history or postponed to the future. It keeps arriving in the present tense, at a particular address, on a particular afternoon.

And it is worth noticing what has to be true for that word to work. He does not say the Scripture will be fulfilled when the nation repents, or when the conditions are right, or when enough people believe. He says it is fulfilled in the hearing of a room that is about to reject him. The today does not depend on the response. It depends on who has just sat down.

verseByVerse.quote: And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, 'Is not this Joseph's son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, Is not this Joseph's son?

The compliment and the problem arrive in the same breath, and it takes a moment to see that the second sentence cancels the first.

They are impressed. Luke's word is that they marvelled — the same word he used of the neighbours after the shepherds came (2:18), and it means what it meant there. Wonder is not faith. It is what a person feels when something has been genuinely interesting and nothing has yet been decided.

Gracious words. The phrase can mean words full of grace, or simply words that were charming — and the ambiguity is probably deliberate on Luke's part. Either way they are appraising the performance. He has just announced that the Jubilee has arrived in their village, and the congregation is admiring his manner.

Then: Is not this Joseph's son?

The question is not hostile. It is the sound of a small community being pleasantly astonished by one of its own. They knew him at nine. They knew the family, the trade, the house, the brothers and sisters. They have watched him buy timber.

And that is exactly the difficulty. It is not open unbelief; it is a settled framework into which the claim will not fit. They do not disbelieve the sermon so much as find the preacher already accounted for. He has been categorised — filed under people we know — and there is no category above it.

Which is worth pressing, because it is the particular danger of everyone who has grown up near the things of God. Familiarity does not usually produce hostility. It produces a mild, pleasant, entirely unthreatened appreciation. The person who has heard the Christmas story every year since infancy has an account of Jesus in place before he ever hears a sermon — and the account is not wrong so much as too small, and it has the enormous advantage of never requiring anything.

There is a way of knowing about someone which is the biggest single obstacle to knowing them. Nazareth had thirty years of information about Jesus Christ, and it was the one town in Galilee where he could do almost nothing.

The people who received him in this Gospel were, almost without exception, people who met him with no prior file: a Roman officer, a Samaritan, a woman with a bad name, a tax collector up a tree, a criminal with six hours to live.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.' And he said, 'Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answers the question they have not asked out loud, and Luke lets us watch him read a room.

Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, Physician, heal yourself. The saying was a common one — look after your own before you go looking further afield. And he spells out what they mean by it: What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.

A reader tracking the narrative will stop here, because Luke has not told us about anything at Capernaum. That comes eight verses later. This is the clearest signal in the Gospel that Luke's orderly account (1:3) means arranged, not chronological — he has lifted the Nazareth visit out of its place in the sequence and set it at the head of the ministry, because it explains everything that follows: why Jesus is based at Capernaum and not at home, why the message goes to outsiders, and how it will end.

Matthew and Mark record a rejection at Nazareth much later (Matt. 13:54-58; Mark 6:1-6). Whether that is this visit told in its chronological place, or a second visit to a town that had not changed its mind, cannot be settled from the evidence — the details differ enough to allow either. What is certain is that Luke knew what he was doing when he put it first.

Now the demand itself, because it is more instructive than it looks. They want a miracle, and they want it on grounds of local loyalty. Not show us you are the Messiah but do for us what you did for them. The claim underneath is one of entitlement: we knew you first, so we have first call.

That is the request Jesus consistently refuses, and it is worth seeing why. A miracle performed to satisfy a hometown's sense of ownership would establish nothing except that he could be leveraged. He has just come from forty days of refusing exactly this — do something spectacular to prove yourself — and the wilderness is still on his clothes.

Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown.

He is not complaining. He is placing himself in a line, and the line is not a comfortable one. Israel's prophets were consistently honoured everywhere except where they came from, and consistently killed by the people who had the Scriptures. He knows what he is stepping into, says so at the start of his ministry, and goes on with it anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the two stories that turn admiration into a lynch mob, and it is important to see that Jesus chose them.

He could have made his point about prophets and hometowns and stopped. Instead he reaches for two episodes from Israel's own Scriptures, both about famous prophets, both about God going somewhere nobody expected.

There were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah… and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. A three-year famine, Israelite widows starving in every village — and the prophet is sent past all of them to a foreign woman in Sidon. Sidon, of all places: Jezebel's country, the homeland of the Baal worship Elijah was fighting.

And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian. Syria was the enemy. Naaman commanded the army that raided Israel's borders; the little servant girl who told him about the prophet was a slave his own troops had kidnapped. He was cleansed, and Israel's lepers were not.

Both stories are in their Bible. Neither is disputed. And put together they say something the congregation understands perfectly: the fact that the blessing is near you does not mean it is for you, and God has a settled habit of taking it past his own people to somebody they despise.

Note what makes this so much worse than an insult. He is not saying they are unworthy and Gentiles are worthy. He is saying that grace is grace — that it is not owed to anyone, and therefore cannot be claimed by anyone, and therefore may land wherever God pleases. The Nazareth congregation's rage is the exact rage of the elder brother in Luke 15, and of the workers hired at dawn. It is what religious people feel when they discover that the thing they thought they had earned is a gift.

So the test this passage sets is not difficult to state and is uncomfortable to answer. There is some category of person you have quietly written off — a nationality, a lifestyle, a political tribe, an individual with a name — for whom you would find it genuinely hard to be glad if God saved them tomorrow and left you exactly where you are.

Whoever came to mind is your Naaman. And Naaman is the one the story is about.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. But passing through their midst, he went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath.

All of them. Six verses ago the same room was speaking well of him. Nothing has happened in between except two Bible stories.

That is worth pausing on. The thing that turned a congregation into a mob was not a miracle withheld, or an insult, or a political provocation. It was the suggestion that God's grace is free — free enough to go to a Sidonian widow and a Syrian general and past the people who had the Scriptures. The gospel had been preached in Nazareth for about ninety seconds and the response was homicide.

And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff.

This is a Sabbath. These are worshippers. They have come from a service in which the Scriptures were read, and they are now marching a man to a precipice — and the men doing the marching have known him since he was a boy. Somewhere in that crowd are people who taught him, sold to him, employed him. Possibly his own relatives.

Luke does not say they intended a trial. There was no trial. This is a village losing its temper at a level that ends in a killing.

But passing through their midst, he went away.

Nine words, and Luke offers no explanation whatever. No miracle is described. He does not vanish, or strike anyone down, or call for angels — which, an hour's walk from where the devil had suggested exactly that, is worth noticing. He simply walks through the middle of them and leaves.

Whatever happened there, the reason it happened is the one Luke will give again and again: it was not the hour. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord — that is John's wording, but it is Luke's conviction (John 10:18). He cannot be killed early, or in the wrong place, or by the wrong hands, or for the wrong reason. His death is not something that will happen to him. It is something he has come to do, on a specified day, in a specified city, and a hillside in Galilee is not it.

So the first congregation Jesus preached to tried to murder him, and he walked away and kept preaching. That is the beginning of the ministry — and it is a fair warning to anyone who imagines that faithful preaching is chiefly a matter of being well received.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From Nazareth, which rejected him, Jesus goes to Capernaum, which will be the base of the Galilean ministry. Within what appears to be a single Sabbath he teaches with authority, casts out an unclean spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law, and at sunset heals a multitude brought to his door.

The contrast with Nazareth is complete. The hometown that had him from childhood loses him; the town that receives him gets a cascade of kingdom power — teaching, healing, and liberation.

The exorcism in the synagogue is Luke's first, and it raises a question that runs through the Gospel: what is the relation between the kingdom of God and the realm of demons? The demon's cry — “What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God” — is the first accurate confession of Christ in Luke, and it comes from a demon. The powers of darkness identify him before anyone in Galilee does, and their knowledge saves them nothing. The demons believe and shudder (Jas. 2:19); they do not trust and rest.

Jesus silences it and casts it out with four words. No ritual, no incantation, no procedure — which is exactly what a first-century reader would have found astonishing, since contemporary exorcists used elaborate techniques. Luke, the physician, adds that the man was left unharmed.

The healing of Simon's mother-in-law is narrated with the same economy: Jesus rebuked the fever, the same verb used of the demon, and it left her. The response is immediate — she rises and serves. That is the New Testament pattern: what is received is not kept. The restored woman becomes the one who provides.

The healings at sunset, when the Sabbath ended and the sick could lawfully be carried through the streets, are the kingdom in miniature: a whole town at one door, and Jesus laying his hands on every one of them, individually, into the night.

Then, at dawn, he leaves for a desolate place, and refuses the crowd's attempt to keep him: “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.” The healings are real and they are not the mission. He was sent to announce a kingdom, and he goes to the next town.
verseByVerse.theology:
The demon's address, “the Holy One of God,” appears elsewhere in the New Testament only at John 6:69, on Peter's lips. The irony is severe: the demon confesses what the disciples will grasp only gradually and the religious leaders will refuse. The spiritual world sees what the natural eye misses.

But knowledge of who Jesus is, without submission to who he is, is not faith. The demons have impeccable Christology and it does them no good whatever. Right doctrine held in terror is still a lost condition.

Jesus's withdrawal at daybreak to a desolate place, and his answer to the crowd who would have kept him, establishes the missionary imperative of the ministry. The word “must” (dei) appears again — the same divine necessity that took him to the temple at twelve, through the wilderness, and will take him to Jerusalem.

And this is the first mention in Luke of the phrase that will dominate the rest of the Gospel: the kingdom of God. It is not a place or a programme but God's rule breaking into a world in rebellion, in the person of the King — which is why its arrival looks like demons evicted, bodies mended, and the poor given news.
verseByVerse.examples:
The demon's terror — “Have you come to destroy us?” — is the correct reading of what the kingdom of God means for the powers of darkness. Wherever the kingdom comes, the dominion of darkness gives ground.

That is the cosmic dimension of every healing, every exorcism, every act of forgiveness in the Gospels. It is not merely a personal benefit to the recipient; it is territory changing hands. The church that prays for the sick, that names fear and guilt and lies for what they are, and that proclaims forgiveness in the name of Jesus, is doing in its own place what he did in Capernaum.

The crowds “would have kept him from leaving them” (v. 42). The wish to possess Jesus — to keep him local, to make him the property of one congregation or one tradition — is a permanent temptation of Christian communities, and it is always well meant. Jesus consistently refuses it.

He came not to be kept but to be followed. The congregation that asks how to keep Jesus to itself has asked very nearly the wrong question. The right one is how to follow him to the next town.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejected at home, he moves to Capernaum — a fishing town on the north shore of the lake, on the trade road, considerably larger than Nazareth and a good deal more mixed. It becomes his base for the whole Galilean ministry. The town that received him got him; the town that had him from childhood lost him.

And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.

The word is exousia, and it is the key to everything that follows in this chapter. It means the right to act, backed by the power to do it.

To feel the force of it you have to know what teaching normally sounded like there. A scribe taught by citation: Rabbi Hillel said this, Rabbi Shammai said that, and the weight of a teaching came from the chain of authorities behind it. Nobody expected originality; originality would have been a defect. The teacher's whole business was to transmit accurately what had been handed down.

Jesus does not do this. He quotes Scripture constantly — he has just quoted Deuteronomy three times in the desert — but he never props himself on a rabbi, and he will shortly be saying but I say to you in a way no scribe on earth would have dared. His word is not commentary on the tradition. It is the thing the tradition had been trying to transmit.

And notice what Luke does with the word next. In four verses the crowd will use it again about something else entirely: with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits (v. 36). The authority in the teaching and the authority over the demons are the same authority. Luke has deliberately put the sermon and the exorcism in the same paragraph so that nobody separates them.

Which is worth holding on to. What went out of his mouth in that synagogue is not a different order of thing from what went out of his mouth to the demon. The word that unmakes a demonic hold and the word that is read on a Sunday morning are one word — and the reason preaching is worth anything at all is that it carries it.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, 'Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first miracle Luke records in the public ministry is not a healing. It is a rescue.

And it happens in church. A man has sat in that synagogue, presumably for years, with the spirit of an unclean demon, and nobody knew — until the presence of Jesus made it impossible to stay hidden. Whatever else that says, it says that a religious setting is no proof of a clean one, and that the arrival of Christ does not create trouble so much as reveal it.

Here the plain question has to be faced, because a modern reader has no framework for any of this. What is a demon, and does this still happen?

Scripture gives less than curiosity would like and enough to go on. Demons are personal, created, spiritual beings in rebellion against God — angels who fell (2 Pet. 2:4; Jude 6). They are not equal and opposite to God; they are creatures, and Luke will shortly show one obeying a two-word command. They are not the explanation of ordinary sin, ordinary illness or ordinary sorrow: Luke, a physician, carefully distinguishes the demonised from the sick in the very next paragraph (v. 40-41). And they are real. The New Testament does not treat them as a first-century way of describing epilepsy.

Does it happen now? The honest answer is that Scripture never suggests the enemy has gone out of business, that missionaries in many parts of the world report encounters they cannot explain any other way, and that a person in the modern West is far likelier to be destroyed by respectable idolatry than by anything dramatic. Both errors are real: to see a demon behind every difficulty, and to have quietly stopped believing in the enemy at all. The second is much the commoner, and it suits him better.

Now what the demon says, because it is extraordinary. Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are — the Holy One of God.

That is the first accurate confession of Christ in Luke's Gospel, and it is made by a demon. Not by a disciple; the disciples have not been called yet. The powers of darkness identify him correctly before anybody in Galilee does, and their theology is impeccable.

And it saves them nothing. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe — and shudder (Jas. 2:19). Here is the proof in a sentence: right doctrine, held with terror, in a being that will be lost. Knowing who Jesus is and being willing to have him are two entirely different things, and this creature has the first and would die rather than have the second.

The shudder is the tell. Have you come to destroy us? He knows exactly what the arrival of this man means for him, and he is right.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, 'Be silent and come out of him!' And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. And they were all amazed and said to one another, 'What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!' And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus rebuked him, saying, Be silent and come out of him!

Two commands, and the first is as striking as the second.

Be silent. The demon has said nothing false. It called him the Holy One of God, which is precisely what he is, and it said so out loud in a crowded synagogue where the truth had been in short supply. And he shuts it up.

He will do it again eight verses later, and repeatedly through this Gospel. He will not accept testimony from unclean spirits, however accurate. Partly because the messenger discredits the message; partly because a public identification at this stage would force the ministry into the wrong shape too early. But mostly because truth spoken by an enemy in terror is not witness. Witness comes from people who have been rescued and love him — and by the end of Luke's second volume there will be thousands of them.

Come out of him. That is the whole exorcism. No ritual, no formula, no repetition, no objects, no name-calling, no contest. Jewish exorcists of the period used elaborate techniques and invoked greater powers; a first-century reader would have expected at minimum a lengthy procedure. Jesus uses four words and it is finished.

Then Luke, the physician, adds a detail nobody else does: having done him no harm. The demon threw the man down on its way out — a last spiteful act by a creature that has lost — and Luke checks the man over and reports that he was unhurt. It is the note of someone who cared what happened to the person and not only to the story.

The crowd's reaction is exactly right: What is this word? They do not ask what technique he used or where he trained. They ask about the word. They have grasped the connection Luke has been drawing since verse 32 — the authority in the teaching and the authority over the spirits are one thing.

Here is the beginning of the war, and here is how it goes. The strong man's house is entered by someone stronger, and there is no struggle in the doorway. Everything that holds a human being — the powers of darkness, and death itself — is under orders it did not choose to take, from a voice that made it. He speaks once, and what has held a man for years lets go and goes out, and the man sits up unharmed on the floor of a village synagogue. There has never been a rival. There has only ever been a King, and a rebellion that had not yet been told it was over.

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Out of the synagogue and straight into a house. The authority that silenced a demon in public now walks into somebody's kitchen.

Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever. Two small things in that sentence.

First, Simon. Luke has not told us who he is; the call of the fishermen comes in the next chapter. It is another mark of his arrangement rather than his chronology — and it fits, because Simon must already have known Jesus before the boat scene in chapter 5, or the story there makes no sense.

Second, the mother-in-law. Simon Peter was married. Paul mentions it in passing years later, noting that Cephas took his wife with him on his travels (1 Cor. 9:5). The fact is worth stating plainly and leaving there.

And Luke, the doctor, grades the fever: literally a great fever, which was a recognised medical classification in the ancient world. He is the only evangelist who does it. Mark says she had a fever; Luke says how bad it was.

And they appealed to him on her behalf. She did not ask. Somebody else did — a household asking on behalf of a woman too ill to ask for herself. That is worth having by anyone who has ever sat by a bed with nothing to offer but a request.

And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. The same verb as the demon: he rebuked it. Luke is not suggesting the fever was demonic; he is describing the same sovereign word applied to a different enemy. Sickness gets spoken to in the imperative.

Now the honest part, because a chapter of instant healings will be read by somebody who has prayed for years and buried the person anyway. Luke is not describing the normal experience of God's people, and he never says he is. Paul left a co-worker sick at Miletus (2 Tim. 4:20) and had a thorn he asked three times to have removed and did not. What these days in Capernaum show is not a policy but a person — what he is like, and what he will finally do, and what has already begun. Every fever he rebuked came back eventually and every person he healed later died. These are signs of the morning, not the noon.

And immediately she rose and began to serve them. No convalescence — the recovery is total. And her first act with a restored body is to feed the people in her house. That is the shape of the thing all through Luke: what is received is not kept. She got up and put the meal on.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. And demons also came out of many, crying, 'You are the Son of God!' But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the sun was setting. Luke gives the hour because it explains the crowd. The Sabbath ended at sundown, and carrying a burden — a sick relative on a mat — was work. So the whole town has been waiting, watching the light go, and the moment the sun is down the doors open all along the street.

Picture it. A single doorway in a fishing village, and a queue forming in the dark that stretches out of sight; families half-carrying people who have not been out of a house for years; the noise; and one man, who has already taught in the synagogue, fought a demon and healed a woman since dawn.

And he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them.

That is the sentence to stop at, and it is the reason this entry exists. He could have done it from the doorway. One word had emptied a man of a demon that morning; a word over a crowd would have been well within his power and would have taken about four seconds.

He touched them one at a time. All of them. Every single person in that queue got his hands, his eyes, his attention — and given the numbers, that means hours of it, going on into the night, with the next face and the next and the next.

Some of those he touched had not been touched by anybody for years. Leprosy, discharges, disfigurement, madness — the conditions in that street were exactly the conditions that made a person untouchable, and the ceremonial law was not a cruelty but it did leave people alone. He put his hands on every one of them.

That is not efficiency. It is not even, strictly, necessary. It is what he is like.

And the demons keep shouting, and he keeps silencing them — because they knew that he was the Christ. Luke gives the reason plainly. It is not that they were wrong; it is that they knew, and he would not be announced by them.

Here he is, then, at the end of the first day anyone recorded. The Son of God, who could have spoken once from a doorway and gone to bed, standing in a Galilean street after dark, putting his hands on one broken person after another until there was nobody left in the queue. He was not tired of them. He has never been tired of them. There is no one so far gone, so long untouched, or so far down the line that he works through the crowd and stops before he gets there.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, but he said to them, 'I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place.

After a night like that, the first thing he does is leave. Luke does not say here what he went to do; Mark, telling the same morning, says he went to pray (Mark 1:35). It is the pattern Luke has already established at the Jordan and will keep returning to — before the Twelve are chosen, before Peter's confession, on the mountain, in the garden.

Note when it happens. Not after a failure, not in a crisis, but the morning after the most spectacularly successful day of his ministry so far. The town is at his feet. That is the moment he walks out into the wilderness alone — which suggests that the hour of greatest danger is not the one that feels like it.

And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them. Luke's verb is strong: they tried to hold on to him. This is not hostility. It is Capernaum at its best — a town that has seen what he can do and does not want to lose it, and there is nothing wicked in wanting him to stay.

He goes anyway.

I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.

There is the must again — dei, the divine necessity that first appeared on the lips of a twelve-year-old in the temple (2:49) and will drive him all the way to Jerusalem. And notice what it is attached to. Not to healing. To preaching.

That is startling given the previous night, and it deserves saying plainly: the healings are real, and they are not the mission. He was sent to announce something, and the healings are the announcement made visible.

And here is the first mention in Luke of the phrase that will dominate the rest of the Gospel: the kingdom of God. It is not a place and it is not a programme. It is God's rule — his reign breaking into a world in rebellion, in the person of the King. Which is why its arrival looks like this: demons evicted, bodies mended, the poor given news, debts cancelled. Wherever he goes, the territory changes hands.

The desire to keep him is a permanent temptation of Christian communities, and it is always well-meant. A church that asks how to hold on to what God is doing among them has asked a natural question and very nearly the wrong one. He was not sent to be kept. He was sent to be followed — to the next town.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence closes the chapter, and Luke uses it to widen the frame.

And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.

A reader with an older translation may find Galilee here instead, and the difference is a genuine textual one worth a note. The manuscripts divide, and Judea is the harder reading — which is generally the stronger claim, since a copyist is far likelier to smooth a difficulty than to create one. Everything in this chapter has happened in Galilee, so Judea looks like a slip and would have invited correction. But Luke uses Judea elsewhere for the whole Jewish homeland rather than the southern province alone (1:5; 23:5), and on that usage there is no difficulty at all. He is saying that the preaching spread through the country of the Jews.

Which is the point of putting the sentence here. The chapter began with one man alone in a desert and ends with a preaching circuit across a nation. Between those two lines he has been offered the kingdoms of the world and refused them, been driven out of his own village, and emptied a street of its sick.

And note what he is recorded as doing at the end of it: preaching. Not consolidating Capernaum. Not building on the momentum of a spectacular night. Moving on, synagogue by synagogue, saying the same thing in the next town — which is exactly what he said in verse 43 he had been sent for.

It is also worth noticing where he preached. In the synagogues: the ordinary weekly gatherings of ordinary Jewish people, the same institution whose Nazareth branch had tried to kill him a fortnight earlier. He did not abandon the synagogue because a synagogue rejected him. He went to the next one.

The trumpet of the Jubilee had sounded in one village and been shouted down. So he took it to the rest of them — and he has never yet stopped taking it to the next town, or run out of patience with congregations that will not have him, or decided that a place has heard enough.

4.text: <sup>1</sup> And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness <sup>2</sup> for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup> The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.” <sup>4</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’” <sup>5</sup> And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, <sup>6</sup> and said to him, “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. <sup>7</sup> If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.” <sup>8</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>9</sup> And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, <sup>10</sup> for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ <sup>11</sup> and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>12</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>13</sup> And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time. <sup>14</sup> And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. <sup>15</sup> And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all. <sup>16</sup> And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. <sup>17</sup> And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written, <sup>18</sup> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, <sup>19</sup> to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.” <sup>20</sup> And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. <sup>21</sup> And he began to say to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” <sup>22</sup> And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, “Is not this Joseph's son?” <sup>23</sup> And he said to them, “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.” <sup>24</sup> And he said, “Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown. <sup>25</sup> But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, <sup>26</sup> and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. <sup>27</sup> And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.” <sup>28</sup> When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. <sup>29</sup> And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. <sup>30</sup> But passing through their midst, he went away. <sup>31</sup> And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, <sup>32</sup> and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority. <sup>33</sup> And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, <sup>34</sup> “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.” <sup>35</sup> But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent and come out of him!” And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. <sup>36</sup> And they were all amazed and said to one another, “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” <sup>37</sup> And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region. <sup>38</sup> And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. <sup>39</sup> And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them. <sup>40</sup> Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. <sup>41</sup> And demons also came out of many, crying, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. <sup>42</sup> And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, <sup>43</sup> but he said to them, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.” <sup>44</sup> And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.

5.title: Calling, Cleansing, and the New Wine
5.overview:
Chapter 5 gathers five scenes that together define what it means to encounter Jesus: a miraculous catch of fish that produces not pride but prostration; the cleansing of a man whose disease had made him untouchable; the healing of a paralytic whose friends refused to be stopped by a crowd; the call of a tax collector from his booth; and a dispute about fasting that opens into the deepest question of the chapter — whether the new thing Jesus is doing can be contained in the old structures of Judaism. The answer is no. New wine requires new wineskins. What Jesus brings is not a reform of the old system; it is something genuinely, radically new.

The call of the first disciples (vv. 1–11) is Luke's fullest account of how Peter, James, and John came to follow Jesus — fuller than the brief summaries in Matthew and Mark, because Luke wants to show not just the what but the why. They did not follow a charismatic teacher because he seemed promising. They followed because they had encountered something that simultaneously exposed their unworthiness and compelled their trust. Peter's “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” is the most honest response to the presence of holiness in the New Testament — the instinct that knows it cannot stand in the presence of what it has just encountered, and is answered not with departure but with the word: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.”

The chapter closes with a theological dispute about fasting (vv. 33–39) that turns out to be the interpretive key to everything that has come before. The Pharisees and John's disciples fast; Jesus's disciples do not. The question is not merely about religious practice; it is about eschatology. Jesus answers with the image of a wedding: the bridegroom is present. The time of mourning is over; the feast has begun. This is not the time for old wineskins; the new wine of the kingdom — the presence of the Son of God himself — cannot be contained in the structures designed for a world still waiting for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Jesus Calls the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The call of the first disciples is set on the shore of the Lake of Gennesaret, where Simon Peter and his partners James and John have fished all night and caught nothing. Jesus borrows Peter's boat as a floating pulpit, teaches the crowd from the water, and then tells Peter to put out into the deep and let down the nets.

The instruction is professionally absurd. Fishermen who have worked the prime hours of the night without result do not take advice on technique from a carpenter, in daylight, with the nets already cleaned. But Peter obeys — “at your word I will let down the nets” — and the catch is so large that both boats begin to sink.

The miracle is not primarily about fish. It is about the person who commanded them. Peter, who knows these waters better than almost anyone alive, has just watched something no expertise can produce, and his response is immediate: he falls at Jesus's knees and says “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.”

That is the language of Isaiah's vision (“Woe is me!
