It is a failure of self-knowledge so complete that the man is entirely sincere.

Which is more frightening, not less. A conscious fraud could stop. This man is doing his best.

Now the part that is routinely missed. Jesus does not say leave your brother's speck alone. He says: first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye. The speck is still to come out. The brother is still to be helped. What is being corrected is the order.

That matters, because this passage is used almost as often to avoid responsibility as to duck it — quoted to mean that nobody may ever say anything to anybody. Jesus assumes the opposite. Christians are meant to help each other see. He is telling you what qualifies you to do it.

And the qualification is not moral superiority; it is honest sight. A man who has faced his own worst and found mercy at the bottom of it is precisely the man who can be trusted with somebody else's failure, because he is no longer using it to feel better.

There is a practical test in it. Before speaking, ask what this conversation would cost you — and whether you are looking forward to it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sermon now shifts from conduct to cause, and the image is agricultural and inarguable.

No good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit. Nobody disputes this. You do not get figs off a thornbush. The fruit does not determine the tree; it reveals it.

That is the direction of the whole passage, and it is worth getting right, because this could be read as a demand to try harder — produce better fruit, or else — and it is the opposite. A tree does not decide what fruit to bear. It bears according to what it is. Which means the question this raises is not what should I be producing? but what am I?

Then the application, and it moves inward twice. First to the heart: the good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good. The word is thēsauros, a treasury — a store, the accumulated deposit. Whatever has been put in over the years is what comes out.

And then to the mouth: for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. Literally, out of the overflow. Speech is not what a person decides to say. It is what spills over when the container is full and no longer being watched.

Which makes this the most usable diagnostic Jesus ever gave, and it can be run on yourself this afternoon.

Not: what do I say when I am trying to make an impression? Anyone can manage that. But: what comes out when I am tired, when I am driving, when the phone call has gone badly, when I am among people I do not need to impress? What do I return to in conversation without meaning to? What is the tone of my speech about people who are not in the room?

That is the overflow, and Jesus says it is a straight readout of the treasury.

Two guards, though. He is not saying that a single bad word proves a bad heart; the language is about what a tree bears, which is a pattern over seasons, not one morning's crop. Every Christian says things they hate having said.

And he is not offering a project. You cannot improve the fruit by working on the fruit, and you cannot change your speech by monitoring your speech — that produces a careful hypocrite, which is where this sermon started. What has to change is the treasury, and only one person restocks it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–49 — Build Your House on the Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The sermon ends with two builders, two houses, and one storm — and everything hangs on a distinction that cannot be seen.

It is preceded by the question that makes the parable necessary: “Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and not do what I tell you?” Jesus does not doubt that they call him Lord, or suggest they are insincere; the doubled address is the language of warmth. The problem is that the word has become detached from its meaning. Kyrios means owner, master, the one whose word settles the matter — and to call a man Lord while deciding independently what to do with his instructions is a contradiction in terms.

The parable is not a contrast between a man who heard and a man who did not. Both come to Jesus. Both hear his words. Both build. From the road, on a fine day, there is nothing to choose between them.

The difference is entirely underground. The wise builder “dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock” — two verbs describing the least rewarding work in construction. Nobody admires a foundation. It takes the longest, produces nothing visible, and the man who skips it gets his house up first.

Then the flood, and Luke is precise: the same stream breaks against both houses. The storm is not sent to test one and spare the other. It is weather, and it comes to everyone — which rules out the reading in which the obedient are protected from trouble. Both are hit equally. What differs is what happens next.

“Immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.” There is no gradual subsidence and no chance to shore it up. A life built on nothing does not fail by inches.

The storm is unspecified, and the vagueness is the point: bereavement, illness, betrayal, the slow attrition of a faith that was never load-bearing, and finally the judgement. Something always comes.

And the rock is not a set of principles. Jesus has spent thirty verses saying things no one can live out by admiration, and he ends by describing a man who hears my words and does them. The digging is obedience, and what it reaches is him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The eschatological note — the house that falls, and “the ruin of that house was great” — places the sermon's ethics in the context of final judgement. This is not moralism; it is eschatology.

The commands of the sermon are not useful guidelines for a better life. They are the description of the life that will stand on the day when every life is tested — which is why the sermon cannot be domesticated into a programme of self-improvement. It describes a life that is only possible through the transformed heart the kingdom produces, which is exactly what the tree-and-fruit teaching has just said.

And it is why the question at v. 46 is not an attack on assurance. It is a question about the relationship between what a person says about Christ and what they do about what Christ says. Every command in this chapter is checkable, and not one of them can be kept by admiring it.

The rock, finally, is not the sermon. It is the one who preached it. To hear these words and do them is to build on Jesus himself, and he is what the digging reaches.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable of the two builders has been used in Christian preaching from the earliest centuries as the description of the difference between nominal and genuine faith. Both builders heard Jesus; both began to build; both appeared to be doing the same thing. The difference was invisible until the storm came.

This is Jesus's own warning against the self-deception that hears the word, feels its power, admires its truth, and then returns to a life built on other foundations. The church in every generation has members who have heard much and built little.

The wise builder “dug deep” — the effort of foundation-laying is not passive. It requires excavation, the removal of everything covering the rock, the work of getting down to what will hold. That is spiritual formation: not merely hearing but digging, through prayer and Scripture, through accountability, through obedience in small things, until the foundation is no longer mood and circumstance and social approval.

The digging is unglamorous and nobody sees it. The house is what people see. But the digging is what determines whether the house stands — and the way to start is not in general. Take one command from this chapter, with an actual name attached, and ask what it means this week.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do what I tell you?

Twenty words, and there is nowhere to stand while reading them.

Notice first what is not being questioned. He does not doubt that they call him Lord, and he does not suggest they are insincere in saying it. The doubling — Lord, Lord — is the language of warmth, even fervour; it is how you address someone you mean it about. The problem is not coldness.

The problem is that the word has become detached from its meaning. Kyrios means owner, master, the one whose word settles the matter. To call a man Lord and then decide independently what to do with his instructions is not a moral failure so much as a contradiction in terms. It is like calling someone your employer and never coming in.

And the question is put as a genuine question. He asks why. There is an answer, and every honest Christian knows roughly what it is: because the saying is warm and the doing is expensive; because the language of discipleship costs nothing and its substance costs everything; because it is entirely possible to love the person of Jesus in a general way and to have quietly arranged one's life so that nothing he said in this chapter applies.

Which is why the question comes exactly here. Read back over what he has just said. Love your enemies. Do good to those who hate you. Bless the man who curses you. Give and expect nothing back. Do not condemn. Take the log out of your own eye. Every one of those is checkable, and none of them can be done by admiring it.

So the verse is not an attack on assurance and it is not a demand for perfection. It is a question about the relationship between what a person says about Christ and what they do about what Christ says — and it is worth answering slowly, with one specific instruction in mind, rather than in general.

Take one. Any one of them from this chapter. Ask what it would mean this week, with an actual name attached.

That is the whole of what the next three verses are about, and it is the difference between two houses that look exactly alike.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sermon ends with two builders, and everything hangs on a distinction that cannot be seen.

Read the description carefully, because the usual telling gets it wrong. This is not a contrast between a man who heard Jesus and a man who did not. Both come to him. Both hear his words. Both build houses. From the road, on a fine day, there is nothing to choose between them.

The difference is entirely underground. He dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. Luke's phrase is two verbs — he dug, and he went deep — and it describes the least rewarding work in construction. Nobody admires a foundation. It takes the longest, costs real effort, produces nothing visible, and the man who skips it gets his house up first and has more of a house to show for the same season's work.

Then the flood. And notice how Luke describes it: the stream broke against that house — the same stream, against both houses. The storm is not sent to test one and spare the other. It is simply weather, and it comes to everyone.

That is worth saying plainly, because this parable is sometimes read as though the obedient are protected from trouble. They are not. Both houses are hit, equally, by the same water. What differs is what happens next.

Could not shake it, because it had been well built. And of the other: immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.

Luke's immediately is grim. There is no gradual subsidence, no chance to shore it up. The first serious pressure and it is over — and the wreckage is described as great, because a life built on nothing does not fail by inches.

The storm can be almost anything: bereavement, a diagnosis, a betrayal, the slow attrition of a faith that was never load-bearing, and finally the judgement. Jesus does not specify, and the vagueness is the point. Something always comes.

And here is the last thing the sermon says. The rock is not a set of principles. He has spent thirty verses saying things no one can live out by admiration, and he ends by describing a man who hears my words and does them. The digging is obedience, and what it reaches is him.

Both men heard the sermon. One of them built his life on the man who preached it.

<sup>17</sup> And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. <sup>19</sup> And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all. <sup>20</sup> And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. <sup>21</sup> “Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. <sup>22</sup> “Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! <sup>23</sup> Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets. <sup>24</sup> “But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. <sup>25</sup> “Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. <sup>26</sup> “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets. <sup>27</sup> “But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, <sup>28</sup> bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you. <sup>29</sup> To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. <sup>30</sup> Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back. <sup>31</sup> And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them. <sup>32</sup> “If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

7.title: Faith, Doubt, and the Extravagance of Grace
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is one of the richest chapters in Luke's Gospel — four scenes that together compose a portrait of the grace of God operating at the edges of what respectable religion thought was possible. A Roman soldier sends word to Jesus about his dying servant; a widow's dead son is raised in a small village; the imprisoned John the Baptist sends messengers to ask if Jesus is really the one; and a woman known as a sinner anoints Jesus's feet with her tears and her perfume at a Pharisee's dinner table. In every scene, the expected is reversed: the Gentile soldier has greater faith than anyone in Israel; the dead man walks; the greatest prophet struggles with doubt; and the sinner, not the Pharisee, demonstrates the love that flows from forgiven debt.

The chapter's theological centre is the exchange between Jesus and John's disciples (vv. 18–35). John's question — “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” — is the most honest expression of faith-under-pressure in the Gospels. The forerunner who announced the Coming One from the womb, who saw the Spirit descend at the Jordan, who proclaimed the axe at the root of the trees — is now in prison, and the Coming One is not doing what John expected. Jesus's answer is not an argument but a recital: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news preached to them. He is, in other words, doing exactly what Isaiah promised the Servant would do. Blessed is the one who is not offended by him — even when he does not do what you expected.

The sinful woman at Simon's house (vv. 36–50) is the chapter's most searching scene. She comes uninvited, she weeps, she wipes Jesus's feet with her hair, she anoints them with perfume. Simon, the Pharisee host, draws the obvious conclusion: if Jesus were really a prophet, he would know who was touching him, and he would not allow it. Jesus's response is the parable of the two debtors — one forgiven a small debt, one a large one; which loves more? And the answer overturns Simon's entire moral framework. The woman's extravagant love is not the cause of her forgiveness; it is the evidence of it. She loves much because she has been forgiven much. Simon's cool hospitality reveals that he considers himself forgiven little — which means he considers himself to owe little, which means he loves little.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Jesus Heals a Centurion's Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The centurion whose servant is sick is the first Gentile whose faith is commended in Luke's Gospel — and it is commended in the strongest possible terms: “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

He is a Roman military officer, commander of a hundred men, the local face of the occupying power in a garrison town. He has also built the local synagogue — an extraordinary act of generosity towards a community he was not part of, and towards a God who was not his. And Luke's first fact about him is that a dying slave was “highly valued by him,” which in a world that classified slaves as speaking tools tells you a great deal before the man opens his mouth.

The Jewish elders who come on his behalf argue from merit: “He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he built us our synagogue.” That is how human beings naturally think about who deserves help. The centurion contradicts every word of it.

“Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.” The elders said he was worthy; he says he is not, and uses a different word from theirs. Nothing he has done puts Jesus under any obligation.

Then the reasoning, and it is the most penetrating theology anyone has produced in the Gospel so far: “For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me.” Note the first phrase. Not a man with authority but a man under it. He knows exactly why his orders are obeyed — when he speaks, Rome speaks — and that such authority operates through words, at any distance the words can travel.

He applies the framework to Jesus and concludes that illness is in the same position as a legionary: under orders. He is right, and he worked it out from twenty years of army life.

This is the faith the church has lived on since the ascension. Nobody now gets Jesus under their roof in the way the centurion declined. What is available is exactly what he asked for and received: the word, spoken at a distance, by one whose authority is not limited by where his feet are.
verseByVerse.theology:
The centurion's analogy is more profound than it first appears. He is not merely saying that Jesus is like a commanding officer. He is recognising that authority over illness has the same character as authority in a chain of command — it operates through words, at a distance, on the basis of what stands behind the speaker.

He knows that a soldier who refuses his order is refusing the emperor whose authority he carries. He perceives that the illness Jesus commands is in the same position, and he is right. The authority Jesus exercises over creation is the authority of its Creator, and creation obeys its Creator.

Jesus's amazement — “he marvelled at him” — is one of only two places in the Gospels where Jesus is said to marvel; the other is at the unbelief of Nazareth (Mark 6:6). Faith where none was expected, and unbelief where all was.

How the eternal Son can be surprised is answered the way Luke answered it at 2:52: two whole natures in one person. According to his divine nature he knows all things and learns nothing; according to his human nature he genuinely encountered this man and was genuinely moved. The wonder was real. He was not acting.
verseByVerse.examples:
“I am not worthy to have you come under my roof” is the model of the humility that genuine faith produces. By every external measure this man is among the most impressive people in the narrative — authority, resources, a reputation for generosity — and he is the one who says he is not worthy. The elders say he is; he says he is not.

It is not false modesty. It is the accurate perception of a man who has understood who he is asking for help, and the awareness of that distance is precisely what Jesus names as great faith.

And there is a quieter thing worth taking from him. Everything remarkable he says about authority he learned at work, in the army, in the ordinary business of command — not from the prophets and not in a synagogue. The best theologian in Galilee that morning was a soldier, and what qualified him was his job.

The centurion never came in person and received everything he asked for. The word of Jesus is not constrained by geography, and the authority he trusted across the streets of Capernaum is the same one trusted across continents in every generation of the church's praying.

verseByVerse.quote: After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sermon ends and Luke turns immediately to a sickroom. He has told us what the kingdom requires; now he shows what the kingdom does.

And the first person the kingdom does it for is a Roman officer.

A centurion commanded a hundred men. He was the backbone of the Roman army — a career soldier, promoted on competence, the rank at which the empire actually worked. In Capernaum, a garrison town on a trade route, he was the local face of the occupying power. Whatever the Jewish population of that town felt about Rome, they felt it about him.

He is also, by the standards of the day, an owner of people. The word Luke uses is doulos, a slave — and that is the relationship the story turns on.

Who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him.

Stop at that last clause, because it is doing more than setting the scene. The Greek is entimos — held in honour, precious. It is not the vocabulary of a man protecting an asset.

And a first-century reader would have felt the strangeness of it. Roman law classified a slave as a speaking tool. The agricultural writers of the period discussed the disposal of worn-out slaves in the same paragraph as worn-out oxen. Nobody expected an officer to spend anything on a dying servant, and certainly not to go looking for a Jewish miracle-worker on his behalf.

So before the man has said a word, Luke has told us something about him. He is a person of considerable power who has not used it in the ordinary way — and the first evidence of his character is not his religion but how he treats somebody who could not have made him do anything.

That is not a small test, and it has not dated. What a person is really like shows most clearly in how they behave towards those who have no leverage over them at all: the junior member of staff, the cleaner, the elderly relative who will not remember, the customer who will never come back.

Everything else the centurion is about to say will be extraordinary. But the thing that opens the door is simply that he loved a slave, and Luke wants that on the record first.

verseByVerse.quote: When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, 'He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion does not go himself. He sends a delegation of Jewish elders — the leading men of the synagogue — to ask on his behalf.

That is not timidity. It is a man who understands exactly what he is and where he stands. A Gentile officer of the occupying army approaching a Jewish teacher directly would put that teacher in an impossible position in front of his own people. So he uses the one channel that costs Jesus nothing, and he evidently has friends enough among the elders to be able to.

And the elders make his case with real warmth: He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.

Note what that means. A Roman officer paid for a Jewish synagogue — the building in which the Scriptures were read and the God of Israel worshipped, in a town he was garrisoning. That is not a bribe or a public-relations exercise; it is an extraordinary act of respect towards a conquered people's God. Archaeologists at Capernaum have found a fourth-century synagogue built on an earlier basalt foundation, and it is entirely possible that the stones the centurion paid for are still there.

Now watch the argument the elders make, because the whole passage turns on it. Their word is worthy, and their evidence is a track record: he loves us, he built us something. It is a case built on merit — he has earned this.

That is exactly how human beings naturally think about who deserves help, and it is entirely reasonable, and the centurion is about to contradict every word of it.

Matthew tells this same story and has the centurion come to Jesus and speak directly, with no elders and no friends in sight (Matt. 8:5-13). A reader who notices will want to know which it was. The answer is that this is how people have always reported such things, then and now. We say a king signed a treaty when his envoy carried it, that a firm wrote to us when a clerk typed the letter; what a man does through those he authorises to speak for him is credited to the man.

Matthew, writing tightly, gives the centurion's own words and leaves out the machinery of how they travelled. Luke, who told us he had gone back to the eyewitnesses (1:3), keeps the machinery — and the extra detail sharpens Matthew's point rather than softening it. The man is so persuaded he has no standing before Jesus that he will not even present himself. He sends others to say he is not worthy to come.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, 'Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus went with them. Four words, and they are worth pausing on. No hesitation, no enquiry into the man's religion, no comment on the ethics of slaveholding or of Roman occupation. A Jewish teacher sets off towards a Gentile officer's house — which would render him ceremonially unclean — because a servant is dying.

And then, before he arrives, a second message comes down the road.

Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof.

The elders had said he is worthy. The centurion says I am not, and he uses a different word from theirs — theirs meant deserving on the strength of a record; his means adequate, of sufficient standing. He is not being modest about his achievements. He is saying that the categories the elders were using do not apply.

Which is the first genuinely theological sentence anyone in this Gospel has spoken about themselves, and it comes from a pagan soldier. He has understood something the men who built the case for him had not: that nothing he has done puts Jesus under any obligation, and that the distance between them is not measured in synagogues built.

Therefore I did not presume to come to you. The reasoning is consistent all the way down. He did not come in person, not out of caution but out of conviction — a man who believes he has no standing does not push to the front.

But say the word, and let my servant be healed.

And there it is. He asks for nothing except a sentence.

Take in how much is contained in that. He does not need Jesus in the room. He does not require a touch, a ritual, a visit, or a sight of the patient. He believes that this man can say something in one place and have it happen in another — and he believes it firmly enough to stop the healer on the road and tell him not to bother coming.

Which is precisely the faith the church has had to live on ever since. Nobody now gets Jesus under their roof in the way the centurion declined. What is available is exactly what he asked for and got: the word, spoken at a distance, by someone whose authority is not limited by where his feet are. Every prayer offered for somebody in another country rests on the thing this soldier worked out on a street in Capernaum.

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the centurion explains his reasoning, and it is the most penetrating piece of theology anyone has produced so far in this Gospel.

For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, Go, and he goes; and to another, Come, and he comes; and to my servant, Do this, and he does it.

Read the first phrase carefully, because it is the key and it is easily skipped. He does not say I am a man with authority. He says I am a man set under authority — and only then mentions the men beneath him.

That is the whole insight. The centurion knows perfectly well why his orders are obeyed, and it is not because he is personally impressive. It is because when he speaks, Rome speaks. The soldier who ignores him is not defying a man; he is defying the empire standing behind the man. His authority is real precisely because it is derived, and it operates entirely through words, at whatever distance the words can travel.

He applies that framework to Jesus, and the application is astonishing. If a centurion can say go in one street and have it done in another, because of who stands behind him — then this man, whatever stands behind him, need only say the word. Illness is in the same position as a soldier: it is under orders.

Notice what he has grasped, and who he has grasped it from. He is a professional in a chain of command, and it is his profession that taught him. He did not read it in the prophets. He worked it out from twenty years of army life and applied it to a man he had never met.

And he was right. The authority Jesus exercises over sickness is the authority of the one who made the body, and creation obeys its Maker as reliably as a legionary obeys Rome — more so.

There is something in that for anybody who has ever felt their ordinary working life to be spiritually irrelevant. The best theologian in Galilee that morning was a soldier, and what qualified him was his job.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, 'I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.' And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him.

Jesus is astonished. That is a remarkable sentence, and it should not be hurried past.

There are only two places in the Gospels where Jesus is said to marvel, and they are exact opposites. Here he marvels at a Gentile's faith. At Nazareth he marvelled at the unbelief of the people who had watched him grow up (Mark 6:6). He was surprised, both times, in the same direction — faith turning up where nobody expected it, and refused where everybody did.

How the eternal Son can be surprised is a question worth facing rather than dodging, and the answer is the one Luke gave at 2:52. In the one person of the Son there are two whole natures. According to his divine nature he knows everything and learns nothing. According to his human nature he genuinely encountered this man, on that road, and was genuinely moved by what he heard. The wonder is real. He was not acting.

Then the public verdict: I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.

He turns away from the messengers and says it to the crowd — which means it is not a private compliment but a deliberate lesson, delivered to a Jewish audience, comparing them unfavourably with a Roman officer. It is the same point that emptied the synagogue at Nazareth in fury (4:25-27), and here it is again in the seventh chapter.

And what exactly is the faith he commends? Not the man's generosity, though it was real. Not his humility, though it was accurate. What Jesus names as faith is his confidence that the word of Christ is sufficient — that nothing further is required, no presence, no procedure, no leverage.

And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well.

Luke reports it flatly and from the messengers' point of view. Nobody saw the healing happen. There was no moment, no gesture, no crowd. A man said something on a road, and in a house some distance away a dying slave stopped dying — and the only people who could testify to it walked in afterwards and found him up.

That is very often exactly how it looks from inside a Christian's life. The word goes out, and nothing visible happens where you are standing, and you come home and find that something has.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Jesus Raises a Widow's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The raising at Nain is one of the most tender scenes in Luke and one of the most deliberately crafted. Two crowds meet at the town gate: the crowd following Jesus, and a funeral coming out.

At the centre of the funeral is a widow carrying out her only son, and Luke underlines both facts because both are load-bearing. A woman's economic and legal standing ran through a man — father, then husband, then son. She has already buried the husband. She is now burying the son, and there is no fourth name on the list. This is not only the worst grief there is; it is destitution.

Nobody asks Jesus for anything. There is no centurion sending elders, no friends taking a roof apart. She has not prayed and does not know who he is. He simply arrives at the intersection of his journey and her grief.

“And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her.” Two things in that sentence. This is the first time Luke himself calls Jesus the Lord in his own narration — not a title on somebody's lips but the evangelist's own description, and he uses it in front of a coffin. And the verb for compassion is esplanchnisthē, a word for something involuntary and physical, felt in the gut. It is the word used of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20) and the Samaritan seeing the man in the ditch (10:33) — and it is the word Zechariah used of God himself, the tender mercy by which the sunrise would visit us (1:78).

He touches the bier, which under the law makes a man unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11) — and, as with the leper in chapter 5, the traffic runs the wrong way. Then four words to a corpse: “Young man, I say to you, arise.”

Luke, the physician, records the result in two clinical stages: he sat up, and he began to speak. And then the sentence that is the point of the whole scene — “and Jesus gave him to his mother” — which is word for word what is said of Elijah at Zarephath (1 Kgs. 17:23).

The crowd's response is fear, and then two acclamations: “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” Both are true, and both fall short. Elijah prayed three times and God raised the boy; this man gave an order.
verseByVerse.theology:
The raising of the widow's son is a sign of the kingdom with both an immediate and an ultimate reference. Immediately it is the reversal of the most final of all reversals, accomplished by the one who will himself die and rise. Ultimately it points forward to the general resurrection, when the dead will rise at the voice of the Son of God (John 5:25-29; 1 Thess. 4:16).

Jesus does not raise this young man permanently; he will die again. What the miracle demonstrates is not the abolition of biological death but authority over death as a power — the authority that reaches its final expression in Jesus's own resurrection.

The echo of Elijah is deliberate, and Luke has been preparing it since 4:26, when Jesus preached about the widow of Zarephath at Nazareth and the town tried to kill him. Both prophets meet a widow whose only son has died; both speak; both give the son back to his mother in the same words.

The echo establishes Jesus as the fulfilment of the prophetic tradition rather than its continuation. Where Elijah stretched himself over the boy and cried out to the LORD three times, Jesus simply speaks. The authority has been concentrated. The prophet gives way to the Lord of the prophets.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's compassion for the widow, unprompted and unsolicited, is the model of the grace that sees before it is asked. She did not pray. She did not seek him out. She was lost in her grief, and he saw her.

He was not the only person at that gate who could see her — the whole town was there. He was the one who looked at the woman rather than the coffin. The posture of compassion begins with seeing, and the Christian who prays to notice what God notices is asking to become like the man who walked into Nain and saw a widow in a crowd.

“Do not weep” — said to a woman at her only son's funeral — would be an outrage from anybody else. It is not a denial of her grief and not a rebuke; he wept himself at a friend's tomb. He says it because he is about to remove the reason.

That is the only circumstance in which the sentence is not cruelty, and it is the circumstance he was standing in. Nobody else may say it. He may — and one day, to everybody, he will (Rev. 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two processions meet at a gate, and Luke has staged it deliberately.

Coming up the road is Jesus, with his disciples and a great crowd — a company full of the energy of what happened in Capernaum, on their way into town.

Coming out of the town is a funeral, with a considerable crowd of its own. In that culture the whole village turned out; the body would have been carried on an open bier, wrapped, with wailing women and pipers, moving towards the burial ground outside the walls, because burial had to happen the same day.

The two crowds meet in the gateway, and one of them is going to have to give way.

Then Luke does something precise. He describes the dead man in three steps, and each one closes a door.

A man who had died. That is the first. Not sick, not sinking. Past every remedy anyone in either crowd could offer.

The only son of his mother. That is the second. Not one of several. The only one.

And she was a widow. That is the third, and it is the one that finishes her.

Take in what those three facts meant in the first century, because our world softens them. A woman had no independent economic standing. Her security ran through a man — first her father, then her husband, then her son. This woman has already buried the husband. She is now burying the son. There is no fourth name on the list.

So she is not merely a mother in the worst grief there is. She is, from that morning, destitute — with no income, no legal advocate, and no prospect of either, walking behind the body of the last person who stood between her and the road.

And notice what is completely absent from this story. Nobody asks Jesus for anything. There is no centurion sending elders, no friends taking a roof apart, no leper on his face in the road. Nobody in that funeral has heard of him or is looking for him. She has not prayed. She is, as far as Luke tells us, entirely lost in what has happened to her.

He simply arrives at the intersection of his journey and her grief.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, 'Do not weep.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the Lord saw her.

Luke has changed something, and a first-century reader would have caught it. Up to this point he has narrated Jesus by name. Here, for the first time in his Gospel, Luke himself calls him the Lord — not as a title on somebody's lips but as his own description of who this is. He does it at the gate of Nain, in front of a coffin.

He saw her. There were two crowds and a body and a great deal of noise, and what he saw was the woman.

She was not the loudest thing at that gate. She was a middle-aged woman walking behind a bier among a crowd of mourners, and every person there had come for the son. He looked at her.

He had compassion on her. The verb is esplanchnisthē, from the word for the inward organs — the Greeks located the strongest feelings in the gut, and this is a word for something involuntary and physical. It is the same word used of the father catching sight of the prodigal on the road (15:20), and of the Samaritan seeing the man in the ditch (10:33). It is not a decision to be kind. It is what happened inside him when he saw her.

And it is the exact word Zechariah had reached for about God himself — the tender mercy of our God, the bowels of mercy, by which the sunrise would visit us (1:78). The thing the old priest sang about in the abstract is now standing in a gateway, looking at a widow.

And said to her, Do not weep.

Those three words would be an outrage from anybody else. Said at a graveside to a woman who has lost her only child, do not weep is the sort of thing that makes people leave the church.

He is not telling her that grief is inappropriate; he does not say that anywhere, and he wept himself at a friend's tomb. He is not offering perspective, or reminding her of the resurrection at the last day, or suggesting she is taking it badly.

He is telling her to stop because he is about to remove the reason. It is the only circumstance in which the sentence is not cruelty, and it is the circumstance he is standing in.

Nobody else may say it. He may — and one day, to everybody, he will (Rev. 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, 'Young man, I say to you, arise.' And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still.

Two things happen in that sentence, and both matter.

He touched the bier. Under the law, contact with a corpse or with what carried it made a man unclean for seven days and required the ritual of the red heifer to undo (Num. 19:11-13). This is not a technicality; it is one of the strongest defilements in the Mosaic code, and everyone in both crowds knew it. A rabbi did not go near a funeral bier.

He put his hand on it — and, exactly as with the leper two chapters earlier, the traffic runs the wrong way. Death does not contaminate him. Life goes the other direction.

Then: the bearers stood still. The procession stops. Nobody has been told to stop; the men carrying the body simply halt, because a stranger has laid a hand on it and something in the moment has changed. For a few seconds, at the gate of a Galilean town, a funeral is standing motionless in the road.

And he said, Young man, I say to you, arise.

He speaks to a dead man, in the second person, by name of address. There is no prayer here — and that is worth setting beside the obvious parallel. Elijah, faced with a widow of Zarephath and her dead son, stretched himself over the boy three times and cried out to the LORD, and God gave the child back (1 Kgs. 17:17-24). Elisha did much the same for the Shunammite's son. The prophets prayed, and God raised.

Jesus gives an instruction.

And the dead man sat up and began to speak. Luke, the physician, records it in two clinical stages: he sat up; he started talking. Whatever the young man said, Luke does not tell us, and there is a restraint in that which is worth noticing — a later writer would not have resisted supplying a report from the other side.

And Jesus gave him to his mother.

Five words, and they are the point of the whole scene. Not and the crowd was amazed, not and the young man followed him. He handed the boy back to the woman he had looked at in the gateway.

They are also, word for word, what is said of Elijah at the end of the Zarephath story: and he gave him to his mother (1 Kgs. 17:23). Luke knew exactly what he was quoting. The prophet prayed three times and God raised the boy. Here the Lord of the prophets says four words, and hands a son back to his mother, and walks on into the town.

verseByVerse.quote: Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, 'A great prophet has arisen among us!' and 'God has visited his people!' And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear seized them all, and they glorified God.

Fear first. It is Luke's consistent report of what the presence of God does to people — the shepherds in the field, the fishermen in the boat, the crowd after the paralytic — and it is not a defect in them. Something has happened at that gate which does not belong in the ordinary world, and the correct response is not delight but awe.

Then two acclamations, and Luke records them as two separate sayings going round the crowd.

A great prophet has arisen among us! They are entirely right, and they are working from the obvious precedent. A prophet, a widow, a dead only son, a boy given back to his mother — anybody who knew 1 Kings 17 would reach for Elijah, and they did. It is the correct identification.

And it is not enough. Elijah prayed and God raised the boy; this man gave an order. The crowd has recognised the category and missed that the category has been exceeded — which is exactly what Luke has been doing since chapter 4, when Jesus preached about Elijah and Elisha at Nazareth and the town tried to kill him for it.

God has visited his people!

This one is larger than the crowd knows. The verb is the one Zechariah used in the Benedictus — he has visited and redeemed his people (1:68) — the word for God coming to see about his people with intent to act, the word from the burning bush. It is the language of the exodus.

They mean: God has taken notice of us again after all these years. What is actually true is that God has arrived in person and is walking through their gate — and the sentence they are saying is more accurate than they can possibly intend.

That is worth holding on to, because it describes most of what happens when God works among ordinary people. The crowd's theology was incomplete and their instinct was sound. They knew they had seen God do something; they had not yet grasped who had done it. Nobody in this Gospel arrives at a full understanding of Jesus in one afternoon, and Luke does not despise the partial recognition. He records it, and moves the story on.

And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country. Which is how the next paragraph begins — because the news reached a cell.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–35 — Messengers from John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John is in prison — Herod arrested him for confronting the tetrarch's marriage (3:19-20) — and the imprisonment has raised the question that was always implicit in his ministry. He sends two disciples with it: “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?”

Take in who is asking. The man who leapt in the womb at Christ's approach (1:41), who saw the heavens open and the Spirit descend, who said “Behold, the Lamb of God” — this man, in a cell, in the dark, wondering whether he had been wrong. If he could come to the edge of that question, the presence of doubt is not proof that a faith was never real. It is very often the mark of a real faith under a real weight.

Jesus's answer is neither a rebuke nor a reassurance but a demonstration. First he works, in that very hour, in front of the messengers. Then: “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them.”

The list is a mosaic of Isaiah — 26:19, 29:18, 35:5-6, 61:1 — the texts describing what it will look like when God finally comes to save. John knew every one by heart. Jesus is answering doubt not with an argument but with evidence, and the evidence is the Scriptures John built his life on, now enacted in front of his own men.

“And blessed is the one who is not offended by me” is a gentle warning that names John's actual difficulty without embarrassing him. He had announced an axe at the root and a winnowing fork (3:9, 17); what he is hearing about is healings and dinner parties. Everything promised is coming. Not everything is coming yet.

After the messengers leave — and only after — Jesus tells the crowd what he thinks of John: not a reed shaken by the wind, not a man in soft clothing, but a prophet, and more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1. “Among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

The section ends with the children in the marketplace. John came fasting and they said he had a demon; the Son of Man came eating and they called him a glutton. The objections were mutually exclusive, which proves the objections were never the reason.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's doubt from prison is the New Testament's most honest portrait of faith under pressure, and it is treated with complete respect. Jesus does not rebuke him, question his faith, or withdraw the commendation he is about to give. He answers the question with careful evidence.

That is the pastoral heart of the passage. Genuine doubt, honestly expressed, receives a genuine answer. A Christian tradition that treats doubt as a mark of spiritual failure has missed the model of Jesus himself. Honest wrestling with “is it really true?” is not the absence of faith; it is faith pushed to its limit by circumstance and still asking — and asking the right person.

The saying about the least in the kingdom is not a demotion of John but an elevation of the kingdom. It concerns position in redemptive history, not personal holiness or usefulness. John stood at the threshold: he announced the Lamb and did not live to see the Lamb slain, or raised, or the Spirit poured out.

The least believer in the kingdom has what John did not yet have — an accomplished redemption, a finished sacrifice, and the indwelling Spirit. Not because that believer is more faithful, but because he lives on the other side of the event John was pointing at.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's question is the question of every sincere believer facing a crisis of expectation: I believed this was true; this is not what I expected; am I wrong? And the answer Jesus gives is not “of course you are right, do not worry.” It is “look at the evidence.”

When faith is under pressure the antidote is not reassurance but the careful examination of what has actually happened — the Scriptures, the cross, the empty tomb, the testimony of those who met the risen Christ. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it is a step towards evidence that has been examined.

Notice too what John did with his doubt. He did not sit in the dark nursing it, and he did not broadcast it. He sent it to Jesus. That is the one move available to a man in a cell, and it is the right one.

And the parable of the children diagnoses a condition that is not confined to Pharisees. There is a way of engaging with the things of God in which one is always, sincerely, weighing an objection — the preaching is too demanding, or too soft; that Christian is a hypocrite, and that one a fanatic. Every objection may be individually reasonable. What gives the game away is that the seat is never vacated. The test is not whether you have a criticism, but whether anything has ever succeeded in getting you up.

verseByVerse.quote: The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, 'Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?' And when the men had come to him, they said, 'John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples of John reported all these things to him. All these things: a centurion's servant healed at a word, a dead man sitting up at a town gate. And John is in prison.

Luke has already told us why (3:19-20). He confronted Herod Antipas about his marriage, and Herod locked him up — in the fortress of Machaerus, according to Josephus, on the far side of the Dead Sea. He has been there for months. He will not come out.

And he sends two men to ask a question.

Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?

Read that slowly and take in who is asking. This is the man who leapt in his mother's womb at the sound of Mary's voice (1:41). Who was filled with the Spirit before he was born. Who stood in the Jordan and saw the heavens open and the Spirit come down like a dove. Who said, of this very man, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29).

That man is now asking whether he got it wrong.

Several things may be going on, and it is honest to say we cannot be certain which. He may be asking for his disciples' sake rather than his own. He may be struggling with the shape of it — he had announced someone with an axe at the root and a winnowing fork in his hand (3:9, 17), and what he is hearing about is healings and dinner parties and no fire at all. Or he may simply be in the darkness that a cell and a death sentence can bring on anybody.

Stay with it a moment longer, because there is more comfort here than a first reading gives.

If this man — the greatest born of women, by Christ's own verdict three verses later — could come to the edge of or shall we look for another?, then the presence of doubt is not proof that a faith was never real. It is very often the mark of a real faith under a real weight.

And notice what he does with it. He does not sit in the dark nursing it, and he does not announce it to the world. He sends it to Jesus. That is the one move available to a man in a cell, and it is the right one.

Luke tells the story twice over — John sends, and then the men arrive and repeat it word for word. He is making sure nobody misses the question.

verseByVerse.quote: In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight.

Before Jesus answers a word, he works — and Luke tells us it happened in that hour, while John's two messengers were standing there watching.

That is the shape of the answer, and it comes before the words. The men were sent to ask a question about identity. What they are given first is an afternoon.

Luke, the physician, distinguishes the categories carefully, as he does throughout: diseases — chronic conditions; plagues — literally scourges, the word for a whip, used of afflictions that lash a body; evil spirits — a separate category again, not collapsed into the medical ones; and then the blind, singled out and given their own clause.

The blind are singled out because they are about to matter. Of everything in the list Jesus is about to send back to the cell, sight to the blind is the one Isaiah repeats most often, and it is the one thing no first-century physician could counterfeit. Luke uses an unusual word for it here — he bestowed sight, granted it as a gift.

And there is something worth noticing about the method, because it is the same method Jesus used at the temptation and will use at the empty tomb. He does not defend himself by assertion. He does the thing, and lets the doing be the evidence.

A man in a prison cell has asked whether the whole of his life's work was pointed at the right person. The reply is not going to be trust me. It is going to be a list of things his own messengers saw with their own eyes that afternoon — checkable, specific, and matching a text John had known since boyhood.

That is how Christ handles honest doubt, and it has not changed. He does not scold it, and he does not ask for a leap in the dark. He points at what has actually happened.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, 'Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go and tell John what you have seen and heard.

Not tell John I am the Messiah. Not a rebuke, not a reassurance, not a word about how disappointing the question was. Jesus sends back a list of observable facts and lets John do the arithmetic.

And the list is not a list of impressive works. It is a quotation.

The blind receive their sight — Isaiah 35:5. The lame walk — Isaiah 35:6. The deaf hear — Isaiah 35:5 again, and 29:18. The dead are raised up — Isaiah 26:19. The poor have good news preached to them — Isaiah 61:1, the very text Jesus had read out at Nazareth.

These are the passages describing what it will look like when God finally comes to save his people. John knew every one of them; he had built his ministry on the chapter that opens prepare the way of the LORD. Jesus is saying: you know what the prophets said would happen when he came. Ask your messengers what they watched this afternoon.

The only item in the list that is not from Isaiah is lepers are cleansed, and its inclusion is its own argument: nobody had ever seen that.

Then the beatitude, and it is unmistakably meant for the man in the cell: blessed is the one who is not offended by me.

The verb is skandalizō — to be tripped up, to stumble over something in the road. It is a gentle word and an honest one, and it names John's actual difficulty without embarrassing him. There is nothing in the list about an axe, or a winnowing fork, or fire, or a prison door opening. Everything John was promised is coming. Not everything is coming yet.

Which is exactly where a great many believers stumble, and the sentence is worth taking personally. The difficulty is rarely that Christ has failed to do what he said. It is that he has not done it in the order we assumed, or on the timetable we needed, or in the shape our expectations had already built for him.

He does not promise John an explanation. He offers him the evidence, and a beatitude for the man who can hold on when the answer is smaller than the question — and John, so far as the record goes, held on, and died in that cell, and was right all along.

verseByVerse.quote: When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When John's messengers had gone. The timing is deliberate and it is one of the kindest details in the Gospel. Jesus waits until the two men are out of earshot, and only then tells the crowd what he thinks of John.

He could have said it in front of them and sent the compliment back with the answer. He did not. John was to be given the evidence, not a testimonial — and the crowd was to be told the truth about a man who was not there to hear it and could not be embarrassed by it.

Then three rhetorical questions, each one demolishing something the crowd might have gone out to see.

A reed shaken by the wind? The Jordan valley is full of them — tall, hollow, bending whichever way the air moves. It is a picture of a man with no fixed convictions, who goes with whatever is blowing. There may be an edge in it, too: Herod Antipas had minted coins stamped with a reed, and it was Herod who had John in a cell.

A man dressed in soft clothing? John wore camel's hair and a leather belt. And Jesus adds the contrast himself: those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts — which is precisely where John is at that moment, though not as a guest.

The crowds went into a desert to hear a man who could not be bribed, bent, or bought a better coat. That is what took them out there, and it is worth asking what takes people out now.

A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.

The first two questions expected the answer no. This one expects yes — and then gets more than it asked for.

What is more than a prophet? A prophet speaks of what is coming. John was the only one who could point with a finger and say that man. Every other prophet in Israel's history described a horizon; John stood at the edge of it and named the person walking over.

And there is a second thing that made him more, which the next verse will say outright: the prophets foretold the Messiah, and John was himself foretold.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is he of whom it is written, Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.

The quotation is Malachi 3:1, and there is something in it that ought to stop a careful reader.

In Malachi, God is speaking about himself. The line reads: Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me — the messenger goes ahead of the LORD, who is coming to his temple.

Jesus quotes it with the pronouns changed. Before your face. Your way before you. The one whose way is being prepared, in Malachi's own words, is the God of Israel — and Jesus applies the text to himself and hands it to a crowd without further comment.

I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John.

Take the measure of that. Not greater than the prophets — greater than anybody. Abraham, Moses, David, Elijah, Isaiah: none of them occupied a higher place in the purposes of God than the man currently sitting in Herod's cell wondering whether he had been wrong.

And then the sentence that has puzzled readers for two thousand years.

Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.

It is not a demotion of John, and it is not about personal holiness or usefulness or reward. It is about position in redemptive history — which side of the cross a person stands on.

John stood at the threshold. He announced the Lamb and did not live to see the Lamb slain, or raised, or the Spirit poured out. He knew the promise and died before the payment. Everything he had was anticipation.

The least believer in the kingdom has what John did not yet have: an accomplished redemption, a finished sacrifice, the forgiveness of sins actually purchased, and the Holy Spirit indwelling. Not because that believer is more faithful — almost certainly he is not — but because he lives on the other side of the event John was pointing at.

Which is worth sitting with rather than skimming. Whatever the least Christian possesses, it is something the greatest man ever born of a woman looked at from a distance and did not live to hold. The temptation is always to measure ourselves against John's heroism and despair. Measure instead what you have been given.

verseByVerse.quote: (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke drops in a parenthesis, and it is one of the most important sentences in his Gospel.

When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John.

The phrase is striking: they declared God just — literally, they justified God. That is not something people usually do. To justify God is to say that he is in the right about you: that his verdict on your life is accurate, that his summons to repent was warranted, that when he says you need washing he is not exaggerating.

And it is the tax collectors who did it. The men whose profession was theft under licence heard John, agreed with God about themselves, and went into the water.

But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.

The men who knew the Scriptures best did not. And Luke's phrasing is very exact — they rejected the purpose of God for themselves. They did not deny that God had purposes; they were entirely orthodox about that. They declined to be included.

Now a reader who has been taught the sovereignty of God will feel a difficulty here, and it is worth facing rather than stepping round. Can the purpose of God be rejected? Does this verse make his plan subject to a committee vote in Jerusalem?

It does not, and Luke of all writers is the last person who thought so — this is the man who will say that Herod and Pilate and the Gentiles gathered to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28). The eternal purpose of God went forward exactly as decreed, and these men were not consulted.

What they rejected was the purpose of God for themselves: the good and gracious intention held out to them in John's preaching, the invitation to repent and be washed. They were offered it, and they would not have it, and the refusal was entirely their own — and God's plan was not delayed by a single day.

Which is where the mystery sits in Scripture and where it is left. What is not mysterious is who did which. The men with nothing to protect said God was right about them. The men with a reputation to defend refused the water, and Luke records it in brackets, as though the thing were almost too sad to put in the main sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: 'To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like?

Jesus reaches for a scene everybody watching would have recognised: children in a village square, playing at the two great public events of adult life.

We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.

The two games are weddings and funerals. One group of children pipes, and the others are supposed to get up and dance. So they change the game and sing a lament, and the others are supposed to beat their breasts and wail. And whichever game is proposed, the second group sits there.

It is a small, exact, slightly comic picture of the most exasperating thing in human relationships: the person who cannot be pleased, and who is never wrong, because the objection simply changes.

What makes it sharp is who is playing which part. It is easy to assume Jesus is casting his generation as the children calling out — the ones with the complaints. He may be; the sentence works either way. But the sting is in the middle of it: the game keeps changing, and the same people keep sitting down.

The next two verses give the two tunes that were actually played. John came with the dirge — fasting, camel's hair, judgement, repentance. Jesus came with the flute — feasts, tax collectors, wine, a wedding. Between them they covered the whole range of what God can send to a nation.

And the response to both was the same, dressed up in two different objections.

That is worth applying carefully, because it describes a real and very common condition and it is not confined to Pharisees. There is a way of engaging with the things of God in which one is always, sincerely, weighing an objection — the preaching is too demanding, or too soft; the church is too formal, or too casual; that Christian is a hypocrite, and that one is a fanatic. Every objection may be individually reasonable. What gives the game away is that the seat is never vacated.

The test is not whether you have a criticism. It is whether anything has ever succeeded in getting you up.

verseByVerse.quote: For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus names the two tunes, and the objections that met them.

For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, He has a demon.

John's austerity was genuine, deliberate, and commanded before he was born (1:15). And the verdict on it was not that he was mistaken but that he was possessed — a fanatic, unbalanced, not right in the head. That is what an ascetic gets: nobody argues with him, they diagnose him.

The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!

And that is what the other kind gets. Jesus went to dinner parties. He went to Levi's house full of tax collectors and he is about to go to a Pharisee's. He turned water into wine at a wedding. And the verdict was that he was a man with no self-control and worse taste in company.

Two ministries, as different as they could be, both from God, both rejected — and the reasons given were mutually exclusive. Which is the proof that the reasons were never the reason.

There is a phrase in that insult worth rescuing, though, because they meant it as an accusation and it happens to be the finest description of him anyone produced in his lifetime. A friend of tax collectors and sinners. They said it to shame him. It is engraved on the hope of every person who has ever come to him ashamed — and the next fifteen verses are about to show exactly what sort of friend he is.

Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.

The saying picks up the language of verse 29 — where the people justified God. Wisdom, in the Old Testament, is God's own wisdom personified, calling in the streets and being ignored (Prov. 1:20-33). Here she is vindicated, and the vindication comes from her children: the people who actually responded.

The argument is not won by debate. It is won by the tax collectors who went into the water, and by the woman who is about to walk into a Pharisee's dining room with a jar of ointment. You cannot argue a generation out of an objection that was never about the evidence. You can only produce the children.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee named Simon invites Jesus to dinner. Jesus accepts — which is worth registering, since two verses earlier they were calling him a friend of tax collectors and sinners. He ate with the disreputable and with the respectable, and seems to have refused nobody.

The setting explains the story. Guests reclined on low couches, propped on the left elbow, feet extending away from the table; and such meals were semi-public, with uninvited townspeople free to come in and stand round the walls. That is how she gets in.

She is “a woman of the city, who was a sinner” — no name, no history, and in that context the description almost certainly means she was publicly known for sexual immorality. She comes uninvited, stands behind him at his feet, weeps enough to wet them, wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and anoints them with ointment from an alabaster flask.

Every one of those acts is either socially ruinous or physically degrading. A respectable woman did not unbind her hair in public. The feet were the dirtiest part of a man in a sandalled country, and the anointing belonged on the head. She does not appear to notice any of it. She never speaks — the only major figure in the chapter who does not.

Simon's response happens entirely behind his face: “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is.” The logic is tidy, and what he cannot conceive is the third possibility — that Jesus knows exactly what she is, better than Simon does, and is letting her touch him anyway. Jesus answers the unspoken thought, which settles Simon's question about prophetic knowledge before the conversation starts.

Then the parable of the two debtors, and Simon walks into it with a hedge that gives him away: “The one, I suppose.” Neither debtor could pay; the lender cancelled both; the one forgiven more loved more.

And then the mirror is turned on the table. No water for the feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for the head — three ordinary courtesies any Galilean host provided without thinking, and Simon omitted all three. Against each, what she did, and each of hers is enormously larger. He withheld the cheap minimum; she gave the costly maximum at the lowest place in the room.

“Your sins are forgiven… Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” Not her love — her faith. The love was the fruit. The faith was what got her through the door.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the two debtors is the theological key to the scene and to the chapter. Forgiveness is the cause; love is the effect. This is the reverse of the moralism that says “love more, and God will forgive you more.” The gospel runs the other way: the more you understand what you have been forgiven, the more you will love.

Her love is extravagant because her sense of her cancelled debt is accurate and large. Simon's love is cool because his sense of his own debt is small — or rather, because he does not yet believe he has one. A man who considers himself basically righteous will never produce the love that flows from a woman who knows she was lost and is not any more.

Verse 47 is regularly misread, and the passage itself supplies three corrections. The parable Simon has just endorsed runs cancellation first and love after. The Greek for “are forgiven” is a perfect — completed in the past, standing in the present; it happened before she entered the house, which is why she came. And three verses later Jesus names what saved her, and it is her faith.

The “for” is the for of evidence, not of cause — as in “it rained last night, for the ground is wet.” The second half of the verse proves it: “he who is forgiven little, loves little.” Forgiveness is the input; love is the output.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman is the chapter's portrait of what it looks like to be genuinely overwhelmed by grace. She is not performing for the guests; she seems unaware of them. She is not observing social convention; she has left it behind. She is not managing her reputation; she forfeited it years ago.

What she is doing is the only thing she can think of in the presence of the one who has forgiven her — giving everything she has left, her tears, her hair, her perfume and her dignity, because what she has received is worth more than all of it together. The question the scene puts to every reader is whether we feel forgiven like that.

Simon's failure is the failure of good morality without grace-shaped self-knowledge. He is not a bad man. He is careful, observant, theologically serious, and he has kept his reputation intact. What he has never seen is the size of his own debt.

A person who does not see the depth of their own sin cannot be overwhelmed by the grace that forgives it, cannot produce the love that flows from it, and cannot understand a woman weeping on the floor. The church that produces more Simons than sinful women has failed at the most basic level of gospel communication: it has not helped people grasp what they have been forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table.

Two verses ago they were calling him a friend of tax collectors and sinners. Here he accepts an invitation from a Pharisee — which is worth registering, because it settles something about him that is often got wrong.

Jesus was not selective in the direction people assume. He ate with the disreputable, and he ate with the respectable, and he seems to have accepted every invitation he was given. He is as willing to sit in Simon's dining room as at Levi's party. If he had refused the Pharisees' tables he would have been exactly the partisan they accused him of being.

The setting needs picturing, because the story depends on it. Guests at a formal meal did not sit on chairs at a table. They reclined on low couches around three sides of a low table, propped on the left elbow, feet extending away from the food. A man's feet were therefore at the outer edge of the room, behind him. And such meals were semi-public: the doors stood open, and uninvited people from the town could come in and stand round the walls to listen to the conversation. That was normal, and it is how she gets in.

And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner.

Luke's behold turns the reader's head, and then he tells us almost nothing. No name. No history. Two descriptions: she is of the city, and she is a sinner — and in that context, applied to a woman and stated as her public identity, it almost certainly means she was known for sexual immorality.

That is what the room knew about her when she walked in. It is what everyone had known about her for years, and it is very likely the only thing about her anybody could have told you.

When she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment.
