She found out where he was. And she went — into the house of a Pharisee, which is the last building in that town where a woman like her would be welcome, carrying something expensive.

She had already worked out what she was going to do before she got there. The flask was bought, or fetched, or dug out from wherever such things were kept.

verseByVerse.quote: and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke slows down and gives five actions in a single sentence, and every one of them is a scandal.

Standing behind him at his feet. She takes the only position available to her, which is also the lowest place in the room.

Weeping. Luke does not say why. She has not been rebuked, and nothing has yet happened. Whatever this is, it started before she arrived.

She began to wet his feet with her tears. The verb is the one used of rain falling. This is not a discreet tear or two; there are enough of them to wash the dust off a man's feet, and they keep coming.

And wiped them with the hair of her head. Here the room would have gone very quiet. A respectable woman did not unbind her hair in public; it was done at her wedding, and after that in private, and to loosen it in front of men was so improper that it appears in rabbinic discussion as grounds for divorce. She takes down her hair in a Pharisee's dining room, in front of his guests, and uses it as a towel.

And kissed his feet. Luke's verb is continuous — she kept kissing them, over and over. The feet: the dirtiest part of a man in a sandalled country, the part a slave washed.

And anointed them with the ointment. The flask was alabaster, which was how the costly ointments were kept. And she pours it on his feet — not his head, which is where you anoint a guest of honour. She does not consider herself entitled to his head.

Now the thing to see. Every one of these acts is either socially ruinous or physically degrading, and she does not appear to notice.

She is not performing; there is no sign she is aware of the audience at all. She is not negotiating; she asks for nothing and says nothing — she is the only major figure in this chapter who never speaks. She is not trying to earn something, and the parable Jesus is about to tell will make that explicit: the debt was cancelled first, and this is what came after.

She has already forfeited her reputation years ago, and now she spends what is left of her dignity in about ninety seconds, in public, on a man's feet — because she has been forgiven, and there is nothing else she can think of to do with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, 'If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.' And Jesus answering said to him, 'Simon, I have something to say to you.' And he answered, 'Say it, Teacher.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself.

Simon says nothing out loud. He is far too well brought up for a scene at his own table. The whole objection happens behind his face.

If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.

The logic is tidy and it is worth laying out, because Simon is not a fool. A prophet has supernatural knowledge; a prophet who knew what she was would not let her touch him; this man is letting her touch him; therefore either he does not know, or he does not care — and either way, he is not a prophet.

What Simon cannot conceive is a third possibility: that Jesus knows exactly what she is, better than Simon does, and is letting her touch him anyway.

Notice also the two words he uses of her — who and what sort. He wants Jesus to know not merely her name but her category. She is, in his mind, a type before she is a person, and the type is the whole of what needs to be said.

And Jesus answering said to him, Simon, I have something to say to you.

Luke's word is answering. Simon has not spoken. Jesus answers him anyway — which is the third time in this Gospel that he replies to an unspoken thought (5:22; 6:8), and it disposes of Simon's question before the conversation has properly started. Simon wanted to know whether this man had prophetic knowledge. He has just had a demonstration and has not noticed.

And observe how it is done. Not I know what you are thinking, and it is disgraceful. He uses the man's name and asks for permission to speak. There is no ambush and no humiliation in front of the guests — a courtesy, incidentally, that Simon had not extended to him.

Say it, Teacher.

Simon is polite, and he is condescending. Teacher is a perfectly respectful word, and it is a good deal less than Lord, which is what the centurion called him in verse 6 without ever having met him.

verseByVerse.quote: 'A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?' Simon answered, 'The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.' And he said to him, 'You have judged rightly.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parable is four sentences long and it dismantles the room.

A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.

A denarius was a day's wage for a labourer. So the debts are roughly twenty months' wages and roughly two months' wages — a serious difference, and both figures are real money. Neither man is being teased with a trifle.

When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both.

Two things are established in one clause, and both matter. First, neither man could pay — the difference in the size of the debts made no difference whatever to the outcome, because fifty denarii a man does not have is as unpayable as five hundred. Second, the cancelling is entirely the lender's act. Nobody negotiated. Nobody offered instalments.

The Greek for cancelled is echarisato — from charis, grace. He graced them both.

Now which of them will love him more?

And Simon walks into it, with a small hedge that gives him away: The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.

That I suppose is beautifully observed. He can see the answer coming and he can also see that it is going somewhere he will not enjoy, so he answers correctly and holds it at arm's length. It is the tone of a man who has just realised he is in a conversation he did not start.

You have judged rightly.

Now hold on to what the parable does and does not say, because this is the theological hinge of the whole scene and it is regularly got backwards.

The love does not produce the cancellation. In the story, the cancelling comes first, and the loving comes after, and it comes in proportion to how much was cancelled. Love is the effect. Grace is the cause.

Which means the question the parable leaves hanging over Simon's dining table is not who is the better person? It is: how big do you think your debt was? Simon is not being told that he is unforgiven. He is being told that his estimate of what he owed is the reason his welcome was so cool.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, 'Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, Do you see this woman?

Two things happen in that sentence, and Luke has arranged them carefully. Jesus turns to face her — for the first time in the scene, since she has been behind him throughout — and he speaks to Simon.

So he is looking at her while he talks about her. She hears every word of what follows with his eyes on her.

Do you see this woman? Simon has seen nothing but a category. He looked at her and read a file. Jesus asks him to look again, and then tells him what is actually there.

What follows is three comparisons, and each has the same structure: you did not… but she has…

I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet. Water for a guest's feet after a dusty road was not an extravagance. It was the minimum — a jug and a basin, usually handled by a servant. Simon did not provide it.

You gave me no kiss. The kiss of greeting was the ordinary courtesy between host and guest, the equivalent of a handshake at the door.

You did not anoint my head with oil. A little olive oil on the head of an honoured guest — cheap, customary, pleasant.

None of the three was legally required. All three were what any host in Galilee did without thinking. And Simon, who had invited this man to his own house in front of his own friends, omitted every one of them.

That is not an oversight. Three courtesies are not forgotten by accident. Simon wanted Jesus at his table and was not prepared to honour him at it — he invited him as a curiosity, and treated him accordingly, and everyone in the room would have registered it as the small public slight it was.

And against each omission, Jesus sets what she did — and every one of hers is enormously larger than the courtesy Simon skipped. No water: she used tears and her own hair. No kiss: she has not stopped kissing his feet since she came in. No oil on the head: ointment from an alabaster flask on his feet.

Simon withheld the cheap minimum. She gave the costly maximum, at the lowest place in the room, to the dirtiest part of a man.

The one who thought he had nothing much to be forgiven gave nothing much.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven — for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.

This is one of the most misread verses in the New Testament, and it is worth taking slowly, because a great deal hangs on it.

Read quickly, her sins are forgiven, for she loved much sounds as though her love bought the forgiveness — that she earned it by the extravagance of what she did on the floor. That reading has a long history, and it is the natural sense of the English as it stands.

It cannot be right, for three reasons drawn from the passage itself.

First, it reverses the parable Jesus has just told and Simon has just agreed with. In the story, the debt is cancelled and then the loving follows in proportion. If love produced forgiveness here, the parable would have to run backwards, and Jesus has spent five verses establishing which way round it goes.

Second, the tense. The Greek for are forgiven is a perfect — an action completed in the past whose result stands in the present. Her sins have been forgiven, and remain so. That happened before she entered the house. It is why she came in.

Third, three verses later he tells her plainly what saved her, and it is not her love: your faith has saved you.

So what does the for mean? It is the for of evidence, not of cause. We use it constantly: it rained last night, for the ground is wet. Nobody thinks the wet ground made it rain. The wet ground is how you know.

That is exactly the logic here, and the second half of the verse proves it: he who is forgiven little, loves little. Notice which way the causation runs in that clause. Not he who loves little is forgiven little. The forgiveness is the input; the love is the output. And Jesus has just used the same test to read the room — Simon's cold hospitality was evidence of Simon's small sense of debt, exactly as her tears were evidence of her large one.

This matters pastorally as much as theologically. If love earns forgiveness, then every anxious believer must ask whether they have loved enough, and the honest answer is always no. If love is the evidence of forgiveness, the question changes entirely — and the way to love more is not to squeeze harder but to look longer at what you have actually been forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven.' Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, 'Who is this, who even forgives sins?' And he said to the woman, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to her, Your sins are forgiven.

He has been speaking about her to Simon. Now he turns and speaks to her, and it is the first time anyone in the scene has addressed her at all.

She already knew. The perfect tense in the previous verse means the thing was settled before she came through the door, and her tears were the evidence of it. So why say it out loud?

Because she needed to hear it said, in that room, in front of those people. A woman who has spent years as the town's byword had just crawled to the feet of a rabbi at a Pharisee's dinner party, and the whole room was watching to see what he would do with her. He tells her, where everyone can hear, that her sins are gone.

There is a great deal of pastoral practice in that. Assurance is not merely a private transaction with God. People need to be told, in words, by somebody with the authority to say it — which is a good part of what preaching and the Lord's Table are for.

Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, Who is this, who even forgives sins?

The same question as at the paralytic's healing (5:21), and it is the right question. Only God forgives sins committed against God; everyone at that table knew it. They have understood the claim perfectly and, once again, drawn no conclusion from it.

And notice what Jesus does with the murmur: nothing. He does not turn to defend himself or argue the point. He has one more thing to say and it is not to them.

And he said to the woman, Your faith has saved you; go in peace.

Not your love has saved you. The love was the fruit; the faith was the root — the trust that got her through a door she had no business entering, to the feet of a man she believed would not throw her out.

And she was right about him. That is all her faith consisted of, and it was enough.

Here, then, is what he is like. A woman with no name in the record, no standing, no argument and no words walks into a room full of men who despise her, and puts everything she has left on the feet of Christ — and he does not flinch, does not distance himself, does not manage the situation. He receives it, defends her to the man whose house it is, tells her out loud that she is forgiven, and sends her out through the same door in peace. There has never been a sinner too far gone for that welcome, and there is not one now.

7.text: <sup>1</sup> After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. <sup>2</sup> Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him. <sup>3</sup> When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. <sup>4</sup> And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy to have you do this for him, <sup>5</sup> for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.” <sup>6</sup> And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. <sup>7</sup> Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed. <sup>8</sup> For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>9</sup> When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.” <sup>10</sup> And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well. <sup>11</sup> Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. <sup>12</sup> As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her. <sup>13</sup> And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.” <sup>14</sup> Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” <sup>15</sup> And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother. <sup>16</sup> Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” <sup>17</sup> And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country. <sup>18</sup> The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, <sup>19</sup> calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” <sup>20</sup> And when the men had come to him, they said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’” <sup>21</sup> In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight. <sup>22</sup> And he answered them, “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. <sup>23</sup> And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” <sup>24</sup> When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? <sup>25</sup> What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. <sup>26</sup> What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. <sup>27</sup> This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ <sup>28</sup> I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.” <sup>29</sup> (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, <sup>30</sup> but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.) <sup>31</sup> “To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? <sup>32</sup> They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’ <sup>33</sup> For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ <sup>34</sup> The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ <sup>35</sup> Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.” <sup>36</sup> One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. <sup>37</sup> And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment, <sup>38</sup> and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment. <sup>39</sup> Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus answering said to him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he answered, “Say it, Teacher.” <sup>41</sup> “A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. <sup>42</sup> When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?” <sup>43</sup> Simon answered, “The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.” And he said to him, “You have judged rightly.” <sup>44</sup> Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. <sup>45</sup> You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. <sup>46</sup> You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. <sup>47</sup> Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.” <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” <sup>49</sup> Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” <sup>50</sup> And he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

8.title: The Word, the Storm, and the Power of the Kingdom
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is organised around the question of hearing and responding to the word — the parable of the sower, the lamp under a jar, and Jesus's redefinition of family as those who hear the word and do it all converge on the same theme before the chapter moves into four great demonstrations of kingdom power. After the teaching section, the chapter becomes a series of astonishing encounters: Jesus calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee, casts a legion of demons into a herd of pigs, heals a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years, and raises Jairus's daughter from the dead. The four miracle stories are not loosely connected anecdotes; they form a theological argument. Jesus has authority over the forces of nature, over the powers of darkness, over the long suffering of a diseased body, and over death itself. Nothing is outside the reach of his word.

The opening note about the women who accompanied Jesus and provided for the ministry out of their means (vv. 1–3) is characteristic Luke — he notices and names women at a point in history when their testimony was not counted and their presence was not recorded. Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Chuza, Susanna, and many others: they are not background figures but named participants in the mission, financing the ministry that will change the world. Luke's Gospel is consistently attentive to those whom history overlooks.

The parable of the sower (vv. 4–15) is the parable about parables — the key to how the whole teaching ministry of Jesus works. The word is the seed; the hearts of the hearers are the soil; the response to the word determines everything. But the parable also functions as a warning and a comfort simultaneously: a warning that most hearers will not bear fruit, for a variety of reasons; a comfort that some will — “an hundredfold.” The harvest is certain; it comes to those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke records that Jesus travelled through cities and villages proclaiming the kingdom of God, accompanied not only by the twelve but by a group of women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities.

The list is striking in its specificity: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; Joanna, the wife of Herod's household manager Chuza; Susanna; and many others. These women “provided for them out of their means” — the verb is diēkonoun, the root behind deacon, and it is continuous. They kept on providing, out of their own money.

So the Galilean ministry was funded by women. Thirteen men walking from village to village for the better part of three years, eating every day, with no visible income — and Luke tells us in half a verse where the money came from.

The significance of the passage is easily underestimated. In a culture where women were excluded from the travelling company of a rabbi, Jesus's entourage included them as named, active participants — and it exposed him to precisely the accusation his enemies had already made (7:34). He did it anyway, and Luke records it without a word of defence.

Each woman is identified by what was done for her rather than by what she brought. The company around Jesus is not a collection of the promising; it is a collection of the rescued.

Mary Magdalene needs rescuing from a long misreading. Magdala was a fishing town on the lake, and the name says only where she came from. What Scripture tells us of her past is that seven demons came out of her — which is affliction, not scandal. She is not the unnamed woman of the previous chapter; the accident of neighbouring paragraphs invited that merger, and a sixth-century sermon fixed it in the Western imagination for a thousand years. There is no basis for it in the text.

Joanna is a court wife whose husband managed the estate of the man who had John the Baptist in a cell. Whatever her presence here cost her at home, she is named again at the empty tomb (24:10) — as is Mary Magdalene, who will still be there at the cross when the men have gone.
verseByVerse.theology:
The inclusion of women in the travelling band is a quiet revolution in the social world of first-century Judaism. Rabbis did not travel with female disciples; the association would have been scandalous, and Jesus's opponents were already looking for material.

His practice reflects the consistent pattern of including those the religious establishment excluded, and it anticipates the full participation of women in the life of the new covenant community (Acts 2:17-18; Gal. 3:28). The kingdom of God does not replicate the social hierarchies of the world it enters.

It matters, too, that the women are introduced immediately before the parable of the soils. Luke has just shown a company of people in whom the word took root and bore fruit — and their fruit was that they gave everything they had to keep the sowing going.

These same women are at the cross when the twelve have scattered (23:49), and at the tomb on the third morning (24:1-11). They are not peripheral figures. On the two occasions when the testimony mattered most, they are the witnesses Luke has.
verseByVerse.examples:
The women who supported the ministry “out of their means” are the New Testament's first and clearest model of financial stewardship in service of the gospel. They did not merely believe; they paid for it, and they kept paying.

The theology of giving that runs through Paul's letters (2 Cor. 8-9; Phil. 4:14-19) has its roots here: those who share in the blessings of the gospel share their resources with those who carry it forward. It is easy to romanticise the finances of the gospel and pretend they were not there. They were. Somebody bought the bread.

And notice what these women could not do. They could not preach in a synagogue, and there is no sign they tried. What they had was money and mobility, and they put both under the mission for years, and were named once and then never mentioned in that connection again.

There is a whole doctrine of unglamorous service in that. The four Gospels exist partly because a group of women paid the bills of an itinerant preacher and did not require anybody to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God.

Luke gives the shape of the ministry in a sentence: town after town, on foot, saying the same thing. Two verbs — proclaiming, the word for a herald making a public announcement, and bringing the good news, which is the verb behind gospel. He is not lecturing. He is announcing something that has happened.

And the twelve were with him, and also some women.

Stop there, because a first-century reader would have. Rabbis had disciples, and disciples were men. A teacher travelling from village to village with a company that included women was not merely unusual; it was the kind of arrangement that generated exactly the accusation his enemies had already made two chapters earlier — a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34).

He did it anyway, and Luke records it without a word of defence.

And notice how they are identified: women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities. Every one of them is described by what was done for her, not by what she brought. The company around Jesus is not a collection of the promising. It is a collection of the rescued.

Then a name, and it needs rescuing from fourteen centuries of misreading. Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.

Magdala was a fishing town on the western shore of the lake, and the surname simply says where she was from. What Luke tells us about her is that seven demons came out of her — which is affliction, not scandal, and it is the only thing Scripture ever says about her past.

She is not the woman who wept at Jesus's feet in the previous chapter. That woman is deliberately left unnamed, sixteen verses earlier; the accident of neighbouring paragraphs is what first invited the merger, and a sermon of Gregory the Great in the sixth century fixed it in the Western imagination for a thousand years. There is no basis for it anywhere in the text. Mary Magdalene was not a prostitute. She was a woman under an oppression so total that Luke has to use a number for it, and she got free.

And of everyone in this list, she is the one who will still be there at the cross when the men have gone (23:49), and first at the tomb on the third morning (24:10).

verseByVerse.quote: and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two more names, and then the sentence that explains how any of this was possible.

Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager. Take in what that means. Chuza managed the estate and finances of Herod Antipas — the man who had John the Baptist in a cell and would eventually have his head brought in on a plate. Joanna is a court wife. She has status, money, and a husband employed by the enemy.

And she is walking around Galilee with an itinerant preacher from Nazareth. Whatever conversations that produced in her household, Luke does not tell us, and they cannot have been comfortable. She is also named again at the empty tomb (24:10), so whatever it cost her, she was still there at the end.

And Susanna, and many others. A name with no story at all, and then a crowd of women whose names nobody wrote down.

Who provided for them out of their means.

Here is the detail that changes how the whole ministry looks. The verb is diēkonoun — the root behind deacon — and it is in the continuous tense: they kept on providing. And out of their means is plain: it was their own money.

So the Galilean ministry of Jesus Christ was funded by women. Thirteen men walking from village to village, eating every day, sleeping somewhere every night, for the better part of three years, with no visible income — and Luke tells us in half a verse where the money came from.

That is worth saying plainly, because it is easy to romanticise the finances of the gospel and pretend they were not there. They were. Somebody bought the bread. And the people who bought it are named here, once, and then never mentioned again in connection with it.

There is a whole doctrine of Christian giving in that half-verse, and it long predates Paul's collection for Jerusalem. These women could not preach in a synagogue and did not try. What they had was resources, and they put them under the mission, quietly, for years — and the four Gospels exist partly because they did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — The Parable of the Sower and Its Explanation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable of the sower is Jesus's own explanation of why his ministry produces such varied responses — and why his disciples should not be surprised or discouraged by it. He tells it publicly (vv. 4-8), then explains it privately (vv. 9-15), with a hard word about the purpose of parables in between.

Note when he tells it. Not to a disappointing turnout, but to the largest crowd of the ministry so far — and what he says is a story in which three-quarters of the sowing comes to nothing. He is telling the truth about crowds.

The picture was entirely ordinary. In that agriculture, sowing came before ploughing: a man walked the field broadcasting seed by the handful, and the ground was turned over afterwards. So the seed genuinely did fall everywhere. The sower is not careless; that is simply how the job was done, and it matters — the same generous scattering reaches all four kinds of ground.

The disciples ask what it means, and Jesus's answer is one of the most important passages in the Gospels on parabolic teaching: “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that 'seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.'” The quotation is Isaiah 6:9-10, the commission given after the vision of the throne — the hardening that follows persistent rejection of revelation.

This should not be softened, and three things hold it together. It is a judgement, and it falls on people who have already refused what they were given; Luke has shown a Nazareth that tried to kill him and a delegation plotting his death. A parable is also a door held ajar, hiding the thing from the casual and rewarding the man who comes back and asks — which is exactly what has just happened in verse 9. And it is mercy as well as judgement: to be told plainly and reject it plainly is a far more terrible position.

The explanation identifies the seed as the word of God, which settles a great deal. The variable in this parable is never the seed; it is the ground. The path is hardened by ordinary traffic. The rock is shallow soil over limestone, where the fastest growth in the field is the first to die. The thorns are already rooted and simply grow at the same time, for the same water and light. And the good soil holds the word fast in an honest heart and bears fruit with patience.

It is not a rigid psychological classification. It is a mirror, and every hearer is invited to hold it up.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the sower is the foundational parable — Mark records Jesus saying, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables?” (Mark 4:13). It establishes the principle governing all his teaching: the response to the word determines everything.

The seed does not change. It is the same word in all four soils, and the same generous hand scattering it. What varies is the condition of the heart it lands in — which is the basis of the New Testament's consistent call to prepare the heart through humility, through the removal of competing loves, through the patient reception of what has been given.

The description of the good soil — “an honest and good heart” — uses a phrase that was a stock expression in the wider culture for a fine and admirable person, and Jesus fills it with different content. The heart he commends is not the morally superior one but the honest one: the heart that will let the word say what it says without negotiating, and does not flinch when the diagnosis is unflattering.

And the last word is hypomonē, patient endurance — the capacity to remain under a weight without moving. The rock soil was the fastest in the field; the good soil is the slowest. Fruit takes a season, and there is no arrangement by which it can be brought forward.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable is a diagnostic tool. The question it puts to every hearer is not “have you heard the gospel?” but “what has happened to the word in you?”

Has it been taken away before it could go in — by distraction, by noise, by a life with no quiet in it? A footpath is not naturally hard ground; it is ordinary soil walked over so often that nothing can get into it, and the traffic that packed it down was perfectly innocent.

The rock soil frightens sincere believers, and it should be handled carefully. It describes someone who fell away — who is no longer there — not someone who is struggling and worried about it. Scripture is consistent that what God begins he finishes (Phil. 1:6; John 10:28), and John's own comment on those who left is that “they went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The remedy is never introspection; a plant cannot inspect its own roots. It is to go deeper, in the unspectacular disciplines nobody sees, before the drought arrives — because the sun in this parable is not a possibility. It is the weather.

The thorns are the most dangerous soil, because nothing appears to be wrong. And not one of the three Jesus names is a sin: cares, riches, and the ordinary pleasures of life. The choking of the word in a comfortable country is done almost entirely by legitimate things — which is exactly why it is so hard to see, and why the outcome is stated so precisely: their fruit does not mature. Not nothing at all. Perpetually promising, and never actually there.

verseByVerse.quote: And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, 'A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great crowd is gathering, people coming from town after town — and this is the moment Jesus chooses to tell a story about how most seed fails.

That is worth noticing before anything else. He is not looking at a discouraging turnout. He is looking at the largest crowd of the ministry so far, and what he says to them is a parable in which three-quarters of the sowing comes to nothing.

He is not being pessimistic. He is telling the truth about crowds, and preparing his disciples for the next three years — and for the next three thousand.

A sower went out to sow his seed.

The picture is entirely ordinary and every person listening had watched it done. In that agriculture, sowing generally came before ploughing: a man walked across the field with a bag at his hip, broadcasting seed by the handful in wide arcs, and afterwards the ground was turned over. Which means the seed genuinely did fall everywhere — on the path worn across the field by villagers, on the thin soil over the limestone shelf, into the corners where last year's thorns were still rooted.

The sower is not careless. That is simply how the job was done, and it matters for reading the parable: the same generous scattering reaches all four kinds of ground.

Some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.

A footpath through a field, packed hard by generations of feet. The seed does not go in at all — it lies on the surface, gets walked on, and the birds have it before the ploughing. Nothing has gone wrong with the seed. It simply never got below the surface, because the surface would not let it.

Luke alone adds trampled underfoot, and it is the detail of a careful reporter. Before the birds even arrive, the ordinary traffic of ordinary life has walked over it.

One more thing before the other soils, and it governs how the whole parable is heard. Jesus never identifies the sower. He identifies the seed (v. 11) and he identifies all four soils, and about the man with the bag he says nothing at all.

That silence is deliberate, and it is a mercy to everyone who has ever tried to sow anything. The parable is not about the skill of the preacher. It is not a study in technique, or timing, or how the message was framed. The sower does one thing: he walks the field and scatters, generously, over ground he cannot control and mostly cannot even see.

verseByVerse.quote: And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.' As he said these things, he called out, 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three more soils, and each fails at a different depth.

Some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture.

This is not bare stone. Much of Galilee is limestone with a thin skin of soil over it, and to a man walking the field it looks like the rest. Seed goes in, germinates fast — precisely because the shallow soil warms quickly — and comes up before anything else in the field. Then the sun comes, and the roots find rock instead of water, and the whole thing is dead by noon.

The fastest growth in the field is the first to die. Luke, characteristically, names the cause exactly: no moisture.

And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it.

Here nothing appears to be wrong at all. The soil is good, the seed goes deep, the plant grows — and so does everything else. The thorns are not planted; they are already there, roots left in the ground from last year. They do not attack the wheat. They simply grow at the same time, for the same water and the same light, and they are better at it.

Note the verb: choked. Strangled. It is a slow death by competition, and the crop is still standing when it happens.

And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.

A hundredfold is an enormous return — a good harvest in that country might be tenfold, and the figure is deliberately extravagant. Whatever the failures, the yield of the fourth soil is not merely adequate. It more than covers everything lost on the other three.

As he said these things, he called out, He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

Luke says he called out — raised his voice, at the end, over a crowd.

And the sentence is itself a test. Anyone can hear a story about farming; what he is asking for is the kind of hearing that goes past the surface and lets the thing in. Which is exactly what the parable is about. A man who listens to the parable of the soils and does not ask which soil he is has just demonstrated the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said, 'To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant.

Notice what the disciples do, because it is the whole point of what follows. They do not assume they have understood. They come back and ask.

That asking is itself the parable being enacted. The crowd heard a story about farming and went home; these men heard the same story and pressed for more. What separates them at this stage is not superior insight — Mark records Jesus telling them plainly that they had not understood it either (Mark 4:13). What separates them is that they came back.

To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God.

The word is mystēria — not puzzles, but things that were hidden and are now being disclosed. And note the passive: it has been given. Their understanding is not an achievement. Somebody handed it to them.

But for others they are in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.

This is one of the hardest sentences in the Gospels, and it should not be softened. Jesus is quoting Isaiah 6:9-10 — the commission God gave Isaiah after the vision of the throne, sending him to a people who would hear and not understand, and telling him in advance that his preaching would harden them.

Does God then deliberately blind people? Three things have to be held together.

First, this is a judgement, and it falls on people who have already refused what they were given. Isaiah's commission comes after generations of ignored prophets, and Luke has already shown us a Nazareth that tried to kill Jesus and a delegation of experts plotting his death. Nobody in this chapter is being blinded on the way in.

Second, a parable is not merely a veil. It is also a door held ajar. It hides the thing from the casual and rewards the man who comes back and asks — which is precisely what has just happened in verse 9. The same story that closed the crowd's ears opened these men's, and the difference was whether they returned.

Third, this is mercy as well as judgement. To be told plainly and to reject it plainly is a far more terrible position than to be told in a story you did not follow. A parable leaves the door open longer than a sermon does.

What cannot be done with this verse is to use it to explain away one's own dullness. The remedy is in verse 9, and it is not complicated. They asked.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.

Before anything else, that identification settles a great deal. The seed is not the preacher, not the technique, not the atmosphere of the meeting, not the personality of the man scattering it. It is the word of God, and it is exactly the same seed in all four soils.

Which means the variable in this parable is never the seed. It is the ground.

That is a hard word for anyone who preaches and a liberating one. Hard, because it removes the excuse that a poor response means the wrong method was used. Liberating, because it removes the burden of believing that a better performance would have produced a better harvest. The sower's job is to scatter the seed. He cannot manufacture soil.

The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.

Two things in that sentence deserve attention.

The first is that there is an enemy, and Jesus names him. This is not a psychological account of inattention. Something intelligent and hostile is at work in the moment between hearing and believing, and its whole strategy here is remarkably modest. It does not need to refute the word. It does not need to produce an argument. It only needs to remove it before it goes in.

The second is the purpose clause: so that they may not believe and be saved. That is what is actually at stake in a distracted hour. Jesus states plainly that the enemy's aim in taking the word away is to prevent a salvation that would otherwise have followed.

Now think about what a footpath actually is. It is not naturally hard ground. It is ordinary soil that has been walked over so many times that nothing can get into it — and the traffic that packed it down was perfectly innocent. Nobody hardened it on purpose.

Which is the exact danger of a life with no quiet in it. The word arrives on Sunday, and by the time the car is out of the car park there has been a conversation, a screen, a plan for the afternoon — and it is gone, and nobody did anything wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.

This is the soil that frightens people, and it should be handled carefully, because it has done real damage to sensitive consciences.

Start with what is genuinely there. The response is real as far as it goes: they receive it with joy, and the joy is not called false. Luke even says they believe for a while. Something happened, and it was visible, and it may have been more visible than what happened in the good soil.

What is missing is root. And root is precisely the part nobody can see — the underground work that nobody applauds and that only shows up in a drought.

In time of testing. The word is peirasmos, the same word as at 4:13 — trial, or temptation, the two senses English keeps apart and Greek does not. The plant does not die because a wind blew it over. It dies because the sun came out and there was nothing beneath it to reach for water.

Now the question that presses on any believer who has ever gone through a bad season: is this me? Have I lost my salvation?

Three things need saying, and they need saying in this order.

First, the passage is not describing someone who is struggling. It describes someone who fell away — who is no longer there. A person worried about this verse is by definition still asking the question, which is not what the rock soil does.

Second, Scripture is consistent that what God begins he finishes. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Phil. 1:6). No one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). John's own comment on those who left is not that they lost something but that they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). The rock soil is not a Christian who was lost; it is a plant that never had root.

Third — and this is the pastoral point — the remedy is never introspection. Staring at your own root system is exactly what a plant cannot do. What can be done is to go deeper: to put the word somewhere it can reach water, in the unspectacular disciplines that nobody sees, before the drought arrives.

Because it will. The sun in this parable is not a possibility. It is the weather.

verseByVerse.quote: And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.

This is the most dangerous soil in the parable, because it is the only one where nothing appears to be wrong.

There is no bird here and no drought. The seed went in properly and the plant is growing. The man is still in the field, still green, still where he was. What is happening is entirely gradual and entirely invisible until harvest, when it turns out there is nothing on the stalk.

And look at the three thorns Jesus names, because not one of them is a sin.

Cares — anxieties, the things that genuinely need worrying about. Money, health, a difficult child, an ageing parent, a job that may not last.

Riches — not theft, simply having things and the work of keeping them.

Pleasures of life — the ordinary enjoyments. Not vice; the word covers the perfectly innocent pleasures of an ordinary existence.

These are the thorns. Which means the choking of the word in a comfortable country is done almost entirely by legitimate things, and that is precisely why it is so hard to see. A man being strangled by an obvious sin usually knows it. A man being strangled by his mortgage, his hobbies and his family's diary has nothing to repent of that he can name.

Note also Luke's phrase: as they go on their way. It does not happen at a moment. There is no decision, no crisis, no turning point. It happens over a decade, in the course of getting on with life.

And the outcome is stated with brutal precision: their fruit does not mature. Not they bear no fruit at all — there is something, and it never ripens. Perpetually promising and never actually there.

Here is a test that takes a minute and is uncomfortable. Not what sins am I fighting? but: what has quietly become non-negotiable in my week, and when did I last examine it? Thorns are not planted. They are simply left, and they were there before the seed was.

verseByVerse.quote: As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.

Four things, and every one of them is unspectacular.

Hearing the word. The same word, from the same sower, that fell on all the other ground. Nothing different has been offered here.

Hold it fast. The verb is katechousin — to hold down, to grip, to retain. It is active and it is continuous. This is not passive reception; it is a man who has taken hold of something and does not let go of it, and the reason the word is needed is that things get taken. The bird came for the path soil. Nobody grips what nothing is trying to remove.

In an honest and good heart. The Greek phrase here was a stock expression in the wider culture for a fine and admirable person — and Jesus fills it with entirely different content. The heart he commends is not the morally superior one. It is the honest one: the heart that is not managing an impression, that will let the word say what it says without negotiating, that does not flinch when the diagnosis is unflattering.

Which is worth naming, because it is the one qualification for good soil that anybody can identify in themselves. Not am I fruitful? — that is not visible yet. But: when the word says something I do not like, do I let it stand?

And bear fruit with patience.

The last word is hypomonē — endurance, the capacity to remain under a weight without moving. And it is the note the whole parable ends on.

That deserves emphasis in a hurry-driven Christianity that measures everything by immediate visible outcome. The rock soil was the fastest in the field; the good soil is the slowest. Fruit takes a season, and it takes the same season whether or not anybody is watching, and there is no arrangement by which it can be brought forward.

So the marks of the only soil that works are these: an honest heart, a firm grip, and time. Nothing here is dramatic. Nothing here is beyond an ordinary believer. And it is the only one of the four that ends with a harvest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Lamp Under a Jar and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two brief teachings follow the parable, and both apply it.

The lamp saying comes first, and its placing is deliberate. Jesus has just explained a parable privately, to a small group, after saying that the secrets of the kingdom are given to some and not others. A disciple could easily draw the wrong conclusion: we have been let into something, and it is ours.

“No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light.” Both absurdities are exact: a jar smothers the flame for lack of air, and a lamp under a bed burns the house down. Neither preserves light; both destroy it while pretending to keep it.

And note the purpose clause — so that those who enter may see. Not so the lamp may be admired, and not for the household's benefit. The secrets of the kingdom were given to be put where strangers can see by them.

“For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest” cuts both ways. Forward, it is a promise: the gospel entrusted to twelve men in a house in Galilee will not stay in the house, and Luke is writing the second volume that proves it. But everything concealed also comes out eventually — which is terrifying for anyone hiding something, and one of the great comforts of Scripture for anyone who has been slandered or quietly written off.

“Take care then how you hear” is the imperative that gathers up the whole chapter. And the principle attached to it — to the one who has, more will be given — is not a cruelty but a description of how understanding actually behaves. Capacity grows by use, and atrophies without it. Luke alone adds the sharpest phrase: “even what he thinks that he has.” The man's holdings were never what he supposed.

Then Jesus's mother and brothers arrive, and he redefines family: “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” It is not a rejection of Mary. It is the good soil of verse 15, four verses on, given a family name — and it is the same hearing-and-doing that ended the sermon at 6:47-49.
verseByVerse.theology:
The lamp saying and the redefinition of family are the application of the parable to the disciples' own vocation. They have been given the secrets of the kingdom (v. 10) — not for private illumination but for public proclamation. The word they received is the lamp; the world they are being sent into is the stand.

The parable of the sower describes what happens when the word meets different soils. The lamp saying describes what those in whom it took root are to do with it.

And the family saying should be read alongside what Luke has already established about Mary. She is not being demoted; she is the founding member of the category. The woman who said “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38) heard the word of God and did it, and Jesus has just told a crowd of strangers that the door into his family is the one she walked through.

Nobody is in it by blood. Everybody is in it by hearing and doing — which is why the brothers standing outside at this point in the story, who did not yet believe in him (John 7:5), are outside in more senses than one.
verseByVerse.examples:
The redefinition of family as those who “hear the word of God and do it” is the basis of the extraordinary community the church creates across every natural human division. People who share nothing by blood, culture, language or class are family because they share the same word and the same response to it.

This is the sociological miracle of the first-century church, which drew together Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women, into a community the ancient world had no category for. It remains the miracle of every congregation that takes hearing-and-doing as its defining identity rather than any natural affinity.

“Take care then how you hear” is worth turning into a practical question, because the parable has just made hearing the decisive variable. Not what was preached, but what was done with it between the car park and Tuesday.

And “even what he thinks that he has” is aimed precisely at the person who is quite sure they are fine. Both the rock soil and the thorn soil had something, and both would have described themselves as having it, and neither had what they supposed — and each found out at the worst possible moment. There is a mercy in being told now, in a season of quiet, rather than in a season of testing.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lamp, and the saying is placed here on purpose.

Jesus has just explained a parable privately, to a small group, after telling the crowd that the secrets of the kingdom are given to some and not to others. A disciple could very easily draw the wrong conclusion from that: we have been let into something, and it is ours.

The lamp saying shuts that down immediately.

No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed.

The picture is a small clay oil lamp — the ordinary domestic kind, holding perhaps an hour or two of light. The two absurdities are exact: a jar over it would smother it for lack of air, and a lamp under a bed would burn the house down. Neither is a way of preserving light. Both are ways of destroying it while pretending to keep it.

But puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light.

Note the purpose clause. Not so that the lamp may be admired, and not so that the household may enjoy it. So that those who enter — people coming in from outside, who do not live there — can see.

The secrets of the kingdom were not given to the disciples for their private illumination. They were given to be put where strangers can see by them.

For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.

This cuts two ways, and both are in the passage.

Forward, it is a promise. What God has revealed is going somewhere; the gospel entrusted to twelve men in a house in Galilee will not stay in the house. Luke is writing the second volume that proves it.

But the sentence has a second edge, and Scripture uses it that way elsewhere. Everything concealed comes out eventually. There is no permanently private life, no version of a man that stays behind the door for ever, and the day is coming when the lighting is universal.

For anyone hiding something, that is terrifying. For anyone who has been misrepresented, slandered, or quietly written off, it is one of the great comforts of Scripture. Nothing stays hidden. Including the truth about you.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care then how you hear.

Not what you hear — Jesus has said that elsewhere and it matters. Here it is how. The whole chapter so far has been about the manner of reception, and this is the imperative that gathers it up: pay attention to the way you are listening, because the four soils were not four kinds of seed.

Then the principle, and it is uncomfortable: for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.

Read at speed, that sounds like a cruelty — the rich get richer. It is nothing of the kind. It is a description of how understanding actually behaves, and everyone who has ever learned anything knows it is true.

Capacity grows by use. A man who acts on what he has understood finds that more is opened to him; the next thing is intelligible because the last one was obeyed. And a man who receives and does nothing loses even the ability to receive — not by punishment but by atrophy. Nothing is confiscated. It simply wastes.

Now the phrase that is easy to skim, and it is the sharpest in the sentence: even what he thinks that he has.

Luke alone has those words. The parallel in Mark says simply what he has. Luke's version says something more disturbing: the man's holdings were never what he supposed. He has been carrying a receipt for something that is not in the vault.

That is precisely the position of the rock soil and the thorn soil. Both had something. Both would have described themselves as having it. Neither had what they thought they had, and the discovery came at the worst possible moment — the drought, and the harvest.

So the warning is not aimed at the person who knows they are empty. It is aimed at the person who is quite sure they are fine.

And there is a mercy in being told now. A man can find out in a season of quiet self-examination what he would otherwise find out in a season of testing. The invitation is still open, and the remedy has not changed since verse 9: he can ask.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. And he was told, 'Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.' But he answered them, 'My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd.

Two things worth registering before the saying itself.

The first is his brothers. Luke mentions them without explanation, exactly as Matthew and Mark name four of them and mention sisters as well (Mark 6:3). The plainest reading of the text is the one it invites: Mary and Joseph went on to have a family, and Jesus grew up the eldest of several children. That was discussed at 2:7 and needs no relitigating here — but the brothers are real, they are outside, and John tells us plainly what they thought of him at this stage: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5).

The second is why they had come. Luke is discreet; Mark is not, and records that his family set out to seize him, because people were saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). Whatever exactly is happening at the edge of this crowd, it is not a social visit.

Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.

And then the answer, which has troubled readers for centuries: My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.

Read as a snub, it is shocking. Read carefully, it is not a snub at all — and two things prove it.

He does not say I have no mother and brothers, and he does not refuse to see them. What he does is redefine the category, in public, in front of a crowd, at exactly the moment the claim of blood was being pressed on him.

And notice what the definition is: those who hear the word of God and do it. That is the good soil of verse 15, four verses on, given a family name. It is also, word for word, the two builders at the end of the sermon (6:47-49). Luke has been circling this since chapter 6, and here he lands it.

Which means the answer is not a rejection of Mary. It is an inclusion of everybody else on the terms Mary herself met first. The woman who said let it be to me according to your word (1:38) is the founding member of the category — and Jesus has just told a crowd of strangers that the door into his family is the same one she walked through.

Nobody is in it by blood. Everybody is in it by hearing and doing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus and the disciples set out across the lake at his own initiative — “Let us go across to the other side.” They are in that boat, in that weather, because he told them to get in. The storm is not a consequence of any failure; obedience put them there.

He falls asleep. It is the only place in the Gospels where he is described as sleeping, and it is one of the plainest windows into his humanity: he had been preaching all day, and the moment the boat was under way he was unconscious in the stern.

Then a windstorm comes down on the lake. The geography explains it — the lake sits some two hundred metres below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines funnelling cold air off the heights into the warm basin without warning. A small, shallow lake goes from flat to lethal in minutes. It still does.

And these are professional fishermen who have worked this water all their lives. When they wake him with “Master, Master, we are perishing!” it is not landsmen panicking. These are the people you would want in the boat, and they have concluded they are going to drown — which is worth saying to anyone taught that fear is always a failure of faith. Sometimes fear is an accurate reading of the instruments.

He “rebuked the wind and the raging waves” — the same verb Luke used of the demon in the synagogue (4:35) and of a fever (4:39). There is no prayer. He speaks to the weather in the imperative.

“And they ceased, and there was a calm.” Luke's word is galēnē, a dead flat calm — and anyone who has been on water knows how strange that is. When wind drops, the swell runs on. Here the wind stops and the water goes flat in the same instant.

“Where is your faith?” is gentler than it looks. He does not ask why they have none; he asks where it has gone, which assumes they have some and mislaid it. What was missing was not courage but the conclusion they should have drawn from everything they had already seen.

And they were more frightened afterwards than during. The wind had threatened their lives; what came next threatened their categories. “Who then is this?”
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm is the New Testament's most direct claim that Jesus exercises the prerogatives of the Creator over the natural world.

In the Old Testament only the LORD commands the wind and the sea. “He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Ps. 107:29). “You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them” (Ps. 89:9). “Who shut in the sea with doors… and said, Thus far shall you come, and no farther?” (Job 38:8-11).

The disciples' question — “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” — has only one available answer, and every man in that boat had sung Psalm 107 since childhood. Luke leaves the question hanging; it will not be answered aloud until Caesarea Philippi.

The sleeping is theologically as significant as the stilling. He is not asleep because he is unconcerned but because he is at peace — the one who will say “do not be anxious” (12:22) practising it in a sinking boat. And it is the fullest possible statement of the incarnation: the Lord of the storm, too tired to stay awake, four feet from men who thought they were dying.
verseByVerse.examples:
The disciples have Jesus in the boat and they are terrified. They have heard the sermon, seen the healings, received the explanation of the parables — and when the storm comes they are afraid and amazed.

That is the honest portrait of early discipleship, and of most later discipleship too. Knowing who Jesus is in the abstract is not the same as trusting him in the specific, wet, embodied crisis. Faith is very seldom lost in a crisis; it is mislaid — and “where is your faith?” is a search rather than an accusation.

The passage is not primarily about the disciples' failure. It is about the one who was in the boat with them. He did not abandon them in the storm and he did not scold them for waking him. He stilled it, and then invited them to examine where their faith had been — not to condemn but to grow.

And the sea does not negotiate. It does not respond to authority, or reputation, or courage; it has drowned better sailors than these. It heard a tired man speak from the back of a small boat, and it lay down.

verseByVerse.quote: One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, 'Let us go across to the other side of the lake.' So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us go across to the other side of the lake.

Hold on to who said that, because it matters for everything that follows. The trip was not the disciples' idea and it was not a detour. They are in that boat, in that weather, because Jesus told them to get in and where to go.

That disposes at the outset of a reading this story often gets: that the storm was a consequence of some failure. It was not. Obedience put them there.

And as they sailed he fell asleep.

It is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus is described as sleeping, and it is one of the plainest windows into his humanity. He is exhausted. He has been preaching to crowds all day, and the moment the boat is under way he is unconscious in the stern — Mark adds the detail that he was on a cushion (Mark 4:38).

The Son of God, asleep, in a fishing boat, because he was too tired to stay awake. That is not a lapse in the narrative. It is the incarnation, doing what a body does.

And a windstorm came down on the lake.

The verb is exact and so is the geography. The Sea of Galilee sits about two hundred metres below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines funnelling down to the water from the Golan heights to the east. Cold air off the heights drops into the warm basin without warning, and the lake — which is small, and shallow — goes from flat to dangerous in minutes. It still does.

And they were filling with water and were in danger.

Luke, who is not a sailor, states the professional verdict plainly: they were in danger. And the men making that assessment include four commercial fishermen who had worked this water their whole lives. This is not landsmen panicking. These are the people you would want in the boat, and they have concluded they are going to drown.

Which is worth saying to anyone who has been told that fear is always a failure of faith. Sometimes fear is simply an accurate reading of the instruments.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and woke him, saying, 'Master, Master, we are perishing!' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Master, Master, we are perishing!

The doubled address is the sound of men shaking somebody awake. And their verdict is in the present tense: not we are going to drown but we are perishing — it is happening.

Notice what they do, though, underneath the panic. They wake him. Whatever they expected of a carpenter in a storm, some instinct sent them to the back of the boat rather than to the oars. It is not much of a faith and it is pointed in exactly the right direction — which is very often what faith looks like at three in the morning.

And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves.

The verb is epetimēsen, and Luke has used it before in this Gospel — of the demon in the synagogue (4:35), and of Peter's mother-in-law's fever (4:39). He rebuked them. It is the word for a sharp word of command to something that has no business behaving as it is.

And here is the thing to sit with. There is no prayer. He does not ask his Father to still the storm; Elijah would have. He speaks to the weather, in the imperative, the way a man speaks to a dog that is out of order.

And they ceased, and there was a calm.

Luke's word for what followed is galēnē — a dead flat calm. Anyone who has been on water knows how strange that is. When a wind drops, the sea does not; the swell runs on for a long time afterwards. Here the wind stops and the water goes flat in the same instant, and the boat is suddenly sitting still on a mirror with twelve soaked men in it.

What they had asked for was rescue. What they got was a demonstration.

Because in the Scriptures they had memorised as boys, there is exactly one person who does this. He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Ps. 107:29). You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Ps. 89:9). Who shut in the sea with doors… and said, Thus far shall you come, and no farther? (Job 38:8-11).

The one who does that is asleep in the stern of their boat, and they had just woken him up.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Where is your faith?' And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, 'Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them, Where is your faith?

The question is gentler than it looks in English, and it repays attention. He does not say why have you no faith? He asks where it has gone — which assumes they have some, and that it was mislaid rather than absent.

And it is worth being clear about what he is not rebuking. Not their fear of the storm; that was an accurate assessment by professionals. Not their waking him; that was the right instinct. What has gone missing is the conclusion they should have drawn from everything they had already seen — that the person in the boat with them was not in the same category as the weather.

They had watched him command a demon and a fever with a word. They had watched a dead man sit up at a town gate. The storm did not find them ignorant; it found them not applying what they knew.

Which is the ordinary condition of most believers in most crises, and there is comfort in seeing it named without contempt. Faith is very seldom lost in a crisis. It is mislaid — and the question is not an accusation but a search: where did you put it?

And they were afraid, and they marveled.

Luke is precise and slightly startling here. They were more frightened after the storm stopped than during it. The wind had merely threatened their lives. What came next threatened their categories.

Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?

There it is — the question this whole Gospel exists to answer, asked out loud for the first time by the men closest to him, sitting in a wet boat on a flat sea.

They do not answer it. Luke leaves it hanging, and he will leave it hanging for another nine chapters until Peter finally says the word at Caesarea Philippi. But everyone in that boat had sung Psalm 107 since childhood, and every one of them knew who it is that hushes the waves.

The sea does not negotiate. It does not respond to authority, or reputation, or courage; it has drowned better sailors than these and will again. And it heard a tired man speak from the back of a small boat, and it lay down. There is only one who has ever been obeyed like that, and he had been asleep four feet away from them the whole time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–39 — Jesus Heals a Man with a Demon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the far shore — Gentile territory, east of the lake, with pigs on the hillsides — a man possessed by a legion of demons meets Jesus and falls at his feet.

The description is harrowing and deliberate. He wore no clothes; he did not live in a house but among the tombs; he had repeatedly broken the chains put on him and been driven into the desert. Stripped of clothing, of community and of self-determination, he is not described as a man with a problem but as a site.

Two puzzles meet a careful reader here. Gerasa lay thirty miles inland, and Gadara six miles off; neither is on the shore. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa, modern Kursi, was the spot — a small place on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water — while Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached that coast. And Matthew names two men where Mark and Luke name one: Matthew adds a second, he does not subtract one, and the other two follow the man who spoke and who was left with a story to tell.

The demons recognise Jesus at once and their theology is impeccable: “Son of the Most High God” — the Gentile form of the title, fitted to the postcode. But look at the verb. They beg. Three times in this scene the powers of darkness plead, which is Luke's way of showing how the balance of power stands the moment Jesus steps ashore.

“Legion” was nominally six thousand men, and a legion is not a crowd but an occupying force. The word would have had an edge in the Decapolis, where people had watched real ones march. And the answer comes from the occupation rather than the man: asked his own name, there is no I left to reply.

They beg not to be sent to the abyss — the sealed prison of rebel spirits (Rev. 20:1-3) — but into the pigs. Jesus permits it, and it is the demons who stampede the herd, doing to two thousand animals in a moment what they had done to one man for years.
