The lake full of drowned swine is the plainest possible evidence of what he had been living under.

The townspeople find him clothed, in his right mind, and sitting at the feet of Jesus — the posture of a disciple. And they ask Jesus to leave. The man himself begs to come along; that is the one request in the chapter that is refused. “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.”
verseByVerse.theology:
This is the most comprehensive exorcism narrative in the Gospels, and it is performed in Gentile territory, on a Gentile man, before an audience of Gentile herdsmen. The geography is the theology: the kingdom of God does not stop at the borders of Israel.

The Gerasene man is the Gentile counterpart to the demonised man in the Capernaum synagogue (4:33) — both liberated by the same word, with the same authority, and neither able to put up the slightest resistance.

The restored man is “in his right mind” — sōphronounta, the word for the sober self-possession the New Testament calls for in Christian character — and he is sitting at Jesus's feet, where a disciple sits (cf. 10:39; Acts 22:3). The demonic occupation has not merely been evicted; the ground has been given to somebody else.

That distinction matters, because a deliverance that only removes does not hold. Jesus said so himself: a house swept and empty gets reoccupied (11:24-26). The sitting at the feet is not incidental colour. It is the theological point of the healing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The townspeople who ask Jesus to leave are the cautionary portrait of a community that values what it can calculate over what it cannot control. The pigs are gone; the man is well. The arithmetic should be straightforward.

But the fear is real, and Luke names it: something has happened here that they do not control. A lunatic in the tombs can at least be chained. Every generation of the church has had to decide whether to welcome the disruptive grace of God or manage it into something more comfortable — and Jesus does not argue with them. He gets into the boat and goes. He will not force himself on a community that has counted the cost and decided against him.

The man's desire to follow, and Jesus's refusal, is the missionary call in its most particular form: go to the people who already know you. That is a harder road than the boat. Everyone who has been converted where their old life is public knowledge understands it.

And he is sent to declare not a doctrine but a testimony — the one subject on which he is the world's leading authority. Then Luke does something quietly enormous and leaves it without comment: Jesus said “declare how much God has done for you,” and the man went and proclaimed “how much Jesus had done for him.” The two sentences sit three words apart, and Luke sees nothing to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They land on the far shore, and everything about the place is foreign.

The country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. This is Gentile territory — the region of the Decapolis, east of the lake, Greek-speaking, with pigs on the hillsides, which tells you at once that no Jewish community is farming here.

Two things about this crossing will stop a reader with a map or a harmony, and both are worth settling.

The first is the place. Gerasa lay some thirty miles inland; no herd could run from there down a bank into the lake. Matthew names the Gadarenes, and Gadara is about six miles off, still not on the shore. Some manuscripts of all three Gospels read Gergesenes. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa — modern Kursi — was the actual spot, a small place on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water, exactly as the story requires, while Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached down to that coast. Each writer named the region by the city his own readers would recognise, much as one might place a village in greater London. The steep bank is still there.

The second is the arithmetic. Luke describes one man, and so does Mark; Matthew says there were two (Matt. 8:28). Neither denies the other — Matthew adds a second man, he does not subtract one. Where a pair is involved and only one does the talking and only one is left with a story to tell, a writer naturally follows him. Mark and Luke keep the camera on the man who spoke, who was called Legion, who begged to come along and was sent home instead. The same thing happens at Jericho, where Matthew has two blind men and Mark names only Bartimaeus.

There met him a man from the city who had demons.

Then Luke sets out what was left of him, in three strokes.

For a long time he had worn no clothes — not an eccentricity but the loss of the most basic mark of human dignity, and Luke's for a long time says this was his settled condition, not a crisis.

And he had not lived in a house — no address, no household, no place at anybody's table.

But among the tombs — which in a Jewish frame is the last word in uncleanness, and in any frame is a man living among the dead because the living will not have him.

He has been stripped of clothing, community and personhood. He is not described as a man with a problem. He is described as a site.

verseByVerse.quote: When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, 'What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.' For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him.

He gets there first. Jesus has just stepped off the boat; the man comes at a run, screaming, and goes down at his feet — which is, whatever else is happening inside him, the posture of worship, forced out of an enemy.

What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.

The opening phrase is a stock formula of confrontation — literally what to me and to you?, the ancient equivalent of what do you want with me? The same words came out of the demon in the Capernaum synagogue (4:34).

And once again the theology is impeccable. Son of the Most High God is exactly right, and it is the title Gabriel used to Mary (1:32). Notice, too, that the demon uses the Gentile form — Most High God was how pagans referred to the God of Israel. Even the vocabulary is fitted to the postcode.

But look at the verb: I beg you. This is the first of four times in this scene that begging happens, and three of them come from the demons. The powers of darkness spend this entire passage pleading — which is Luke's way of telling you exactly how the balance of power stands the moment Jesus steps ashore.

Do not torment me. They are not asking to be left alone. They are asking about timing, and they know there is a schedule. Matthew records the same demons saying it outright: have you come here to torment us before the time? (Matt. 8:29). They have better eschatology than most of the people in this Gospel.

Then Luke's parenthesis, and it is the detail the older commentary skipped entirely: For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.

Two facts about the town are buried in that. They had tried. Somebody bought chains, and posted guards, and did it repeatedly — this was a community attempting, in the only way it knew, to manage a man it could not help. And every attempt failed, and each failure sent him further out into the desert.

That is what human management of a spiritual bondage looks like. Restraint is not deliverance. Chains can stop a man harming anybody; they cannot give him back his mind.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then asked him, 'What is your name?' And he said, 'Legion,' for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus then asked him, What is your name?

It is the only question Jesus asks in the whole encounter, and it is worth asking why he asks it.

Not for information. The likeliest reason is the simplest: a name is what a person has, and this man has not been addressed as a person in years. The town called him a danger; the tombs were his address. Jesus asks him who he is.

And he said, Legion, for many demons had entered him.

The answer is horrifying on two counts.

First, what it means. A Roman legion was nominally six thousand men. Whether the number is literal or a way of saying an army, the sense is the same — and a legion is not a crowd. It is an occupying force: organised, disciplined, under orders, and in possession of ground.

Second, who answers. The question was put to the man, and what comes out is the occupation speaking in the first person. He has been so comprehensively taken over that when asked for his own name he gives theirs. There is no I left to reply.

And there is an edge in the word that a man in the Decapolis would have felt. The people of that region knew what a legion was; they had watched them march. The word for what has destroyed this man is the word for what occupied his country.

And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.

The abyss is the deep — in the Greek Old Testament it renders the primeval waters of Genesis 1, and in later Jewish writing and in Revelation it is the prison of rebel spirits, the pit that is shut and sealed (Rev. 9:1-2; 20:1-3).

So they know where they are going, and they know he can send them, and they know they cannot stop him. Everything in this exchange is negotiation from a position of total defeat. The one thing they never attempt is resistance.

Between the arrival at verse 27 and the request at verse 31, there has not been a struggle. There has only been begging.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission.

Two questions press on any thoughtful reader here, and both deserve straight answers rather than being hurried past.

Why did Jesus permit it? And what is the drowning meant to say?

Start with who does the drowning. Jesus does not command the pigs into the lake. He grants a request, and it is the demons who stampede the herd to its death — doing to two thousand animals in a moment what they had been doing to one man for years. The destruction is theirs, and it unmasks them.

That is the first answer. This is what these powers always do to whatever they occupy. The town had been looking at a naked man in the tombs and calling it madness. Now they have a hillside of evidence about what had actually been living in him, and it is impossible to misread.

The second answer is about arithmetic, and the objection has to be met honestly: sceptics have long pointed to the drowned herd as proof that Jesus was careless of property and cruel to animals.

Weigh the exchange as it stands. One human being — made in the image of God, somebody's son — is pulled out of a living death. A herd of pigs is lost. Jesus refuses the calculation that counts the livestock and forgets the man. Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! he says elsewhere (Matt. 12:12), and the scale holds here. A Saviour who would leave a man among the tombs to protect a herd would be no Saviour at all.

There is a third thing, and the next verses will show it. The ruined herd forced the district to a decision it could no longer avoid. It put a price on the table.

Scripture does not linger over the owners' loss — not because the loss did not happen, but because the point of the story is about to be standing there clothed and in his right mind. The pigs are the price tag the town could see. The man is the treasure it could not.

verseByVerse.quote: When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind.

Luke sets the restoration against the ruin, item by item, and every term answers something in verse 27.

He had worn no clothes: he is clothed. He had lived among the tombs, driven into the desert: he is sitting. He had been out of his mind: he is in his right mind — sōphronounta, the word for sober, self-possessed sanity.

And the fourth item is the one that is not merely a reversal: at the feet of Jesus. That is where a disciple sits. It is where Mary of Bethany will sit (10:39), and where Paul says he sat under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). The man has not simply been emptied. He has been re-seated.

That distinction matters, because deliverance that only removes is not deliverance for long. Jesus said so himself: a house swept and empty gets reoccupied (11:24-26). What happened here is that the ground was taken back and then given to somebody.

And they were afraid.

Then the sentence that is the real indictment of the passage: all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear.

Look at what they are looking at. The man everyone in that district had given up on — the one they had chained, and guarded, and finally left in the graveyard — is sitting quietly in his right mind, dressed, listening. It is the best thing that has happened in that region in years.

And they want the man who did it to leave.

Two things are moving in them, and Luke names one and implies the other. The stated reason is fear — and it is the same fear that fell on the fishermen when the sea went flat. Something has come into their district that they cannot manage, and that is genuinely more unsettling than a lunatic in the tombs, because a lunatic can at least be chained.

The unstated one is the hillside. There is a herd in the lake and somebody has to account for it.

And notice what Jesus does with the request. He does not argue, or press, or stay to reason with them. So he got into the boat and returned. He came a long way across a dangerous lake for one man, and when the district asked him to go, he went.

That is a sobering mercy. He will not force himself on a community that has counted the cost and decided against him.

verseByVerse.quote: The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, 'Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.' And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him.

This is the fourth begging in the passage, and the first that comes from a human being. The demons begged not to be tormented, and begged not to go to the abyss, and begged to enter the pigs. Now the man begs to stay with Jesus.

And it is the only request in the chapter that is refused.

Consider what he was asking for and why it was reasonable. His neighbours had just told Jesus to leave. Every person in that district knew what he had been; there is no starting again in a place like that. The boat was leaving, and on it were twelve men who had also left their trades to follow, and he wanted a place among them. Given what he had come out of, it is difficult to imagine a more understandable request.

But Jesus sent him away, saying, Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.

Two commands, and both cost him something.

Return to your home. Back to the house he had not lived in, to relatives who had watched him deteriorate, to a town that had chained him and then given up. That is a harder road than the boat, and everyone who has ever been converted in a place where their old life is public knowledge knows it.

Declare how much God has done for you. He is not sent to argue, or to teach, or to explain the kingdom of God — he has had perhaps an hour's instruction. He is sent to tell people what happened to him, which is the one subject on which he is the world's leading authority.

That is worth holding on to by anybody who has ever felt disqualified from saying anything. The first missionary to Gentile territory had no training, no Scriptures, and no theology, and he had a before and an after that an entire district had witnessed.

And then Luke does something quietly enormous, and leaves it without comment.

Jesus said: declare how much God has done for you. And the man went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.

He was told to speak about God. He spoke about Jesus. Luke sets the two sentences side by side, three words apart, and does not explain — because as far as he is concerned there is nothing to explain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–56 — Jesus Heals a Woman and Raises Jairus's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final section is Luke's most carefully interlaced double narrative — a healing folded inside a raising, with each story interpreting the other.

Jairus is a ruler of the synagogue: a lay official who organised the services and carried the community's respect, and a member of the class that had been watching Jesus with hostility since chapter 5. He falls at Jesus's feet in the road, in front of people who know exactly who he is. His only daughter, about twelve, is dying, and every consideration of position has gone.

Jesus goes with him. The crowd presses. And a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years — exactly as long as the girl has been alive — reaches through the crowd and touches the tassel on the corner of his garment.

Her twelve years had cost far more than health. Leviticus 15:25-27 put a woman in her condition under continuing ritual uncleanness, and not only her: anything she sat on, anyone who touched her. Twelve years without the synagogue, without normal contact, very likely without a husband — and none of it her fault. Luke, a doctor, records the failure of his own profession without flinching: she had spent everything and was no better.

Her approach is furtive because it had to be; by the law she understood, her touch would defile him. And once again the traffic runs the wrong way. The bleeding stops.

Jesus stops the whole procession to ask who touched him — a question he already knows the answer to. Peter's exasperation is reasonable and Luke lets it stand. But he will not take a transaction where a person is available: she had tried to take the gift and stay invisible, and that would have left her physically healed and socially exactly as she was. He makes her say it out loud, in public — which puts her restoration on the record where her whole town can hear it — and then calls her “Daughter,” the only time in the Gospels he uses that word to a woman.

And while he is still speaking, the message comes: “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” From where Jairus stands, the delay killed her. Somebody else's twelve-year problem was attended to first, and his child ran out of time.

“Do not fear; only believe.” Then the mourners are put out, the girl is taken by the hand — “Child, arise” — and her spirit returns. And the first thing Jesus says afterwards is that somebody should get her something to eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
The interlacing of the two stories is a masterpiece of narrative theology. The woman healed on the way to Jairus's house teaches Jairus — and the reader — that the delay did not diminish Jesus's power or exhaust his compassion. The one who felt power go out of him for her has more than enough for a dead girl.

Jairus is being taught, at his own cost and in real time, to resist the word that says “it is too late.” The “too late” of the messengers is not too late for the Lord of life, and Jairus had just watched, at close range, what this man does for somebody who ran out of options twelve years ago.

“She is not dead but sleeping” is not a correction of the diagnosis, and Luke — a physician — gives three signals that she was genuinely dead: the professional mourners had arrived, the crowd knew, and “her spirit returned.” Jesus is changing a category, not disputing a fact. Sleep is the condition from which you are expected to get up, and that is now what death is for those who belong to him (1 Thess. 4:13-15; John 11:11).

The woman's touch of the “fringe” may point to the tassels of Numbers 15:38-40, worn as a reminder of the commandments. Malachi 4:2 had promised that the sun of righteousness would rise “with healing in its wings,” and the Hebrew for wings is the word for the corners of a garment. She may have been reaching, knowingly or not, for exactly that.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's twelve years, her exhausted resources, her uncleanness and her invisibility are the conditions in which she finally comes. She did not come while she still had options; she came when she had nothing left.

And Jesus's response — stopping in the middle of a crowd, insisting on finding her, calling her “daughter,” declaring her faith in front of everyone — is the public vindication of a person who arrived at the bottom of her resources. Her faith was ignorant in its theology, furtive in its method and frightened in its execution, and he calls it faith and commends it aloud.

Jairus's journey is faith pushed to its absolute limit. He did everything right: he found Jesus, he fell at his feet, he asked in time. Then the delay, and then the word that it was over. This has to be said plainly, because it is what a great many lives feel like and pious hurry past it is worthless.

“Only believe” is not a technique, and it is not an instruction to generate a quantity of faith sufficient to raise the dead — that reading crushes bereaved people. It is a word to a man who has just been told it is finished, asking him to keep hold of the person beside him for another ten minutes.

And the last instruction in the house is the one that could not have been invented. A girl has been raised from the dead, the room is beyond speech, and the Son of God says: get her something to eat. She is a child, and she has been ill, and she will be hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him.

The contrast with the last verse is deliberate and painful. One shore asked him to leave; the other has been standing about waiting for the boat to come back.

And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue.

Luke gives us his name and his office, and both matter. A ruler of the synagogue was not a priest but a lay official — the man who organised the services, appointed the readers, kept the building, and carried a good deal of the community's respect. In a Galilean town he was somebody.

He is also, by definition, a member of the class that has been watching Jesus with increasing hostility since chapter 5. The men who came from every village of Galilee and Judea to sit and observe (5:17) were his colleagues.

And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him.

He goes down in the road, in front of a crowd of people who know exactly who he is. Whatever position he held in that town, and whatever the synagogue authorities had been saying about this preacher, it is all gone in a second. He is not managing his reputation. He has a dying child.

That is one of the things suffering does, and it is not always a cruelty. It strips away the calculations we cannot ordinarily get past. There are people who have arrived at Christ by roads they would never have chosen, and Jairus is one of them: he did not come because his theology changed. He came because his daughter was dying and there was nowhere else.

For he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying.

Luke's detail is a physician's and a storyteller's at once. Only — the same word he used of the widow's son at Nain (7:12), and it does the same work. About twelve, which in that culture is the edge of womanhood, the year a girl becomes marriageable. She has had exactly one life's-worth of a childhood, and it is ending.

And the number will matter again in ten verses.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke interrupts himself. Jesus is on his way to a dying child, the crowd is pressing, and the narrative stops for a woman nobody has noticed.

And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years.

Twelve. Jairus's daughter has been alive for twelve years; this woman has been bleeding for exactly as long. Luke has set the two side by side on purpose: one has had a life, and the other has been losing hers, over the same span.

Take in what those twelve years had cost her, because it is far more than a medical condition. Leviticus 15:25-27 puts a woman with a chronic discharge under continuing ritual uncleanness — and not only her. Anything she sat on was unclean. Anyone who touched her was unclean until evening. Which means twelve years without the synagogue, twelve years unable to handle food for her household, twelve years in which every human contact carried a consequence for the other person.

If she was married when it began, she is very unlikely to be married now.

So the isolation is total and it is enforced by the law of God, and it is not her fault. She has done nothing.

And though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone.

Luke, a doctor, records the failure of his own profession without flinching — and Mark is blunter still, saying she had suffered much under many physicians and had grown worse (Mark 5:26). Twelve years of treatments, each one costing money and hope, and at the end of it she is bankrupt and no better.

She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment.

Everything about that is furtive, and it had to be. She is ceremonially unclean in a dense crowd, touching a rabbi — and by the law she understood, her touch would defile him. She has no right to be there at all.

The fringe is probably the tzitzit, the tassel on the corner of the outer garment that every observant Jewish man wore as a reminder of the commandments (Num. 15:38-40). It is the furthest edge of him that a person crouching in a crowd could reach.

And immediately her discharge of blood ceased.

Twelve years, and it stops. And once again the traffic runs the wrong way: the uncleanness does not travel from her to him. Wholeness travels from him to her.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Who was it that touched me?' When all denied it, Peter said, 'Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!' But Jesus said, 'Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said, Who was it that touched me?

He is on his way to a dying child and he stops the whole procession to ask a question he already knows the answer to.

When all denied it, Peter said, Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!

Peter's exasperation is entirely reasonable and Luke lets it stand. There are hundreds of people jammed against him; the question is, on the face of it, absurd. It is also the second time in this chapter that Peter has spoken to Jesus in a crisis, and the first was we are perishing.

But Jesus said, Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.

He distinguishes between the crowd's pressing and this touch, and the distinction is the point. Hundreds were in physical contact with him. One person took something.

Power has gone out from me — dynamis, and Luke has used it before of the healing that flowed from him (6:19). Whatever exactly it means, it was not automatic and it was not free. Something went out of him, and he felt it go.

Now the real question: why stop? He knows what happened. She has what she came for. The child is dying up the road and every second matters.

He stops because a healing is not the same as a person, and he has not come for transactions.

She had tried to take the gift and remain invisible — which is entirely understandable for a woman in her position, and it would have left her exactly as she was in every way except the physical. Still unspoken-of. Still, as far as her town was concerned, unclean. Still nobody's daughter.

He will not let her have it that way. He is going to make her say it out loud, in front of everyone, and then he is going to say something to her that she can carry for the rest of her life — and he holds up a dying child's father in the road while he does it.

Which is worth registering by anyone who has ever wanted the benefits of Christ without the exposure of being known by him. He asks the question. He always asks the question.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling.

Luke's phrasing is exact. She did not come forward; she came when she saw that hiding had failed. And she is shaking.

Why? Not, presumably, because she doubted the healing — she could feel it. She is frightened because of what she has just done: an unclean woman has touched a rabbi in public and taken something without asking. In front of a crowd, and a synagogue ruler, she is about to be exposed as both ceremonially defiling and presumptuous.

And falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed.

She tells the whole thing. Twelve years of it, out loud, to a street full of strangers — the condition she has never been able to name in public, the money spent, the doctors, and what happened when she reached the tassel.

That is the confession he stopped the procession to get, and it is worth seeing why it was worth the delay. Her testimony is now on the public record. Everyone in that crowd has heard, from her own mouth, that she is well — which means she can go back into the synagogue, and into her family's kitchen, and into ordinary human contact, and nobody can say otherwise.

He did not merely stop the bleeding. He put her back into the community, and he did it by making her speak.

And he said to her, Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.

Daughter. It is the only time in the Gospels that Jesus addresses a woman with that word. She has been nobody's for twelve years — untouchable, unmentionable, very likely unmarried by now — and the first word out of his mouth gives her a family.

And notice what he says her faith did, and what it did not. It did not manufacture the power; that came out of him. Her faith was simply the hand that reached. It was ignorant in its theology, furtive in its method, and frightened in its execution, and he calls it faith and commends it in public.

Go in peace. Not merely you are cured. Peace is shalom — wholeness, everything put back in its right place. She came for one thing and he gave her the lot: her body, her standing, her place among people, and a name to be called by.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, 'Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.' But Jesus on hearing this answered him, 'Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking.

The timing is unbearable, and Luke means it to be. Jesus is in the middle of the sentence that gives the woman her peace, and the messenger arrives.

Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.

Consider what that means for Jairus, who has been standing there through all of it. He came running with minutes to spare. Then the crowd slowed them. Then a woman touched a tassel, and Jesus stopped, and would not move on until she had told her entire story in public — and while she was telling it, his daughter died.

From where Jairus was standing, the delay killed her. Somebody else's twelve-year problem, which had waited twelve years and could surely have waited another hour, was attended to first — and his child ran out of time.

That has to be said plainly, because it is what a great many people's lives feel like, and pious hurry past it is worthless. Jairus is the man who did everything right, asked in time, and watched the answer arrive too late.

And notice the messenger's advice, which is kindly meant and entirely rational: do not trouble the Teacher any more. There is nothing more to be done. The category has changed from illness to death, and everybody knows the difference. The word for trouble means to bother, to put to inconvenience — the man is being gently told to let the poor rabbi get on.

But Jesus on hearing this answered him, Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.

He intercepts it. Luke's construction has Jesus overhearing the message and answering before Jairus can absorb it — cutting in before the sentence can land and take root.

Only believe. Two words, and they are not a technique. Jesus is not telling him to generate a quantity of faith sufficient to raise the dead; that is the reading which crushes bereaved people, and it is not what the sentence says. He is telling a man who has just been informed that it is over to keep holding on to the person standing next to him for another ten minutes.

And this is where the woman's healing was for Jairus as much as for her. He has just watched, at close range and at his own cost, what this man does for somebody who had run out of options twelve years ago.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, 'Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.' And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child.

Five people, and the composition is worth noticing. The three disciples who will also be on the mountain at the transfiguration (9:28) and in the garden at Gethsemane (22:39-45) — the three who see him raise the dead, see him in glory, and see him on his face in the dirt. And the parents, because this is their daughter and not a demonstration.

Everybody else is put out.

And all were weeping and mourning for her.

The house is full of noise. In that culture the mourning began immediately and it was loud; even a poor family was expected to provide professional mourners and flute-players, and the wailing was a formal, public performance of grief. It had started within the hour.

But he said, Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.

Now, what does that mean? Because it is regularly used to argue that she was never dead — that this was a coma, and Jesus was correcting a medical error.

That cannot be what Luke means, and Luke is a doctor. The messenger reported a death. The professional mourners had arrived, and they did not come for the unconscious. Luke's own next sentence says the crowd knew she was dead. And when she revives, Luke writes that her spirit returned (v. 55) — which is not the language of waking from a faint.

Jesus is not correcting a diagnosis. He is changing a category. Sleep is the condition from which you are expected to get up, and in his vocabulary that is now what death is — which is exactly how the New Testament will go on to speak of dead Christians: those who have fallen asleep (1 Thess. 4:13-15; John 11:11; Acts 7:60).

The word is not a denial of death. It is a claim about who is standing in the room.

And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.

Luke's phrasing is careful and it is not kind to them: they laughed knowing. This is not a misunderstanding; it is derision from people who were right about the facts.

They are the only people in this Gospel who laugh at Jesus, and they had every reason. He said something absurd. And within five minutes, the girl they had been paid to mourn walked past them out of the room.

verseByVerse.quote: But taking her by the hand he called, saying, 'Child, arise.' And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But taking her by the hand he called, saying, Child, arise.

He takes her hand. Again — as with the leper, as with the bier at Nain — he touches what the law says will defile him. Contact with a corpse meant seven days' uncleanness (Num. 19:11), and he reaches out and takes hold of a dead twelve-year-old.

And the word he uses is a family word. Mark preserves it in the original Aramaic — Talitha cumi — and it is the ordinary domestic phrase a mother uses in the morning. Little girl, get up. The greatest power in the universe is exercised in the tone of voice used to wake a child for school.

And her spirit returned, and she got up at once.

Luke's language is precise about what happened: her spirit returned. She had gone, and she came back. No process, no recovery, no gradual return of colour — she stood up.

And he directed that something should be given her to eat.

This is the sentence that gives the passage away, and it is the reason no one could have invented it.

A twelve-year-old has just been raised from the dead in front of her parents and three grown men. The room must be beyond speech. And the first thing the Son of God says, having conquered death in a bedroom in Galilee, is: get her something to eat.

She is a child, and she has been ill, and she will be hungry.

There is more of what he is like in that instruction than in the miracle before it. The one who commands the wind and the abyss and the grave, and who has just called a girl's spirit back into her body, is also the one who notices that nobody has thought about her breakfast.

And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

Which is, on the face of it, impossible — a houseful of mourners is outside, and they had watched her die. But he is not asking them to keep a secret so much as refusing to be turned into a spectacle, and Luke has recorded the same instruction twice before.

He came across a lake through a storm, was asked to leave by one district, stopped for a woman nobody could see, and walked out of that house leaving a family with their daughter and a strict instruction to say nothing about it. He was not building a reputation. He was going to a cross, and on the way he was raising the dead and asking whether anyone had fed the child.

8.text: <sup>1</sup> Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, <sup>2</sup> and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, <sup>3</sup> and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means. <sup>4</sup> And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, <sup>5</sup> “A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. <sup>6</sup> And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. <sup>7</sup> And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. <sup>8</sup> And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>9</sup> And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, <sup>10</sup> he said, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’ <sup>11</sup> Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. <sup>12</sup> The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. <sup>13</sup> And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away. <sup>14</sup> And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature. <sup>15</sup> As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience. <sup>16</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>17</sup> For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light. <sup>18</sup> Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.” <sup>19</sup> Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. <sup>20</sup> And he was told, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.” <sup>21</sup> But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” <sup>22</sup> One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side of the lake.” So they set out, <sup>23</sup> and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger. <sup>24</sup> And they went and woke him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm. <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Where is your faith?” And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” <sup>26</sup> Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. <sup>27</sup> When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. <sup>28</sup> When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.” <sup>29</sup> For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.) <sup>30</sup> Jesus then asked him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Legion,” for many demons had entered him. <sup>31</sup> And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. <sup>32</sup> Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. <sup>33</sup> Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. <sup>34</sup> When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. <sup>35</sup> Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>36</sup> And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. <sup>37</sup> Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned. <sup>38</sup> The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, <sup>39</sup> “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.” And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him. <sup>40</sup> Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. <sup>41</sup> And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, <sup>42</sup> for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. <sup>43</sup> And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. <sup>44</sup> She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased. <sup>45</sup> And Jesus said, “Who was it that touched me?” When all denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!” <sup>46</sup> But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.” <sup>47</sup> And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” <sup>49</sup> While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus on hearing this answered him, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.” <sup>51</sup> And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. <sup>52</sup> And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, “Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>53</sup> And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. <sup>54</sup> But taking her by the hand he called, saying, “Child, arise.” <sup>55</sup> And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. <sup>56</sup> And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

9.title: The Turning Point: Cross, Glory, and the Road to Jerusalem
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the pivot of Luke's Gospel — the hinge on which the whole narrative turns. Everything before it is the Galilean ministry of proclamation, healing, and gathering; everything after it (from 9:51 onward) is the great journey to Jerusalem, the road that leads to the cross. Within this single chapter, the Galilean ministry reaches its theological summit and its geographical end. The chapter contains the feeding of the five thousand, Peter's confession, the first and second passion predictions, the transfiguration, the healing of the epileptic boy, and the setting of the face toward Jerusalem. It is the most theologically dense chapter in Luke's Gospel.

The pivot on which chapter 9 turns is v. 51: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” The phrase “set his face” is the language of prophetic determination — Isaiah uses it of the Servant who “set his face like a flint” (Isaiah 50:7) in the face of suffering and shame. From this moment, every step Jesus takes in Luke is a step toward the cross. The transfiguration (vv. 28–36), which precedes this turning point, is the divine confirmation of the way that is being chosen — Moses and Elijah appear and speak of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word translated “departure” is exodos. The cross is not a defeat; it is the Exodus, the supreme act of divine liberation toward which all of Israel's history has been moving.

The chapter's central theological contribution is the collision between two kinds of glory. The crowds see a miracle-worker; Herod is perplexed by a rumoured prophet; the disciples feed five thousand from five loaves; Peter confesses the Christ of God — and immediately Jesus reframes everything. The Son of Man must suffer. Anyone who wants to follow must take up their cross daily. Whoever tries to save their life will lose it. The glory of the transfiguration is flanked on both sides by the shadow of the cross — and that is exactly the point. The glory and the cross are not opposites; they belong together. The cross is the path to the glory; the glory is the validation of the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Twelve Sent Out; Herod's Perplexity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus calls the twelve together, gives them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. Two words, and not synonyms: power (dynamis) is the capacity, authority (exousia) is the right. Both are given, and neither is earned.

The instructions are deliberately spartan — no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic. Between them those five items cover security, supply and comfort, and he takes all five away. The messengers are to depend entirely on the hospitality of those they visit, staying in whatever house first receives them and not moving on to a better one.

A reader comparing Gospels will find a difficulty: Mark records that they were to take nothing except a staff (Mark 6:8). The likeliest explanation turns on two different verbs. Mark's is about what to pick up — the stick already in your hand may come. Luke's is about what to acquire — do not go to the market first. Both fit the point of the list, which is not a uniform but a posture: do not equip yourself against the possibility that God will not provide.

Where they are not received, they are to shake the dust from their feet — the gesture a Jew used at the border when returning from Gentile territory, here applied to Jewish villages that refuse the kingdom's messengers. The old boundary has moved. It now runs not around the nation but around the message.

Luke reports the whole mission in one verse: they went, they preached, they healed, everywhere. What is absent is as striking as what is there — no account of the first house, the first refusal, the first demon. The instructions were not an ideal held up for admiration; they were the actual conditions under which twelve ordinary men walked into actual villages, and it worked.

Herod's perplexity closes the section. He has killed the greatest of the prophets and is now hearing that something greater is happening. The three theories on offer — John raised, Elijah appeared, one of the old prophets risen — are all respectful and all too small. His question, “who is this about whom I hear such things?”, is exactly the right question. And “he sought to see him” is the tragedy: he gets his wish at the trial (23:8), and Jesus does not answer him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sending of the twelve is the first instance of the apostolic mission. The word apostle means simply one who is sent; it says nothing about the man's qualities and everything about his commission.

The authority they receive is delegated — the same authority Jesus has been exercising since chapter 4, now given to them to exercise in his name. This is the pattern that will run through Acts: the Spirit-empowered community carrying the same authority of the same word into the same world.

Note who receives it. These are the men who will shortly argue about which of them is greatest (v. 46), fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), propose incinerating a Samaritan village (v. 54), and desert him in a garden. He does not wait until they are ready.

And the errand has two halves held together: to proclaim and to heal. Luke will not let them come apart. A ministry that heals and says nothing has withheld the reason; a ministry that talks and touches nothing has announced a kingdom that apparently changes nothing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The instructions to take nothing are not a travel policy but a structural embodiment of dependence. The messengers carry no resources that would make them independent of those they are sent to, which creates a bond of mutual vulnerability: the messenger depends on the receiver, and the receiver depends on the message.

The rule about staying in the first house is more pointed than it looks. A travelling teacher who attracted interest could expect better offers as the week went on. A messenger who upgrades has begun to be paid — and the moment his comfort depends on the standing of his host, his message is for sale.

The shaking of the dust takes a refusal seriously enough to mark it, without bitterness and without a backward argument. Two instincts are common and both are wrong: to keep pressing until the gospel becomes an irritation attached to a person, or to shrug it off and privately conclude they were never going to anyway. The dust does neither.

And Herod is the standing warning that the right question is not enough. A man can be genuinely interested in Jesus Christ for years, ask exactly the correct question, and go to his grave having done nothing about the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have been watching for four chapters. Now he hands them the equipment and sends them out.

He called the twelve together and gave them power and authority. Two words, and they are not synonyms. Power is dynamis — the capacity, the raw ability to do the thing. Authority is exousia — the right to do it. A man may have one without the other: a burglar has the power to open your door and no authority; a magistrate has the authority to arrest and may not have the strength. The Twelve are given both, and they are given them. Nobody in this sentence earned anything.

And notice the scope: over all demons and to cure diseases. That is exactly what Luke has shown Jesus doing since chapter 4 — the same two categories, kept carefully distinct, that a physician would keep distinct. What has been his alone is now delegated.

Which is worth pausing over, because of who is receiving it. These are the men who will shortly argue about which of them is greatest (v. 46), fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), want to incinerate a Samaritan village (v. 54), and desert him in a garden. He does not wait until they are ready. He never has.

And he sent them out. The verb is apesteilen, and it is the root of apostle — one who is sent. That is the whole meaning of the title. It says nothing about the man's qualities and everything about his commission; an apostle is not a rank but an errand.

And the errand has two halves, held together: to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. Word and work, announcement and demonstration. Luke will not let them come apart. A ministry that heals and says nothing has withheld the reason; a ministry that talks and touches nothing has announced a kingdom that apparently changes nothing.

There is something here for anyone who has ever felt unqualified to do anything for God, and it is not a compliment about hidden potential. It is better than that. What the Twelve took into those villages was not theirs. They had it because it was put into their hands that morning by somebody who had it to give — which is still the only way anyone has ever had anything worth carrying.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics.

Five items, and the list is not random. The staff is for the road and for defence; the bag is the beggar's or traveller's satchel; the bread is the day's food; the money is the reserve; the second tunic is the change of clothes and the blanket for a cold night. Between them they cover security, supply, and comfort. He takes all five away.

A reader comparing Gospels will find a genuine difficulty here. Mark records the same commission and says they were to take nothing except a staff (Mark 6:8); Luke and Matthew say no staff.

The likeliest explanation is the plainest, and it turns on the two different Greek verbs. Mark's phrasing is about what they should pick up — take nothing along, except that the stick already in your hand may come. Luke's is about what they should acquire or provide for themselves — do not go and get one. A man already carrying a staff keeps it; nobody is to go to the market first. That reading fits both texts without straining either, and it fits the point of the whole list, which is not a uniform but a posture: do not equip yourself against the possibility that God will not provide.

And notice how far that goes. They are sent to preach the kingdom of God with no food and no money — which means that within a day of setting out, every one of them will be hungry and dependent on somebody who has not yet heard the message.

And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart.

This is more pointed than it looks. In that culture, a travelling teacher who attracted interest could expect better offers as the week went on — a larger house, a wealthier host, a more comfortable room. The rule forbids it. Stay where you first landed, whoever they turn out to be.

The reason is not hard to see. A messenger who upgrades has begun to be paid, and the moment his comfort depends on the standing of his host, his message is for sale. It is also simply a matter of not humiliating the first family who took him in.

None of this is a dress code for modern missionaries, and turning it into one misses it. What it is, permanently, is a description of the posture: go without the equipment that would let you pretend you are not dependent, and do not let your accommodation start deciding your message.

verseByVerse.quote: And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.

He tells them in advance that some places will refuse. That is worth registering before anything else: rejection is not treated as a possibility to be prayed against but as a certainty to be prepared for. The men going out with power over demons are told, in the same breath, that some towns will simply not have them.

The gesture itself was a familiar one. A Jew returning from Gentile territory would shake the dust of the pagan road off his feet at the border, so as not to carry it into the land. It said: that place and this place are not the same, and I am bringing none of it home.

Which makes its use here extraordinary. These are Jewish villages. To shake the dust off in Galilee is to say that a town of Israelites which has refused the kingdom of God has put itself, by that refusal, outside — that the old boundary has moved, and it now runs not around the nation but around the message.

Note also what it is not. It is not a curse; the disciples call down nothing. It is not revenge; there is no argument, no denunciation in the street. It is a piece of theatre performed at the town limits, and it is called what it is: a testimony. The last thing that town gets is a picture of what it has just done.

And there is something in this for the ordinary business of speaking about Christ to people who do not want to hear. Two instincts are common and both are wrong. The first is to keep pressing — to treat a refusal as a problem of technique, and to go back with a better argument, and again, until the relationship is ruined and the gospel has become an irritation attached to a person. The second is to shrug it off, decide it never mattered, and privately conclude that they were never going to anyway.

The dust does neither. It takes the refusal with complete seriousness — this was not nothing, and something real has been declined — and then it leaves, without bitterness and without a backward argument, and walks to the next village.

Which means there is a point at which a faithful messenger stops. Not because he has given up on the people, and not because the message has lost its power, but because the responsibility has changed hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere.

One verse for the whole mission, and Luke tells us four things: they went, they preached, they healed, everywhere.

What is not here is as striking as what is. No account of how it felt to set out with no money. No record of a debate about the instructions. No description of the first house, or the first refusal, or the first demon. Luke — who is perfectly capable of narrating a mission in detail, and does so at length in his second volume — gives this one a single sentence.

The effect is to make the instructions of the previous verses land differently. They were not an ideal held up for admiration. They were the actual conditions under which twelve ordinary men actually walked into actual villages, and it worked.

Notice the order, too, because Luke keeps it consistent: preaching the gospel and healing. The proclamation is named first here, as it was in verse 2 and as it will be at 4:43, where Jesus said preaching was what he was sent for. The healings authenticate the announcement; they are not a substitute for it.

Everywhere. Luke's word is emphatic and it sits at the end of the sentence. Twelve men, on foot, in an unbroken circuit of villages that had never had anything like this — and the total time available before Jesus moves on is short. They did not concentrate on the promising places. They went through.

And there is a plain encouragement in the compression itself. The mission that Luke can summarise in nineteen words was, for the men doing it, weeks of dust, strange houses, meals they had not paid for, and conversations they had no way of preparing. It looked, from the inside, like ordinary hard work with no guarantee. It was, from the outside, the kingdom of God arriving in villages that had waited centuries.

Most obedience is like that. It is only ever visible as a summary afterwards.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. Herod said, 'John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?' And he sought to see him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mission has been so effective that the news reaches the palace, and Luke turns the camera on a man who will not appear again until the trial.

Herod the tetrarch — Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea. Tetrarch means ruler of a quarter, and it is a deliberately modest title; he wanted to be called king and Rome never allowed it.

Heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed. Luke's word is diēporei — thoroughly at a loss, unable to find a way through. It is the same word he will use of the women standing in front of an empty tomb (24:4).

The three theories he is hearing are all serious ones. John raised. Elijah appeared — the forerunner Malachi promised. One of the old prophets risen. Every explanation on offer puts Jesus somewhere in the prophetic tradition, and every one of them is too small, which is precisely the trouble: the categories available to that court cannot hold what is happening in the villages.

John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?

Luke gives Herod six words of autobiography and they are the six he would least want quoted. Notice the grammar: the pronoun is emphatic and the verb is his own. Not John was executed; not there was an unfortunate business at a banquet. John I beheaded. Whatever else this man is, he is not lying to himself about what he did.

Who is this? It is the right question. It is the question the disciples asked in the boat (8:25) and the question the whole Gospel exists to answer, and it has just been asked, correctly and urgently, by a murderer in a palace.

And he sought to see him.

There is the tragedy, and Luke will pay it off. Herod wants to see Jesus, and he keeps wanting it, and eventually he gets exactly what he asked for. At the trial, Pilate sends Jesus to him, and Luke tells us Herod was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him (23:8). He questions him at some length. And Jesus does not answer him — the only person in the Gospels to whom he says nothing at all.

The question was right and the wanting was real, and neither was ever going to be enough. A man can be genuinely interested in Jesus Christ for years, ask the correct question, and go to his grave having done nothing about the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Jesus Feeds the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The twelve return from their mission and Jesus withdraws with them to Bethsaida for rest. Mark gives his reason in his own words: “Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while.” The crowds find out where the boat is going and get there first.

So the rest lasts as long as it takes a crowd to work out the destination — and Luke records that “he welcomed them.” The verb means received gladly. He met the people who had wrecked his only plan for the week as though they had been invited, and spoke to them of the kingdom of God, and cured those who had need of healing, until the day was nearly over.

The disciples' suggestion is sensible and they are right about almost everything: it is late, the place is desolate, thousands need food and lodging, and the villages are the only source of either. Sending away is not wickedness; it is arithmetic, done honestly, by tired men. What the arithmetic never includes is the person standing next to them.

“You give them something to eat” is emphatic in the Greek — you give them — and there is no reading on which the twelve can obey it. Their answer is what an honest man says when handed an impossible order: here is the inventory. Five barley loaves and two fish, which John tells us belonged to a boy. They have even costed the alternative: Mark records two hundred denarii, two-thirds of a year's wage, and even that would not be enough.

They are right. Five loaves and two fish do not feed five thousand men — and Luke's andres means adult males specifically, so with women and children the real number is far higher. No amount of faith changes that arithmetic and Jesus never suggests otherwise. What he does is ask for the loaves. Nothing in this passage is multiplied before it is handed over.

The four verbs over the bread — took, blessed, broke, gave — are the ordinary actions of a Jewish householder, and Luke fixes them in the reader's memory because they return twice: at the Last Supper (22:19) and at Emmaus, where “their eyes were opened, and they recognised him” (24:30-31).

All ate and were satisfied — echortasthēsan, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the satisfaction God gives (Ps. 107:9; 132:15). And twelve baskets of fragments were gathered: one for each man who had done the arithmetic.
verseByVerse.theology:
The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle besides the resurrection recorded in all four Gospels, which signals its weight. The typology is dense: a multitude fed in a desolate place, as Israel was fed in the wilderness; the crowd seated in ordered companies of fifty, as Moses set the people in fifties (Exod. 18:25); the one greater than Moses giving bread not prayed down from heaven but broken from his own hands.

It is the New Testament's great sign of the messianic banquet — the feast Isaiah promised (Isa. 25:6-9) and Revelation describes as the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9). Every time the church gathers at the Lord's table it is taking a foretaste of that feast.

And the eucharistic action defines the church's life: receiving grace, returning it in blessing, breaking it in service, giving it away. He could have distributed the bread himself. Instead it goes from his hands into the disciples' and from theirs to the people — so that the men who said “send them away” spent the next hour giving away food they did not have.

The twelve baskets left over say what the whole scene says: the kingdom of God does not issue minimum rations. There was more at the end than at the beginning, and it was not close.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Send the crowd away” is the reasonable option in far more situations than this one — the pastoral problem genuinely beyond a church's capacity, the person whose needs are more than anyone in the congregation can carry, the ministry that cannot be staffed.

And notice what had just happened to these men. They had come back that same week from a mission in which they healed the sick with nothing in their pockets, and were still telling him about it two verses earlier. Experience of God's provision has a remarkably short half-life, and it is almost never available in the moment it would be most use.

“Bring what you have” can be preached as though the trick were to be optimistic about the loaves. It is not. The loaves are genuinely insufficient and everyone in the story knows it. The command is to put them in his hands anyway, in full knowledge that they will not do, and see what he does with them.

The rhythm of withdrawal and interruption is worth having by anyone who works with people and has learned, rightly, to guard their time. The guarding is not unspiritual — Jesus withdrew constantly. But the plan is not the master. There will be a day when what was properly and prayerfully arranged is taken by people who need something, and the question is whether they are met as an intrusion or as guests.

verseByVerse.quote: On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On their return the apostles told him all that they had done.

They come back full of it, and he listens. Then, Luke says, he took them and withdrew apart — Mark records the reason in Jesus's own words: Come away by yourselves to a desolate place and rest a while (Mark 6:31). The men have been working, and he is taking them away to recover.

When the crowds learned it, they followed him.

So the rest lasts as long as it takes a crowd to work out where the boat is going. Mark says they ran round the shore on foot and got there first.

Here is the moment, and everything about the reaction is worth watching. Jesus has just brought twelve exhausted men to a quiet place for the express purpose of resting, and several thousand people have arrived and taken it.

And he welcomed them.

The verb is apodexamenos — received gladly, made welcome. Not tolerated, not endured. He met the people who had wrecked his only plan for the week as though they had been invited.

And spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing.

He does both, and he keeps doing them until the day is nearly over (v. 12). Luke's phrase for the sick is careful: those who had need of healing — not everyone in the crowd, but those who had come with a need. He attended to the ones who required attention.

This pattern runs right through Luke, and it should not be flattened into a lesson about being available at all times, because that is not what Jesus does. He withdraws constantly. He gets into boats to get away. He goes up mountains alone at night. The rhythm is real and he defends it — right up to the moment when the need is standing in front of him, and then the rhythm gives way, every time.

Which is worth having by anyone who works with people and has learned, rightly, to guard their time. The guarding is not unspiritual; Jesus did it. But the plan is not the master. There will be a day when the thing you had properly and prayerfully arranged is taken from you by people who need something, and the question is whether they are met as an intrusion or as guests.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, 'Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the day began to wear away.

Luke's phrase is almost elegiac — the day was declining, the light going. And with the light goes the margin: a crowd of thousands, in open country, several hours from anywhere, with night coming.

And the twelve came and said to him, Send the crowd away.

Before this is criticised, it should be admitted that they are right about everything except one thing.

They are right that it is late. They are right that the place is desolate — erēmos, the wilderness word. They are right that thousands of people need lodging and food and that neither is available where they are standing. They are right that the surrounding villages are the only realistic source of either. And they are right that somebody has to say something, because Jesus has been teaching and healing all day and the sun is going down.

This is not laziness or hard-heartedness. It is twelve men who have taken responsibility for a logistical problem their teacher appears not to have noticed, and their solution is the only sensible one available: send them off now, while there is still enough light for them to walk.

Notice too what has just happened to them. These are men who have come back this same week from a mission in which they cast out demons and healed the sick with nothing in their pockets. Two verses ago they were telling him all about it. And now, facing a crowd with no food, their instinct is to calculate the resources and organise a dispersal.

That is not a special failing of theirs. Experience of God's provision has a remarkably short half-life in all of us, and it is almost never available in the moment it would be most use.

Send the crowd away. It is worth hearing the phrase on its own, because it is the reasonable option in more situations than this one — the pastoral problem that is genuinely beyond the church's capacity; the person whose needs are more than anyone in the congregation can carry; the ministry that cannot be staffed. Sending away is not wickedness. It is arithmetic, done honestly, by people who are tired.

What the arithmetic never includes is the person standing next to them.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'You give them something to eat.' They said, 'We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to them, You give them something to eat.

The pronoun is emphatic in the Greek: you give them. He does not dispute their assessment of the situation. He hands it back.

It is a shocking instruction, and it is meant to be. There is no possible reading on which the Twelve can obey it. He is telling twelve men with nothing to feed a crowd they have just correctly identified as unfeedable.

They said, We have no more than five loaves and two fish.

Their answer is exactly what an honest man says when handed an impossible order: here is the inventory. Five loaves — small barley cakes, John tells us, the food of the poor — and two fish, probably salted, the ordinary relish that went with bread. It is one packed lunch. John adds that it belonged to a boy in the crowd.

Unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.

There is a note of something in that clause, and it is not quite sarcasm but it is close. Mark supplies the figure they were working with: two hundred denarii, which is two-thirds of a labourer's annual wage, and even that would only give each person a little (Mark 6:37; John 6:7). They have costed it. It cannot be done.

And they are right. That has to be said plainly, because the disciples in this story are usually treated as slow, and here they are simply accurate. Five loaves and two fish do not feed five thousand men. No amount of faith changes that arithmetic, and Jesus never suggests otherwise.

What he does is ask for the loaves.

Which is the shape of the thing, and it is worth getting right, because bring what you have can be preached as though the trick were to be optimistic about the loaves. It is not. The loaves are genuinely insufficient and everyone in the story knows it. The command is not to believe in the bread. It is to put the bread in his hands anyway, in full knowledge that it will not do, and see what he does with it.

Nothing in this passage is multiplied before it is handed over. That is the whole point of the order of events.

verseByVerse.quote: For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, 'Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.' And they did so, and had them all sit down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there were about five thousand men.
