Luke's word is andres — adult males, specifically, not people in general. Matthew makes the implication explicit: besides women and children (Matt. 14:21). The real number in that field is very likely somewhere between ten and twenty thousand.

And he said to his disciples, Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.

Consider what that instruction commits the Twelve to. They have just told him it cannot be done. He now sends them out into a crowd of thousands, in failing light, to organise it into roughly a hundred separate companies of fifty — which is an hour's work at least, in front of hungry and increasingly irritable people, with five loaves in a bag and no explanation of what is about to happen.

They have to seat the whole crowd before they know there is anything to serve.

That is obedience with no visible warrant, and Luke records it in four words: and they did so. Whatever else may be said about these men, they went out into that field and did it.

Why groups of fifty? Two reasons suggest themselves, and both are in the text.

The practical one is distribution. A crowd of thousands cannot be fed by twelve men passing baskets through a mob; it can be fed by twelve men working a hundred defined companies, each one a manageable size, in order, with nobody missed.

The other is older. When Israel came out of Egypt and was fed in the wilderness, Moses set them in ordered companies — chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties (Exod. 18:25; cf. Num. 31:14). A crowd in a desolate place, arranged in fifties, about to be fed by God, is not an image any Jew would fail to recognise.

And there is something in the shape of it worth keeping. He did not feed a mass. He fed people in groups small enough to see each other's faces, seated on the grass, sharing out of the same basket — which is a good deal closer to a hundred suppers than to one enormous distribution, and it is the first picture in this Gospel of what the church would turn out to look like.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.

Four verbs, and Luke has chosen them with great care: he took, he blessed, he broke, he gave.

Every Jewish household head did exactly this at the start of a meal. He lifted the bread, looked up, said the blessing — Blessed are you, LORD our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth — broke it, and handed it round. There is nothing esoteric in the actions. What Luke is doing is fixing them in the reader's memory.

Because the same four verbs come back twice more, and both times they matter enormously. On the last night: he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them (22:19). And at Emmaus, in the house, with two men who have walked seven miles with a stranger: he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognised him (24:30-31).

Take, bless, break, give. It is how five thousand were fed on the grass; it is how the new covenant was instituted; it is how the risen Christ was recognised. Luke has laid a thread through his Gospel, and this is where he ties the first end of it.

Notice also the sequence in this verse. He does not multiply the bread and then break it. He gives thanks over five loaves — the actual, insufficient five — and it is in the breaking and the giving that there turns out to be more. Luke does not describe the miracle happening. There is no moment at which the pile visibly grows. There is a man breaking bread and handing it to twelve others, and it does not run out.

And gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd.

He could have handed it out himself. Instead the bread goes from his hands into theirs, and from theirs to the people — so that the men who had said send them away spend the next hour walking up and down a hillside giving away food they did not have.

He took what was offered him, and he gave thanks for it before it was anything like enough. That is the sentence to sit with. Five small loaves, held up in two hands in front of a hungry multitude, and a blessing spoken over them by the one through whom every field of barley in Galilee had been made.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they all ate and were satisfied.

All — every one of the thousands, women and children included, down to the last group of fifty at the far edge of the field. Nobody was missed and nobody got the end of the supply.

Were satisfied is echortasthēsan, and it is a strong word. It was used of animals grazed to the full, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the satisfaction God gives: I will abundantly bless her provisions; I will satisfy her poor with bread (Ps. 132:15); he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things (Ps. 107:9).

They were not given enough to take the edge off. They were fed until they had had enough, in a wilderness, at the end of a long day, by a man with five loaves.

And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces.

Twelve baskets. Not twelve crumbs — kophinoi, the stiff wicker baskets a traveller carried. There was more at the end than at the beginning, and it was not close.

The number is unlikely to be accidental. Twelve is the number of the tribes, and it is the number of the men who had said it could not be done — one basket each, carried back by the very people who had done the arithmetic. Whatever else they were going to remember about that afternoon, each of them walked off the field holding the evidence.

And note the instruction implied in picked up. The one who had just produced a meal for thousands out of a boy's lunch had the leftovers gathered. Nothing was wasted. Extravagance and carefulness sit in the same paragraph without the slightest tension.

What was brought to him was five loaves and two fish, and it was not enough, and everyone knew it was not enough, and the men who brought it said so out loud. And there was food on that hillside until thousands of people had eaten all they could hold, and then there was more left over than had been there to start with.

He has never yet been handed something too small to work with. He has never yet run short at the far end of the field. And whatever is put into his hands comes back multiplied, in baskets, with the ones who said it was impossible carrying them home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Peter's Confession and the Cost of Discipleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying — Luke alone tells us so, as he does at every hinge of this Gospel — and out of that prayer comes the question the whole book exists to answer.

“Who do the crowds say that I am?” The answers are the same three that reached Herod's court: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets risen. Every one is respectful; every one is wrong in the same way, placing him within the prophetic tradition rather than beyond it.

“But who do you say that I am?” The Greek puts the pronoun first and hard. It is a question no survey can answer. Peter says: “The Christ of God.”

And immediately, without celebration, Jesus charges them to tell no one — and begins to teach what the title actually means. “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.”

The silence is not modesty. In Galilee in that decade Messiah meant a son of David who would raise an army and break Rome; John records a crowd trying to make him king by force (John 6:15). The word is embargoed until it can carry the meaning he is about to give it. And the rejection is specified by office — the Sanhedrin, which is to say the entire official religious leadership of the people of God. Not Rome. The men who had the Scriptures.

The call to discipleship follows on the same terms, and Luke marks the audience: “he said to all.” This is not advanced material for the twelve. “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”

To deny the self is not to deny oneself things. The verb is the one Luke will use of Peter in the courtyard saying “I do not know him” (22:57). And “take up his cross” was not a metaphor to anyone hearing it: crucifixion was a live Roman practice, and the phrase described a condemned man carrying the beam of his own execution to the place where he would be nailed to it.

Then “daily,” which is Luke's addition — Matthew and Mark do not have it. It takes the most final image available and makes it a routine, which means it is not chiefly about martyrdom and not reserved for the exceptional.

The section closes with a promise that has troubled readers ever since: “there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” Luke answers it in the very next sentence.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter's confession is correct, and Luke records no commendation of it — Matthew's account has the blessing on Peter; Luke, writing for a Gentile church, moves straight to the reframing. The Christ of God is the suffering, dying, rising Son of Man.

“Son of Man” is not, as it sounds in English, a modest way of saying “a human being.” It comes from Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion and a kingdom that shall not pass away. It is a claim of enormous weight wrapped in a phrase that sounds humble — which is exactly why he could use it in public.

The word must (dei) is the divine-necessity word Luke uses at every turning point. The cross is not an accident, a miscalculation, or the defeat of the mission. It is the appointment. And he never once announces the death without the rising in the same breath.

On “will not taste death,” three answers are given and they are not equally strong. The weakest strains the words. The second, and much better, takes the kingdom in Luke's usual sense — God's reign breaking in — and points to the resurrection, Pentecost, and the spread Luke describes in his second volume, all within the lifetime of the hearers. But the strongest is the one Luke himself supplies: eight days later, three of them went up a mountain and saw the Son of Man in glory.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Daily” is the word that brings the cross within reach of an ordinary believer. It is not the dramatic act of martyrdom reserved for the exceptional disciple; it is the ordinary Tuesday in which the self is again told it does not rule here.

And self-denial needs guarding, because it can be twisted into something poisonous. It is not self-hatred, and it is not the erasure of a personality God made. It is the dethroning of the self as the thing every decision is finally referred back to.

“What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself?” is put at the extreme deliberately: if the trade fails at the maximum price it fails at every price below it. Nobody reading this will gain the whole world. The prices most people actually pay are small — a working life arranged around security, a set of decisions taken to keep a reputation intact, a marriage kept comfortable by never saying the true thing.

And shame is the right word, chosen over “deny” or “reject.” Very few people in a Western country will be asked to renounce Christ; a great many are embarrassed by him, and by his words particularly. What is actually being weighed, in the moment of going quiet at a dinner table, is the estimate of a roomful of people against the estimate of the Son of Man in the glory of the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, 'Who do the crowds say that I am?' And they answered, 'John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.' Then he said to them, 'But who do you say that I am?' And Peter answered, 'The Christ of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him.

Luke's sentence is slightly odd in English and deliberately so: praying alone, with the disciples there. It is his way of saying that Jesus was in prayer and they were nearby — and Luke alone tells us this. Matthew and Mark both record the question; only Luke says where it came from.

That is worth noticing, because it is a habit of this Gospel. The baptism, the choosing of the Twelve, the transfiguration, Gethsemane, the cross — Luke puts Jesus at prayer before every hinge in the narrative. The most important question in the book comes up out of a conversation with the Father.

Who do the crowds say that I am?

The answers are the same three that reached Herod's court eleven verses earlier: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the old prophets risen. The crowds are not hostile and they are not stupid. Every one of those answers is respectful, and every one puts him in the prophetic line — a great man in a great tradition.

And every one is wrong in the identical way. They are all attempts to fit him into a category that already exists.

Then he said to them, But who do you say that I am?

The Greek puts the pronoun first and hard: you — what do you say? It is the pivot of the Gospel, and it cannot be answered by a survey. Everything up to this point has been evidence; the question is what has been made of it.

And Peter answered, The Christ of God.

Three words in Greek, and they are the right ones. Christos is the Greek for Messiah, the Anointed — the one Israel had been promised since David, the king who would come. Peter has stopped putting him in the line of the prophets and named him as the one the whole line was pointing at.

Two things follow, and they will occupy the rest of the chapter.

The first is that the confession is correct and Luke records no commendation of it — Matthew's account has the blessing on Peter, and Luke, writing for a Gentile church, moves straight past it to what comes next.

The second is that being right about the title is not the same as understanding it. Peter has the correct word and, as the next ten verses will show, entirely the wrong picture. He is about to hear what the Christ of God actually involves, and within moments of getting it right he will be arguing with it.

Which is a fair description of most people's first real confession. The word is true. The content arrives later, and usually costs something.

verseByVerse.quote: And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying, 'The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one.

Two verbs, both forceful, stacked one on the other. Peter has just said the right thing and Jesus immediately puts a lid on it.

Why silence a true confession? Because in Galilee in that decade, Messiah meant something specific and largely political — a son of David who would raise an army, break Rome, and restore the kingdom. John's Gospel records a crowd trying to make him king by force after the feeding (John 6:15). A public messianic claim would have started a movement he had not come to lead, and finished with soldiers.

So the word is embargoed until it can carry the meaning he is about to give it — which he does in the very next sentence.

The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.

Take the title first. Having accepted Christ, he immediately calls himself the Son of Man, which is his own preferred self-description and is not, as it sounds in English, a modest way of saying a human being. It comes from Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom that shall not pass away. It is a claim of enormous weight, wrapped in a phrase that sounds humble — which is exactly why he could use it in public.

Then must. The Greek is dei, divine necessity, and Luke uses it at every hinge of this Gospel — a boy in the temple (2:49), a preacher who must go to the next town (4:43), and now this. The cross is not a miscalculation, a tragedy, or a plan that went wrong. It is the appointment.

Then the four things, in order: suffer, be rejected, be killed, be raised. The rejection is specified by office — the elders and chief priests and scribes, which is the Sanhedrin, which is to say the entire official religious leadership of the people of God. Not Rome. Not the pagans. The men who had the Scriptures.

And note where he puts the resurrection: in the same sentence, first time of telling. He never once announces the death without the rising. The disciples will still be devastated, and Luke will tell us why — they did not understand it (v. 45), and they were afraid to ask.

What Peter has confessed and what Jesus has just described are the same person. That is the hardest thing in the chapter, and everything after it is the working out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to all, 'If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to all. Luke marks the audience deliberately. What follows is not advanced material for the Twelve. It is the terms of entry, said to everyone standing there.

If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.

Three clauses, and the middle one has a word in it that is Luke's alone. Matthew and Mark record the saying without daily (Matt. 16:24; Mark 8:34). Luke adds it, and it changes the shape of the whole thing.

Deny himself. This is the first thing, and it is regularly misheard. It is not deny himself things — that is self-denial in the ordinary sense, giving up sugar or television, and it is not what the word says. The verb is aparneomai, and Luke will use it again in this Gospel for exactly one other thing: Peter, in a courtyard, saying I do not know him (22:57). To deny the self is to say about your own claims what Peter said about Jesus — I do not know this person; he has no standing here.

Which is worth guarding, because it can be twisted into something poisonous. It is not self-hatred, and it is not the erasure of a personality God made. It is the dethroning of the self as the thing every decision is finally referred back to.

Take up his cross. The picture was not a metaphor to anyone hearing it. Crucifixion was a live and public Roman practice, and the phrase described one thing: a condemned man carrying the beam of his own execution through the streets to the place where he would be nailed to it. Everyone in that crowd had seen it.

So the image is not bear your hardships. A difficult marriage, a chronic illness, a hard employer — those are real, and Scripture has a great deal to say about them, but they are not this. The cross is what a man picks up when he has already been sentenced and is on his way out of the city.

And then daily, and this is where Luke does his work. A cross is carried once. Luke's addition takes the most final image available and makes it a routine — which means it is not chiefly about martyrdom, and not reserved for the exceptional. It is the ordinary Tuesday of an ordinary believer, in which the self is again told it does not rule here.

For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.

The word for life is psychē — the self, the whole person. And the sentence is not a moral exhortation but a statement about how reality is built. A life organised around its own preservation is being lost in the act of being protected. There is no third option on offer, and the man who declines to choose has chosen.

verseByVerse.quote: For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself?

It is a commercial question, and the vocabulary is commercial: profit, gains, forfeits. He is asking about a transaction, and inviting the hearer to check the arithmetic.

And he sets the exchange rate at the most extreme point available. Not a good salary, not a comfortable life — the whole world. Everything. Every currency, every pleasure, every honour, every acre. Put all of it on one side of the scale.

Against it he sets one item: himself. Not his soul as some detachable religious component, but the man — the self who was going to enjoy all that. And the point is that the trade is not merely bad; it is incoherent. The buyer has purchased everything and disposed of the only person who could have had it.

Nobody in that crowd would ever gain the whole world, and nobody reading this will either. That is why the question is put at the extreme: if the trade fails at the maximum price, it fails at every price below it. And the prices most people actually pay are small — a working life arranged around security, a set of decisions taken to keep a reputation intact, a marriage kept comfortable by never saying the true thing.

For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory.

Shame is the right word for what usually happens, and it is worth saying that he chose it rather than denies or rejects. Very few people in a Western country will be asked to renounce Christ. A great many are embarrassed by him — by the words particularly, which is what he specifies: me and of my words. It is one thing to hold a private faith and quite another to be the person at the table who believes what he said about sin, or judgement, or himself.

The warning is exact and it is symmetrical: what is done to him now is what will be done then. And the then is described in a way designed to reframe the now — in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. The man whose association is currently a social liability is going to arrive in a company like that.

Which puts the embarrassment in proportion. What is actually being weighed, in the moment of going quiet at a dinner table, is the estimate of a roomful of people against the estimate of the Son of Man in the glory of the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.

This is one of the hardest sentences in the Gospels, and it should not be hurried, because sceptics have built a case on it and honest readers stumble over it.

The charge is simple. Jesus told the people in front of him that some of them would still be alive when the kingdom of God arrived. They all died. Therefore he was mistaken, and the church has been explaining away a failed prediction ever since.

Three answers are given, and they are not equally strong.

The weakest treats see the kingdom of God as the second coming and then argues about what taste death means. That does not work; the words are plain, and straining them does the text no favours.

The second, and much better, takes the kingdom to mean what Luke consistently means by it — not the end of the world but the reign of God breaking in. On that reading the promise was kept within the lifetime of the hearers, and spectacularly: in the resurrection, when the King came out of a tomb; at Pentecost, when the Spirit fell and three thousand entered the kingdom in a morning; and in the years Luke describes in his second volume, when the thing spread from Jerusalem to Rome. Men standing on that hillside saw all of it.

But the strongest answer is the one Luke himself supplies, and he supplies it in the very next sentence.

Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain (v. 28). All three Synoptic Gospels put the transfiguration immediately after this promise, and none of them does it by accident. Some standing here — and eight days later exactly three of them are taken up a mountain and shown the Son of Man in his glory, with Moses and Elijah beside him and the voice of the Father over him.

He said some of them would see the kingdom before they died. Eight days later, three of them did.

And the placing is a mercy as well as a fulfilment. He has just told them he is going to be rejected, killed, and raised, and told them all to pick up a cross. Then he takes three men up a mountain and lets them see, for a few minutes, what is on the other side of it.

Which is more or less how it still works. Nobody gets the mountain permanently, and nobody is asked to walk to Jerusalem without ever having seen anything.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
About eight days after the confession and the first passion prediction, Jesus takes Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray — and Luke alone tells us that is why he went. It happened while he was praying.

Luke is careful with his verbs. Mark and Matthew use metamorphōthē, the word behind metamorphosis; Luke, writing for Greek readers in a world full of stories about gods changing shape, avoids it and describes what was seen: his face became different, his clothing turned a white that flashed. Nothing was added to him. This is not Jesus becoming something more than he was; it is the covering coming off something always there.

Moses and Elijah appear in glory — the Law and the Prophets. Both had met God on the same mountain, Sinai and Horeb; both had asked in their way to see him and been given a back and a whisper. Now they stand in the light, talking with him.

And Luke alone tells us the subject. They “spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word is exodos. The man who led the first one — out of Egypt, through the blood of a lamb, through the sea — is standing there while the word is applied to a death in Jerusalem. It is the interpretation of the cross, given from heaven, before it happens: not a defeat but a deliverance, accomplished by a lamb, on a fixed date, by a leader who goes ahead of his people. And the verb is accomplish, not suffer.

The three were heavy with sleep and nearly missed it — the same three Luke will find asleep in Gethsemane (22:45). Peter's proposal to build three tents comes as Moses and Elijah are leaving: a man trying to stop something ending, and Luke's aside is candid and gentle, “not knowing what he said.” The proposal is wrong in a specific way: one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah, three equals.

The cloud interrupts him mid-sentence. It is the shekinah — the cloud of Sinai, of the tabernacle, of Solomon's temple, unseen in Israel for centuries — and the verb “overshadowed” is the one Gabriel used to Mary (1:35).

“This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” Then the cloud lifts, and Moses is gone, and Elijah is gone, and there are not three figures on that mountain requiring three tents.
verseByVerse.theology:
The transfiguration is at once christological and eschatological — revealing who Jesus is, and what the coming kingdom will look like. What the disciples see is not a separate divine form he can put on and take off; it is the radiance belonging to who he always is, momentarily unrestrained. The humanity that veiled the glory at Bethlehem is for a few minutes transparent to it. This is what John means by “we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (John 1:14).

Moses and Elijah's conversation is the most extraordinary discussion never recorded — two of the greatest figures of the Old Testament speaking with the Son of God about the cross that will accomplish the ultimate Exodus. Everything either of them ever wrote or did had been leaning towards it.

Some Bibles read “my Beloved” at v.35 rather than “my Chosen One,” and the manuscripts do differ. “Chosen One” is very likely what Luke wrote, and it is the harder reading — a copyist would naturally smooth it to match the baptism and the parallel in Matthew. And the phrase is deliberate: “my chosen” is Isaiah's word for the Servant (Isa. 42:1). On a mountain where they have just discussed his exodus, the Father names him with the Servant's title.

“Listen to him” is the only imperative in the scene, and it is aimed with precision at three men who have spent eight days failing to accept one particular thing he said.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter's desire to build three tents is the perennial temptation to institutionalise a moment of glory — to capture the experience, preserve it, replicate it. Every significant encounter with the living God carries it. The glory was never given to be housed; it was given for the road down.

And the road down is where nearly all Christian work is actually done. Jesus comes off that mountain the next morning into a crowd, a boy in convulsions, and a ministry that has failed. Moses came down Sinai with his face shining and found a golden calf.

“Listen to him” is the transfiguration's practical legacy. The disciples have been given an extraordinary visual confirmation, and are told the appropriate response is not to build but to listen. The Christian life is not primarily about spectacular experiences of divine glory, though God gives those in his mercy. It is about listening to the voice of the Son, in Scripture, in prayer, in the community of faith.

And the placing of it is a mercy as well as a fulfilment. He has just told them he will be rejected and killed, and told them all to pick up a cross. Then he takes three men up a mountain and lets them see, for a few minutes, what is on the other side of it. Nobody gets the mountain permanently, and nobody is asked to walk to Jerusalem without ever having seen anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now about eight days after these sayings.

Luke ties it to what came before. Eight days ago Peter said the Christ of God, and Jesus said the Son of Man must suffer, and everyone was told to take up a cross. Now three of them are going up a mountain.

Mark and Matthew both say six days; Luke says about eight. There is no difficulty here — Luke's about is doing exactly the work it appears to do, and the two are the same span counted inclusively or loosely, in the ordinary way people speak.

He took with him Peter and John and James.

The same three who were in the room when Jairus's daughter was raised (8:51), and the same three he will take deeper into the garden at Gethsemane (22:39-46). They see a dead girl stand up, they see him in glory, and they see him on the ground with his sweat like blood — and the third scene is unintelligible without the second.

And went up on the mountain to pray.

There it is again, and Luke is the only one who says it. Matthew and Mark have him take them up the mountain; Luke says why he went. He did not go up to be transfigured. He went up to pray, and it happened while he was praying.

And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.

Luke is careful with his verbs, and there is a reason. Mark and Matthew use metamorphōthē — he was transformed, the word behind metamorphosis. Luke, writing for Greek readers in a world full of stories about gods changing shape, avoids it entirely and describes what was seen: his face became different; his clothing turned a white that flashed.

And altered is the right sense. Nothing was added to him. This is not Jesus temporarily becoming something more than he had been; it is the covering coming off something that was there all along. The glory that filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exod. 40:35) was, that evening, standing on a hillside in a borrowed body, praying — and for a few minutes the body did not hide it.

Which is why the detail about prayer matters so much. It happened while he was praying. Whatever passed between the Son and the Father on that mountain, the glory of God broke through the surface of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah.

Of all the figures in Israel's history, these two. Moses, who gave the law; Elijah, the greatest of the prophets. Between them they are the Law and the Prophets — the whole Old Testament, standing on a hillside, in conversation.

There is a second thing they share, and it is not usually noticed. Moses died on a mountain in Moab and God buried him, and no man knows the place (Deut. 34:5-6). Elijah did not die at all; he was taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kgs. 2:11). Both of them had also met God on a mountain — Moses at Sinai, Elijah at Horeb, which is the same mountain — and each was hidden in a cleft or a cave while the glory passed by (Exod. 33:22; 1 Kgs. 19:9-13).

Each of them once asked, in his own way, to see God, and was allowed a back and a whisper. Now they are standing in the light, talking with him.

Who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.

Luke alone tells us the subject of the conversation, and the word he uses for it is startling. Departure translates exodos.

They are talking about his exodus.

Consider who is standing there while that word is used. The man who led the first one — out of Egypt, through the blood of a lamb on a doorpost, through the sea, out of slavery into a land. And the word for what he did is now being applied, in his hearing, to a death in Jerusalem.

That is the interpretation of the cross, given from heaven, before it happens. It is not a defeat, not an accident, not a tragedy to be redeemed afterwards. It is an exodus — a deliverance of a people out of a slavery deeper than Egypt's, accomplished by a lamb, through blood, on a specified date, by a leader who goes ahead of them.

And note the verb: which he was about to accomplish. Not suffer. Not undergo. Accomplish — to fulfil, to bring to completion. The cross is spoken of on that mountain the way a man speaks of a work he is going to finish.

Moses and Elijah are in glory, and they are not talking about glory. They have the attention of the Son of God on a mountaintop with the light of heaven on them, and what they discuss is Calvary. Everything either of them ever wrote or did had been leaning towards it, and now the date is fixed and the road runs downhill from here to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, 'Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah'—not knowing what he said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep.

They almost missed it.

Luke alone records this, and it is not a flattering detail to preserve. The three of them are on a mountain where the Son of God is shining and two of the greatest figures in redemptive history have arrived to discuss the salvation of the world, and the disciples are struggling to stay awake.

It is worth noting where else Luke tells us this about the same three men. In Gethsemane he finds them sleeping for sorrow (22:45). Twice — on the mountain of glory and in the garden of agony, at the two most significant nights of their lives — Peter, James and John cannot keep their eyes open.

There is no rebuke attached to it here. They are tired, it is presumably late, and they have climbed a mountain. It is simply what men are like.

But when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him.

They did see it. Luke is careful to say so, because he is going to depend on Peter's testimony for this scene and he wants it clear that the man was awake for it. Peter himself will write about it decades later: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty… we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain (2 Pet. 1:16-18).

And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents.

Notice the timing. He speaks as Moses and Elijah are leaving — which suggests a man trying to stop something ending.

The tents are almost certainly a reference to the Feast of Booths, when Israel lived in shelters for a week to remember the wilderness, and which had come to carry expectations of the age to come. Peter has grasped that this is a foretaste of the kingdom. His instinct is to set up camp.

And the proposal is wrong in a specific way: one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah. Three tents, three equals. The next verse will correct that from the cloud, and the correction will leave Jesus standing alone.

Not knowing what he said. Luke's aside is candid and gentle. Peter is not being wicked; he is doing what people do in the presence of something overwhelming, which is to talk, and to propose a project.

The instinct to build something that will keep the moment is a permanent one, and it always fails for the same reason. The glory was never given to be housed. It was given for the road down.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!' And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them.

Peter is interrupted mid-sentence. It is the only answer his proposal gets.

And the cloud is not weather. It is the shekinah — the cloud of the presence that came down on Sinai (Exod. 24:15-18), that filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exod. 40:34-35), that went before Israel in the wilderness, that filled Solomon's temple until the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kgs. 8:10-11). Israel had not seen it for centuries.

The verb overshadowed is episkiazō, and Luke has used it once before in this Gospel: Gabriel told a girl in Nazareth that the power of the Most High will overshadow you (1:35). The same word, the same presence, at the conception and at the mountain.

And they were afraid as they entered the cloud. Of course they were. Everything Israel knew said that men do not walk into that and come out.

And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!

The Father speaks twice in this Gospel and both times about the same person. At the Jordan it was you are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22), spoken to Jesus. Here it is this is my Son, spoken to the three of them.

Some Bibles read my Beloved here rather than my Chosen One, and the manuscripts do differ. Chosen One is very likely what Luke wrote, and it is the harder reading — a copyist would naturally smooth it to match the wording at the baptism and the parallel in Matthew. And the phrase is deliberate: my Chosen One is Isaiah's word for the Servant — Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights (Isa. 42:1). On a mountain where they have just been discussing his exodus, the Father names him with the Servant's title.

Then the command, and it is the only imperative in the whole scene: listen to him.

Not look at him, though the light was extraordinary. Not build for him. Listen. And it is aimed with precision at three men who have spent the last eight days failing to accept one particular thing he said — that the Son of Man must suffer and be killed and be raised. Moses spoke and Elijah spoke and Israel was to hear them; the Father says the listening now goes to his Son.

And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone.

The cloud lifts. Moses is gone, and Elijah is gone, and there are not three figures on that mountain requiring three tents. There is one, and he is the one they are to hear. The Law and the Prophets have said what they came to say and have stepped back, and what is left standing in the ordinary evening light is a man they are going to follow down the hill to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–50 — Healing, Humility, and the Second Passion Prediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Coming down from the mountain, Jesus meets a father whose only child is seized by a spirit that convulses him — and the disciples who were not on the mountain had tried and failed.

The father's description is clinical, and a modern reader will recognise it: sudden onset, a cry, convulsion, foaming, then flattened exhaustion. So was the boy ill or possessed? Luke is the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician, and he consistently keeps the categories apart: those sick with various diseases, and demons also came out of many (4:40-41); a crowd healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits (6:17-18). Jesus speaks the same way: “I cast out demons and perform cures” (13:32). Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this boy something else was behind them.

Two errors do real harm and Luke's care rules out both — that every seizure or darkness of mind is the enemy's work, and that “demon” was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose. But Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you.

“O faithless and twisted generation” is addressed to the whole scene, not the father — the word “twisted” is Moses' word for Israel in the wilderness (Deut. 32:5). And it is followed immediately by “Bring your son here.” He names the faithlessness and then heals the boy anyway.

Luke ends the miracle as he ended the one at Nain: “he gave him back to his father” (cf. 7:15). Not “the boy was healed.” A son handed back to the man who brought him.

Then, at the height of the crowd's enthusiasm, the second passion prediction — “let these words sink into your ears,” literally put these words into your ears. They did not understand, it was concealed from them, and they were afraid to ask. Afraid of the answer, almost certainly; Mark records Peter, after the first prediction, taking Jesus aside to rebuke him for it (Mark 8:32).

And what fills the silence is an argument about which of them is greatest. Jesus takes a child — a person with no legal standing and nothing to offer — and stands the child beside himself. Then John reports that they stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus's name, and gives his reason: “he does not follow with us.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples' failure at v.40, after their success in vv.1-6, raises the question of what changed. Matthew records Jesus naming it as “little faith” (Matt. 17:20). The lesson is what the whole chapter teaches: the authority delegated to them is not their own. It flows from the one who gives it and is sustained by the relationship of trust with him.

“Delivered into the hands of men” uses paradidotai, the verb that will be used of Judas throughout the passion, and which the Greek Isaiah uses of the Servant who was delivered up for our sins (Isa. 53:12). There is a bitter wordplay the English keeps: the Son of Man is handed over into the hands of men.

Luke's “it was concealed from them” is a passive without an agent, and probably deliberately so. Two things are true at once: there is a hiddenness God appoints (cf. 19:42; 24:16), and there is a hiddenness they are manufacturing, since the next verse shows exactly what they were thinking about instead.

On “the one who is not against you is for you” — a reader will notice the apparent opposite at 11:23, “whoever is not with me is against me.” The difference is in the pronouns. There the subject is a man's own relation to Christ, where there is no neutral ground. Here it is one servant's judgement of another. About my own standing, assume nothing; about another doing good in his name, assume the best.
verseByVerse.examples:
The child placed beside Jesus is a searching challenge to every form of Christian leadership measured by influence, platform, numbers or reputation. A first-century child had no legal rights, no property, no voice, and no capacity to confer honour on anybody — which is exactly why he was chosen for an argument about greatness.

So the test is not how a man behaves towards those above him; everyone is attentive upwards. It is how he treats those who cannot advance him, repay him, report him, or do him any good at all. The person who cleans the building. The member of the congregation whose conversation goes nowhere. The child in the room, who has nothing and is watching.

“I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not” is an honest report of ministry failure, said out loud, in front of a crowd, by the man it failed. It belongs in the Gospel and it is a comfort of a hard kind: the record of the church's work has always included the things that did not work.

And John's “he does not follow with us” — not “he does not follow you” — names the instinct precisely. It is the assumption that the boundary of my group is the boundary of the kingdom, and that work God is doing outside it is at best suspect and at worst competition. Christ has servants who do not attend your church, use your vocabulary, or share your history, and they are not to be stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, 'Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him.

The mountain was last night. This is the morning, and the crowd is waiting at the bottom.

Luke has built the contrast deliberately and it is the same one Moses walked into. He came down Sinai with his face shining, carrying the words of God, and found the people round a golden calf (Exod. 32). Jesus comes down with the voice of the Father still in the disciples' ears, and finds a boy in convulsions and a ministry that has failed.

That descent is where nearly all Christian work is actually done. Not on the mountain, and not in the memory of it, but the next morning at the bottom of the hill, among people who were not there and have a problem that will not wait.

And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.

Every word of that is a father's.

He cried out — he shouted over a crowd. He does not open with a theological claim or a request for a miracle; he asks Jesus to look at the boy. He has stopped expecting anything and is asking for attention.

And then the detail that does the work: he is my only child. Luke has used that phrase twice already — the widow's only son at Nain (7:12), Jairus's only daughter (8:42). It is his way of saying there is nothing behind this. No other children, no second chance, and in that world no future for the family either.

This man is not a disciple, and Luke does not tell us his name. He is a father in a crowd who has been living for years with a child who is destroyed in front of him at unpredictable intervals, and who has come, presumably having heard something, to a preacher's followers, and been let down.

Anybody who has cared for a severely ill or disabled child will recognise the exhaustion in the request. He does not ask for much. He asks to be looked at.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him.

The father's description is clinical, and a modern reader will recognise it immediately: sudden onset, a cry, convulsion, foaming, and then the flattened exhaustion afterwards. Any doctor today would read that paragraph and name it a seizure.

So was this boy ill, or was he possessed? And behind that sits the sharper question people actually mean: were these pre-scientific people simply calling a disease of the brain a devil?

The answer comes from Luke himself, and it is worth having, because he is the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician, and his Gospel is full of his clinical eye — the woman who had spent all she had on doctors (8:43), the grading of a fever (4:38), the sweat like drops of blood (22:44). And he consistently keeps the two categories apart.

He writes that they brought Jesus those who were sick with various diseases, and that demons also came out of many (4:40-41). He describes a crowd who came to be healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits who were cured (6:17-18) — two groups, named separately, in a single breath. Jesus himself speaks the same way: I cast out demons and perform cures (13:32). A man who thought every convulsion was a devil would not write like that.

Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this particular boy something else was behind them.

Two errors do real harm here, and Luke's own care rules out both. The first makes every seizure, every darkness of the mind, a work of the enemy — a cruelty this Gospel forbids by the plain fact that its author lists sickness and spirits as different things. A Christian with epilepsy is not in the devil's grip; he needs good medicine and the love of his church, not an interrogation about hidden sin. The second is the fashionable error, that demon was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose properly. But notice what happens in two verses' time: Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you.

And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.

That sentence has to be sat with, because it is the honest report of a ministry failure, said out loud, in front of a crowd, by the man it failed.

These are the same men who came back a chapter ago full of what they had done. Whatever happened in those villages was real. And here, at the bottom of the mountain, with a father watching, nothing worked.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, 'O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.' While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples,
verseByVerse.commentary:
O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you?

It is the sharpest thing Jesus says in this Gospel, and the first question is who it is aimed at.

Not the father. The man has done nothing wrong; he came, he asked, and he told the truth about what happened. Not the boy. The address is to a generation — the crowd, the disciples, the whole scene at the foot of the mountain, and the word twisted is the one Moses used of Israel in the wilderness (Deut. 32:5).

And there is something in the tone worth noticing, because it is not simply anger. How long am I to be with you and bear with you? is the sound of a man carrying something heavy. He has come down from the light of his Father's presence into a valley where nothing works, and he says so.

Then, without pausing: Bring your son here.

That is the whole answer to the question of whether the exasperation was the last word. He names the faithlessness and then heals the boy. He does not make the father's help conditional on the crowd improving.

While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him.

One last violent display, and it happens on the way. Luke wants it seen: the thing is at its worst in the final seconds before it is finished. That is not unusual, and it is worth knowing by anyone who has watched a besetting sin or a long oppression flare up hardest just as ground is being taken.

But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.

Three verbs, and the third is the one Luke chose to end on. He gave him back to his father — exactly the phrase used at Nain, where he gave him to his mother (7:15).

Not the boy was healed. Not the demon departed. A son was handed back to the man who had brought him. Luke will not let a miracle be reported as an event when it can be reported as a gift, from one person to another, in front of witnesses.

And all were astonished at the majesty of God.

The word is megaleiotēs — greatness, magnificence. The crowd does not credit a technique or a healer. Something of the size of God has been visible in a valley, in a boy who could stand up, in the arms of a father who had stopped hoping.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.' But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples, Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.

The timing is the point. The crowd is at the height of its enthusiasm — a boy has been restored, God's greatness is on everyone's lips — and Jesus turns away from all of it to tell his disciples something that will spoil it.

Let these words sink into your ears. The Greek is more physical than English allows: put these words into your ears. Set them down there. He is not making an announcement; he is asking them to store something they will need later and cannot use yet.

The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.

This is the second passion prediction, and it is much shorter than the first — and one word in it is new. Delivered is paradidotai, the verb for handing over, and it is the word that will be used of Judas throughout the passion. It is also, in the passive, the word Isaiah's Greek text uses of the Servant who was delivered up for our sins (Isa. 53:12).

And there is a bitter wordplay in the sentence that the English keeps. The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. The one who came as the representative man is going to be handed over to men, by a man, and killed by them.

But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it.

Luke's phrasing raises a question. Concealed by whom?

He does not say, and the passive is probably deliberate. Two things are true at once, and the Gospel holds both. There is a hiddenness that God appoints — Luke will say the same of the Emmaus pair, whose eyes were kept from recognising him (24:16), and of the crowd in Jerusalem from whom the things that make for peace are hidden (19:42). And there is a hiddenness the disciples are manufacturing themselves, because the next verse shows exactly what they were thinking about instead, and it was which of them was greatest.

And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.

There is the human half, stated plainly. They did not understand, and they did not ask, and Luke tells us why: they were afraid.

Afraid of what? Almost certainly of the answer. There is a kind of not-understanding that is genuinely stuck, and there is a kind that has grasped enough to know it does not want the rest. Mark records Peter, after the first prediction, taking Jesus aside to rebuke him for it (Mark 8:32). They had understood more than they wanted to.

And the pattern is a familiar one. The question that most needs asking is very often the one nobody in the room will raise — not because it is difficult, but because everyone present suspects what the answer will cost.

verseByVerse.quote: An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side
verseByVerse.commentary:
An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest.

Read that sentence with the previous one still in the air. He has just told them he is going to be handed over to men and killed. They did not understand it, and were afraid to ask. And what fills the silence is an argument about rank.

Luke sets the two side by side without a word of comment, and the effect is devastating.

It is worth asking what they were arguing about, because the timing suggests an answer. Three of them had just been up a mountain and come back different, and would not say why (v. 36). Peter had been the one to name him the Christ. Someone had presumably not managed to cast out the demon. There was material for a dispute, and it was fresh.

So this is not a general failing of ambitious men. It is what happened in the hours after the glory, among people who had been let in on something — which is precisely where this particular sin lives. Nobody argues about greatness who has not first been given something.

But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts.

Luke does not say they told him. He knew — and the phrase he uses is the reasoning of their hearts, which is where the argument actually was. Whatever was being said aloud, the thing being weighed was internal, and he could see it.

That is worth pausing on before the child arrives. This is not a man detecting a squabble. It is the one who knows what is in man (John 2:25) reading the interior of twelve people at once, including the parts they would not have admitted to each other.

Took a child and put him by his side.

He does not answer the argument. He does not name a winner, or rebuke the ambition, or deliver a lecture on humility. He walks over, picks up a child — paidion, a young one, small enough to be taken — and stands the child next to himself.

The visual is the argument. Twelve grown men are ranking themselves, and he places beside himself the one person present with no rank whatsoever.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.

To understand the force of this, the modern picture of childhood has to be set aside entirely.

A first-century child was loved, certainly. But in law and in society a child was a person of no standing: no legal rights, no property, no vote, no voice, no capacity to confer honour on anybody. A child could do nothing whatever for a man's position. That is why Jesus chose one to stand beside him in the middle of an argument about greatness.

Receives is the key verb, and it is the language of hospitality — to welcome, to take somebody in. So the question is not who is willing to be like a child?, though that is true elsewhere. The question here is: who will you make room for, when the person can do nothing for you?

And then the chain, which is startling. Receive the child, and you receive Christ. Receive Christ, and you receive the Father who sent him. The one with the least standing in the room is connected, in three steps, to the throne of God.

That is not sentiment. It is a claim about where Christ has chosen to be found, and it will be made again more sharply — as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matt. 25:40).

For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.

And there is the answer to their argument, and it is not the answer that the argument was wrong. He does not abolish greatness. He tells them the measurement is inverted, and then leaves them holding it.

This is worth making concrete, because it is easy to admire and hard to run. The test is not how a man behaves towards those above him — everyone is attentive upwards. It is how he treats the people who cannot advance him, cannot repay him, cannot report him, and will never be in a position to do him any good at all.

The person who cleans the building. The member of the congregation whose conversation goes nowhere. The child in the room, who has nothing and is watching.

Whatever is being said to them is being said to Christ, and whatever is being given them is going to the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, 'Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.' But Jesus said to him, 'Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John answered, Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.

The word answered is odd, because nobody had asked John anything. He is responding to what Jesus has just said about receiving a child — and what he offers, apparently as a contribution, is an account of something they did.

The timing is not accidental and Luke has left it exposed. Jesus has just placed a child beside himself and said the least is the greatest. John, who is one of the three who went up the mountain, immediately produces an incident in which the disciples enforced a boundary.

Now look at what he actually reports, because it is very carefully worded.

The man was casting out demons. It was working. The disciples had failed at precisely this a few verses earlier (v. 40), and this outsider had not. And he was doing it in your name — not in his own, not as a rival, but under the authority of Jesus.

So the ground for stopping him is not that he was a fraud, and not that he was doing harm. John states the reason himself, and it is the only reason he has: because he does not follow with us.

Not he does not follow you. Us.

But Jesus said to him, Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.

The correction is immediate and it is unqualified.

A reader will notice that Jesus says something apparently opposite two chapters later: whoever is not with me is against me (11:23). The two are not in conflict, and the difference is in the pronouns. There, the subject is a man's own relation to Christ, and there is no neutral ground: no one is uncommitted where he is concerned. Here, the subject is one servant's judgement of another, and the presumption runs the other way. About my own standing before Christ, assume nothing. About another man doing good in his name, assume the best.

What is being corrected is a specific instinct, and it is thoroughly religious. It is the assumption that the boundary of my group is the boundary of the kingdom, and that work God is doing outside it is at best suspect and at worst competition.

Note also that this is not a licence for indifference about truth. The man in question was doing something unmistakably good in the name of Jesus. That is a long way from saying it does not matter what anyone believes.

But within those limits the principle stands, and it is generous. Christ has servants who do not attend your church, use your vocabulary, or share your history — and they are not to be stopped.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 51–62 — The Face Set Toward Jerusalem; The Cost of Following
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” With that sentence Luke's narrative pivots. The Galilean ministry is over, and the journey that runs from here to 19:44 begins. Everything that follows — the parables, the healings, the controversies — happens on the road that leads to the cross.

“Taken up” is analēmpsis, a noun used nowhere else in the New Testament, reaching past the cross to the ascension. Luke has the whole arc in one word: the death, the rising, the going home.

“Set his face” is the language of the Suffering Servant: “I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame” (Isa. 50:7) — from a passage whose preceding verse reads, “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard.” He is not swept toward the cross by events, or cornered by his enemies. He turns and starts walking.

The route runs through Samaria, which most Jewish pilgrims avoided by going round through the Jordan valley. He goes straight through. And the village refuses him precisely because his face is set toward Jerusalem — the ancient dispute over Gerizim and Jerusalem. On the first day of the journey to the cross, what he is rejected for is going to the cross.

James and John ask to call down fire, reasoning from Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:10-12), and reasoning badly: Elijah faced armed men sent to seize a prophet, and these two are facing a village that declined to provide beds. Jesus rebukes the disciples, not the Samaritans, and they go on to another village. That village would be evangelised within a few years (Acts 8:5-8), and no one there was burned.

Three encounters close the chapter. A man volunteers to follow anywhere and is told the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head — a report on the previous night, not a general statement. A second is called and asks to bury his father first; in that world burial happened the same day, so the request almost certainly means “let me stay until my father dies,” an indefinite postponement. A third asks only to say goodbye — which is what Elisha was granted (1 Kgs. 19:20) — and is answered with a ploughing image, the difference being that Elisha destroyed his plough.
verseByVerse.theology:
The travel narrative beginning at 9:51 is Luke's unique structural contribution. Matthew and Mark move quickly from Galilee to Jerusalem; Luke devotes ten chapters to the journey. The structure is theological before it is geographical: to follow Jesus is to be on the road to Jerusalem, which is to say on the road to the cross. The whole of it is lived in the shadow of the set face of 9:51.

“Leave the dead to bury their own dead” is among the most shocking sayings in the Gospels — an apparent violation of the fifth commandment and of an obligation so weighty that the Old Testament names its absence as a mark of judgement (Jer. 22:18-19). It is not an abolition of family duty. It is a refusal of one word, and the word is first. And the saying is wordplay, not cruelty: let those who are spiritually dead attend to the socially necessary; you have been called by the one who gives life.

“Fit for the kingdom of God” uses the ordinary word for useful or suitable. It is not a statement about whether such a man is saved. It is a statement about whether he is any use at the plough while facing the wrong way.

And the instinct James and John show — to destroy those who reject Jesus — is answered by the direction he is walking. The one who has set his face toward a cross does not call down fire on those who refuse him; he presses on toward the sacrifice that will make it possible for even Samaritans to receive him.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ancient plough was light, single-handled, and pulled through stony ground; it had to be held down with constant pressure and steered by eye on a fixed point ahead. A man who turns to look behind loses the line in a moment, and a crooked first furrow makes every furrow after it crooked, because they are all set by the first. The issue is not affection for home. It is that the eyes are not on the work.

The three would-be disciples represent three ways of not following. The first underestimates the cost — “wherever you go” sounds easy until it means homelessness. The second and third both say first. There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish before following becomes convenient, and the reasonable things are genuinely reasonable, which is exactly what makes them so effective at postponing everything.

Luke does not tell us what any of the three decided. He never does. The stories are left open, which is itself the point: the road is still going, and the question is still standing.

And a comfortable church needs the first exchange plainly, because a certain kind of preaching promises the opposite — that coming to Christ secures a settled life. The one making the offer had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards an execution, and he thought the volunteer was owed that information before signing.

verseByVerse.quote: When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.

This is the hinge of Luke's Gospel. Everything from here to chapter nineteen happens on a road, and the road has one destination.

The days drew near — literally, the days were being fulfilled, filled up. Time is running out on purpose, and it is being counted.

For him to be taken up. Luke's noun is analēmpsis, and it is used nowhere else in the New Testament. It means the taking up, and it reaches past the cross to the ascension — the same root as the verb in Acts 1, where he was lifted up (Acts 1:9). Luke is describing the whole arc in one word: the death, the rising, and the going home.

He set his face to go to Jerusalem.

The phrase is Hebrew in shape and it is not merely a decision. It is the language of the Suffering Servant: I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame (Isa. 50:7). And it belongs to a passage in which the Servant says, three verses earlier, I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting.

So the face that is set towards Jerusalem is set with Isaiah's words already in it, and the man knows exactly what is at the other end. He is not swept toward the cross by events, or cornered by his enemies, or overtaken by a plot. He turns and starts walking.

And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans.

The route from Galilee to Jerusalem runs through Samaria, and most Jewish pilgrims went round it — down the Jordan valley, east of the river, adding days to the journey rather than cross that ground. He goes straight through, and sends men ahead to arrange lodging.

But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.

The hostility was ancient and mutual. Samaritans held that God was to be worshipped on Mount Gerizim; Jews held it was Jerusalem, and the two communities had been at it for centuries. So the refusal is not personal. It is a village looking at a party of pilgrims heading for the wrong mountain, and declining to house them.

What he is rejected for, on the first day of the journey to the cross, is going to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, 'Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?' But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?

James and John. Mark tells us Jesus had nicknamed the pair of them Boanerges, Sons of Thunder (Mark 3:17), and it is difficult to read this verse without concluding that the name was earned.

And notice: they ask permission. They do not act. There is even a kind of deference in it — do you want us to? — which makes the request more disturbing rather than less, because they genuinely expect the answer might be yes.

Their precedent is scriptural. Elijah, on a hillside in this same country, called down fire from heaven on two companies of soldiers sent to arrest him (2 Kgs. 1:10-12). These two have just come down a mountain where they saw Elijah in glory eight days ago. They are not making it up; they are reasoning from the Bible, and reasoning badly.

Because the situation is not the same at all. Elijah faced armed men sent by an apostate king to seize a prophet. James and John are facing a village that declined to provide beds.

But he turned and rebuked them.

The one rebuked in this passage is not the Samaritans. Luke records no word to the village at all. The reprimand goes to the disciples, and Luke does not tell us what was said.

Which brings up something a reader may notice with two Bibles open. Older translations have more here. The King James adds to v. 55 that Jesus said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. For the Son of man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them.

Those words are absent from the earliest and best manuscripts, and the modern versions drop them to a footnote — which is why one Bible may be shorter than another at exactly this point. Two things are worth saying, and they pull in opposite directions.

The words are almost certainly not what Luke wrote. A scribe appears to have supplied the content of a rebuke Luke deliberately left unstated, and once written in a margin it moved into the text.

But the sentence that was added is entirely true, and it is true from Luke's own pages. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10) is in this Gospel in Jesus's own words. And within one chapter the hero of his most famous story will be a Samaritan (10:33). The copyist guessed the theology exactly right. He simply had no business putting his guess into the Gospel.

And they went on to another village.

That is the whole response to rejection: no fire, no argument, no curse. They walked on. The village that turned him away that evening would be evangelised within a few years by the church in Acts (Acts 8:5-8) — and no one there was burned.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going along the road, someone said to him, 'I will follow you wherever you go.' And Jesus said to him, 'Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three men now meet him on that road, and Luke puts them together because between them they cover most of the ways a person fails to follow.

As they were going along the road, someone said to him, I will follow you wherever you go.

The offer is unprompted, enthusiastic, and unlimited. Nobody called this man. He volunteers, and he volunteers everything — wherever you go.

Matthew tells us this one was a scribe (Matt. 8:19), which adds something: a trained man, used to attaching himself to a teacher, and probably expecting the arrangement to look like the ones he knew.

And Jesus said to him, Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

It is not a refusal. It is a disclosure — and it is worth noticing that Jesus does not respond to enthusiasm by capitalising on it. He gives the man the one piece of information his offer did not account for.

The comparison is exact and slightly bitter. Foxes have dens. Birds have nests. The animals of the land he made have somewhere to sleep. He does not.

And the timing matters, because he has just been refused lodging by a Samaritan village. This is not a general statement about his lifestyle; it is a report on last night. The man has said wherever you go on a road where the last village would not have him.

There is something in this that a comfortable church needs to hear plainly, because a certain kind of preaching promises the opposite — that coming to Christ secures a settled life. The one making the offer had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards an execution, and he thought the volunteer was owed that information before signing.

Luke does not tell us what the man decided. He never does with any of the three. The stories are left open, which is itself the point: the road is still going, and the question is still standing.

verseByVerse.quote: To another he said, 'Follow me.' But he said, 'Lord, let me first go and bury my father.' And Jesus said to him, 'Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
To another he said, Follow me. But he said, Lord, let me first go and bury my father.

This one does not volunteer. He is called — the same two words that were said to Levi at the tax booth (5:27), and to fishermen at a lakeside.

And his reply sounds like the most reasonable sentence in the chapter. Burying a father was among the most sacred obligations in Jewish life. It was a duty that took precedence over the study of the law, over prayers, even over the Passover pilgrimage. A son who did not bury his father had failed at the commandment to honour him.

Leave the dead to bury their own dead.

Which is, on the face of it, shocking — and it is worth knowing one thing before it hardens into a picture of Jesus refusing a grieving son a funeral.

In that world burial happened the same day, or the next at the latest. A man whose father had died that morning would be at the tomb, not standing on a road listening to a travelling preacher. The request almost certainly means what the identical phrase still means in parts of the Middle East: let me stay until my father dies. It is not a plea for three days off. It is a request for an indefinite postponement — a few years, perhaps many, until the duty is discharged and the inheritance settled and the man is free to go with nothing owing.

That is why the answer lands as it does. Jesus is not being cold about a coffin. He is refusing one word, and the word is first.

And the saying itself is a piece of wordplay, not a cruelty. Leave the dead to bury their own dead uses the word in two senses in a single line: let those who are spiritually dead attend to the socially necessary; you have been called by the one who gives life. The village will manage the funeral. It cannot manage the proclamation.

But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.

The commission is the reason for the severity. This is not a man being told to abandon his family for no purpose; he is being given a different one, and it is urgent.
