There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish before following becomes convenient, and the reasonable things are genuinely reasonable — which is exactly what makes them so effective. The kingdom does not accept a place in the queue behind the rest of a life.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet another said, 'I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.' Jesus said to him, 'No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet another said, I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.

The third man volunteers like the first and asks for a delay like the second, and his request is the smallest of the three. He does not want to wait for a death or negotiate terms. He wants to go home and say goodbye.

And there is a precedent for exactly this, which he may well have had in mind. When Elijah threw his cloak over Elisha at the plough, Elisha said, Let me kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you — and Elijah let him go (1 Kgs. 19:20). He went back, slaughtered his oxen, burned his ploughing equipment for the fire, fed the people, and then followed.

So the man is asking for what the prophets allowed. And this time the answer is no.

No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

Notice that Jesus answers him with a ploughing image, which suggests the Elisha story is in view on both sides. And the difference between the two cases is instructive: Elisha destroyed the plough. This man wants to keep the option of the house.

The picture itself is precise and any farmer would have felt it. The ancient plough was light, single-handled, and pulled by oxen through stony ground. It had to be held down with constant pressure and steered by eye on a fixed point ahead. A man who turns to look behind him loses the line in a moment, and a crooked first furrow makes every furrow after it crooked, because they are all set by the first.

The issue is not affection for home. It is that the eyes are not on the work.

Fit for the kingdom of God — the word is the ordinary one for useful, suitable, well-placed for a purpose. It is not a statement about whether such a man is saved. It is a statement about whether he is any use at the plough while he is facing the wrong way.

And so the chapter ends, on a road, with three unfinished conversations and a man walking towards Jerusalem. The first would not count the cost; the second and third both said first. None of them is told he cannot come.

What each is told is that the road is going somewhere, and it is going there now, and the one leading it has already set his face.

9.text: <sup>1</sup> And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, <sup>2</sup> and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. <sup>3</sup> And he said to them, “Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. <sup>4</sup> And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart. <sup>5</sup> And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>6</sup> And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. <sup>7</sup> Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, <sup>8</sup> by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. <sup>9</sup> Herod said, “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” And he sought to see him. <sup>10</sup> On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. <sup>11</sup> When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing. <sup>12</sup> Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, “Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.” <sup>13</sup> But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.” <sup>14</sup> For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” <sup>15</sup> And they did so, and had them all sit down. <sup>16</sup> And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd. <sup>17</sup> And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces. <sup>18</sup> Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” <sup>19</sup> And they answered, “John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.” <sup>20</sup> Then he said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” And Peter answered, “The Christ of God.” <sup>21</sup> And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, <sup>22</sup> saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.” <sup>23</sup> And he said to all, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. <sup>24</sup> For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. <sup>25</sup> For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? <sup>26</sup> For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. <sup>27</sup> But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” <sup>28</sup> Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>29</sup> And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white. <sup>30</sup> And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, <sup>31</sup> who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. <sup>32</sup> Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. <sup>33</sup> And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah”—not knowing what he said. <sup>34</sup> As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. <sup>35</sup> And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” <sup>36</sup> And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen. <sup>37</sup> On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. <sup>38</sup> And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child. <sup>39</sup> And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. <sup>40</sup> And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” <sup>41</sup> Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.” <sup>42</sup> While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. <sup>43</sup> And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples, <sup>44</sup> “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” <sup>45</sup> But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying. <sup>46</sup> An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. <sup>47</sup> But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side <sup>48</sup> and said to them, “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.” <sup>49</sup> John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus said to him, “Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.” <sup>51</sup> When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. <sup>52</sup> And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. <sup>53</sup> But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. <sup>54</sup> And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” <sup>55</sup> But he turned and rebuked them. <sup>56</sup> And they went on to another village. <sup>57</sup> As they were going along the road, someone said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>58</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>59</sup> To another he said, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>60</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” <sup>61</sup> Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.” <sup>62</sup> Jesus said to him, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

10.title: The Seventy-Two, the Samaritan, and the Better Part
10.overview:
Chapter 10 gives us three of Luke's most theologically rich scenes — each one, in its own way, a complete world. The sending of the seventy-two (vv. 1–24) expands the mission beyond the twelve, shows what kingdom authority looks like in practice, and culminates in the most intimate expression of Jesus's joy in the entire Gospel. The parable of the Good Samaritan (vv. 25–37) is the world's most famous story about neighbourly love — and simultaneously one of its most searching challenges to religious self-justification. And the scene at the home of Martha and Mary (vv. 38–42) is the New Testament's most precise statement about the one thing that is necessary in a life pulled in every direction by legitimate demands.

The chapter is the opening movement of the great travel narrative (9:51–19:44) — the long road to Jerusalem during which Jesus pours himself into his disciples and into the crowds that gather around him. The sending of the seventy-two models the missional multiplication that will characterise the church after Pentecost. The Samaritan parable models the ethics of the kingdom in the most concrete possible terms. The Mary-and-Martha scene models the devotional centre that makes the mission and the ethics sustainable. Together, the three scenes answer three questions: What does the kingdom produce in the world? What does the kingdom demand of its citizens? And what does the kingdom require of those who would receive it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Jesus Sends Out the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus appoints seventy-two others — beyond the twelve — and sends them ahead of him in pairs to every town and place he is about to go.

If your Bible says seventy, nothing is wrong: the manuscripts divide almost evenly here and at v. 17, and both figures carry the same symbolism. Moses appointed seventy elders to help carry a burden he could not carry alone (Num. 11:16), and two more prophesied in the camp (Num. 11:26); the table of nations in Genesis 10 comes to seventy in the Hebrew and seventy-two in the Greek. Either way, the expansion from twelve signals that the mission is wider than the twelve tribes.

They go two by two — the two witnesses the law required (Deut. 19:15) — and they go ahead of him. They are not independent agents but an advance party, and everywhere they arrive he is coming behind them.

“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” inverts the instinctive picture. The field is not the problem; the field is ready. And faced with a labour shortage, Jesus does not say “go” but “pray” — and he says it to the seventy-two he is about to send out that hour. The crop is not ours, the field is not ours, and the shortage is not finally ours to solve: it is “the Lord of the harvest” and “his harvest,” twice in one sentence.

“Lambs in the midst of wolves” is candid. A lamb among wolves is food; there is no version of that scene where the lamb wins. Jesus does not promise safety, and the whole security of the arrangement is in the person doing the sending.

The instructions echo those to the twelve, with additions. “Greet no one on the road” is not rudeness but urgency — an Eastern roadside greeting could consume a large part of a day, and Elisha said the same to Gehazi on an errand that would not wait (2 Kgs. 4:29). The “son of peace” is a Semitic idiom for a person already prepared to receive what is being brought; and where there is none, the peace “returns” — nothing is wasted.

“Eat what is set before you” is far more than manners. It sends Jewish men into households whose kitchens were the daily boundary of the covenant, and it plants the seed of Peter's rooftop vision (Acts 10:14-15).

And the woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum are the harshest words in Luke's Gospel — aimed not at pagan cities but at the three villages where most of the ministry had happened.
verseByVerse.theology:
The chain of representation in v.16 — “the one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me” — governs all Christian mission. It rests on the ancient principle that an authorised envoy carries the standing of the one who sent him: insult the ambassador and you have insulted the king.

The comfort in that is enormous. A believer stammering through an explanation to a colleague is not offering a private opinion; if the colleague hears, he has heard Christ. The messenger's inadequacy does not degrade what is carried.

The weight is equally real. There is no neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken. But note the limit, or the verse becomes a tyrant: the chain runs through the message, not through everything a messenger happens to want. It has been used to shield leaders from criticism, as though disagreeing with the man were rejecting Christ. What could not be refused without consequence was a specific announcement: the kingdom of God has come near.

The woes introduce graduated accountability — judgement proportional to light received. Paul develops it (Rom. 2:12-16), and Hebrews applies it to those who have known the covenant (Heb. 10:26-31). The privileged place in the kingdom is also the most exposed position under judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Chorazin appears in the whole New Testament exactly twice — here and in the Matthew parallel — and not one miracle done there is recorded anywhere in the four Gospels. Yet Jesus speaks of “the mighty works done in you” as though his hearers knew what he meant. It is a quiet reminder of how much is not in the books (cf. John 21:25): a town condemned for a history of miracles no evangelist thought to write down.

“It will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town” is not a claim that inhospitality outranks Sodom's sins. It is that Sodom never had this. Nobody stood in her streets announcing that the kingdom of God had come near.

And the last word a rejecting town hears is not a curse but the offer, repeated. “Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near” is word for word what the receiving towns were told (v. 9). The kingdom came as near to Chorazin as to anywhere — and nearness is not reception.

The principle bites hardest where most has been given (12:48), which in the modern world means anyone with a Bible on the shelf, a church down the road, and a lifetime of sermons behind them.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. And he said to them, 'The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If your Bible says seventy where this one says seventy-two, nothing is wrong and nothing much hangs on it. The manuscripts divide almost evenly, here and again at v. 17, and translators go different ways. Either figure carries the same symbolism, since the Old Testament supplies both — the elders Moses appointed number seventy (Num. 11:16), but two more were left in the camp and prophesied anyway (Num. 11:26); and the table of nations in Genesis 10 comes to seventy in the Hebrew and seventy-two in the Greek. A copyist working from either tradition could tidy the other towards it.

What the number says is the same on both counts. Moses' seventy were appointed to carry a burden he could not carry alone. Genesis' seventy are the nations of the world. This mission is larger than the Twelve and it is pointed outward.

Two by two. Not for company, though that helps. Under the law, a matter was established by two witnesses (Deut. 19:15), and what these men are carrying is testimony. It also makes them harder to discredit and harder to discourage.

Into every town and place where he himself was about to go. They are not independent operators. They are an advance party, and everywhere they go he is coming behind them. That is the whole shape of Christian mission and it has not changed: the messenger arrives first, and the Lord follows into the place the message has opened.

The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few.

Turn that over, because it is the opposite of what most people assume. The instinctive picture of evangelism is a small harvest and a resistant field — a few interested souls in a world that has stopped listening. Jesus says the opposite. The field is not the problem. The field is ready.

Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.

And here is the surprise. Faced with a shortage of workers, he does not say go. He says pray — and he says it to seventy-two men he is about to send out that very hour. The people being sent are told to pray for more of themselves.

The verb is strong: deēthēte, beg. And the one being begged owns the field. It is the Lord of the harvest and his harvest — twice in one sentence. Which quietly settles a great deal of anxiety about Christian work. The crop is not ours, the field is not ours, and the labour shortage is not finally our problem to solve. It is his, and he has told us how to raise it with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves.

It is one of the most candid sentences he ever spoke, and it is worth noticing that he says it as he sends them, not afterwards.

Take the picture seriously. A lamb among wolves is not an underdog with a fighting chance. It is food. There is no version of that scene in which the lamb wins, and no shepherd who ever put one there on purpose — which is exactly what he says he is doing.

And he does not promise it will be all right in the sense they would want. He does not say the wolves will turn out to be friendly, or that the lambs will be made into something more formidable. He says I am sending, and the whole security of the arrangement is in the person doing the sending.

There is something here that a comfortable church habitually softens. The vulnerability of the mission is not a design fault to be engineered out. It is the design. A church that has made itself safe — culturally powerful, financially insulated, politically protected — has not improved on this arrangement. It has swapped it for another one.

Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals.

The list is even shorter than the Twelve's (9:3). No purse, no traveller's satchel, and no spare sandals — the ancient equivalent of no wallet, no bag, no change of shoes for a journey on foot.

And greet no one on the road.

This sounds rude until you know what a greeting was. An Eastern roadside greeting was not a nod; it was an extended exchange of enquiries after family, health and business, and it could consume a large part of a day. There is also a precedent that is almost certainly in view: Elisha, sending Gehazi urgently to a dead child, told him, if you meet anyone, do not greet him, and if anyone greets you, do not reply (2 Kgs. 4:29).

So it is not a rule about manners. It is a rule about urgency, and it is temporary and specific — this is a single sweep through the towns he is about to visit, with a deadline attached, and the men have been told not to let the ordinary courtesies of the road eat the daylight.

Which is the honest reason it is in the Gospel. There are seasons when the ordinary good things have to give way to something that will not wait, and knowing which season you are in is most of the skill.

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever house you enter, first say, Peace be to this house!

The greeting is shalom, and in Hebrew it never meant merely the absence of trouble. It means wholeness, everything in its right place, a life not at war with God or itself. And in the mouth of a man sent by Jesus it is not a pleasantry. Notice how the next sentence treats it: as something that goes somewhere, settles or does not, and can come back.

And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you.

Son of peace is a Semitic idiom — a person characterised by the thing named, in this case one who belongs to the peace being offered and is ready for it. Somebody in that village has been prepared before the messengers arrive.

That is worth registering by anyone who has ever felt that evangelism is a matter of manufacturing interest out of nothing. It is not. The instruction assumes there is already a person in the street whose heart has been made ready by somebody else, and the work is largely to find him.

And if there is not: it will return to you. Nothing is lost. A blessing offered to a house that will not have it is not wasted; it comes back to the one who offered it. Which is a quiet mercy for every believer who has spoken and been rebuffed and felt they had spent something they could not get back.

And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.

Stay put. The rule is the same as the Twelve's and for the same reason: a messenger who trades up has begun to be paid, and a man whose lodging depends on the standing of his host will eventually trim his message to keep it.

But there is a phrase here worth stopping on, because of what happened to it later. The laborer deserves his wages.

Paul quotes that sentence in a letter to Timothy — and quotes it as Scripture. He writes: For the Scripture says, You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain, and, The laborer deserves his wages (1 Tim. 5:18). The first half is Deuteronomy 25:4. The second half is this verse.

Which means that within Paul's lifetime, the words of Jesus recorded in Luke's Gospel were being set alongside the Law of Moses under the single heading the Scripture says. That is not a later church council conferring authority on a book. It is an apostle, writing to a colleague, treating what Jesus said exactly as he treats what God said through Moses — because he could see no difference.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you.

It sounds like a rule about manners and it is a great deal more than that.

These are Jewish men, sent by a Jewish teacher, into towns that in this part of the country would have included Gentile and Samaritan households. What is set before a travelling Jew in such a house is not necessarily food he can eat, and the whole architecture of Jewish identity ran through the kitchen. The food laws were not a dietary preference; they were the daily, physical boundary of the covenant people.

And he tells them to eat what they are given.

Luke, who is writing for a Gentile church, knows exactly where that instruction is going. In his second volume Peter will be on a rooftop in Joppa, shown a sheet full of unclean animals and told to kill and eat, and will protest that he has never eaten anything common or unclean — and be answered, What God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:14-15). Within an hour he will be in a Roman centurion's house.

The seed of that is here, in a travel instruction, years before anyone understood what it meant.

There is a plainer point too, and it is about the receiving end of hospitality. To eat what a poor household puts in front of you, without inspecting it, is to accept the person. Anybody who has been served a meal by people who had very little will know that scrutinising it would have been the one unforgivable thing.

Heal the sick in it and say to them, The kingdom of God has come near to you.

Again the two together, and in that order — the touch and then the word. The healing is not a strategy to earn a hearing, and the word is not an explanation of the healing. They are one announcement made in two ways.

And the announcement itself is precise: not the kingdom of God will come, but has come near. It is close enough to be reached. The perfect tense means the nearness is a settled state — it has arrived and it is standing there — which is exactly what a village would conclude on watching its sick get up.

verseByVerse.quote: But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say…

Notice that he does not tell them to leave quietly. He tells them to go out into the public street and make an announcement — which takes a good deal more courage than staying, and is the last thing a rejected messenger would naturally want to do.

Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you.

The gesture is the one the Twelve were given (9:5): the dust a Jew shook off at the border on returning from pagan ground. Performed in an Israelite street it says something devastating — that this town has put itself outside, and the line no longer runs where they think it does.

But look at what is added, because it changes everything about the tone.

Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.

That is the same sentence they were told to say to the towns that received them (v. 9). Word for word. The only difference is the nevertheless.

So the last thing a rejecting town hears is not a curse. It is the offer, repeated. The kingdom came near to Chorazin exactly as near as it came to the village that took the messengers in — and nearness is not the same as reception. It came near, and they were standing there, and they said no.

Which is the whole tragedy of the verse. The kingdom of God is not a distant possibility that unfortunate towns never had a fair chance at. It walked up the street.

I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.

Sodom is the Bible's byword for a place beyond saving — a city destroyed by fire from heaven, whose name became shorthand for the outer limit of wickedness (Gen. 19).

And a Galilean village that declined to give a bed to two travelling preachers will fare worse.

The logic is not that hospitality outranks Sodom's sins. It is that Sodom never had this. Nobody stood in the streets of Sodom announcing that the kingdom of God had come near, and nobody healed her sick in the market square. These towns did have it, and they had it in daylight, and they preferred not to.

Note also the phrase on that day — a fixed, known day, with degrees of judgement on it. Whatever else is true of the last day, it is not a single undifferentiated verdict. It is weighed.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the woes, and they are the harshest words in Luke's Gospel. It is worth being clear who is receiving them.

Not Rome. Not the Sanhedrin. Not the towns that never heard. Three small fishing villages on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee — the places where he had lived and worked and where most of his ministry so far had happened.

Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!

And here is something that ought to stop a careful reader. Chorazin appears in the whole of the New Testament exactly twice — here, and in the parallel in Matthew 11:21. Not one miracle done in Chorazin is recorded anywhere in the four Gospels. Yet Jesus speaks of the mighty works done in you as though everyone listening knew what he meant.

Which is a quiet reminder of how much is not in the books. John says as much at the end of his Gospel: there are also many other things that Jesus did (John 21:25). Chorazin is the evidence — a town condemned for a history of miracles that no evangelist thought to write down.

For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.

Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician port cities on the coast, wealthy, pagan, and denounced by the prophets for centuries (Isa. 23; Ezek. 26-28). A Galilean listener would have filed them under hopeless.

And Jesus says they would have repented. Not might have — would have, and long ago.

That sentence tells us something about the mind of God that is not comfortable and is not optional: he knows what people would have done under circumstances they were never given. Which raises questions no one can fully answer. What it does not do is give anyone an excuse, because the towns being addressed are the ones that did get the circumstances.

And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.

Capernaum was his base — the town he moved to after Nazareth threw him out (4:31), where he taught in the synagogue, healed Peter's mother-in-law, and emptied a street of its sick in one evening.

And the language he uses about it is borrowed. Will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down is the taunt Isaiah aimed at the king of Babylon, who said in his heart I will ascend to heaven and was told you are brought down to Sheol (Isa. 14:13-15). The most privileged village in Galilee is addressed in the words written for the archetype of proud rebellion.

The principle underneath is stated plainly enough elsewhere: everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required (12:48). It cuts hardest at those who have had most — which in the modern world means anyone with a Bible on the shelf, a church down the road, and a lifetime of sermons behind them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.

One sentence, and it holds the whole doctrine of Christian mission in a chain of four links.

Follow it backwards, because that is the direction the authority runs. The Father sends the Son. The Son sends the seventy-two. Therefore what is done to the seventy-two is done to the Son, and what is done to the Son is done to the Father.

This rests on something older than the Gospel. In the ancient world an authorised envoy carried the standing of the man who sent him; the rabbinic principle was that a man's representative is as the man himself. Insult the ambassador and you have insulted the king, and every court in the world understood it.

What Jesus does here is put ordinary men in that position — men with no money, no bag and no spare sandals — and connect them by a direct line to the throne of heaven.

Two things follow, and they pull hard in opposite directions.

The first is an extraordinary comfort. A believer stammering through an explanation of the gospel to a colleague is not conducting a private conversation about a personal opinion. If the colleague hears, he has heard Christ. The messenger's inadequacy — and it is usually considerable — does not degrade what is being carried. Nobody ever thought less of a king because his letter arrived in the hands of a tired man.

The second is a weight. It means there is no such thing as a neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken, and it means the person declining is not declining you. That distinction matters in both directions. It should stop a rejected Christian from taking it as a personal verdict on himself — and it should stop him from being casual about what has actually just happened in the conversation.

And notice one limit, or the verse becomes a tyrant. The chain runs through what you say, not through everything a messenger happens to want. It has been used to protect leaders from criticism, as though disagreeing with the man were rejecting Christ. The seventy-two were carrying a specific message: the kingdom of God has come near. That is what could not be refused without consequence — not their preferences, and not their opinions.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Return of the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seventy-two return elated: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” The word even gives them away — they expected the preaching to work and did not expect that. And they are careful about the mechanism: in your name.

“I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” is one of the most startling sentences in the Gospels. It may look back to the primordial fall, or forward to the cross and the final defeat (cf. Rev. 12:9); but the tense and the context favour a comment on what has just happened. They came back talking about demons submitting, and his answer begins “I saw.” He is telling them what their preaching tour looked like from where he was standing.

Seventy-two men had spent a fortnight in small towns nobody has heard of, saying an unimpressive sentence to farmers, with no money and no shoes. The Son of God, watching the same fortnight, saw the ruler of this world come down out of the sky like a strike of lightning. There is no ordinary Christian work — only work whose real scale is invisible from inside it.

Then the authority over serpents and scorpions, and the promise that nothing shall hurt them — both of which have been badly misused and both of which the passage itself guards.

And then the redirection: “do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” The joy was not wrong; it was aimed at the wrong thing. Authority is about what they can do, and anything resting on what a man can do rises and falls with his last performance.

Jesus then rejoices in the Holy Spirit — one of the very few places where Luke tells us what he was feeling, and the verb is exultation, the word used of a child leaping in the womb (1:44). The Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father, and the occasion is a group of nobodies coming home from a preaching tour.

The prayer thanks the Father for a hiding as well as a revealing, and then makes one of the highest claims in the Synoptic Gospels: all things handed over, and a mutual knowing of Father and Son that admits no third party except by the Son's choosing.

Finally the private beatitude: “blessed are the eyes that see what you see.” Not blessed for perceptiveness — blessed for what happens to be in front of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The joy of Jesus “in the Holy Spirit” is a Trinitarian moment: the Son's joy is given in the Spirit and directed to the Father in prayer. The mutual delight of Father, Son and Spirit overflows into the mission and into the lives of those who share in it.

Verses 21-22 have long been called the Johannine thunderbolt, because they drop into Matthew and Luke sounding exactly like the fourth Gospel. “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” is not authority in a defined area but everything. And the mutual knowing is not the language of a teacher who understands God better than others; it is a claim to stand inside the life of God, on the near side of a door only he can open. That he opens it is why the prayer is joy rather than terror.

“The wise and understanding” are not scholars in general — the man saying it is the finest interpreter of Scripture who ever lived, and Luke, who records it, is the most educated writer in the New Testament. They are the professionally religious who have watched everything and concluded he is a problem. And the “little children” are the seventy-two. The dividing line is not intelligence but whether a man will come with empty hands; learning is no obstacle to that, it simply supplies one more thing to hold onto.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” reorients the worker's identity from achievement to grace. The image is a citizen register — the book of life in which names are written (Ex. 32:32; Ps. 69:28; Dan. 12:1; Phil. 4:3; Rev. 21:27).

Every feature of it reverses what they were celebrating. The authority was given for a task; the name is written for good. The authority varies with the day; the writing was done before they were sent. The authority is theirs to exercise; the name was entered by somebody else — and it is in heaven, which is the one place nothing can be got at.

This belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by his usefulness. The minister whose standing before God rises and falls with the size of the congregation. The parent who reads his children's faith as a report card on himself. The Christian who has been ill for two years, can no longer do any of the things he used to do, and quietly suspects he has become surplus.

And the beatitude of vv.23-24 is a rebuke to the boredom that settles on people who have been in church a long time. Abraham died with one son and a burial plot. Moses asked to see God's glory and was shown a back. Isaiah described the Servant's wounds seven centuries early and never met him. Every one of them longed for this. Isaiah would have given everything he owned for an afternoon with a New Testament and a quiet room.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!' And he said to them, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!

The word even gives them away, and it is delightful. They expected the preaching to work. They expected the healings, more or less. They did not expect that.

And they are careful about the mechanism: in your name. Whatever the exhilaration, they have not confused whose authority it was.

And he said to them, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.

It is one of the most startling sentences in the Gospels, and the first question is when he saw it.

Three readings are possible. It may look back to the primordial fall — the rebellion of the great adversary before human history began, which Scripture gestures at rather than narrates. It may look forward to the cross and the final defeat, seen in advance, as Revelation describes it (Rev. 12:9). Or it may be a comment on exactly what has just happened: as seventy-two unremarkable men walked through Galilean villages saying the name of Jesus, he watched the enemy's position collapse.

The tense favours the third, and the context settles it. They came back talking about demons submitting; his answer begins I saw. He is telling them what their preaching tour looked like from where he was standing.

And the image is exact in two ways. Lightning is sudden — not a slow retreat, a fall. And lightning comes down; whatever height the adversary held, he is not holding it.

What that does to the scale of the thing is the point. Seventy-two men had spent a fortnight in small towns nobody has heard of, saying an unimpressive sentence to farmers, with no money and no shoes. That is what they experienced. And the Son of God, watching the same fortnight, saw the ruler of this world come down out of the sky like a strike of lightning.

There is no ordinary Christian work. There is only work whose real scale is invisible from inside it — which is why the report and the reply in these two verses do not sound like they belong to the same event.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.

Two things in that promise need guarding, because both have been badly misused.

The first is the serpents. Set beside the longer ending of Mark — they will pick up serpents with their hands (Mark 16:18) — this verse has been made the charter of the snake-handling churches, where believers lift live rattlesnakes in worship to demonstrate their faith, and where people have died doing it.

But look at what Jesus is actually saying. Serpents and scorpions are standard biblical shorthand for hostile and demonic power; the language comes straight from Psalm 91:13, you will tread on the lion and the adder. And the sentence explains itself in its own next clause: and over all the power of the enemy. He is describing the authority the seventy-two have just been exercising over demons, not issuing an invitation to pick up vipers.

And there is a sharper point still, from Luke's own pages. Psalm 91 is the very psalm the devil quoted in the wilderness, urging Jesus to throw himself from the temple because angels would catch him — and Jesus refused with a single line: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test (4:9-12). To engineer a danger in order to make God prove a promise is not faith; it is precisely the thing Jesus called temptation. A man who deliberately handles a rattlesnake to demonstrate his trust is not obeying this verse. He is repeating the devil's use of Scripture.

The second is the phrase nothing shall hurt you, which, read as bodily immunity, is contradicted by almost everyone who first heard it. James was killed with the sword (Acts 12:2). Stephen was stoned. Paul was beaten, stoned and shipwrecked, and finally beheaded — though he was also, once, shaken off a viper into a fire without harm (Acts 28:3-6), which shows that God can preserve, not that he always will.

So what does the promise mean? Luke answers it himself, and he does it by putting both halves in a single breath: some of you they will put to death… but not a hair of your head will perish (21:16-18). Both sentences are true at once, which settles the sense beyond argument.

The protection is not a guarantee that the body will be untouched. It is a guarantee that the enemy cannot finally destroy them — that nothing done to a disciple's body can undo what has been secured for his soul.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.

He has just confirmed the authority in the strongest terms. Now he tells them not to build their happiness on it.

Note that he does not say the joy was wrong. He says it was aimed at the wrong thing — which is a much finer correction, and a much more necessary one. What they came back rejoicing in was real, granted by him, and worth being pleased about. It is simply not what a person can stand on.

Why not? Because it is about what they can do.

And anything resting on what a man can do rises and falls with his last performance. There will be a day like the one at the foot of the mountain, where the disciples tried and nothing happened (9:40). There will be seasons when the work does not go. A joy founded on effectiveness is a joy on a schedule, and the schedule is not in your hands.

But rejoice that your names are written in heaven.

The image is a citizen register — the roll of a city, listing those who belong to it. Scripture uses it repeatedly: the book of life, in which names are written (Ex. 32:32; Ps. 69:28; Dan. 12:1; Phil. 4:3; Rev. 21:27).

And every feature of it is the reverse of what they were celebrating. The authority was given for a task; the name is written for good. The authority varies with the day; the writing was done before they were sent and is not being reviewed. The authority is theirs to exercise; the name was entered by somebody else, and — this is the part that carries the weight — it is in heaven, which is the one place nothing can be got at.

Which is why this verse belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by his usefulness, and there are a great many. The minister whose sense of standing before God rises and falls with the size of the congregation. The parent who reads his children's faith as a report card on his own. The Christian who has been ill for two years and can no longer do any of the things he used to do for God, and quietly suspects he has become surplus.

The word to all of them is that the thing worth rejoicing in was never the doing. It is a name, already written, in a book they cannot reach and cannot lose.

verseByVerse.quote: In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit.

Luke stops to tell us what Jesus was feeling, which he almost never does. The verb is ēgalliasato — not quiet contentment but exultation, the word used of a child leaping in the womb (1:44). And it happens in the Holy Spirit.

This is one of the clearest windows in the Synoptic Gospels into the life of God. The Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father. Three persons, one delight, and the occasion for it is a group of nobodies coming home from a preaching tour.

I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children.

He thanks the Father for a hiding as well as a revealing, and that has to be faced rather than smoothed.

But notice who the wise and understanding are in this Gospel. They are not scholars in general, and this is emphatically not a commendation of ignorance — the man saying it is the finest interpreter of Scripture who ever lived, and Luke, who records it, is the most educated writer in the New Testament. The wise here are the professionally religious of Galilee and Jerusalem: men with the texts, the training and the standing, who have watched all of it and concluded he is a problem.

And the little children — nēpioi, infants — are the seventy-two. Fishermen and farmers who could not have argued a point of law and had just come back from casting out demons.

So the dividing line is not intelligence. It is whether a man will come with empty hands. Learning is no obstacle to that whatsoever; it simply supplies one more thing that can be held onto.

Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. Literally, because thus it was well-pleasing before you. He does not merely accept the Father's arrangement. He is delighted by it.

All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

Scholars have long called this the Johannine thunderbolt, because it drops into Matthew and Luke sounding exactly like the fourth Gospel — and it is one of the strongest claims Jesus makes anywhere.

All things. Not some authority in a defined area. Everything, handed over.

Then a mutual knowing that admits no third party: the Father knows the Son; the Son knows the Father; nobody else knows either except by the Son's choosing. That is not the language of a teacher who understands God better than others. It is a claim to stand inside the life of God, on the near side of a door that only he can open.

And he opens it. That is the last clause, and it is why this prayer is joy rather than terror.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning to the disciples he said privately, 'Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then turning to the disciples he said privately.

Luke marks it carefully: he turns, and he speaks to them alone. What follows is not for the crowd.

Blessed are the eyes that see what you see!

Not blessed are you for being perceptive. Blessed are the eyes — for what happens to be in front of them. The blessing is entirely a matter of where they are standing in history, and they did nothing to arrange it.

For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.

Put names to that and it becomes almost unbearable.

Abraham, who was told that all nations would be blessed through his offspring and died with one son and a burial plot. Moses, who asked to see God's glory and was hidden in a rock and shown a back. David, promised a son whose throne would stand for ever, who went to his grave a thousand years before the child was born. Isaiah, who described the Servant's wounds seven centuries early in such detail that sceptics still refuse to believe he wrote it, and never met him. Daniel, who saw one like a son of man receiving an everlasting kingdom, and was told to seal the book and go his way.

Every one of them wanted this. Not one of them got it. And a group of Galilean labourers had spent the past few weeks walking around with him, eating with him, and coming home to tell him how the trip went.

The word for desired is a strong one — longed, yearned. These were not men with a mild curiosity. They spent their lives leaning towards something they were told they would not see.

Which puts a familiar problem in a hard light. There is a boredom that settles on people who have been in church a long time — the sense that the gospel is a known quantity, the Bible a familiar book, the whole thing slightly worn. It is not usually unbelief. It is simply the effect of proximity on the extraordinary.

And there is a further turn, because it goes further than the disciples. They saw him at a distance from the cross and understood almost nothing of it; anyone reading this has the finished account of the death and the rising, the whole of the Scriptures, and the Spirit given. Isaiah would have given everything he owned for an afternoon with a New Testament and a quiet room.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–37 — The Parable of the Good Samaritan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A lawyer — an expert in the law of Moses — stands up to test Jesus: “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” The wording gives him away twice over. What shall I do assumes the answer is an action; and an inheritance is the one thing nobody works for, since it comes by belonging to a family. He has put a doing-word and a receiving-word in the same sentence without noticing.

Jesus answers with two questions. “What is written in the Law?” asks for the text. “How do you read it?” asks for the man — and a reading is never neutral. The examination has quietly moved.

The lawyer's answer is superb: Deuteronomy 6:5 welded to Leviticus 19:18, the spine of the law in a sentence. And Jesus commends it: “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.”

Which is perfectly true. Anyone who loved God with the whole heart, soul, strength and mind, and his neighbour as himself, without a lapse, from first breath to last, would indeed live. The catch is not in the offer but in the doer. Jesus is using the law as it was meant to be used — not a ladder to climb but a mirror to look into (Rom. 3:20; Gal. 3:24).

And it works. The lawyer does not go home content; he starts negotiating, “desiring to justify himself.” His question — “who is my neighbour?” — sounds like scholarly precision and is a search for a boundary. If neighbour has edges, there are people outside them, and a man can be entirely obedient and still walk past the rest. It was a live question with real answers on offer: neighbour was generally taken to mean a fellow Israelite, and the Qumran sect required its members to hate the sons of darkness.

The story refuses him a category from its first line: not a Jew, not a Gentile, just “a man.” Stripped and beaten unconscious, he has lost the two things — clothing and speech — by which anyone could have identified him.

A priest passes. A Levite passes. Every listener now expects the third man to be an ordinary Israelite; that is the shape of the joke. What arrives is a Samaritan — and the hostility was ancient, mutual and violent. It is only two chapters since a Samaritan village refused Jesus a bed and James and John asked to burn it.

Then the reversal: not “who is my neighbour?” but “which of these three proved to be a neighbour?” The lawyer cannot say the word. He says “the one who showed him mercy.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The usual defence of the priest is ritual purity: contact with a corpse made him unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11-13), and he could not tell from a distance whether the man was dead. But note the direction of travel — he was going down, away from Jerusalem, towards Jericho, where many priests lived between rotations. His duty is behind him, not ahead.

And the law he was protecting had a clause about exactly this. The same Torah commands a man to help even his enemy's fallen animal (Ex. 23:4-5), and forbids standing by the blood of your neighbour (Lev. 19:16) — three verses before the command the lawyer had just quoted.

Luke offers the priest and Levite no mitigation whatever. He simply says they passed by on the other side, and adds of the second that he “came to the place” — he got closer, looked from nearer, and crossed anyway. The Samaritan, by contrast, “when he saw him, had compassion.” The difference is not in the seeing. It is in what the seeing was allowed to do.

The parable has been read allegorically since Origen: the traveller is humanity, the robbers the devil, the priest and Levite the law and prophets that cannot save, the Samaritan Christ, the inn the church, the two denarii the sacraments. The reading is not without insight — Jesus is indeed the one who binds wounds, pays the debt and promises to return. But the surface command is non-negotiable: “Go and do likewise.”
verseByVerse.examples:
The verb translated “had compassion” is esplanchnisthē, from the word for the inward organs — compassion felt physically, the thing that turns over inside a person. Luke uses it exactly three times: of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20), and of the Samaritan.

The care is worth itemising, because Jesus itemises it. Bandages torn from his own clothing; his own oil and wine, the standard first-century treatment, now gone; his own animal, which means he walked; a night spent nursing a stranger; two denarii, two days' wages, enough for a fortnight's board; and then an open-ended undertaking — “whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.” A blank cheque, in a foreign town, for an unconscious man of the race that despised him.

“Go and do likewise” is not “go and feel compassion,” which is sentiment, or “go and have good intentions,” which are cheap. It is the specific, costly, schedule-wrecking, wallet-opening action of the Samaritan.

Which is unbearable if read honestly — and that is the moment it matters who is telling the story. One person has kept this command whole. He came down a far longer road, to where we were lying, when we were in no condition to ask; he paid what we could not, and he has promised to come back. The order is never mercy shown in order to earn mercy, but mercy received and then passed on (1 John 4:19). The command remains binding — and it is addressed to people who have already been picked up out of a ditch.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, 'Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' He said to him, 'What is written in the Law? How do you read it?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test.

A lawyer here is not an advocate in a court but an expert in the law of Moses — a scholar of Scripture, a man whose whole training was in what God had said and what it required.

And Luke tells us his motive before he opens his mouth: he stood up to put him to the test. This is not an enquiry. It is an examination, conducted in public, by a professional, of a Galilean teacher with no formal qualifications.

Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?

The question is enormous and the wording gives the man away. What shall I do? — the assumption is already in place before the answer arrives. Eternal life is a thing achieved by an action, and what he wants is the specification.

And there is a second thing buried in it that only shows up on a second reading. He asks what he must do to inherit. An inheritance is the one thing nobody works for. It comes by belonging to a family, and the beneficiary contributes nothing but a relationship. He has put a doing-word and a receiving-word in the same sentence and not noticed.

He said to him, What is written in the Law? How do you read it?

Jesus does not answer. He asks two questions back, and both are respectful — this man knows the law, and he is being invited to say so.

But the second question is doing something the first is not. What is written asks for the text. How do you read it asks for the man.

That distinction is worth having, because it is the difference between two things that are constantly confused. Any two people in a disagreement about Scripture usually have the same words in front of them. What differs is the reading — and a reading is never neutral. It is done by a person, with a history and a set of interests, who wants some things to be true and others not to be.

So Jesus has, in six words, moved the examination. The lawyer came to test him on the content of the law. He is about to be tested on what he has been doing with it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered, 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.' And he said to him, 'You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.

The lawyer's answer is superb, and it deserves saying so. He puts together Deuteronomy 6:5 — the Shema, which every Jew recited twice a day — and Leviticus 19:18, a single line buried in a chapter of miscellaneous statutes, and welds them into one command.

Nobody had to teach him that. He has read the law and seen its spine.

And the four terms are not a checklist of separate compartments; they are a way of saying all of you, with nothing held back. Heart, soul, strength, mind — the affections, the life, the effort, the thinking. There is no part of a man left over that is not commanded.

You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.

Which raises the question that ought to trouble anyone reading this with Paul in mind. Is Jesus really telling a man he can earn eternal life by keeping the law?

Take the sentence at face value and it is perfectly true. Anyone who loved God with the whole heart, soul, strength and mind, and his neighbour as himself, without a lapse, from first breath to last, would indeed live. God has never said otherwise. The catch is not in the offer. It is in the doer, and there has never been one — apart from the man saying it.

So Jesus is using the law exactly as the law was meant to be used: not as a ladder to climb but as a mirror to look into. Through the law comes knowledge of sin (Rom. 3:20); it was our guardian until Christ came (Gal. 3:24), and its work is to bring a man to the end of himself so that he will look elsewhere.

And watch how well it works here. Jesus says do this and you will live, and the lawyer does not say amen and go home content. The very next thing he does is start negotiating the terms — desiring to justify himself (v. 29).

That is a man who has just felt the floor move. He asked how much he had to do, and has been handed a standard that leaves him nowhere to stand; and rather than fall, he reaches for a definition small enough to survive on.

The parable that follows is not a softening of the demand. It takes his last handhold away.

verseByVerse.quote: But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, 'And who is my neighbor?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, And who is my neighbor?

Luke gives the motive again, and this time it is the hinge of the whole chapter. Desiring to justify himself — wanting to come out of this conversation still standing, still right, still able to say that he had done what was required.

The question that produces the world's most famous story is asked by a man looking for somewhere to hide.

And notice what a clever question it is. It is not evasive on the surface at all. It sounds like precision — the reasonable request of a careful scholar wanting to know the scope of a term before he applies it. Any lawyer would ask it.

But run it out and see where it goes. If neighbour can be defined, then it has edges. And if it has edges, there are people outside them. And if there are people outside them, then a man can love everyone inside the line, be entirely obedient, and walk past the rest with a clear conscience.

That is what he is after. Not whom should I love? but whom am I permitted not to?

And it was a live question with real answers on offer. The rabbinic discussion of Leviticus 19:18 turned on the surrounding phrase, the sons of your own people — so neighbour was generally taken to mean a fellow Israelite. Some communities of the period drew it tighter still: the Qumran sect required its members to love the sons of light and hate the sons of darkness. Every one of those definitions gave a man a boundary and let him rest.

Which is worth pressing on, because the instinct is universal and it does not present itself as wickedness. It presents itself as realism. Nobody can help everybody; a line has to be drawn somewhere; the question is where. And the moment a line is agreed, the people beyond it stop being a claim on anyone.

Every version of that reasoning was standing behind this question, and Jesus is about to tell a story in which the line the lawyer most wanted — the racial one — is crossed by the man he least wanted to admire.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus replied, 'A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho.

Note what we are not told. No name, no trade, no nationality, no religion. He is simply a man, and the omission is deliberate: the lawyer asked for a category, and the first thing the story refuses him is a category.

The road is real and it was notorious. Jerusalem sits about 2,500 feet above sea level; Jericho lies roughly 800 feet below it, seventeen miles away. The road drops over three thousand feet through limestone gorges and blind bends, with caves and rocks all along it. Jerome, living nearby centuries later, says it was still called the Red Ascent, and it was known as bandit country.

He fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead.

Stripped and beaten and unconscious. Which matters more than it looks, because those two details remove the only two things a passer-by could have used to identify him. Clothing told you a man's nationality and status; speech told you the rest. Naked and silent, he is unclassifiable.

He is a human being in a ditch, and there is no way to work out whether he is one of ours.

Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side.

The usual defence of the priest is ritual purity: contact with a corpse made a priest unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11-13) and barred him from temple service, and he could not tell from a distance whether the man was dead.

But look at the direction of travel. He was going down — away from Jerusalem, towards Jericho, which is where a great many priests lived between their rotations. His duty is behind him, not ahead. Whatever else was in his mind, a defiling contact on the way home would have cost him a week of inconvenience, not a lost turn at the altar.

And it is worth saying plainly that the law he was protecting had a clause about exactly this. The same Torah commands that a man help even his enemy's fallen animal (Ex. 23:4-5), and forbids standing by the blood of your neighbour (Lev. 19:16) — three verses before the command the lawyer had just quoted.

So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.

Luke adds a phrase for the second man: he came to the place. He got closer. He looked, from nearer, and crossed anyway.

And every listener now knows what comes next, because these stories run in threes and the third man is always the ordinary Israelite. Priest, Levite, layman. It is the joke shape, the sermon shape, the shape of every story anyone has ever told about the temple establishment failing while the common man does right.

What arrives instead detonates the entire structure.

verseByVerse.quote: But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But a Samaritan.

It is difficult now to feel what those words did to that audience.

The hostility was ancient, mutual and violent. Samaritans were the descendants of the northern kingdom's remnant, mixed with settlers brought in after the Assyrian conquest; they had their own temple on Mount Gerizim, their own edition of the Pentateuch, and no use for Jerusalem. Jews regarded them as heretics and half-breeds. Within living memory Samaritans had scattered human bones in the temple courts at Passover to defile it. The Gospel of John records the flat statement that Jews had no dealings with Samaritans (John 4:9), and it is only two chapters since a Samaritan village refused Jesus a bed and James and John asked to burn it (9:52-54).

This is the man Jesus makes the hero of the story — to a Jewish scholar of the law, in answer to a question about who counts as a neighbour.

And when he saw him, he had compassion.

The verb is esplanchnisthē — from the word for the inward organs, the gut. It describes compassion felt physically, the thing that turns over inside a person. Luke uses it exactly three times: of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the father seeing the prodigal on the road (15:20), and here.

And note the sequence, because it is the same sequence the priest and Levite had and broke. They saw and crossed over. He saw and was moved and went to him. The difference is not in the seeing. It is in what the seeing was allowed to do.

Then the care, and it is worth itemising, because Jesus itemises it.

He bound up his wounds — with strips of his own clothing, since there is nothing else on that road. He poured on oil and wine: the standard first-century treatment, wine to disinfect and oil to soothe, and both of them his own travelling supplies, now gone. He set him on his own animal, which means the Samaritan walked, at the pace of an injured man, for however many miles remained. He brought him to an inn and took care of him — that is a night, spent nursing a stranger.

And in the morning: two denarii, two days' wages for a labourer, which would have covered board for a fortnight or more. Then the sentence that goes furthest of all: whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.

He has just written a blank cheque, in a foreign town, for an unconscious man of the race that despises him, and bound himself to return.

verseByVerse.quote: Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?' He said, 'The one who showed him mercy.' And Jesus said to him, 'You go, and do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?

The question has been turned inside out, and that is the parable's most important move.

The lawyer asked who is my neighbour? — which puts the other person under examination and the questioner safely in the chair. Jesus asks which of the three proved to be a neighbour, which puts the questioner in the road and asks what he did.

It is no longer a question about the boundaries of obligation. It is a question about what kind of man is walking past.

He said, The one who showed him mercy.

He cannot say it. The answer is one word — the Samaritan — and he takes six to avoid it. Luke leaves that exposed without a syllable of comment, and it is the most human moment in the chapter: a man who has understood the story perfectly and cannot get the word out of his mouth.

And Jesus said to him, You go, and do likewise.

And there the parable stops, which is unbearable if you have been reading honestly. The command is not lowered by an inch at the end. Go and be the Samaritan — cross a racial hatred, spend your own money, give your own time, take on an open-ended liability for a stranger who can never repay you.

Anyone who finds that manageable has not understood it. Anyone who has understood it is standing exactly where the lawyer is standing, looking for somewhere to put his feet.

Which is the moment it matters enormously who is telling the story.

One person has kept this command whole. He came down a far longer road than the one from Jerusalem to Jericho, to where we were lying, when we were stripped and half dead and in no condition to ask. He bound up the wounds at his own expense. He paid what we could not, and he has promised to come back. And he is on the road to Jerusalem as he speaks, to settle the account himself.

The order is never mercy shown in order to earn mercy. It is mercy received, and then mercy passed on — we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Go and do likewise remains a command and it remains binding. But it is addressed to people who have already been picked up out of a ditch, and that is the only reason it is good news and not a sentence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes in a house in a village — Bethany, though Luke does not name it — and the placing is deliberate. The Samaritan has just poured out his time and money on a road, with “go and do likewise” still in the air. Now a woman does exactly that, and is gently told she has missed something.

Martha “welcomed him into her house” — her house, Luke says, which is unusual enough to notice, and the verb is the one for receiving a guest with honour. She is not a woman lacking spiritual interest. She is the one who let him in.

Mary “sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching,” and both halves of that would have struck a first-century reader. Sitting at a teacher's feet is the technical posture of a disciple — Paul describes his own training as being brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel” (Acts 22:3). And that place was not open to a woman. Mary sat down in it, Jesus let her, and in three verses he will defend her right to be there against her own sister. Luke reports it in a subordinate clause, as though it were ordinary — which, from now on, it is.

Martha is “distracted with much serving” — the verb means pulled around, dragged in different directions. It is not a word for being busy but for being torn. And the thing tearing her is diakonia, the word that will become the church's term for ministry: she is doing exactly what the women of 8:3 were commended for.

Her complaint takes three steps and each goes further. She interrupts his teaching; she accuses her sister in front of the guests; and then she accuses him. “Do you not care?” is not a request but a charge, levelled at the Lord she has just welcomed in — and then “tell her,” which does not even ask him to intervene but tells him what to say.

Every word of it is what an exhausted person says, and she is not wrong about the facts. What has happened is that a service began as a gift and turned, somewhere between the door and the fire, into a grievance — and the sign of it is that she is now keeping score.

“Martha, Martha” is the address of someone who sees the whole of a person: the same register as “Simon, Simon” (22:31), “Jerusalem, Jerusalem” (13:34), “Saul, Saul” (Acts 9:4). And the diagnosis is not of her workload but of her interior — “anxious,” the word for the worry he forbids in the sermon and the same root as the thorns that choke the word (8:14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Mary sitting at the Lord's feet is the posture of discipleship, and Luke has used the phrase once already of the Gerasene man restored to his right mind (8:35). In the first century women did not ordinarily receive rabbinic instruction, and the posture of female discipleship was itself a quiet revolution. Jesus does not redirect Mary to help; he defends her right to receive what he is giving.

“The good portion” plays on a word for a share at a meal — and Martha, of all people, would have felt it, since she is in the kitchen dividing portions while Mary has taken the one that matters.

“Which will not be taken away from her” carries the force of a promise. What Mary is receiving cannot be confiscated. The dinner will be eaten by nightfall and forgotten by the week's end; the word Mary is taking in is permanent, the living and abiding word of God (1 Pet. 1:23).

Some manuscripts read “few things are necessary, or only one” at v.42; the shorter reading is very likely original and the sense is unaffected either way. What lasts defines what is necessary, and what is necessary defines what must not be sacrificed to the urgent.
verseByVerse.examples:
The scene speaks to the perennial tension between doing and being. It does not abolish the tension; it orders it. Martha's service is not wrong — her anxiety is. And this is not a rebuke of practical work: Luke has just spent a chapter praising a man who bandaged a stranger and paid his bills.

It is a statement about order. Martha's work was needed. What was not needed was for it to be done by a woman who had stopped sitting down.

“Do you not care?” is worth naming for anyone who has prayed like it, because a good many have. It is the same accusation the disciples threw at him in the boat (Mark 4:38) — what resentment sounds like when it finally reaches God. And notice what he does with it: he does not rebuke her for the tone. He answers what is underneath it.

The Christian who serves without ever receiving will end up exactly where she is: efficient, indispensable, exhausted, and quietly furious with the people who are not helping — including, in the end, with the Lord it was all being done for. The cure is not less service. It is the recovery of the one thing that makes service a gift rather than a grievance.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village.

Luke does not name it. John does — Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem, the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus (John 11:1).

And the placing is deliberate. The chapter has just finished with a Samaritan pouring out his time and money on a road, and go and do likewise still hanging in the air. Now a woman does exactly that, and is gently told she has missed something.

Anyone who thinks Luke has arranged these two stories carelessly has not read him.

And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house.
