It is her house — Luke says so, and it is unusual enough to be worth noticing. And welcomed is the word for receiving a guest with honour. In a culture where hospitality was a sacred obligation and a travelling teacher with disciples meant a great deal of work, Martha opened her door to the lot of them.

This is not a woman being criticised for lacking spiritual interest. She is the one who let him in.

And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching.

Two details, and the first-century reader would have caught both.

Sat at the Lord's feet is a technical phrase. It is the posture of a disciple under a rabbi — Paul describes his own training as being brought up at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), and Luke has used the same phrase once already, of the Gerasene man restored to his right mind (8:35). It does not mean Mary was sitting on the floor being decorative. It means she had taken a student's place.

And that place was not open to her. Women were not disciples of rabbis. They were taught the law as it applied to their duties, and the formal relationship of teacher and student was a male arrangement.

Mary sat down in it, and Jesus let her, and in three verses' time he will defend her right to be there against her own sister.

Luke reports it without a flourish, in a subordinate clause, as though it were the ordinary thing. Which, from now on, it is.

verseByVerse.quote: But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, 'Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Martha was distracted with much serving.

The verb is periespato — literally to be pulled around, dragged in different directions. It is not a word for being busy. It is a word for being torn.

And the thing tearing her is much serving — diakonia, the word that will become the church's term for ministry. She is doing exactly what the women of 8:3 were commended for doing.

So the problem in this house is not that Martha chose work over devotion. The problem is what the work has become inside her, and Luke marks the moment it surfaces.

And she went up to him and said, Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.

Three things in one sentence, and each is a step further than the last.

She interrupts his teaching. She accuses her sister in front of the guests. And — this is the sharp one — she accuses him. Do you not care?

That is not a request. It is a charge, and it is levelled at the Lord she has just welcomed into her house. She has moved from serving him to reproaching him, and the distance between those two things was crossed in an afternoon, in a kitchen, doing a good thing.

Then tell her — she does not even ask him to intervene. She tells him what to say.

It would be easy to be hard on her, and it would be a mistake. Every word of her complaint is what an exhausted person says. She is not wrong about the facts: she is serving alone, and the meal does have to be produced, and somebody has to do it.

What has happened is that a service began as a gift and turned, somewhere between the door and the fire, into a grievance — and the sign of it is that she is now keeping score.

There is something worth naming for anyone who has ever prayed like this, because a good many have. Do you not care? is the same accusation the disciples threw at him in the boat (Mark 4:38). It is what resentment sounds like when it finally reaches God. And notice what he does with it: he does not rebuke her for the tone. He answers what is underneath it.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord answered her, 'Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Martha, Martha.

The doubled name is not impatience. Luke records it three other times in his two volumes, and the register is always the same: Simon, Simon, Satan demanded to have you (22:31); Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered your children (13:34); Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

It is the address of someone who sees the whole of a person and is about to say something they need and will not enjoy.

You are anxious and troubled about many things.

Two verbs, and neither is busy. Anxious is merimnas, the word for the worry Jesus forbids in the sermon (12:22-26), the same root as the thorns that choke the word in the parable of the soils (8:14). Troubled means agitated, thrown into turmoil.

He is not diagnosing her workload. He is diagnosing her interior, and it is worth being clear that these are the words he uses of unbelief rather than of overwork. She is not too busy. She is worried.

But one thing is necessary.

If your Bible has a footnote here, it is a real one: some manuscripts read few things are necessary, or only one. The shorter reading is very likely original and the sense is unaffected either way.

Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.

Two words carry it. Portion is the word for a share at a meal, and there is a play on it that Martha, of all people, would have felt — she is in the kitchen dividing up portions, and Mary has taken the one that matters. And will not be taken away is a promise: what Mary is receiving cannot be confiscated. The dinner Martha is making will be eaten by nightfall and forgotten by the week's end. The word Mary is taking in is permanent.

Now the pastoral point, and it must not be turned into what it is not.

This is not a rebuke of practical service, and Luke has just spent a chapter praising a man who bandaged a stranger and paid his bills. It is not a recommendation of contemplation over action. And it is certainly not an instruction that meals should go uncooked.

It is a statement about order. Martha's work was needed. What was not needed was for it to be done by a woman who had stopped sitting down.

The Christian who serves without ever receiving will end up exactly where she is: efficient, indispensable, exhausted, and quietly furious with the people who are not helping — including, in the end, with the Lord she is doing it all for.

10.text: <sup>1</sup> After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. <sup>3</sup> Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. <sup>4</sup> Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road. <sup>5</sup> Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ <sup>6</sup> And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. <sup>7</sup> And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house. <sup>8</sup> Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. <sup>9</sup> Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’ <sup>10</sup> But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, <sup>11</sup> ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ <sup>12</sup> I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town. <sup>13</sup> “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. <sup>14</sup> But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. <sup>15</sup> And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades. <sup>16</sup> “The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.” <sup>17</sup> The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” <sup>18</sup> And he said to them, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. <sup>19</sup> Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. <sup>20</sup> Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” <sup>21</sup> In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. <sup>22</sup> All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” <sup>23</sup> Then turning to the disciples he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! <sup>24</sup> For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” <sup>25</sup> And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>26</sup> He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” <sup>27</sup> And he answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” <sup>28</sup> And he said to him, “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.” <sup>29</sup> But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” <sup>30</sup> Jesus replied, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. <sup>31</sup> Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. <sup>32</sup> So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. <sup>33</sup> But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. <sup>34</sup> He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. <sup>35</sup> And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’ <sup>36</sup> Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” <sup>37</sup> He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” And Jesus said to him, “You go, and do likewise.” <sup>38</sup> Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. <sup>39</sup> And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching. <sup>40</sup> But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.” <sup>41</sup> But the Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, <sup>42</sup> but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

11.title: Prayer, Darkness, and the Woes of the Pharisees
11.overview:
Chapter 11 divides into three movements of escalating intensity. It opens with the disciples' request — “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples” — and Jesus's response: the Lord's Prayer and two parables about persistent asking. It continues with the controversy over Beelzebul, where Jesus is accused of casting out demons by the power of the prince of demons, and responds with the parable of the strong man, the sign of Jonah, and a warning about the darkness that replaces expelled light. And it closes with the most sustained series of woes in Luke's Gospel — six pronouncements against the Pharisees and lawyers that are simultaneously the most confrontational and the most sorrowful words Jesus speaks in public.

The chapter's movement from prayer (vv. 1–13) to spiritual warfare (vv. 14–36) to religious condemnation (vv. 37–54) is not a random sequence. The prayer section establishes the relationship with the Father that makes spiritual life possible. The Beelzebul controversy shows what happens when the kingdom's power is at work in the world — it provokes opposition, demands decision, and warns against the neutrality that is actually a form of hostility. And the woes reveal what becomes of religious life when it loses the relationship with the Father — when the form of religion remains but the substance has been evacuated, replaced by the performance of piety for the wrong audience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying, and when he finishes one of the disciples asks: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” Of everything on offer in three years beside the Son of God — the healings, the stilled storm, the knowledge of men's thoughts — the one thing a disciple asked to be taught was how to talk to his Father.

Luke's version is shorter than Matthew's (Matt. 6:9-13), and that difference has unsettled readers who learned the prayer by heart as children. Where is “who art in heaven”? Where is “thy will be done”? An older Bible will have them at this very verse and a modern one will not.

There is nothing sinister in it. Luke's prayer was always the shorter of the two, but the version the church actually prayed aloud, week after week for centuries, was Matthew's — and scribes copying Luke knew that fuller wording by heart. Line by line, over generations, they filled Luke out to match what their lips already said. It is one of the most understandable corrections in the history of copying and one of the easiest to detect: the earliest manuscripts of Luke are short, and the additions match Matthew word for word. Nothing was lost. Every phrase you were taught is genuinely the Lord's; it is simply Matthew who recorded it.

And Luke's shorter form is worth having in its own right, because two versions tell us something one could not. Jesus plainly gave this prayer more than once, and not in identical words. Matthew says “pray then like this”; Luke says “when you pray, say.” Set them side by side and the conclusion is unavoidable: this was never handed down as a formula to be recited syllable-perfect on pain of not counting. It is a shape for praying — a floor to build on, not a ceiling.

The prayer opens with one word that was a revolution. The Old Testament calls God Father perhaps a dozen times, nearly always of his relation to Israel as a nation; what is almost entirely absent is an individual addressing him that way in prayer. Behind Luke's Greek stands the Aramaic Abba, the word Jesus uses in Gethsemane — family vocabulary, and no Jew of that period prayed with it.

Then five petitions: his name, his kingdom, our bread, our forgiveness, our protection. God first, then us — and the order is not decoration. A prayer that begins with God's honour can bring every human need afterwards without becoming a list submitted to a dispenser.
verseByVerse.theology:
The address “Father” is the theological revolution of this prayer. Paul will name what has happened: “you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'” (Rom. 8:15). The address is not a warmer name for the same relationship; it is a different relationship — the Son's own, opened to people with no natural claim to it.

“Hallowed be your name” asks that God be treated as holy, since his name cannot be made more holy than it is. A name in Hebrew thought is the person as he is known, so the petition asks that he be known, honoured and reverenced as what he actually is — first by the one praying, and then by everybody else. It is a request the person praying is volunteering to be part of the answer to.

“Your kingdom come” is the central petition and the shortest, and it cannot be prayed at a distance. To ask for God's rule to come is to ask for one's own to end, and there is no version of the sentence that leaves the person praying in charge of the parts he was hoping to keep. Every honest praying of it is a small abdication.

The word behind “daily” is epiousios, one of the strangest in the New Testament — so rare that Origen, a native Greek speaker, concluded the evangelists had coined it. It most likely means “for the coming day.” It is a small request, deliberately: enough for today, asked today, and again tomorrow.
verseByVerse.examples:
The “for” in “forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive” has troubled readers, and it must not become a bargain. God's forgiveness is not purchased by ours; the prayer has just called him Father, which nobody earns.

What the clause does is make our forgiving the evidence that his has landed — a diagnostic, not a transaction. A man who has grasped the size of what has been cancelled on his own account cannot go on with a ledger open against his neighbour; and if he can, the honest question is whether he has understood the first half of the sentence at all. Matthew makes the connection explicit (Matt. 6:14-15).

Note the tense, too: “we ourselves forgive,” present and continuing. Not “we forgave, once, years ago.” It is a standing policy.

And “lead us not into temptation” uses peirasmos, the same word as at 4:2, covering both testing and enticement. It is not a fear that God might try to make us sin, which James forbids (Jas. 1:13). It is the prayer of a person who knows his own weakness well enough to ask not to be brought to the edge of it — which is a far more realistic prayer than asking for strength to survive the edge.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, Lord, teach us to pray.

Notice the order. He prays; they watch; and when he has finished, one of them asks.

They had been with him long enough by now to have seen a great deal. They had watched him still a storm, feed thousands, raise the dead, and silence a legion of demons with four words. Any one of those would have been worth asking about.

What they asked for was this.

Luke does not tell us what they saw in his praying, and he does not need to. He has been noting it since the Jordan — at the baptism (3:21), before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before the great question at Caesarea Philippi (9:18), on the mountain where his face changed (9:29). Something about the way this man prayed was different enough that men who had grown up saying prayers three times a day concluded they did not know how.

As John taught his disciples.

That is a useful detail. Rabbis and movements had characteristic prayers; they functioned as a kind of identity, a way of marking out what a group was for. John had given his followers one, and Jesus's disciples want the same from him — not merely instruction in the discipline, but a prayer that belongs to them.

And there is one further thing worth stopping on. The request is not teach us to preach, or teach us to heal, though they had just come back from a mission where both were happening. It is not teach us how you know what people are thinking. Of everything on offer in three years of walking beside the Son of God, the one thing a disciple asked to be taught was how to talk to his Father.

Which is a fair diagnosis of where most people are. Almost every Christian who has been at it for a while will admit, if pressed honestly, that prayer is the part that never quite settles. It is the first thing to go in a busy week and the last thing to come back.

The answer to that is not a technique, and it is not more determination. It is what the disciple did here: to say out loud, to the one person who can do anything about it, that he does not know how.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you pray, say: Father.

One word, and it was a revolution.

The Old Testament calls God Father perhaps a dozen times, and nearly always of his relation to Israel as a nation — is not he your Father, who created you? (Deut. 32:6); you, O LORD, are our Father (Isa. 63:16). What is almost entirely absent is an individual Israelite addressing God that way in prayer. The standard addresses were LORD, God of our fathers, King of the universe — titles that keep a proper distance.

Behind Luke's Greek stands the Aramaic Abba, the word Jesus uses in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). It is not baby-talk, as is sometimes said; grown men used it of their fathers. But it is family vocabulary, and no Jew of that period prayed with it.

He hands it to them as the first word.

And Paul will later say exactly what has happened: you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba! Father! (Rom. 8:15). The address is not a nicer name for the same relationship. It is a different relationship, and it is the Son's own, opened to people who have no natural claim to it whatsoever.

Hallowed be your name.

A name in Hebrew thought is the person as he is known. To hallow it is to set it apart as holy — and since God's name cannot be made more holy than it is, the petition asks that he be treated as holy: known, honoured, and reverenced as what he actually is, first by the one praying and then by everybody else.

Which is a startling thing to put first. The prayer opens by asking that God's reputation be repaired in a world that has trampled it — and it is a request the person praying is volunteering to be part of the answer to.

Your kingdom come.

The central petition of the prayer, and the shortest. It asks for the reign of God to arrive — in the world finally, and in this life now.

And it cannot be prayed at a distance. To ask for God's rule to come is to ask for one's own to end, and there is no version of the sentence that leaves the person praying in charge of the parts he had been hoping to keep. Every honest praying of it is a small abdication.

verseByVerse.quote: Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the prayer turns to us, and it asks for three things: bread, forgiveness, and protection. Body, past, future. There is nothing else a human being needs.

Give us each day our daily bread.

The word behind daily is epiousios, and it is one of the strangest words in the New Testament. It occurs here and in Matthew's version and almost nowhere else in surviving Greek — so rare that Origen, three centuries later and a native speaker, concluded the evangelists must have coined it. It most likely means for the coming day: the bread needed to get through today.

So it is a small request, deliberately. Not a year's security, not a pension, not the removal of uncertainty — enough for today, asked for today, and again tomorrow.

Anyone who has ever wished God would settle their finances once and for all, so that the matter could be closed and no longer prayed about, has been asking for something this prayer will not give. Israel in the wilderness got manna that rotted overnight (Ex. 16:19-20), and it was not a punishment. It was a daily appointment.

And forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us.

Luke says sins where Matthew says debts, and then keeps the debt language in the second half — everyone who is indebted to us. The two ideas are the same. A sin is something owed and not paid.

The for in the middle has troubled people, and it should not become a bargain. It does not mean God's forgiveness is purchased by ours; the whole of Scripture forbids that reading, and this same prayer has just called him Father, which no one earns.

What it does is make our forgiving the evidence that his has landed. It is a diagnostic, not a transaction. A man who has genuinely grasped the size of what has been cancelled on his own account cannot go on with a ledger open against his neighbour — and if he can, the honest question is whether he has understood the first half of the sentence at all.

And note the tense: we ourselves forgive, present, continuing. Not we forgave, once, years ago. It is a standing policy.

And lead us not into temptation.

The word is peirasmos — the same word as at 4:2, covering both testing and enticement. It is not a fear that God might try to make us sin; James settles that (Jas. 1:13). It is the prayer of a person who knows his own weakness well enough to ask not to be brought to the edge of it. Which is a far more realistic prayer than asking for the strength to survive the edge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–13 — Ask, and It Will Be Given
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two illustrations follow the prayer, and both argue from the lesser to the greater.

The first is the friend at midnight. To feel it you have to see the house: one room, the family asleep together on a raised platform, a single door barred at night with a beam that cannot be lifted quietly. Getting up wakes everybody. And there is no bread in the house, because bread was baked daily and eaten daily.

The man banging on the door is not being inconsiderate. Hospitality in that culture was an obligation with the weight of law, and a traveller arriving at night was the whole village's guest; to fail him was a public disgrace. He asks a friend, at the worst possible hour, for three loaves — enough for one meal — and he asks to borrow them.

The sleeper's excuses are all true. The door is barred, the children are asleep, getting up will wake them. And he gets up anyway, “because of his impudence” — anaideia, shamelessness.

Whose shamelessness has been argued over. The traditional reading takes it as the asker's brazen persistence. A second reading, with a good deal to be said for it, takes it as the sleeper's — he rises to avoid the disgrace of being the man who had bread and would not open the door. Both land in the same place: if even this man gives, how much more the Father, who is neither asleep nor inconvenienced.

What the parable licenses is boldness. Most prayer dies of good manners, and this story was told to kill that.

Then “ask, seek, knock” — all three in the present tense, all three continuous — and a promise unconditional in form: “everyone who asks receives.” Which raises the honest problem, because a great many people have read that verse and then buried someone they prayed for.

Jesus answers it with a picture of a father and a child. A fish and a snake are roughly the same shape; an egg and a coiled scorpion are roughly the same shape. What is described is not a father refusing his son but a father handing him something that looks like what he asked for and will hurt him — and no father does that.
verseByVerse.theology:
The three imperatives are in the present tense, implying continuous action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. And there is a progression. Asking is words; seeking involves the feet; knocking is standing at a closed door that has not yet opened, and staying there.

On the difficulty in v.10, three things have to be said. Scripture itself never treats the promise as a blank cheque and says so in the same breath: “if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14), and “you ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (Jas. 4:3). Jesus himself prayed a prayer not granted in the form he asked it — “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). And the next four verses are his own commentary, which is where the weight lies.

A request denied is not a father who is deaf. It is a father who has looked at what was asked for and seen a snake where the child saw a fish. That does not make unanswered prayer painless, and it is not meant to. What it removes is the one conclusion that would be unbearable — that the silence means indifference.

And Luke's ending is his own. Matthew has “how much more will your Father give good things” (Matt. 7:11); Luke has “the Holy Spirit.” Luke's version tells you what good things finally means. The best thing the Father has to give is not a solution to a circumstance; it is himself, present, in a person.
verseByVerse.examples:
“You, who are evil” is dropped in without emphasis, as agreed common ground. He is talking to ordinary decent parents and takes it as obvious that they are bad — and that even so, they would not hand a child a scorpion.

The parable of the friend at midnight is also worth noticing for what the man needs. He is not asking for himself. He wants bread because someone has arrived and he has nothing to give them — which is the position of everyone who has ever tried to help another person and found himself empty.

And “give us each day our daily bread” has a hard edge for anyone who has wished God would settle their finances once and for all, so the matter could be closed and no longer prayed about. Israel in the wilderness got manna that rotted overnight (Ex. 16:19-20), and it was not a punishment. It was a daily appointment.

For anyone praying about something that has not moved in years, this is where the passage lands. Whatever else has or has not been given, the one gift explicitly promised to everyone who asks is God himself — and he is the only gift that cannot arrive in the wrong shape.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, Friend, lend me three loaves.

To feel this parable you have to see the house.

A peasant home in a Galilean village was one room. The family slept together on a raised platform at one end, on mats, with the animals below at the other. There was a single door, and it was barred at night with a heavy wooden beam that could not be lifted quietly. Getting up meant waking everyone.

And there was no bread in the house at midnight, because bread was baked daily and eaten daily. There was no cupboard to raid.

For a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.

Here is the pressure the parable turns on, and a modern reader will miss it entirely without help.

Hospitality in that culture was not a courtesy. It was an obligation with the weight of law, and it was not a private matter between host and guest — it was a village matter. A traveller arriving at night was the whole community's guest, and to fail him was a public disgrace that attached to everyone.

So the man banging on the door is not being inconsiderate. He is doing what any neighbour would expect. And the request is modest and specific: three loaves, enough for one meal, and lend — he will bake tomorrow and return them.

Notice too that he asks a friend. This is not a stranger's door. There is an existing relationship, and he presumes on it at the worst possible hour, which is precisely what friendship is for.

And that is the picture Jesus has chosen for prayer, immediately after teaching them to say Father. Not a subject petitioning a distant monarch through the correct channels at an appointed hour. A man in the dark, out of bread, with somebody depending on him, walking round to a house where he knows he will be heard.

The need in the parable is also worth noticing. He is not asking for himself. He wants the bread because someone has arrived and he has nothing to give them — which is, as it happens, the position of everyone who has ever tried to help another person and found himself empty.

verseByVerse.quote: and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything.

The excuses are entirely accurate. The door is barred; the children are asleep on the mat beside him; getting up will wake the household. Every word of it is true.

And it is worth saying plainly, before anything else, that this man is not God. The parable is not a picture of a reluctant deity who has to be worn down. It is what the ancients called an argument from the lesser to the greater, and it works by contrast, not by comparison — if even this, how much more that.

Yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.

The word is anaideia, and it is rare enough that its sense here has been argued over for a long time. Literally it is shamelessness: the absence of the ordinary restraint that would stop a man knocking at midnight.

The traditional reading takes it as the asker's — his brazen persistence wears the neighbour down. That is a natural reading and it fits what follows in v. 9, where the verbs are continuous: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking.

But there is a second reading with a good deal to be said for it, and it is worth knowing. On this view the shamelessness belongs to the sleeper — he gets up to avoid the disgrace of being the man who had bread and would not open the door. In a village where everyone would hear about it by morning, his own honour is at stake.

Both readings land in the same place, which is why the argument need not be settled here. Either the asker's boldness prevails, or the host's regard for his own name does. And in both cases the point is the same: how much more the Father, who is neither asleep, nor inconvenienced, nor concerned to protect a reputation he does not have to defend.

What the parable licenses is the boldness. Not politeness, not the carefully worded petition submitted through proper channels — a man banging on a door in the dark because he has nothing and knows where the bread is.

Most prayer dies of good manners. It is possible to be so respectful of God that nothing is ever actually asked for, and this parable was told to kill that.

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

Three imperatives, and all three are in the present tense: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. That is not a technicality. It rules out the reading where a single well-formed request is submitted and the matter is closed.

And there is a progression in them. Asking is words. Seeking involves the feet — it is what a man does when the thing is not lying where he can point at it. Knocking is standing at a closed door that has not yet opened, and staying there.

For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

Which brings us to the honest problem, and it must not be stepped over, because a great many people have read this verse and then buried someone they prayed for.

The promise as it stands is unconditional in form. Everyone who asks receives. And a Christian who has asked for years for a marriage to be saved, a child to come home, a body to be healed — and watched none of it happen — is entitled to put the verse and the experience side by side and ask what is going on.

Three things have to be said, and the third is the one that carries the weight.

The first is that Scripture itself never treats this as a blank cheque, and it says so in the same breath as the promise. John writes: if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 John 5:14). And James is blunter: you ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions (Jas. 4:3). The New Testament that records this promise is the same New Testament that qualifies it, and it is not embarrassed to do both.

The second is that Jesus himself prayed a prayer that was not granted in the form he asked. Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me (22:42). If everyone who asks receives meant what the anxious reading takes it to mean, that sentence could not exist.

The third is that the next four verses are Jesus's own commentary on this one, and he chose to answer the question with a picture of a father and a child. Which is where he takes it, and it settles more than any argument.

verseByVerse.quote: What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?

Two pairs, and both are chosen with care. A fish and a snake are roughly the same shape; an egg and a coiled scorpion, pale and about the size of a fist, are roughly the same shape too. What is being described is not a father refusing his son but a father handing him something that looks like the thing he wanted and will hurt him.

And every parent listening knows the answer instantly. Nobody does that. It is not even a temptation.

If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children.

He drops it in without emphasis, as an agreed fact: you, who are evil. Not you, who are imperfect or you, who mean well. He is talking to ordinary decent parents, and he takes it as common ground that they are bad — and that even so, they would not hand a child a scorpion.

How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!

Here is the answer to the difficulty in verse 10, and it is not a qualification of the promise but a description of who is keeping it.

What a good father will not do is give a child something harmful that resembles what was asked for. Which means that a request denied is not a father who is deaf; it is a father who has looked at what was asked for and seen a snake where the child saw a fish.

That does not make unanswered prayer painless. It is not intended to. What it does is remove the one conclusion that would be unbearable — that the silence means indifference.

And then Luke does something that ought to stop the reader, because Matthew's version of this saying ends differently. Matthew has: how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him (Matt. 7:11). Luke has the Holy Spirit.

Both are the Lord's words, and Luke's is the one that tells you what good things finally means. The best thing the Father has to give is not a solution to a circumstance. It is himself, present, in a person.

Which is worth holding by anyone praying about something that has not moved for years. Whatever else has or has not been given, the one gift explicitly promised to everyone who asks is God himself — and he is the only gift that cannot arrive in the wrong shape.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–28 — Jesus and Beelzebul; True Blessedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus casts out a demon that has made a man mute, and the crowd marvels. Two responses come from the critics, and they are the only two available to anyone who does not want to accept him.

The first is the Beelzebul charge — that he works by the prince of demons. Notice what it concedes: nobody disputes that the man is speaking, and nobody suggests a trick. The miracle is granted and the source reassigned, which is in its way the strongest testimony in the chapter to the fact that it happened.

The second is a demand for “a sign from heaven” — a real one, not this business with a local demoniac. Made by people standing in the presence of the evidence, that is not scepticism; it is a way of postponing a decision indefinitely while appearing reasonable.

Jesus dismantles the charge twice over. A divided kingdom cannot stand, so Satan casting out Satan is destroying his own operation. And “by whom do your sons cast them out?” exposes a standard applied to him and not to their own exorcists — which means the objection is not the real reason.

Then his own account: “if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.” The phrase occurs three times in the Old Testament — Pharaoh's magicians conceding they are out of their depth (Ex. 8:19), and the tablets written by God's own finger (Ex. 31:18; Deut. 9:10). Deliverance from slavery and the giving of the covenant, in three words. And the verb is “has come upon you” — not near, as the seventy-two announced (10:9), but arrived.

The parable of the strong man is the interpretation of everything he has done. The strong man is fully armed, on his own ground, and while that holds his goods are safe. Then one stronger attacks, overcomes, strips the armour he trusted in, and divides the spoil. And the goods, in this context, are people.

The section closes with two warnings. Neutrality is abolished — “whoever does not gather with me scatters.” And the swept house: a life cleaned up and left empty is not a neutral state on the way to better. It is a vacancy, advertised.
verseByVerse.theology:
The warning about the returning spirit is the parabolic form of the New Testament's consistent warning against reformation without regeneration. Everything in the description is good news — swept, put in order, the mess dealt with, the habits sorted. One word is missing, and it is the whole point: nobody is living there.

Jesus's assessment of that condition is not “an improvement, as far as it goes.” It is “worse than the first,” because an empty swept house has been made attractive. The remedy is not more sweeping but occupation — and Luke has just named who is available, and how he is described: one stronger, who walks into an occupied house and takes it (v. 22). The Gerasene man was not left empty either; he was found sitting at the feet of Jesus (8:35).

“Whoever is not with me is against me” must be read alongside 9:50, “the one who is not against you is for you,” and the two sit together once you watch the pronouns. There the subject is you — the disciples' judgement of a stranger. Here it is me — a person's own standing before Christ. Generous outward, rigorous inward. Reverse those two and you get exactly the religion Jesus is about to spend fifteen verses dismantling.

And note what Jesus assumes in passing while making his argument: that the kingdom of darkness is a kingdom — organised, unified, under command, and pursuing an interest it will not act against. He says it as something too obvious to argue.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's beatitude on Jesus's mother is well meant and entirely ordinary in that culture: praise the son by praising the woman who produced him. Elizabeth said something very like it in this Gospel's first chapter (1:42).

The word “rather” is doing careful work in the reply. It is not a contradiction but a redirection, and it refuses the assumption underneath the compliment — that blessedness is a matter of proximity. If that were true the whole thing would be closed to everybody else, since there is exactly one womb that bore him.

What he offers instead is open to the entire crowd: “hear the word of God and keep it” — two things anybody can do, in any century, at any distance from Nazareth. And Mary is the outstanding instance of exactly that: “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38). The correction takes nothing from her. It says that what made her blessed was not the biology, which nobody can share, but the faith, which everybody can.

And the swept-house warning is worth turning into a question by anyone whose Christianity consists mainly of things they have stopped doing. Not “what have you got rid of?” but “who lives there now?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. But some of them said, 'He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,' while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now he was casting out a demon that was mute.

Luke's phrasing is compressed — the demon is named by its effect. The man could not speak, and when the demon went out he did.

And the crowd's reaction is the same as everywhere else: the people marveled. Wonder, which is not the same as faith and never has been.

Then two responses from the critics, and they are the only two available to anyone who does not want to accept him.

He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons.

Notice what this concedes. Nobody disputes that the man is speaking. Nobody suggests a trick. The miracle is granted and the source is reassigned — which is, in its way, the strongest testimony in the chapter to the fact that it happened. His enemies were reduced to explaining it, not denying it.

The name itself has a history. Baal-zebub — lord of the flies — was the god of Ekron whom a king of Israel once sent to consult instead of the LORD, and Elijah met the messengers on the road with a message about it (2 Kgs. 1:2-3). The Hebrew name may itself be a deliberate mockery of Baal-zebul, lord of the exalted dwelling. By the first century the word had become a title for the chief of the demons.

So the charge is as serious as a charge can be. Not he is mistaken, not he is unqualified, but the power in him is the enemy's. And they are saying it about a man who has just given a mute person his voice back.

While others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.

The second response is subtler and it is worse. They want a sign — a real one, from the sky, not this business with a local demoniac.

Which is a way of not counting what has just happened in front of them. The demand for further evidence, made by people standing in the presence of the evidence, is not scepticism. It is a way of postponing a decision indefinitely while appearing reasonable, and it is available to anyone at any time, because there is always one more thing that could be asked for.

Luke says they were doing it to test him. The verb has been used once before in this Gospel — in the wilderness, of the devil (4:2).

verseByVerse.quote: But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, 'Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he, knowing their thoughts.

Luke says the Beelzebul charge was made by some of them, and the sign-seeking by others. Whether either was said to his face, Jesus answers what is in the room.

Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls.

He begins with a proposition nobody would dispute, drawn from politics and from family life — two things everybody in that crowd had watched fail. Then he applies it.

And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand?

The logic is simple and it is airtight. If the prince of demons is expelling demons, he is dismantling his own operation. No commander destroys his own positions.

Notice what is assumed along the way, though, because it is easy to miss under the argument. Jesus takes it as given that the kingdom of darkness is a kingdom — organised, unified, under command, and pursuing an interest it will not act against. That is a good deal more than most modern readers assume, and he says it in passing as something too obvious to argue.

And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out?

Now the second argument, and it is devastating.

Your sons almost certainly means Jewish exorcists of their own party — the practice existed, Luke records an instance in his second volume (Acts 19:13-14), and it was not controversial among them. So the critics have a standard they apply to Jesus and do not apply to their own.

That is the shape of the thing, and it is worth naming because it recurs. The objection is not being applied consistently, which means it is not really the reason. Something else is doing the work, and the argument has been assembled afterwards to justify a conclusion already reached.

Therefore they will be your judges.

Their own people will testify against them — not because those exorcists were remarkable, but because the double standard is on the record.

And there is a hard word in this for anyone who has ever constructed a reason for not accepting something they did not want to accept. The reasoning is usually sound. It simply is not what is actually going on.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

Having dismantled the alternative, he states his own account of what is happening — and he does it with a phrase that would have gone off like a bell in that crowd.

The finger of God occurs three times in the Old Testament, and each is worth having.

The first is in Egypt. Pharaoh's magicians have matched Moses trick for trick — the staffs, the blood, the frogs. Then comes the plague of gnats, and they cannot reproduce it, and they go to Pharaoh and say: This is the finger of God (Ex. 8:19). It is the moment the opposition concedes that it is out of its depth, spoken by professional practitioners of the dark arts about a power they recognise and cannot copy.

The other two are the tablets: tablets of stone, written with the finger of God (Ex. 31:18; Deut. 9:10).

So the phrase carries deliverance from slavery and the giving of the covenant in the same three words — and Jesus takes it, in a Galilean street, in an argument with men who have just accused him of witchcraft, and applies it to what he has done for one mute man.

The parallel in Matthew reads by the Spirit of God (Matt. 12:28), which is the same thing said plainly. Luke keeps the Exodus wording.

Then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

This is one of the most important sentences in Luke, and the verb is the point. Not is near, which is what the seventy-two were sent to announce (10:9). Has come upon you — arrived, landed, already here.

The kingdom of God is not, in the first instance, a place or a programme or a future era. It is God reigning; and where the King acts, the reign is present. Which is why the evidence he offers for its arrival is not a throne or an army but a man who can suddenly talk.

And note the pronoun. Upon you — spoken to the people accusing him. The kingdom had arrived in their street, on their afternoon, in front of them. Nearness is not the issue and never was. They were standing in it.

verseByVerse.quote: When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe.

A short parable, and it is the interpretation of everything he has just done.

Take the picture as it stands. The strong man is not weak, and he is not asleep. He is fully armed. He is in his own house, on his own ground, guarding property he regards as his. And Jesus grants the premise: while that arrangement holds, his goods are safe.

That is a sober assessment of the world before he came. The human race was not a neutral territory awaiting instruction. It was occupied, and the occupier was armed, and the goods were secure.

But when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil.

Four verbs, and each is worse than the last for the strong man.

Attacks — the initiative is not his. Overcomes — it is not a contest; it is a result. Takes away his armor — the man is not merely beaten but disarmed, and Luke adds the detail that this was armour in which he trusted, so what is removed is also his confidence. And divides his spoil — the property is not merely recovered; it is distributed, handed out, given away.

Then note what the goods in this parable are. Not gold. The context is exorcism, and the thing carried out of the strong man's house is a human being who could not speak.

So this is what a healing means, seen from above. Every demon evicted, every sickness reversed, every sin forgiven is plunder — property taken off an armed occupier by someone who walked in and was not stopped.

And there is no struggle recorded anywhere in this Gospel. He speaks and it is over. The demons in Luke do not fight him; they beg (8:28, 8:31). The strong man in this parable never lands a blow.

Here, then, is what was actually happening in a village street while men argued about the source of his power. The house of the great occupier was standing open, the armour he had trusted in was on the floor, and the goods he had held for the whole of human history were being carried out and handed back to the people they were taken from.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.

The middle ground is abolished in one sentence, and it is worth seeing why it is placed here.

Two groups have just been described. One accused him of working by Beelzebul; the other wanted a further sign. Neither has committed to anything. The second group in particular would have thought of itself as open-minded — not hostile, merely waiting for more evidence.

Jesus tells them there is no such position.

The reason is in the second half, and the image is agricultural. Gather and scatter are harvest words, and the harvest has already been named two chapters earlier: the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few (10:2). There is a gathering going on. Anyone not part of it is, by the simple fact of standing in the field doing nothing, part of the loss.

Which is the sharp edge of the saying, and it has nothing to do with hostility. Scattering does not require malice; it requires only absence. Grain left ungathered is lost by exactly the same amount whether it was trampled deliberately or simply not picked up.

Now a reader with a good memory will object, because two chapters ago Jesus said what sounds like the opposite. John reported that they had stopped a man casting out demons in his name, and was told: do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you (9:50).

The two sit together once you watch the pronouns.

There, the subject was you — the disciples' judgement of a stranger. Here the subject is me — a person's own standing before Christ. And the two run in opposite directions on purpose. About somebody else, doing good in Christ's name outside your circle: assume the best, and do not stop him. About yourself, in relation to Christ: assume nothing, because neutrality is not on offer.

Generous outward, rigorous inward. Reverse those two and you get exactly the religion Jesus is about to spend fifteen verses dismantling.

verseByVerse.quote: 'When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, I will return to my house from which I came.

A strange little story, and its point is one of the most searching things in the chapter.

Note the pronoun the spirit uses: my house. It has been evicted and it has not conceded ownership. And it comes back to inspect.

And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order.

Everything in that sentence is good news, and that is what makes the story so unsettling.

Swept — cleaned. Put in order — tidied, arranged, set right. This is not a person who relapsed. This is a person whose life visibly improved: the mess dealt with, the habits sorted out, the household running properly.

And there is one word missing, and it is the whole point. Nobody is living there.

Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.

The house was not merely available. It had been made attractive.

Which is the warning, and it is aimed squarely at something the church produces in quantity: reformation without regeneration. A man gives up the drink, or the affair, or the temper. He tidies the house. He is, by any external measure, better than he was — and everyone around him says so, which makes it harder rather than easier to see what has not happened.

What has not happened is that anyone has moved in.

And Jesus's assessment of that condition is not an improvement, as far as it goes. It is worse than the first. An empty swept house is not a neutral state on the way to something better. It is a vacancy, advertised.

The remedy is not more sweeping. It is occupation — and Luke has just told us in the same paragraph who is available to do it, and how he is described: one stronger, who walks into an occupied house and takes it (v. 22). The Gerasene man was not left empty either. He was found sitting at the feet of Jesus (8:35).

Anyone whose Christianity consists mainly of things they have stopped doing should read this paragraph slowly. The question it puts is not what have you got rid of? but who lives there now?

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, 'Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!' But he said, 'Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!

It is one of the most human interruptions in the Gospels. In the middle of an argument about demons and kingdoms, a woman shouts a blessing on his mother.

And it is entirely well meant. It is also a very ordinary way to honour a man in that culture — praise the son by praising the woman who produced him. There is no criticism in what she says, and no error in it: Elizabeth said something very like it, filled with the Holy Spirit, in this Gospel's first chapter (1:42).

But he said, Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!

The word rather is doing careful work. It is not a contradiction; it is a redirection — yes, and here is where the blessing actually lies.

And notice what he does not do. He does not deny that his mother is blessed. He said as much himself when the same question came up in a different form and he redefined his family as those who hear the word of God and do it (8:21) — which is the same sentence as this one, four chapters earlier, with the same two verbs.

What he refuses is the assumption underneath the compliment: that blessedness is a matter of proximity, and that the closest person to Jesus of Nazareth is necessarily the most blessed.

If that were true, the whole thing would be closed to everybody else. There is exactly one womb that bore him. Nobody else can compete for that, and nobody else can have it.

What he offers instead is open to the entire crowd, including the woman who shouted. Hear the word of God and keep it — two things anybody can do, in any century, at any distance from Nazareth.

And it is worth adding, because it is often missed in the anxiety to keep Mary in her place, that she is the outstanding example of the very thing he commends. When the angel finished speaking she said, let it be to me according to your word (1:38). She heard the word of God and kept it.

So the correction takes nothing from her. It says that what made her blessed was not the biology, which nobody can share, but the faith, which everybody can.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — The Sign of Jonah; The Light in You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowds are increasing — and Luke notes it, because that is when Jesus says “this generation is an evil generation.” Popularity has never once altered what he told people.

They want a sign from heaven, and he refuses; but the refusal is not of evidence. It is of evidence on demand, produced to specification, for people who have already decided what would count. A sign given to someone resolved not to believe becomes one more thing to explain — which is exactly what happened fifteen verses earlier when an exorcism was credited to Beelzebul.

The sign of Jonah works two ways, and they are not rivals. Jonah himself was a sign to Nineveh: a foreigner walking into the greatest city of the ancient world with eight words of judgement and no miracle whatever, and the city repented (Jon. 3:4-9). And behind that stands what happened before he arrived, which Matthew makes explicit — three days in the belly of the fish, and three days in the heart of the earth (Matt. 12:40). Luke leaves it unstated and lets the reader who knows Jonah do the arithmetic.

Two witnesses are then called, and both are chosen to sting. The Queen of Sheba travelled over a thousand miles by camel, on a rumour, under no obligation to anybody's God. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria — the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom, a byword for a people beyond hope — and it repented at the preaching of a man who did not want to be there and was furious when it worked.

Neither had a fraction of the light this generation has. And twice the refrain: “something greater than Solomon is here… something greater than Jonah is here.” Not someone greater but something — the neuter, broader and stranger. No prophet in Israel's history ever spoke about himself like that.

The lamp sayings close the section. The lamp is not hidden; it has been on a stand in Galilee for three years. So the problem cannot be the lighting — it is the window. “Your eye is the lamp of your body,” and the words for its two conditions are not medical: haplous means single, undivided, generous; ponērous is the “evil eye” of Jewish idiom, the grudging and tight-fisted disposition (cf. Deut. 15:9; Prov. 28:22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The queen and the Ninevites will rise at the judgement and condemn this generation, because both responded to far lesser messengers. It is the graduated-accountability principle of the woes on Chorazin and Bethsaida, sharpened: it will not be the ignorant who are condemned by Nineveh, but the well-informed.

“Something greater than Solomon” is worth weighing. Solomon was the wisest man who ever lived, and Wisdom itself is standing in the street. Jonah was swallowed by the deep and given back, and the one who will actually break death is speaking. Jesus does not argue for it; he says “behold,” and leaves it there.

The eye sayings are not about eyesight or intellect. Ancient thinking often understood the eye as a window through which light entered and filled the person — so the picture is a house with a window: clear, and the house is bright; blocked, and the house is dark however strong the sun outside.

Which explains the whole chapter. The men in front of him are not short of information. They have the Scriptures, the traditions, and a mute man talking in the street. What they have is a blocked window, and the block is not ignorance. It is what they want. That is an uncomfortable diagnosis, because it means a person's capacity to see the truth is not independent of what he would prefer to be true — and nobody ever thinks that is happening to them.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Be careful lest the light in you be darkness” is the warning that ought to keep a religious person awake. It does not say “be careful in case you are in the dark” — a man in the dark generally knows it and can ask for a light. It says: be careful in case the thing you have been navigating by is itself darkness.

That is a different order of danger. It is not the traveller who knows he is lost; it is the traveller with a compass that is wrong, walking confidently in the wrong direction, and getting further away the harder he tries. And the verb is skopei — look carefully, examine. It is an instruction to inspect the instrument.

The context names who it is for. The next paragraph is a dinner party with a Pharisee that ends in six woes. The people at greatest risk are not the irreligious but those with the most exposure — long church attendance, real biblical knowledge, doctrine they could defend in an argument. All of that can be light, and all of it can be the darkness a man is steering by, and from the inside the two feel identical.

And then, after the warning, the promise, which is unexpectedly warm. “Having no part dark” is the condition — not a life with most of the rooms lit and one door kept shut. And the result is not an impressive person but a useful one: “as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” A life fully lit becomes a lamp, and a lamp is not for the room it stands in.

verseByVerse.quote: When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, 'This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, This generation is an evil generation.

Luke marks the moment carefully: the crowd is increasing, and that is when he says this. Popularity has never once altered what he told people.

It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.

They had asked for a sign from heaven (v. 16). He refuses — and the refusal is instructive, because he has spent the chapter performing signs. A mute man is standing there talking. What is being refused is not evidence but evidence on demand, produced to specification, for people who have already decided what would count.

And there is a reason that request can never be satisfied. A sign given to someone who has resolved not to believe becomes one more thing to explain, which is precisely what happened fifteen verses ago when the exorcism was credited to Beelzebul.

For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.

How was Jonah a sign to Nineveh? Two answers, and they are not rivals.

The obvious one is his preaching. Jonah walked into the greatest city of the ancient world with eight words of judgement and no miracle whatever, and the city repented — king, nobles, and commoners, in sackcloth (Jon. 3:4-9). The prophet himself was the sign: a foreigner arriving with a word from a God they did not worship.

The other is what happened before he arrived, and Matthew's parallel makes it explicit: as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matt. 12:40). A man swallowed by death and given back.

Luke leaves it unstated, which is characteristic — he lets the reader who knows Jonah do the arithmetic. But the shape is unmistakable, and it means the sign this generation is being promised is not something they will be shown next week. It is a grave outside Jerusalem, and it is the only sign that will ever be given, and it is enough.

Which is worth saying to anyone still waiting for God to prove himself in some more convenient way. The proof has been offered. It was offered once, in public, and it involved a tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two witnesses are called, and both are chosen to sting.

The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon.

The Queen of Sheba, from what is probably modern Yemen — a journey of well over a thousand miles by camel, undertaken on a rumour, by a foreign monarch under no obligation to anybody's God. She came, and she listened, and she said the half had not been told her (1 Kgs. 10:1-7).

The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah.

And Nineveh was the capital of Assyria — the empire that had destroyed the northern kingdom and deported ten tribes, whose armies were remembered for cruelty a hundred years afterwards. If a first-century Jew had a byword for a people beyond hope, it was these.

They repented at the preaching of a man who did not want to be there, who had run in the opposite direction, and who was furious when it worked.

So the two witnesses are a pagan queen and a pagan city — and neither had a fraction of the light this generation has. Sheba had a rumour about a king's wisdom. Nineveh had eight words from an unwilling foreigner. The men listening to Jesus have him.

And behold, something greater than Solomon is here… something greater than Jonah is here.

Twice, and the wording is worth noticing. Not someone greater but something greater — the neuter, which is broader and stranger. It is not merely that a better teacher than Solomon has turned up, or a better preacher than Jonah. Something of a different order is present.

Solomon was the wisest man who ever lived and Wisdom itself is standing in the street. Jonah was swallowed by the deep and given back, and the one who will actually break death is speaking.

He does not argue for it. He says behold, and leaves it there — and no prophet in Israel's history ever spoke about himself like that.

And the warning underneath is the one from the previous chapter, sharpened: judgement is proportional to light. It will not be the ignorant who are condemned by the Ninevites, but the well-informed. A pagan queen who travelled a thousand miles for a rumour of wisdom will stand up at the last day beside people who could not be troubled to cross a room.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light.

The saying has been used before in this Gospel (8:16), and its placing here gives it a different edge.

He has just said that something greater than Solomon and Jonah is here. That is the lamp, and it has not been hidden. It has been standing on a stand in the middle of Galilee for the better part of three years, healing people in daylight, in front of crowds, with witnesses.

So the problem in this generation cannot be the lighting.

Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.

The image shifts, and it takes a moment to follow. The lamp on the stand is outside; now there is a lamp inside — and it is the eye.

Ancient thinking about vision worked differently from ours; the eye was often understood as a window through which light entered and filled the person. So the picture is of a house with a window: if the window is clear, the house is bright; if the window is blocked, the house is dark, however strong the sun outside.

And the words for the two conditions are not medical. Healthy is haplous — single, undivided, and in the wider usage of the day, generous. Bad is ponēros — evil, and in Jewish idiom the evil eye meant a grudging, envious, tight-fisted disposition (cf. Deut. 15:9; Prov. 28:22).

So this is not really about eyesight or even about intellect. It is about whether a person is undivided and openhanded, or grasping and calculating — and Jesus says that condition determines what light can get in.

Which explains the whole chapter. The men in front of him are not short of information. They have the Scriptures, the traditions, and a mute man talking in the street. What they have is a blocked window, and the block is not ignorance. It is what they want.

That is an uncomfortable diagnosis, because it means a person's capacity to see the truth is not independent of what he would prefer to be true. Nobody ever thinks that is happening to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness.

Of all the warnings in Luke's Gospel, this is the one that ought to keep a religious person awake.

It does not say be careful in case you are in the dark. A man in the dark generally knows it, and can ask for a light. It says: be careful in case the thing you have been navigating by is itself darkness.

That is a different order of danger entirely. It is not the traveller who knows he is lost; it is the traveller with a compass that is wrong, walking confidently in the wrong direction, and getting further away the harder he tries.

And the verb is worth having: skopei, look carefully, examine. It is an instruction to inspect the instrument.

Who is it for? The context answers. The next paragraph begins a dinner party with a Pharisee and ends with six woes. The men being warned are the most religiously informed people in the country — men who could recite the law, tithed their garden herbs, and had built their whole lives around getting this right.

Which means the people at greatest risk from this verse are not the irreligious. They are the ones with the most exposure: long church attendance, real biblical knowledge, doctrine they could defend in an argument. All of that can be light, and all of it can be the darkness a man is steering by, and from the inside the two feel identical. That is the point. Nobody has ever known they were in this condition.

If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.

And then, after the warning, the promise — and it is unexpectedly warm.

Having no part dark is the condition. Not a life with most of the rooms lit and one door kept shut; the whole of it, with nothing reserved. And the result is not a person who has achieved something impressive. It is a person who has become useful — as when a lamp with its rays gives you light, which is to say, someone others can see by.

Which is where the paragraph has been going since verse 33. The lamp is put on a stand so that those who enter may see. A life fully lit becomes a lamp, and a lamp is not for the room it stands in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–54 — Woes to the Pharisees and Lawyers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee invites Jesus to dine, and he goes. Luke records three such meals in this Gospel and every one ends badly — and Jesus accepts every invitation. Whatever is said in this room is said by a guest who came when he was asked.

He does not perform the ritual handwashing, and the omission is deliberate. That washing was not hygiene and it was not in the law of Moses; nothing in the Torah requires an ordinary Israelite to wash before eating. The Pharisees had taken the priestly standard and applied it to everybody, all the time — a serious and, in its way, admirable ambition. They wanted the whole nation to live as though it were serving in the temple.

His answer takes their own debating point about the cleansing of vessels and turns it on them. A cup polished outside and filthy within is not a partly clean cup; it is a cup nobody can drink from, and the polish makes it worse, because it gets the cup put back on the table. And the word for what is inside is harpagē — plunder, what is seized. Something is being taken.

“Give as alms those things that are within” is his prescription, and it is remarkable: they asked how to be clean and the answer is not a better ritual but to give the contents away. The remedy for plunder is not scouring the cup; it is returning what was taken.

Then six woes — three against the Pharisees and three against the lawyers. The word itself needs setting straight: ouai is the prophets' word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict, the sound a man makes watching somebody walk towards a cliff. Jesus uses it over Jerusalem a few chapters later, and Luke tells us he was weeping (19:41).

They tithe mint and rue and neglect justice and the love of God — and “these you ought to have done” refuses to abolish the small duty. They love the best seat and the public greetings. They are unmarked graves. The lawyers load burdens they will not touch, build the tombs of prophets their fathers killed, and have taken away the key of knowledge.

And it hardens them. The chapter ends with respectable men following a guest out of a house, firing questions to get a sentence they can use.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tithing woe turns on a trade nobody consciously makes. The law required a tithe of grain, wine and oil (Deut. 14:22-23); it said nothing about the pot of mint on the windowsill. These were not lazy men — they were taking God seriously at a level of detail most people never attempt. And “these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others” is regularly ignored: he does not condemn the herb-tithing.

The mechanism is universal. The measurable duty is genuinely satisfying: it can be completed, checked off, and known to be done. Justice and the love of God can never be checked off — and a man who spends his religious energy on things that finish will find he has run out before he reaches the things that do not.

The unmarked-grave woe depends on a detail of the law.
