Contact with a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Num. 19:16), so graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover, conspicuously, so pilgrims could see them and go round. The marking was a public service; it kept people clean. An unmarked grave is the exact opposite — one a man walks straight over and finds out afterwards, if he finds out at all.

And “the key of knowledge” is the heaviest charge. The knowledge in question is not information about God but the thing the Scriptures exist to produce. These men were the keyholders legitimately — and they did not enter themselves, and they blocked the door for people who were already moving towards it.
verseByVerse.examples:
The lawyer's interruption — “in saying these things you insult us also” — is wonderfully revealing. He does not say “that is untrue.” He concedes the accuracy and objects to the tone, which is one of the commonest ways a person defends himself against a word he cannot answer: change the subject from whether it is right to whether it was polite.

The burdens woe puts a simple test to anyone who teaches. Does what you say make it harder or easier for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? There is a way of preaching high standards that lifts people and a way that flattens them, and the difference is usually whether the preacher has any intention of getting under the load himself. Set it against “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

The tomb-building is a way of being on the right side of a controversy that is safely over. It costs nothing to honour a dead prophet; he has stopped saying the things that got him killed. Meanwhile a living one is at the table, and they are about to arrange his death. Every generation of the church admires the awkward men of the previous one, whose battles are settled and whose statues are uncontroversial, and finds the equivalent figure in its own congregation intolerable. A dead prophet requires a subscription; a live one requires repentance.

And the key-of-knowledge woe puts a question to anyone who teaches anything to anybody. A teacher does not chiefly transmit doctrine; he transmits an impression of God, and people believe the impression long after they have forgotten the doctrine. Not whether what you say is correct, which is the easier test — whether someone who listened to you for a year would find the door easier to walk through, or harder.

verseByVerse.quote: While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table.

Two things to register before the confrontation starts.

The first is that a Pharisee invited him, and he went. Luke records three such meals in this Gospel (here, 7:36, and 14:1), and every one of them ends badly — and Jesus accepts every invitation. Whatever is about to be said in this room, it is being said by a guest who came when he was asked.

That is worth holding on to when the woes arrive, because it decides how they should be heard. This is not a man denouncing his enemies from a safe distance. It is a man eating their food.

The second is reclined at table, which tells you the kind of meal. Ordinary daily meals were eaten sitting. Reclining on couches around a low table was for a formal dinner with guests — which means there was an audience, and that the whole exchange took place in front of the Pharisee's friends.

The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.

The washing in question was not hygiene. It was a ritual — water poured over the hands in a prescribed way to remove any ceremonial defilement picked up in the course of the day, particularly from contact with people or things outside the community of the observant.

And it was not in the law of Moses. Nothing in the Torah requires an ordinary Israelite to wash before eating; the rules were for priests handling holy things. What the Pharisees had done was to take the priestly standard and apply it to everybody, all the time — a serious and, in its way, admirable ambition. They wanted the whole nation to live as though it were serving in the temple.

Jesus does not wash, and Luke says the Pharisee was astonished.

It is worth being clear that this was deliberate. He had done it before, in front of a delegation from Jerusalem (Mark 7:1-5), and he knew exactly what omitting it would say at a formal dinner. He is not being careless or rude. He is declining, in front of witnesses, to endorse a system — and he is about to explain why.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said to him, 'Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness.

He answers the unspoken criticism with an image drawn from the table in front of him.

The picture is exact, and it was not merely rhetorical: rabbinic law had extended discussions about the ritual cleansing of vessels, including whether the inside and outside of a cup could be clean or unclean independently of each other. Jesus takes their own debating point and turns it on them.

A cup polished on the outside and filthy within is not a partly clean cup. It is a cup nobody can drink from, and the polish makes it worse rather than better, because it gets the cup put back on the table.

And note the two words for what is inside: greed and wickedness. The first is harpagē — plunder, robbery, what is seized. It is a startling charge to bring against the most scrupulous men in the country, and it means the problem is not merely that they are inwardly unimpressive. Something is being taken.

You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also?

The argument is from creation and it is unanswerable. The same God made the visible and the invisible parts of a man. A religion that attends to one and not the other has not understood who it is dealing with — as though God could see the hands and not the heart.

But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.

This is a genuinely difficult sentence and translators differ over it. The likeliest sense is: give what is inside — the contents of the cup and dish, that is, the food and the wealth it stands for — as alms, and then the whole thing is clean.

Which is a remarkable prescription. They had asked how to be clean, and the answer is not a better ritual. It is: give the contents away.

And it goes straight at the word he has just used. The inside is full of plunder; the remedy for plunder is not scouring the cup but returning what was taken. Generosity is the exact opposite of grasping, and it reaches the place where the actual defilement is.

There is a sharp practical test buried in that, and it is not comfortable. It is entirely possible to be meticulous about religious observance and tight-fisted, and Jesus treats the second as the diagnosis and the first as the cover.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But woe to you Pharisees!

Six woes follow, three against the Pharisees and three against the lawyers, and the word itself needs setting straight before any of them are read.

Ouai is not a curse and not an insult. It is the prophets' word — Isaiah's, Amos's, Habakkuk's — and it is a cry of grief as much as a verdict. It is the sound a man makes looking at somebody walking towards a cliff. Jesus will use the same word over Jerusalem a few chapters later and Luke will tell us he was weeping when he did it (19:41).

For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God.

The law required a tithe of the produce of the field — grain, wine, oil (Deut. 14:22-23). It said nothing about the pot of mint on the windowsill. The Pharisees, wanting to be certain they had not fallen short anywhere, tithed the herbs too, counting out leaves.

There is something genuinely admirable in that, and it should be admitted before it is criticised. These were not lazy men. They were taking God seriously at a level of detail most people never attempt.

And neglect justice and the love of God.

And there it is. The same men counting mint leaves were failing at the two largest things in the law — justice, which is how you treat people, and the love of God, which is everything else.

These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.

This clause matters enormously and is regularly ignored. He does not abolish the herb-tithing. He says they were right to do it. What he condemns is the trade — the quiet substitution of the small and achievable for the large and demanding.

Which is worth naming plainly, because the mechanism is universal and it is not hypocrisy in the ordinary sense. Nobody decides to swap justice for mint. What happens is that the measurable duty is genuinely satisfying: it can be completed, checked off, and known to be done. Justice and the love of God can never be checked off, and a man who spends his religious energy on things that finish will find he has run out before he reaches the things that do not.

The modern equivalents write themselves. Attendance is countable. Reading plans are countable. Positions on secondary matters are defensible. Whether I am just, and whether I love God, are neither — and they are the two things this verse says were being neglected.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.

The second woe is about seating arrangements, and it is more searching than it sounds.

The best seat — literally the first seat — was a real and visible thing. Synagogues had a bench at the front, facing the congregation, near the chest where the scrolls were kept. To sit there was to be seen by everyone for the whole service, and to be seen in the act of being religious.

And greetings in the marketplaces: the elaborate public respect paid to a recognised teacher, in the open square, where the transaction could be observed by passers-by.

Notice what is not being condemned. Not the seats — somebody has to sit at the front, and honouring teachers is not wicked. The word is love. What is diagnosed is an appetite.

And it is worth being exact about what that appetite does, because it is not merely vanity. A man who loves the front seat has acquired a second audience, and the second audience is standing between him and the first. Every act of piety now has two possible payments, and one of them arrives immediately — which is precisely the problem Jesus names elsewhere: they have received their reward (Matt. 6:2).

The reason this is a woe and not a scolding is that it is self-defeating in a way the man cannot see. He is doing genuinely good things and being paid for them in the wrong currency, and the payment is instant and pleasant and leaves nothing outstanding.

Two things are worth saying to anyone who has felt this and recognised it.

The first is that the desire to be well thought of is not curable by pretending not to have it. Public modesty about one's own achievements is one of the front seats.

The second is where the actual remedy lies, and it is not in trying harder to be humble. It is in the fact that a man who already has the approval he most needs stops shopping for the substitute. The whole prayer at the top of this chapter begins Father — and a person who has heard that word settle on him has considerably less use for a bench at the front.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.

The third woe is the worst of them, and it depends entirely on a detail of Jewish law that a modern reader has to be told.

Contact with a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Num. 19:16). It was one of the most serious defilements available, and it disqualified a man from worship until the full ritual of purification had been completed.

Because of this, graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover — painted a conspicuous white so that pilgrims travelling to Jerusalem could see them and go round. The marking was a public service. It kept people clean.

An unmarked grave is therefore the exact opposite: a grave a man walks straight over, and finds out afterwards, if he ever finds out at all.

Now put the charge together, because it is devastating in three distinct ways.

First, they are graves — which is to say, whatever is on the surface, the contents are dead. He has just said the inside of the cup is full of plunder; now he says what is inside the man.

Second, they defile. This is not a criticism of their private spiritual condition. Contact with them makes other people unclean, and Jesus is talking about the effect of these men's ministry on the people they teach.

Third, and worst, nobody can tell. They are unmarked. There is no warning, no visible sign, nothing about their bearing or reputation to make a person step round. The whole reason the damage is done is that they look entirely safe.

And this is not a description of obvious hypocrites, who are much less dangerous because everybody eventually spots them. It is a description of respected men — men whose seriousness about God is genuine, whose knowledge is real, whose lives are outwardly admirable, and who are quietly transmitting something that kills.

What passes over the grave is very often the sincere. A young believer takes his cue from the most impressive religious person he knows, and if what that person actually has is scrupulosity without justice and knowledge without love, that is what he will catch — and he will catch it without any idea that a transfer has taken place.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the lawyers answered him, 'Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.' And he said, 'Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the lawyers answered him, Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.

It is a wonderfully revealing interruption.

The lawyers — experts in the interpretation of the law of Moses, the scholars behind the Pharisees' practice — have been listening to three woes aimed at somebody else, and one of them speaks up to point out that the criticism is landing on his profession too.

Note what he does not say. Not that is untrue. Not you have misunderstood us. He says you insult us — which concedes the accuracy and objects to the tone.

That is the response of a man who has heard something true and has decided to be offended rather than to look. And it is worth naming, because it is one of the commonest ways a person defends himself against a word he cannot answer: change the subject from whether it is right to whether it was polite.

He might have hoped the interruption would end it. It doubles it.

Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.

The picture is of pack animals and their drivers. These men had built an elaborate structure of rulings around the law — the oral tradition that specified exactly how each command was to be kept — and the ordinary Israelite was expected to carry it.

And they do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. The charge is not that they broke their own rules. It is that they never helped anyone else carry them: no allowance made, no weight shared, no interest in whether an ordinary man with a farm and five children could actually do it.

Set that against what he says about himself: my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matt. 11:30). The contrast is the point of the woe.

And the test it puts to anyone who teaches is uncomfortable and simple. Does what you say make it harder or easier for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? There is a way of preaching high standards that lifts people and a way that flattens them, and the difference is usually whether the preacher has any intention of getting under the load himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed.

The fifth woe has a sting that takes a moment to feel.

Building and beautifying prophets' tombs was a genuine piety of the period, and archaeology confirms it — elaborate monuments went up in the first century for figures centuries dead. On the face of it, it is the most respectful thing imaginable: honouring the men their ancestors murdered, publicly, at their own expense.

And Jesus calls it complicity.

So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.

The logic is compressed, and there is a bitter play in it: the fathers put the prophets in the ground, and the sons put up the masonry over them. One buries, the other seals. The joint operation is complete.

But the real charge is deeper than wordplay, and it is this: the tomb-building is a way of being on the right side of a controversy that is safely over.

It costs nothing to honour a dead prophet. The dead prophet has stopped saying the things that got him killed. His words have been polished into Scripture, quoted approvingly, and inscribed on the monument these men are paying for. There is no danger anywhere in it.

Meanwhile a living prophet is sitting at their table telling them that their religion is a whitewashed grave, and they are about to arrange his death.

That is what makes the monument an endorsement rather than a repudiation. A man who says he would never have joined the mob, while queuing to join this one, has not broken with his fathers. He has simply arrived late.

And the pattern outlives the first century entirely. Every generation of the church admires the reformers, martyrs and awkward men of the previous one, whose battles are settled and whose statues are uncontroversial — and finds the equivalent figure in its own congregation intolerable. The reason is not hypocrisy. It is that a dead prophet requires a subscription and a live one requires repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute.

The quotation matches no Old Testament passage exactly, and the likeliest explanation is the plainest: Jesus is speaking as the Wisdom of God — the one who sent the prophets — and summarising in his own words what that sending has always cost. Note the word apostles. He is not only reviewing history; he is looking at the men who will be sent after him.

So that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah.

The two names are the bookends of the Hebrew Bible. Abel is the first murder in Genesis; Zechariah, stoned in the temple court on the king's orders (2 Chr. 24:20-22), is the last recorded martyr in Chronicles — which stands last in the Hebrew ordering. It is a way of saying from the first page to the last.

And that raises the hardest question in the paragraph: how can the blood of Abel, spilled at the dawn of the world, be charged against this generation? Is God punishing men for what their ancestors did?

Scripture appears to forbid exactly that. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezek. 18:20); fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers (Deut. 24:16). If this verse means inherited guilt, it contradicts the law and the prophets outright.

It does not, and Jesus has already said why — one verse earlier. You are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers (v. 48). Nothing is charged to these men that they have not personally ratified. The guilt is not inherited down a bloodline; it is incurred by choosing, in your own generation and with your own eyes open, to do the identical thing.

And there is a reason the reckoning falls here. This is the generation to whom the Son himself has come — the one to whom every murdered prophet was pointing. A long account is closed not because these men are worse than their ancestors but because they have more light than any of them and are about to do worse with it. The judgement is proportional to the privilege, exactly as at Chorazin (10:13-15).

One further word is necessary, because this verse and others like it have been quarried for centuries to justify appalling treatment of Jewish people. Note who is addressed: not a nation and not a race, but the scribes and lawyers in that room, whose conduct Jesus has just described. The speaker is himself a Jew, as are his disciples, as is every prophet whose blood he invokes — and within a few chapters he will weep over this city rather than gloat over it (19:41). To take a rebuke that a Jewish prophet delivered to Jewish leaders about the killing of Jewish prophets, and turn it into a charge against Jewish people as such, is to misread it so completely as to end up standing exactly where the men being rebuked are standing.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.

The last woe is the heaviest, and the image is worth taking slowly.

There is a door. Behind it is the knowledge of God — not information about him, but the thing the Scriptures exist to produce: knowing him. And there is a key.

These men were the keyholders. That was precisely their office. They had the texts, the training and the languages; they were the ones ordinary people came to when they wanted to know what God had said. The key was in their hands legitimately.

You have taken away the key. Not lost it, not misplaced it — removed it. The door that God had provided a way through is now shut, and the thing that would open it is not available to anybody.

Then two charges, and the second is worse than the first.

You did not enter yourselves. They had the key and never used it. A lifetime handling the Scriptures of the living God and they never went in. That is possible, and it is possible in every generation, and it is one of the strangest facts about religious work.

And you hindered those who were entering. Note the tense: people were on their way in. Not people who might have thought about it — people already moving towards the door. And these men got in the way.

How? The whole chapter has shown it. By burying the law under rulings so that no ordinary person could carry it (v. 46). By making the entry requirements ceremonial rather than moral (v. 39). By modelling a religion of counted herbs and front seats. By teaching so that God came out looking like the sort of person these men were.

That last is the real mechanism, and it is why this is the final woe. A teacher does not chiefly transmit doctrine. He transmits an impression of God, and people believe the impression long after they have forgotten the doctrine.

Which puts a serious question to anyone who teaches anything to anybody — a preacher, a parent, a small-group leader. Not whether what you say is correct, which is the easier test. Whether somebody who listened to you for a year would find the door easier to walk through, or harder.

verseByVerse.quote: As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

The dinner is over. He has said everything, and Luke records what it produced.

Not repentance. Not even argument. Something colder.

The verbs are strong and they are all hunting words. Press him hard — the Greek suggests a violent, sustained assault. Provoke him to speak is a single word used of interrogating a witness with the aim of extracting something usable. And lying in wait is the vocabulary of an ambush: the word was used of hunters setting a trap for an animal.

So the scene at the end of chapter 11 is a group of respectable men following a guest out of a house, firing questions, not to learn anything but to get a sentence they can use.

And this is the turn. Up to now the opposition in Luke has been sceptical, then hostile, then organised. From here it is a hunt with a purpose, and it will run without interruption to a courtyard and a trial and a cross.

It is worth sitting for a moment with what has just happened, because it is one of the most sobering things in the Gospel. The word of God had been spoken to these men as clearly and as directly as it has ever been spoken to anybody. Every woe was accurate. Every one of them was delivered by a guest at their own table who had come when he was invited.

And it hardened them.

That is not an accident and it is not a failure of the message. Scripture has said from early on that this happens: Pharaoh, whose heart set harder with every plague; the commission given to Isaiah, that this people would hear and not understand (Isa. 6:9-10); and Luke's own account of a word that falls on a beaten path where nothing can get in (8:12).

The truth is never neutral. It softens or it sets, and which one it does is decided by what it lands on. These men had heard the finest teaching ever given, delivered in person, in their own dining room, and they left the house looking for a way to kill him.

11.text: <sup>1</sup> Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. <sup>3</sup> Give us each day our daily bread, <sup>4</sup> and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, <sup>6</sup> for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’; <sup>7</sup> and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>10</sup> For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>11</sup> What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; <sup>12</sup> or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? <sup>13</sup> If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” <sup>14</sup> Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. <sup>15</sup> But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,” <sup>16</sup> while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven. <sup>17</sup> But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. <sup>18</sup> And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. <sup>19</sup> And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>20</sup> But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>21</sup> When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; <sup>22</sup> but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil. <sup>23</sup> Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>24</sup> “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ <sup>25</sup> And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. <sup>26</sup> Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.” <sup>27</sup> As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!” <sup>28</sup> But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!” <sup>29</sup> When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. <sup>30</sup> For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation. <sup>31</sup> The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>32</sup> The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>33</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>34</sup> Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. <sup>35</sup> Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. <sup>36</sup> If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” <sup>37</sup> While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. <sup>38</sup> The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner. <sup>39</sup> And the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. <sup>40</sup> You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? <sup>41</sup> But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you. <sup>42</sup> “But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>43</sup> Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces. <sup>44</sup> Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.” <sup>45</sup> One of the lawyers answered him, “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.” <sup>46</sup> And he said, “Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. <sup>47</sup> Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. <sup>48</sup> So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs. <sup>49</sup> Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ <sup>50</sup> so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, <sup>51</sup> from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation. <sup>52</sup> Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.” <sup>53</sup> As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, <sup>54</sup> lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

12.title: Fear, Greed, Anxiety, and the Coming Fire
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is one of the most urgent chapters in Luke's Gospel — a sustained call to a particular quality of life in the light of the coming judgment. Jesus addresses a massive crowd (v. 1 — “so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another”) and then moves between the crowd and the disciples in a series of teachings that together form a comprehensive call to undivided allegiance. Do not fear those who can kill the body; fear the one who can destroy both body and soul. Do not covet or stockpile; the wealthy fool who built bigger barns died the night he finished them. Do not be anxious about food and clothing; seek the kingdom first. Be dressed for action, with lamps burning, waiting for the master to return.

The chapter's emotional register is high throughout. Jesus speaks of fire he has come to cast on the earth and a baptism he has to undergo before it — and he is distressed until it is accomplished. He warns that he has not come to bring peace but division — the sword of truth that separates the family. He rebukes the crowd for its ability to read the weather and its inability to read the present moment. And he calls everyone to settle accounts with their adversary before they arrive at the judge — because once you are before the judge, the outcome is fixed. The urgency is eschatological: the crisis of the kingdom's arrival is not a background hum; it is the defining emergency of every human life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Fear God, Not Man; Acknowledge Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowd is so large that people are being trampled — and in the middle of it Jesus turns his back on the thousands and addresses the handful. This is a word for those inside about a temptation specific to religious people.

“The leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” Leaven was a lump of soured dough kept back from the last batch: small, invisible once mixed in, working by itself, changing everything it touches. And Luke alone gives us Jesus's own definition. The Greek hypokritēs was a stage actor speaking his lines from behind a mask — which is not the same as failing to live up to what you believe, the condition of every honest Christian. It is playing a part.

The argument against it is not moral but practical: “nothing is covered up that will not be revealed.” The performance has a fixed run and a closing date. Whether that sentence is the most frightening in the chapter or the most liberating depends entirely on whether a person has anything he is currently maintaining.

The teaching on fear is the application. Do not fear those who kill the body — after that, Jesus says, they have nothing more. The threat runs out. What is commanded instead is a right ordering of fear, not a quantity of terror; and the effect is the opposite of paralysis, since a man who fears God properly has been made unafraid of everything else. Every tyranny in history has run on the fear of what can be done to a body, and this sentence cuts the supply line.

Which is why “fear him” is followed two verses later by “fear not.” The bridge is a bird nobody wanted: sparrows were the cheapest meat in the market, and Matthew's parallel prices them two for a penny (Matt. 10:29), so two pennies buys five — the fifth thrown in free, because it is not worth counting. Not one of them is forgotten.

Then the stakes rise. To acknowledge Christ before men is to be acknowledged before the angels of God; to deny him is to be denied. And then the hardest verse in the chapter — the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit — followed immediately by the promise that in the hour of trial the Spirit himself will supply the words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word for hell is Gehenna, and it is not a mythological invention. It is a place: the Valley of Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech under two of Judah's worst kings (2 Kgs. 23:10; Jer. 7:31), and which the prophets turned into a byword for judgement. Everyone listening could have pointed at it.

The one to be feared is God, not the devil — Scripture never gives the enemy authority to cast anyone anywhere, and nowhere are believers told to fear him. And the whole force of the passage depends on the fact that the one who has authority over death is the same one who does not forget a sparrow and knows a number about you that you do not know yourself.

On the blasphemy against the Spirit, the context is decisive. This saying stands in Matthew and Mark immediately after the Beelzebul accusation — which Luke gave us in the previous chapter (11:15). Men had watched the Spirit of God work in the open and called it the devil, and Mark states the reason plainly: “for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit” (Mark 3:30).

It is not a word said in a bad moment. It is the settled, eyes-open decision to call the light darkness. And since the Spirit's work is to convict of sin and point to Christ (John 16:8-14), a man who has finally refused that work has stopped caring what the Spirit thinks. He is not troubled. The anxiety itself is therefore the disproof: nobody who has committed this sin is afraid of it.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light” uses the architecture everyone lived in. The “private rooms” are the windowless inner storeroom where valuables were kept — the one place a conversation could not be overheard; the housetops were flat, adjoining, and where public announcements were made. The most private place in the house, and the most public place in the town.

The saying cuts both ways, and the context decides which is uppermost. Much of what Christians say for Christ is said quietly, in rooms with no audience, and looks unrecorded; Jesus says it is being minuted. But the primary force here is the other: everything a man is when nobody is watching is going to be read out. And a man who has decided in advance that everything will be known has no further use for the machinery of managing an impression — which is a considerable amount of energy returned to him.

The confession sayings must not become a performance requirement, and the safeguard is in the Gospel itself: Peter denied him three times, in public, under oath, and was restored on a beach. What is described is a settled position, not a single failure of nerve. Yet it should not be softened into nothing either. Very few Western Christians will stand in a court; the moments that count are the conversation at work, the family gathering where silence is taken for agreement, the friendship of a decade in which the most important fact about your life has never been mentioned.

And “the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour” is not a licence for unprepared preaching — the situation named is arrest and interrogation — nor a promise that the defence will succeed. Stephen made the longest speech in Acts under exactly this promise and was stoned at the end of it. What is promised is not acquittal but that the right words will be there.

verseByVerse.quote: In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, 'Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another.

Luke sets the scene with a detail nobody would invent. The crowd is so large that people are being walked on. This is the height of his popularity, and it comes immediately after a dinner party that ended with the religious establishment following him into the street to trap him (11:53-54).

And in the middle of that crush, he began to say to his disciples first — he turns his back on the thousands and addresses the handful.

Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.

Leaven in the ancient world was not a sachet of yeast. It was a lump of dough kept back from the last batch and left to sour, then worked into the new one. Its properties are the point of the image: it is small, it is invisible once mixed in, it works by itself, and it changes everything it touches. Nobody adds leaven twice.

Note also who is being warned. Not the Pharisees. The disciples. This is a word to people already inside — and it is the first thing he says to them after watching what religion had done to the men at that dinner table.

And Luke, alone of the evangelists, gives us Jesus's own definition: which is hypocrisy. The Greek word had a specific origin — hypokritēs was a stage actor, a man who spoke his lines from behind a mask. It is not the same as inconsistency, and it is not the same as failing to live up to what you believe, which is the condition of every honest Christian. It is playing a part.

Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known.

And here is the argument against it, and it is not moral. It is practical.

He does not say that hypocrisy is wrong, though it is. He says that it does not work — that the performance has a fixed run and a closing date, and that everything behind the mask is going to be public.

Which is either the most frightening sentence in the chapter or the most liberating, and which it is depends entirely on whether a person has anything he is currently maintaining.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops.

The picture is precise and it uses the architecture everyone in that crowd lived in.

Private rooms translates a word for the innermost storeroom of a house — the windowless space at the back where valuables were kept, and the one place where a conversation could not be overheard through a doorway. It is the same word Jesus uses for where to go and pray in secret (Matt. 6:6).

And the housetops were flat, used for sleeping and drying grain, and in a village where the roofs adjoined, a man standing on his could be heard by the whole street. It was where public announcements were made.

So: the most private place in the house, and the most public place in the town. What is said in the first is going to be repeated from the second.

Now, which way does this cut? Both ways, and the context decides which is uppermost.

The disciples are about to be told they will be hauled before synagogues and rulers (v. 11), and much of what they say for Christ will be said quietly, to individuals, in rooms with no audience. That work looks small and unrecorded. Jesus says it is being minuted.

But the immediate context is a warning about hypocrisy, and the primary force is the other one. Everything a man is when nobody is watching — the private appetites, the things said about people who are not in the room, the version of himself that exists only behind a closed door — is going to be read out.

Which is worth sitting with rather than hurrying past. Most people maintain a gap of some size between the public self and the interior one, and manage it so habitually that they no longer notice they are doing it. This verse says the gap is temporary.

And there is one entirely practical consequence. A man who has decided in advance that everything will be known has no further use for the machinery of managing an impression — which is a considerable amount of energy returned to him for other purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: 'I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, my friends.

He has never called them that before in this Gospel, and the placing is deliberate. He is about to say the hardest thing in the chapter, and he opens by naming the relationship it is being said inside.

Do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do.

Take the sentence at its full weight. He is not saying that persecution will not come. He is saying that when it comes, and does its worst, it will have reached the end of its resources — and that its worst is death.

That is a startling assessment of what the powers of this world can actually do to a Christian. They can kill him. After that, Jesus says, they have nothing more. The threat runs out.

But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him!

Who is meant? The devil, some have suggested — but Scripture never gives him the authority to cast anyone anywhere, and nowhere are believers told to fear him. The one who has authority over both death and what follows it is God, and the repetition — yes, I tell you, fear him — makes it plain.

The word for hell is Gehenna, and it is not a mythological invention. It is a place: the Valley of Hinnom, on the south side of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech under two of Judah's worst kings (2 Kgs. 23:10; Jer. 7:31), and which the prophets turned into a byword for judgement. Everyone listening could have pointed at it.

Now the pastoral question, because a sensitive reader will stop here. Are Christians meant to be afraid of God?

The answer is that this is spoken to my friends, and the two things are not in tension. What is commanded is a right ordering of fear, not a quantity of terror. And the effect is the exact opposite of paralysis: a man who fears God properly has been made unafraid of everything else, because the worst any human power can do to him has been placed in its true proportion.

Every tyranny in history has run on the same fuel, which is the fear of what can be done to a body. This sentence cuts the supply line. That is why the next thing he says is fear not.

verseByVerse.quote: Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies?

Two verses after fear him comes fear not, and the bridge between them is a bird nobody wanted.

The detail is exact and it is worth having. Sparrows were the cheapest meat in the market, food for the very poor. The coin named is the assarion, roughly a sixteenth of a day's wage. And there is a further touch in the arithmetic: Matthew records the price as two sparrows for one penny (Matt. 10:29). Buy two pennies' worth and you get five, not four. The fifth is thrown in — the one with no value at all, added because it is not worth counting.

And not one of them is forgotten before God.

Including that one.

Notice the form of the statement, because it is unexpected. He does not say God feeds them, or watches them, or values them. He says none of them is forgotten — which is the language of memory, and it means that the death of a bird thrown in free with a purchase is registered.

Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered.

Not counted once, at some point. The perfect tense means the number is known and stands known — a figure that changes daily and is never out of date.

It is the most useless piece of information imaginable, and that is precisely the point. Nobody needs to know how many hairs are on a man's head. The fact that God does tells you not that the information is important but that the attention is total.

Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.

Here, then, is the answer to the fear of what men can do. It is not that the danger has been overstated — he has just conceded that they can kill you. It is that the God who has authority over death is the same God who does not forget a sparrow, and who knows a number about you that you do not know yourself.

Which is why the two commands sit four verses apart without contradiction. The one to be feared and the one who counts the hairs are the same person, and the second fact is what makes the first bearable.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.

The word translated acknowledges is literally confesses in me — an unusual construction that suggests not merely stating a fact about him but declaring an allegiance to him. And the setting for both halves is public: before men, then before the angels of God.

So there are two courtrooms, and what happens in the second corresponds exactly to what happened in the first.

This must not be turned into a performance requirement, and the safeguard is in the Gospel itself. The man who wrote the sharpest denial in the New Testament was forgiven and restored and became the leader of the church. Peter denied him three times, in public, under oath, in a courtyard (22:57-60) — and was recommissioned on a beach.

So the saying is not describing a single failure of nerve. It is describing a settled position: the person who, over a life, will not own him.

And yet it should not be softened into nothing either, because the context makes the intended situation exact. The disciples are about to be dragged before synagogues and rulers (v. 11). The confession in view is the one made when it costs something — and it is not a confession at all if it is only made where it is free.

Which is worth being concrete about, because very few Western Christians will ever stand in a court. The moments that count are smaller and more frequent than that: the conversation at work where the subject comes up and it would be easier to say nothing; the family gathering where a view is expressed and the silence is taken for agreement; the friendship maintained for a decade in which the most important fact about your life has never been mentioned.

None of those is a denial in the courtroom sense. But a man can spend his whole life quietly declining to be identified, and never once decide to.

And the promise on the other side is worth as much as the warning. Whatever is said for him in a difficult room is said again, by him, in front of the angels of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.

This is the verse that has caused more terror in sincere Christians than any other in the Bible, and it must be handled slowly.

Start with what is being contrasted. A word spoken against the Son of Man is forgivable — and that is an extraordinary concession, since Jesus has just spent this Gospel demonstrating who he is. Men can insult him, mock him, misjudge him, and be forgiven. Paul was doing exactly that, in an organised way, on the Damascus road.

So what is the other thing?

The context supplies it, and it is the context that unlocks the verse. This saying appears in Matthew and Mark immediately after the Beelzebul accusation — and Luke has just given us that accusation in the previous chapter (11:15). Men had watched the Spirit of God work through Jesus, in the open, and called it the devil.

That is the sin. It is not a word said in a bad moment. It is the settled, deliberate, eyes-open decision to call the light darkness — and Mark records the reason it cannot be forgiven in the plainest terms: for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit (Mark 3:30).

And now the pastoral point, which needs stating flatly.

The Spirit's work is to convict of sin and to point to Christ (John 16:8-14). A man who has finally and permanently refused that work has, by definition, stopped caring what the Spirit thinks. He is not troubled. He does not lie awake. He has no interest in the question.

Which means the anxiety itself is the evidence. The fear of having committed this sin is a fear the Spirit produces, and he does not trouble the hearts he has stopped working on. Nobody who has committed it is afraid of it.

So if you are reading this with your stomach tight, and have been for years: that tightness is not the symptom. It is the disproof. The unforgivable sin has never once been committed by a person who wanted to be forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities.

Not if. When. He tells them plainly that this is coming, and Luke's second volume will show it happening repeatedly — Peter and John before the Sanhedrin, Stephen before the council, Paul before governors and a king.

And note the range: synagogues, which is the religious court, and rulers and authorities, which is the civil one. Opposition will come from both, and sometimes from both at once.

Do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say.

The word for defend yourself is apologēsēsthe — the root behind apologetics, and in that world a technical term for a courtroom defence speech. A man in the dock had to make one, and men trained for years to do it well.

They are told not to prepare.

For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.

Two things need guarding here, because this verse has been misused in both directions.

It is not a licence for unprepared preaching. The situation named is precise — arrest, trial, an official interrogation about the faith — and it has nothing to do with a man who has not opened his Bible all week and intends to trust the Spirit at eleven o'clock on Sunday. Paul, who lived through more of these trials than anyone, is also the man who told Timothy to do your best to present yourself to God as one approved… rightly handling the word of truth (2 Tim. 2:15).

And it is not a promise that the defence will succeed. Stephen made the longest recorded speech in Acts under exactly this promise and was stoned at the end of it (Acts 7). What is promised is not acquittal. It is that the right words will be there.

Which is the actual comfort, and it is worth naming for a much more ordinary situation than a courtroom. The dread of not knowing what to say — at a hospital bedside, in a conversation that has suddenly turned serious, in front of someone hostile — is one of the commonest reasons Christians stay quiet. The promise here is not that you will be eloquent. It is that in the hour, and not before it, you will not be alone in the room.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Parable of the Rich Fool
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A man interrupts a discourse on hell and martyrdom to ask for help with a family estate — and it was not an unreasonable request in that world, since rabbis routinely arbitrated inheritance disputes. But notice what he actually asks: not “settle the dispute between us” but “tell my brother.” He has already reached his verdict and wants it enforced.

Jesus refuses, and the address is cold — “Man,” not “friend” — with an echo of what was said to Moses when he intervened between two Hebrews in Egypt (Ex. 2:14). Then he diagnoses the plaintiff and says it to the whole crowd, so the man is not singled out: “be on your guard against all covetousness.” Not merely the greed a man would recognise as greed, but every form of it — including the perfectly legitimate-sounding conviction that one is owed what one is owed. This man had a case. He may well have been in the right.

The parable is not a warning against prosperity or against prudent planning. Notice how it opens: not “a rich man made a fortune” but “the land produced.” He did not do it. The harvest came out of soil he did not make, watered by rain he did not arrange — which is the first thing he forgets.

Then the pronouns. In four verses of soliloquy he says I or my eleven times, and God is mentioned by nobody but God. There is no wife in this man's head, no labourers, no neighbour, and above all no giver. The question “what shall I do?” had an obvious answer standing in plain sight in his own Scriptures, and he never considers it. There were poor people within a mile of that farm.

And then the strangest thing in the parable: he opens a conversation with his own soul, which is what a person does when there is nobody else — and tells it that its needs have been met by grain. Every clause is a category error. Ample goods; many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry. He is treating the ache of the soul as a supply problem.

The thing to see is that it very nearly works. He is not miserable. He had done it, and he was content, and he went to bed satisfied. And God's first word is “Fool.”
verseByVerse.theology:
“Fool” in Hebrew thought is not an insult about intelligence. The fool of the Psalms is the man who says in his heart “there is no God” (Ps. 14:1) — which is not a philosophical position but a working assumption. This farmer would have denied being an atheist. He simply ran his entire life without reference to anybody but himself.

“This night your soul is required of you” uses a financial verb — the word for calling in a loan. Which reframes everything he has said. He has spent the parable talking about what is his, and the soul he was addressing turns out to have been on loan the whole time.

And note the timing against his own words: he said “many years,” God says “this night.” The gap between those two is the whole distance between what a man can see and what is actually the case.

“Rich toward God” is the positive alternative and one of the most compact phrases in Luke. It is worth noticing that the alternative is not poverty. Jesus does not say “so is the one who is rich.” He says “so is the one who lays up treasure for himself” — rich in the wrong direction. To be rich toward God is to live in the awareness that every good thing was received and is to be used toward his purposes; the opposite is to treat what one has as one's own achievement, for one's own use, accountable to nobody.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man's problem is not the abundance; it is the accounting. He has a genuine agricultural difficulty and his solution is reasonable, practical, and completely self-oriented. There are exactly two things a man can do with a surplus — distribute it or store it — and he never considers the first. He demolishes serviceable barns to build larger ones, which is a considerable investment of time and money in the business of retention.

Watch also what happens to the ownership across the parable. It begins as “the land” producing. It becomes “my barns,” “my grain,” “my goods.”

“And the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” is left unanswered, and it is devastating precisely because everyone knows the answer is “somebody else's.” He tore down good barns for a harvest he would never eat, and by morning it belonged to people he had not thought about once in five verses.

Which leaves a test that takes about a minute and is uncomfortable. Not “how much have I got?” but: if my accumulation were described out loud by somebody else, in whose direction would it be pointing?

verseByVerse.quote: Someone in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.' But he said to him, 'Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?' And he said to them, 'Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.

It is one of the strangest interruptions in the Gospels. Jesus has just been talking about hell, martyrdom, the unforgivable sin and the courts, and a man in the crowd wants help with a family estate.

And it was not an unreasonable request in that world. Rabbis routinely arbitrated inheritance disputes; the law had detailed provisions, with the elder son taking a double portion (Deut. 21:17). The man is asking a respected teacher to do something teachers did.

Notice, though, what he actually asks for. Not settle the dispute between us. Tell my brother. He has already reached his verdict and wants it enforced.

Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?

The address is cold — Man, not friend — and the refusal is flat. And there is an echo in it: it is almost word for word what was said to Moses when he intervened between two Hebrews in Egypt (Ex. 2:14).

Why refuse? Not because the grievance was necessarily unjust; Jesus never enquires. He declines because this is not what he came to do, and because becoming the arbiter of one man's estate would have made him a functionary in somebody's dispute rather than the Lord of both brothers.

Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.

He refuses the case and diagnoses the plaintiff — and then turns to the whole crowd and says it to everybody, so the man is not singled out.

Two warnings, doubled for emphasis: take care, watch out, and be on your guard, guard yourselves. It is the language for a threat that is not obvious.

And all covetousness. Not merely the greed a man would recognise as greed, but every form of it — including the perfectly legitimate-sounding conviction that one is owed what one is owed.

Which is the sting. This man had a case. He may well have been in the right. And what Jesus saw, watching him push through a crowd of thousands to raise it, was not a wronged brother but a man whose grip had closed.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable, saying, 'The land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land of a rich man produced plentifully.

Notice how the parable opens. Not a rich man made a fortune. The land produced.

He did not do it. He may have ploughed and sown and hired well, but the harvest came out of soil he did not make, watered by rain he did not arrange, under a sun he had no hand in. Every Israelite knew this; it is why the firstfruits were brought to the temple, and why the law required corners of the field to be left standing for the poor (Lev. 19:9-10).

And it is the first thing the man will forget.

And he thought to himself, What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?

His problem is real. He is not a fraud or an oppressor; the parable gives him no vices at all. He is a competent farmer with a genuine logistical difficulty, and the question he asks is the sensible one.

What is worth watching is the pronouns, and they begin here. He thought to himself. In the four verses of his soliloquy he will say I or my eleven times, and God will be mentioned by nobody but God.

There is nobody else in this man's head. No wife, no children, no labourers who brought the harvest in, no neighbour, and above all no giver.

And there is something almost claustrophobic in the phrase he thought to himself, because the whole discussion of what to do with an enormous surplus takes place inside one man's skull. He has more than he can hold and nobody to talk to about it — which is not an accident of the story. It is what the surplus has done to him.

The question what shall I do? had an obvious answer standing in plain sight in his own Scriptures, and he never considers it. There were poor people within a mile of that farm.

And one further thing is worth registering before the parable turns. Jesus does not say the man was dishonest, and the story gives him no vices at all. He is not an oppressor, not a swindler, not a defrauder of labourers — which would have been the easy way to tell it, and would have let every hearer off.

He is a competent farmer having a good year. That is the whole of his character, and it is precisely why the parable is dangerous. It removes every handhold a decent person might reach for.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods.

The solution is entirely rational and entirely revealing.

He has a surplus. There are exactly two things a man can do with a surplus: distribute it or store it. He never considers the first — and note that he does not merely keep the barns he has and fill them. He demolishes serviceable buildings in order to construct larger ones, which is a considerable investment of time and money in the business of retention.

And notice what has quietly happened to the ownership. It began as the land producing (v. 16). It is now my barns, my grain, my goods.

And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.

This is the sentence the parable is built to reach, and it is the strangest thing in it. The man opens a conversation with his own soul.

Which is what a person does when there is nobody else. He has been talking to himself for four verses, and now he addresses the last available party — and what he tells his soul is that its needs have been met by grain.

Take the promise apart, because every clause is a category error. Ample goods — quantity, offered as an answer to a soul. Laid up for many years — a guarantee about a future he does not own. Relax, eat, drink, be merry — comfort, appetite and cheerfulness, which are all real goods and not one of which a soul can live on.

He is doing what every wealthy society trains its people to do: treating the ache of the soul as a supply problem, and answering it with more.

And the thing to see is that it very nearly works. He is not miserable. There is no suggestion in the parable that he was unhappy or unfulfilled or secretly hollow. He had done it, and he was content, and he went to bed satisfied.

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God said to him, Fool!

The first word God speaks in this parable is the last word the man expected, and the timing is the whole point: it comes in the same breath as be merry.

He has not been called wicked. He is called a fool — and in Hebrew thought that is not an insult about intelligence. The fool of the Psalms is the man who says in his heart there is no God (Ps. 14:1), which is not a philosophical position but a working assumption. This farmer would have denied being an atheist. He simply ran his entire life, and made every plan, without reference to anybody but himself.

This night your soul is required of you.

The verb is a financial one — it is the word for calling in a loan. Which reframes everything the man has said. He has spent the parable talking about what is his, and the soul he was addressing turns out to have been on loan the whole time, and it is being called in tonight.

Note the timing against his own words. He said many years. God says this night. The gap between those two is the whole distance between what a man can see and what is actually the case.

And the things you have prepared, whose will they be?

The question is left unanswered, and it is devastating precisely because everyone knows the answer is somebody else's. He tore down good barns to build larger ones for a harvest he would never eat, and by morning it belonged to people he had not thought about once in five verses.

So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.

The two phrases define each other. For himself is the diagnosis; rich toward God is the alternative — and it is worth noticing that the alternative is not poverty. Jesus does not say so is the one who is rich. He says so is the one who is rich in the wrong direction.

Which leaves a test that takes about a minute and is uncomfortable. Not how much have I got? but: if my accumulation were described out loud by somebody else, in whose direction would it be pointing?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “therefore” ties this to the barns. A man has just died with full storehouses, and the lesson drawn is not “store less” but “worry less” — aimed at a different group. The parable was for a crowd with a covetous man in it; this is for disciples, most of whom had nothing to store. And the two problems are the same underneath: both are attempts to secure a life by managing supplies.

Note what is named — food and clothing, not luxuries. This is spoken to people who might actually go hungry. The word for anxiety, merimnate, means the divided mind, and it is the same root as the thorns that choke the word (8:14).

The ravens are chosen deliberately. They were unclean under the law (Lev. 11:15), they are scavengers, and there is a psalm about exactly this — “he gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry” (Ps. 147:9; cf. Job 38:41). The argument is set at the lowest available point. And the ravens are not idle; they fly all day looking. What they lack is a storehouse.

“Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?” is an audit. Anxiety presents itself as responsible — the alert mind doing necessary work — and the question exposes the claim. And then the sharper turn: he calls adding an hour to a life a small thing. From where we stand it is not small at all; it is what a person at a bedside would give everything for. He calls it the little end of the problem.

The lilies are probably the wild anemones that carpet the Galilean hillsides in spring, and the two activities they do not do — toil and spin — were the two halves of a household's labour. And the argument turns hard on where the grass ends up: gathered as fuel, because wood was scarce, and burned in a peasant oven within the week. God takes trouble over the appearance of something that will heat somebody's bread.

Then the alternative, and it is not serenity but a different pursuit: “seek his kingdom.” And behind it the tenderest address in the Gospel — “fear not, little flock” — with a gift that is not a wage but the kingdom itself, given because the Father enjoyed giving it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The argument from ravens and lilies is not an argument for passivity. The ravens still fly; the lilies still grow; the farmer still plants. What is addressed is not the activity of provision but the anxiety about it — the energy spent worrying about what worry cannot secure.

“O you of little faith” is a single word, oligopistoi, and Jesus uses it only of disciples. It is never aimed at outsiders; nobody is called little-faith who has none. And the diagnosis is worth noting: not “you have too much to do” and not “your circumstances are difficult,” both of which may be true. The problem named is a shortage of faith in the character of a particular Father — which makes anxiety a theological condition rather than a temperamental one.

“Nor be worried” in v.29 uses a curious verb, meteōrizesthe — used of a ship tossed on the swell, or something suspended in mid-air, and the root of the English meteor. To be up in the air, unanchored. Anybody who has lain awake at three in the morning will recognise the picture.

“The nations” is not an insult but a description of a real difference. The pagan world had a crowded pantheon of local deities who had to be managed — offerings at the right time, none of them notably fond of you, none reliable. Anxiety in that setting is not a failure of nerve; it is a rational response to the facts as understood. If nobody is certainly looking after you, somebody had better.

Against which stand seven words: “your Father knows that you need them.” Not a force, not a committee of powers. He knows — so it does not have to be brought to his attention, and a great deal of anxious praying is really lobbying. And the needs are not dismissed as unspiritual.
verseByVerse.examples:
Knowing that anxiety is useless does not cure it. Nobody was ever argued out of worry by being told it achieves nothing; anxious people generally know. What the argument does is clear the ground, so the question becomes the right one: not “how do I stop worrying?” but “what am I going to trust instead?”

“Little flock” is a double diminutive in Greek, and an honest one — a small group in an occupied province with the authorities already hunting their teacher. He does not tell them they are stronger than they look. He tells them who the shepherd is, and the word carries the whole weight of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34, where God says “I myself will search for my sheep.” And “good pleasure” is eudokēsen, the same root as the voice at the Jordan: it delighted him.

“Sell your possessions” must be faced, because it is not a metaphor — and Luke supplies the answer across his two volumes. Zacchaeus gives away half and salvation comes to his house that day (19:8-9). The women of 8:3 supported the ministry out of means they must therefore still have had. And Peter's rebuke to Ananias turns on it: “while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?” (Acts 5:4). The selling was never compulsory; the sin was the lie.

So the command is a transfer of ownership, not a rule about percentages. What it can never mean is a Christian who has settled the matter, drawn a line, and considers the rest his own. Ask not what proportion you have given away, but whether there is anything left that you would refuse him.

And “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” reverses the order everyone assumes. We think the heart chooses and the money follows. He says the heart goes after the treasure — which means the affections can be steered, and that there is a reliable way of finding out what you actually love. Not the confession of faith. The bank statement, and the diary.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious.

The therefore ties this directly to the barns. A man has just died with full storehouses, and the lesson drawn is not store less but worry less — which is a different point, and aimed at a different group. The parable was for a crowd with a covetous man in it. This is for disciples, and most of them had nothing to store.

Which is worth noticing at the outset. The rich man's problem and the anxious disciple's problem look opposite and are the same: both are trying to secure a life by managing supplies.

Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on.

Food and clothing. Not luxuries — the two irreducible necessities, and for most of his hearers a genuine daily question. This is not a rebuke to the comfortable for fretting about trivialities. It is spoken to people who might actually go hungry.

The word is merimnate, and it means the divided mind — being pulled apart by a concern. It is the same root as the thorns that choke the word in the parable of the soils (8:14).

For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing.

A short sentence doing heavy work. Whatever life is, it is not the sum of what sustains it — and the proof is that a man can have all the food and clothing he needs and be, as the last parable showed, a fool who dies that night.

Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them.

The choice of bird is not random and would have registered. Ravens were unclean under the law (Lev. 11:15). They are scavengers. And there is a psalm about exactly this: he gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry (Ps. 147:9); Job is asked, who provides for the raven its prey? (Job 38:41).

So the argument is deliberately set at the lowest available point. If God feeds the birds nobody wants, on ground he owns, without a barn between them —

Of how much more value are you than the birds!

And note what is not being said. The ravens are not idle; they fly all day looking. What they do not have is a storehouse. The verse is not against work. It is against the belief that security comes from the size of the reserve.
