The synagogue ruler is indignant, and he does not address Jesus. He addresses the people — public instruction aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the actual target. And his argument is not stupid: the fourth commandment says what he quotes. What he has done is classify a healing as work.

Which produces the sentence that gives the whole thing away: “come on those days and be healed.” He is proposing a schedule for a miracle, to a woman who has not been healed on any working day of any week for eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
“A spirit of disability” should not be flattened either way. Luke, who keeps sickness and spirits carefully apart everywhere else, does not call her possessed or record a demon being cast out; Jesus says Satan had bound her — the same binding language as the strong man of the previous chapter (11:21-22). What is described is a physical condition with something darker underneath it: the fallen world's disorder, exploited.

“Daughter of Abraham” occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham without hesitation; the title is handed to a bent, unnamed, ceremonially awkward woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries. Luke will pair it later with Zacchaeus — “he also is a son of Abraham” (19:9).

The argument from lesser to greater is unanswerable because it is drawn from their own practice. An animal tied in a stall cannot reach water, and leaving it thirsty for a whole day was not an option any farmer would entertain; the rulings of the period permitted untying and leading, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work. So the principle they already hold is that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering.

And the final word is the one they thought was the problem: “on the Sabbath day.” Not in spite of it. Of all the days in the week, the day commemorating a people brought out of slavery is the day for a knot to be undone.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ruler's manoeuvre is worth naming because it is recognisable. Public instruction, aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the target — the sermon everyone knows is about one person, the general remark about standards made in front of the one who fell short. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

And underneath it is the real failure, which is not legalism exactly: he did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building and what registered was a diary problem. There is a kind of religion that can watch God act and think first about procedure, and it does not feel like hardness from the inside. It feels like carefulness.

The woman glorifies God before anyone can tell her what she should feel — not the carefully considered religious expression calibrated for an audience, but the overflow of a life that has just been changed.

Two responses close the section, set side by side in a single verse: the adversaries put to shame, the people rejoicing. Nothing in the evidence separated them. They all saw a woman who had been folded double for eighteen years stand up, and what divided them was what they brought into the building. That is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel: the same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, and the difference is never in the act.

And there is a small mercy at the end. Being put to shame is not the end of a man; shame is the last stop before repentance for anyone willing to take it. Luke does not tell us what the ruler did next. The door was still open when the paragraph closed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath.

Luke notes it almost in passing, and it is the last time in this Gospel that Jesus is recorded teaching in a synagogue. The doors are closing.

And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years.

The behold is Luke pointing. She is not mentioned by anyone else in the room.

The phrase is literally a spirit of weakness, and it should not be flattened either way. Luke, who keeps sickness and spirits carefully apart everywhere else, does not here call her possessed or say a demon was cast out of her; Jesus will say Satan had bound her (v. 16). What is described is a physical condition with something darker underneath it — the fallen world's disorder, exploited.

She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.

Luke the physician gives the clinical picture in a line, and it is the detail of a man who has examined such people. She is folded forward and cannot lift herself upright.

Consider what that means for eighteen years of ordinary life. She has not seen the sky except by turning her whole body. She has not looked another adult in the face; every conversation of nearly two decades has been conducted with the top of her head. She sees feet, floors, and the lower half of the world.

And she is in the synagogue. That is the thing to sit with. Eighteen years bent double, in a culture that read affliction as a verdict, and she is still coming to worship on the Sabbath.

Nobody in that building had a better reason to have stopped coming. She has been asking God for eighteen years and receiving nothing, and she is in her place.

Luke does not tell us she prayed for healing, and she asks for nothing when he arrives. It is likely she had stopped expecting anything — which is what makes what happens next entirely one-sided.

Eighteen years is also worth measuring rather than reading past. It is longer than a childhood. Whatever she was doing when it began — and she was young enough for it to have taken most of her adult life — she has now spent the greater part of her existence looking at the ground.

And nobody in that synagogue had done anything about it. She had presumably been coming for most of those years, past the same faces, and it had become the settled furniture of the place: the bent woman at the back, whom everybody knew and nobody expected to change.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, 'Woman, you are freed from your disability.' And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw her, he called her over.

Three things happen in that half-verse, and all three are his.

He saw her. In a crowded synagogue, teaching, with a woman folded double at the back and probably out of the sightline of everyone facing the front, he noticed her. Luke uses the same verb of him seeing the widow at Nain (7:13) and it always precedes an action.

He called her over. Which means she had to cross the room, slowly, bent, with every eye following her — and it means he made her healing a public event when he could have done it quietly. Whatever else is coming, nobody in that building will be able to say afterwards that they did not see it.

And she has still asked for nothing.

Woman, you are freed from your disability.

The verb is a perfect passive — you have been released, and the release stands. It is the vocabulary of untying, and it is the same root Jesus will use four verses later of the ox untied from its manger.

He does not say be healed. He says the knot has been undone.

And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight.

He touched her, which nobody had needed to do for a long time. And Luke, a doctor, uses a word for straightening that appears in medical writing of setting a limb upright.

Eighteen years, and it takes one sentence and a pair of hands.

And she glorified God.

The first thing she does with her new body. Not thank him, though presumably she did; Luke records that the first use she made of standing upright was worship.

Which is worth seeing exactly. For eighteen years she had not been able to lift her face towards heaven in a building built for lifting faces towards heaven. She stands up straight for the first time since the middle of another decade — and the direction she looks is the one she had been unable to look for eighteen years.

verseByVerse.quote: But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, 'There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.

A woman has just stood upright for the first time in eighteen years and is praising God at the front of his synagogue, and this man is angry.

Notice first who he speaks to. Not to Jesus, who did it. To the people — and effectively to her, since she is the one being told when to come for healing. He has a grievance against a man he does not dare address and takes it out on a congregation that cannot answer back.

That is a recognisable manoeuvre and it is worth naming. Public instruction, aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the actual target — the sermon that everyone knows is about one person, the general remark about standards made in front of the one who fell short. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

And look at his argument, because it is not stupid. He is right that the Sabbath forbids work, and the fourth commandment says so in the words he is quoting: six days you shall labour, and do all your work (Ex. 20:9). He is not inventing a rule.

What he has done is classify a healing as work.

Which leads to the sentence that gives the whole thing away: come on those days and be healed. Say it slowly and it collapses. He is instructing a woman who has been bent double for eighteen years — who has not been healed on any of the six working days of any week for nearly two decades — to come back on Monday.

He is proposing a schedule for a miracle. As though the healing were a service Jesus provided on request, and the only issue were the opening hours.

Underneath that is the real failure, and it is not legalism exactly. It is that he did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building and what registered was a diary problem.

There is a kind of religion that can watch God act and think first about procedure. It is not rare, and it does not usually feel like hardness from the inside. It feels like carefulness.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Lord answered him, 'You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You hypocrites!

The plural is deliberate. One man spoke; Jesus answers a whole way of thinking, and everyone in the room who agreed with him is included.

Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it?

The argument is unanswerable because it is drawn from their own practice, and everybody present did it.

An animal tied in a stall cannot get to water. Leaving it thirsty from Friday evening to Saturday evening was not an option any farmer would have entertained, and the rabbinic rulings of the period made allowance for exactly this — untying and leading were permitted, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work.

So the principle they already hold is that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering. Jesus is not asking them to adopt a new rule. He is asking them to apply the one they use every week of their lives.

And now the comparison, which is the sharpest thing in the chapter.

And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?

Every term is chosen.

This woman — over against his ox or his donkey. The animal has an owner who will take trouble for it. The woman has been in that congregation for years.

A daughter of Abraham. The phrase occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham without hesitation; the title is being handed to a bent, unnamed, ceremonially awkward woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries.

Whom Satan bound. He names the one who tied the knot — the same binding language as the strong man in the previous chapter (11:21-22). This is not a medical misfortune. It is an occupation, and someone is being dispossessed.

Eighteen years — against the ox's overnight thirst.

Be loosed from this bond. The same verb as the untying of the animal, which is the hinge of the whole argument: they untie; he unties.

And the final word is the one they thought was the problem. On the Sabbath day. Not in spite of the Sabbath. Of all the days in the week, the day commemorating a people brought out of slavery is the day for a knot to be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.

One verse, two reactions, and Luke sets them side by side without comment.

All his adversaries were put to shame. The verb means to be humiliated by exposure — not shouted down, but shown up. And it is the passive: something was done to them. Nobody argued them into silence; the argument and the standing woman did it between them.

Note also the word adversaries. It is the first time Luke has used it, and it is a legal term — those set against him, opponents in a case. The synagogue ruler is no longer merely indignant. He belongs to a party.

And all the people rejoiced.

The ordinary crowd, who had nothing invested in the ruling about Sabbath work, are simply delighted. And the word Luke chooses for what they were delighted about is endoxois — glorious things, splendid things.

It is an unusual word for a healing. They have not merely observed something useful. Something of the weight of God has been visible in their synagogue, and they know it.

Two responses, then, to exactly the same event — and this is the point of putting them in one sentence. Nothing in the evidence separated these people. They all saw a woman who had been folded double for eighteen years stand up. What divided them was what they brought into the building.

Which is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel, and for the rest of the story. The same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, and the difference is never in the act.

And there is a small mercy at the end of the verse that is easy to miss. Being put to shame is not the end of a man. Shame is what a person feels when he has been shown to be wrong, and it is the last stop before repentance for anyone willing to take it. Luke does not tell us what the synagogue ruler did next. The door was still open when the paragraph closed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Mustard Seed, Leaven, and the Narrow Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “therefore” ties the parables to the healing. He has just untied one bent woman in a village synagogue, been attacked for it, and sent a happy crowd home — and it is a fair question whether that is what the kingdom of God amounts to.

The mustard seed was proverbially the smallest thing anyone handled. And it is sowed in his garden — deliberately put in the ground, which is a picture of a man doing something that could not possibly be worth the effort. Black mustard grows fast and reaches ten or twelve feet; calling it a tree is a stretch, and probably meant to be.

Because the image of a great tree with birds nesting in its branches is not invented here. It is Ezekiel's and Daniel's, and it always means a kingdom under whose shelter the nations live (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6; Dan. 4:12). Jesus takes the image of the imperial cedar and puts it on a garden herb. The empires of the world start large and end in ruins; this starts with a seed you could lose in the palm of your hand, and the nations end up living in it.

The leaven parable ought to bring a reader up short, since one chapter ago leaven was the picture of everything that ruins (12:1). That is its usual role in Scripture — scoured out before Passover (Ex. 12:15), and Paul's image for malice and evil (1 Cor. 5:6-8).

But the sentence refuses the warning reading. Jesus does not say the kingdom is threatened by leaven; he says it is like leaven — the identical construction he has just used of the mustard seed, as the matching half of a pair. Leaven is a picture of how a thing spreads, not a verdict on what is spreading, and everything that makes it a good image for hypocrisy makes it a good image for the kingdom.

Then someone asks whether the saved will be few, and gets no number. “Strive to enter through the narrow door” — agōnizesthe, the word for what an athlete does in a contest. And the door is narrow: not locked, not hidden, not high. Narrow says nothing about how hard it is to open and everything about how much can be carried through it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The question “will those who are saved be few?” was a live one in the rabbinic schools, and notice how it is framed — a question about a number, and a number relating to other people. The man asking has placed himself outside the calculation.

That is one of the commonest ways of handling a subject that ought to be handled quite differently. There is a particular safety in the general: as long as the topic is the size of the saved population, the conversation can go on for a long time and cost nothing. And Jesus's reply is to them, plural, though one man asked.

If striving is required, is salvation earned? No — and notice what the striving is for. Not to become worthy, and not until enough has been done. Strive to enter. Everything in Luke pushes against the earning reading: the tax collector who can only beat his breast goes home justified (18:13-14), and the dying criminal with nothing to offer is told “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43). Nobody buys this door open — but plenty intend to go through it later, and later is a door that shuts.

“I do not know where you come from” is not a failure of memory. To know, in the Hebrew idiom, is relational (Amos 3:2), and “where you come from” is a householder's question about people at his door: whose are you, and what is your connection to this house?

The closing vision fulfils Isaiah's feast on the mountain for all peoples (Isa. 25:6-8) and the gathering from far off (Isa. 49:12). The seats do not stand empty; the table is full of people nobody in that synagogue expected to see there.
verseByVerse.examples:
The plea of those outside is entirely true and entirely beside the point. They had eaten in his company — very possibly at one of the meals Luke has been recording — and he had taught in their streets and they were there. These are not people making things up.

But every claim is about proximity. We were near you. We were in the room. We were in the town where you preached. Nobody says we trusted you — and a modern reader can produce the identical list without effort: I was at that church for thirty years; I sat under good preaching; I took communion. All of it true, and all of it a description of where a man was standing rather than what he did about it.

Which raises the question that keeps people awake: how do I know I am inside? The door is not a standard you climb to; in this Gospel it is a Person you come to, and Luke has been showing the entering all along in ordinary people. The centurion who says “only say the word” (7:7). The woman told “your faith has saved you; go in peace” (7:50). The leper who came back (17:19). The blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38-39). Not one was admitted for being impressive; each came to Jesus himself, with nothing, and would not be turned aside.

And “some are last who will be first” should not be softened into a general maxim about the underdog. What determines the order is not disadvantage but grace — and grace can only be received by people with empty hands. Those most confident of their standing are the last to ask for mercy, and asking is the only way in.

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore, 'What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said therefore, What is the kingdom of God like?

The therefore ties this to the healing. He has just untied one bent woman in a village synagogue, and been attacked for it, and the crowd went home happy. Now he explains what that was.

It is a fair question to have been asking. If this is the kingdom of God arriving, it does not look like much. One woman. One synagogue. One argument won against a minor official, and the establishment more hostile than it was that morning.

It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden.

The mustard seed was proverbially the smallest thing anyone handled — rabbinic sayings used it as the standard unit of the negligible, and Jesus uses it that way himself when he talks about faith (17:6).

And note that it is sowed in his garden. Not scattered in a field, and not dropped by accident. Somebody deliberately put a thing that small into the ground, which is a picture of a man doing something that could not possibly be worth the effort.

And it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.

Black mustard in that country grows fast and reaches ten or twelve feet — large enough for birds to perch and shelter in, which is what the text says, though calling it a tree is a stretch and is probably meant to be. There is a touch of exaggeration in the picture and it is doing work.

Because the image of a great tree with birds nesting in its branches is not invented here. It is Ezekiel's, and Daniel's, and it always means the same thing: a kingdom under whose shelter the nations live (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6; Dan. 4:12). Ezekiel's version is a promise — God will plant a sprig on a high mountain and it will become a noble cedar, and birds of every sort will nest in the shade of its branches.

So Jesus takes the image of the imperial cedar and puts it on a garden herb.

Which is the joke, and it is also the whole doctrine of how God works. The empires of the world start large and end in ruins. This starts with a seed you could lose in the palm of your hand, and the nations end up living in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he said, 'To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.

The second parable ought to bring a reader up short, and if it does not, it is worth stopping to notice why it should.

One chapter ago, in this same Gospel and from this same speaker, leaven was the picture of everything that ruins: beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy (12:1). That is leaven's usual role in Scripture. Israel scoured it out of the house before Passover (Ex. 12:15); the feast at the start of the passion is the feast of Unleavened Bread (22:1); and Paul takes the image for granted — a little leaven leavens the whole lump — and means malice and evil by it (1 Cor. 5:6-8).

So when Jesus says the kingdom of God is like leaven, some have concluded he must be issuing a warning: corruption spreading quietly through the church.

That reading cannot stand, and the sentence itself refuses it. He does not say the kingdom is threatened by leaven; he says the kingdom of God is like leaven — the identical construction he has just used of the mustard seed, in the same breath, as the matching half of a pair. Both parables answer one question: how does something this small end up being everything? Turn the second into a warning and you have broken the pair in half.

The resolution is simpler than the difficulty suggests. Leaven is a picture of how a thing spreads, not a verdict on what is spreading. Everything that makes it a good image for hypocrisy — that it is small, hidden, works from the inside, and does not stop until the whole batch is changed — is exactly what makes it a good image for the kingdom. The same yeast that ruins the loaf when it is the wrong yeast transforms it when it is the right one. Luke's own two uses prove the point rather than embarrassing it: at 12:1 something false permeates a community; here something true permeates the world.

And do not miss the quantity, because Jesus chose it. Three measures of flour is something near fifty pounds — not a household baking but bread for a hundred people and more, an absurd amount for one woman to be kneading in a kitchen. The comedy is deliberate. A pinch of yeast, invisible the moment it goes in, and a mountain of dough; and the pinch wins.

That is the answer to anyone who has looked at the size of the world and the size of the church and quietly concluded that the arithmetic is hopeless.

verseByVerse.quote: He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. And someone said to him, 'Lord, will those who are saved be few?' And he said to them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem.

Luke reminds us where the road is going. This is the fourth time since 9:51 that he has stopped to note the direction of travel, and it is not filler. Everything in these chapters is being said by a man walking towards his own execution.

And someone said to him, Lord, will those who are saved be few?

The question was a live one in the rabbinic schools, and it was discussed with some relish. How many of Israel would have a share in the age to come? Some held that all Israel would be saved except a named list of exceptions; others were considerably tighter.

And notice how the question is framed. It is a question about a number, and a number relating to other people. The man asking it has placed himself outside the calculation and is enquiring about the statistics.

That is worth naming, because it is one of the commonest ways of handling a subject that ought to be handled quite differently. Questions like what about those who have never heard? and are most people lost? and what happens to those who die as infants? are genuine questions, and some of them have good answers. They are also, very often, a way of discussing eternity in the third person.

There is a particular safety in the general. As long as the topic is the size of the saved population, the conversation can go on for a long time and cost nothing.

And he said to them.

Two small things before the answer itself.

He does not tell him the number. Anywhere in the Gospels where curiosity presses for information God has not given — the times and seasons, who is greatest, what will happen to that man — the answer is a redirection, and it is never rude and never satisfies.

And the reply is to them, plural, though one man asked. Whatever was said next was aimed at everybody in earshot, and the questioner was not going to be allowed to receive it as a matter of general interest.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strive to enter through the narrow door.

He does not answer the question asked. He answers the question that should have been asked, and it is not how many? but are you going in?

The verb is agōnizesthe — the root of agony, and in ordinary Greek the word for what an athlete does in a contest. It means to strain, to exert everything, to compete as though something depended on it.

And the door is narrow — not locked, not hidden, and not high. Narrow. Which says nothing about how hard it is to open and everything about how much can be carried through it.

Two questions come straight off this verse, and a reader deserves both answered.

The first: if I must strive, am I not earning my way in after all?

No — and notice what the striving is for. He does not say strive to become worthy, or strive until you have done enough. He says strive to enter. The effort is not payment offered at the door; it is the urgency of a man who will not be talked out of going through it. Everything in Luke pushes against the earning reading: the tax collector who can only beat his breast goes home justified (18:13-14), and the dying criminal who has nothing whatever to offer is told today you will be with me in Paradise (23:43).

Nobody buys this door open. But plenty of people intend to go through it later, and he is telling them that later is a door that shuts.

For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.

Which raises the second question, and it is the one that keeps people awake: how do I know I am inside?

The passage is about to be unsparing on false assurance, so it is worth saying plainly what genuine entering looks like. The door is not a standard you climb to; in this Gospel it is a Person you come to, and Luke has been showing us the entering all along in ordinary people. It is the centurion who says only say the word (7:7). It is the woman told your faith has saved you; go in peace (7:50). It is the leper who came back (17:19), and the blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38-39).

Not one of them was admitted for being impressive. Each came to Jesus himself, with nothing, and would not be turned aside. If that is what you are doing, you are not outside knocking.

verseByVerse.quote: When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door.

The scene changes from a doorway to a house at night, and the decisive action has already happened before the verse begins. The master has got up and shut the door, and everything after that is on the wrong side of it.

Note that he is not described as refusing to open it. He shut it, once, at a time of his choosing, and the shutting is presented as ordinary — what any householder does at the end of the day.

And you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, open to us.

They know the address. They know what to call him. They are at the right house, and they are asking the right person, and the tense suggests they keep at it.

Then he will answer you, I do not know where you come from.

It is a strange formula, and it is not a failure of memory. To know in the Hebrew idiom is relational — God knew Israel among all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). And where you come from is the question of a householder about people at his door: whose are you, and what is your connection to this house?

The answer is that there is none.

Then you will begin to say, We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.

And here is the plea, and every word of it is true.

They had eaten in his company — very possibly at one of the meals Luke has been recording all through this Gospel. He had taught in their streets, and they had been there to hear it. These are not people making things up. Their credentials are entirely genuine.

They are also entirely beside the point, and it is worth being exact about why. Every claim is about proximity. We were near you. We were in the room. We were in the town where you preached.

Nobody says we trusted you.

Depart from me, all you workers of evil.

Which lands hardest on the most religiously exposed people in any generation. A modern reader can produce the identical list without effort: I was at that church for thirty years. I sat under good preaching. I took communion.

All of it true, and all of it a description of where a man was standing rather than what he did about it.

verseByVerse.quote: In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out.

Weeping is grief and gnashing of teeth is rage — and the pairing is worth noticing, because they do not usually sit together. What is described is not merely sorrow but sorrow with fury still in it.

And the specific torment named is a sight. They will see the patriarchs inside. Whatever else exclusion means, this text says it involves knowing exactly what has been lost and who is at the table.

Note who the people outside are. Not pagans. Men who could recite their descent from Abraham, and whose whole assurance rested on it — we have Abraham as our father, which John the Baptist had already demolished at the start of this Gospel (3:8).

And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God.

Four directions, which is the ancient way of saying everywhere, and it is a deliberate echo of the prophets. Isaiah had promised a feast on the mountain for all peoples, with the covering removed and death swallowed up (Isa. 25:6-8), and the gathering from far off, from the north and from the west (Isa. 49:12).

So the seats do not stand empty. The table is full, and it is full of people nobody in that synagogue would have expected to see there.

And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.

This is Luke's signature and it has been running since the Magnificat — the mighty brought down and the humble exalted (1:52). But it should not be softened into a general maxim about the underdog.

What determines the order is not disadvantage. It is grace, and the fact that grace can only be received by people with empty hands. Those most confident of their standing are the last to ask for mercy, and asking is the only way in.

Which is why the warning falls where it does. It is not aimed at people far from God. It is aimed at people who were sure they were near him — and the seats were taken by strangers who knew they had no claim at all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Some Pharisees warn him that Herod wants to kill him — the only occasion in the Gospels on which Pharisees warn Jesus of a danger, and their motive is genuinely uncertain. Not every Pharisee was an enemy; Luke records three who invite him to dinner. But Herod ruled Galilee, and a man frightened out of that territory would be driven towards Judea, where his real opponents were waiting.

“That fox” is contemptuous in a specific way. In Jewish usage the fox was not primarily crafty but the small predator set against the lion — a rabbinic saying speaks of being the tail of lions rather than the head of foxes. Herod is being called a nuisance rather than a power, which is what he was: Rome never let him be king, and he ended his days exiled to Gaul.

The reply is a timetable, and it belongs to somebody else. Herod does not set the date. The verb for finishing is teleioumai, the language of completion — the same root as the word from the cross, “it is finished.” And the last clause is grim irony: he is not saying Jerusalem is dangerous but that it is the appointed place, and that a prophet is therefore safe from Herod because he is booked in somewhere else.

Then the lament. “How often” is not the language of a man who has been in Jerusalem three or four times in three years. It is the language of someone who has been trying for a very long time — and behind it stands every prophet who was sent and killed. The one speaking is the one who sent them.

The image has a long history in Israel's Scriptures: the eagle stirring her nest (Deut. 32:11), the wings under which Ruth took refuge (Ruth 2:12), the shadow of the wings in the Psalms (17:8; 36:7; 57:1; 91:4). But a hen is not an eagle, and the difference matters. A hen has no talons and cannot fight; what she has is a body and a pair of wings, and the way she saves her chicks in a fire is to spread them and stay where she is. Farmers have found them afterwards, burnt through, with the chicks alive underneath.

That is the image he chose for himself, in the week he set his face towards a city that was going to kill him.
verseByVerse.theology:
“Your house is forsaken” is devastating in two words. It had never been their house — Solomon built it and God filled it, and it is called “my house” in every prophet, as Jesus himself will say in that very building within a week (19:46). To hand it back with the possessive changed is to say the owner has moved out.

Israel had seen it before. Ezekiel watched the glory rise from the cherubim, move to the threshold, and go out of the city to the mountain on the east (Ezek. 10:18-19; 11:23) — and the temple stood a few more years and was then flattened. A building God has left is not a temple; it is masonry.

If your Bible reads “left to you desolate,” that is the longer form found in some manuscripts and in Matthew's parallel. The shorter reading is very likely what Luke wrote, and it is if anything sharper.

The closing quotation is Psalm 118:26, sung by pilgrims arriving at the temple for the feasts, and the crowd will shout it over him within six chapters (19:38). Some read the promise as fulfilled there, and the words match exactly; but the entry is days away, not an era, and what follows it does not look like a welcome. Others read it as pointing further on — to a day when the city that would not be gathered finally says it and means it, which is the hope Paul holds out (Rom. 11:26). It is better not to force the choice.
verseByVerse.examples:
The lament is the model of prophetic grief — the sorrow a faithful preacher feels for those who hear the word and do not receive it. It is not anger; it is love that has been refused, and the grief of knowing what the refusal costs.

Every pastor who has watched someone hear the gospel clearly and walk away, every parent who has prayed for a child who will not turn, every evangelist who has seen the door closing on someone who came so close, has tasted something of it.

“And you were not willing” is four words and the whole tragedy. Every verb before them is his — I would have gathered. The willingness was entirely on one side and the refusal entirely on the other. He does not say they were unable; he says they were not willing, which is worse, and it is the only thing standing between those chicks and those wings.

And what matters most about the last verse is its shape. It ends with until. He has just pronounced the most terrible sentence in the Gospel over the city he was born to save, and he did not stop at the desolation. He put a door in the last line — and the words on the far side of it are not a demand for reparations or a list of terms. They are a welcome, which is the one thing that city never gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, 'Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.' And he said to them, 'Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.

It is the only recorded occasion in the Gospels on which Pharisees warn Jesus of a danger, and their motive is genuinely uncertain.

They may mean it. Not every Pharisee was an enemy — Luke records three who invite him to dinner, and Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were both of that party. Or the warning may be a manoeuvre: Herod ruled Galilee and Perea, and a man frightened out of that territory would be driven towards Judea, which is where his real opponents were waiting. Luke does not tell us, and it is better not to decide.

Either way, the threat is credible. This is the Herod who had beheaded John (9:9), and who has been wanting to see Jesus ever since.

Go and tell that fox.

The message is sent back to Herod personally, and the word is contemptuous in a specific way. In Jewish usage a fox was not primarily crafty; it was the small predator, set against the lion — a rabbinic saying speaks of being the tail of lions rather than the head of foxes. Herod is being called a nuisance rather than a power.

Which is what he was. Rome never let him be king; he was a tetrarch, ruler of a quarter, and he would end his days exiled to Gaul.

Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.

The reply is not defiance for its own sake. It is a timetable, and it belongs to somebody else.

Herod does not set the date. Jesus will go on doing exactly what he is doing until the work is finished — and the verb for finishing is teleioumai, the language of completion and of a thing brought to its proper end. It is the same root as the word from the cross: it is finished (John 19:30).

Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.

There is the must again — dei, the divine necessity that has driven this Gospel since a boy in the temple (2:49).

And the last clause is grim irony. He is not saying Jerusalem is dangerous. He is saying it is the appointed place — that the city which exists to bring men to God has a settled record of killing the men God sends, and that a prophet is therefore safe from Herod because he is booked in somewhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Jerusalem, Jerusalem.

The doubled name again — the same register as Martha, Martha and Simon, Simon. It is what he says when he sees the whole of someone and grieves.

The city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it.

Both verbs are present tense: this is what the city does, habitually, as a settled practice. And the charge is historical, not rhetorical. Zechariah was stoned in the temple court on the king's orders (2 Chr. 24:21). Jeremiah was thrown into a cistern to die. Tradition held that Isaiah was sawn in two under Manasseh.

How often would I have gathered your children together.

How often is the phrase to stop at, because it is not the language of a man who has been in Jerusalem three or four times in three years. It is the language of someone who has been trying for a very long time — and behind it stands every prophet who was sent and killed. The one speaking is the one who sent them.

As a hen gathers her brood under her wings.

The image is maternal, and it is the tenderest thing Jesus ever says about himself.

It has a history in Israel's Scriptures, and he is drawing on it deliberately: the eagle stirring up her nest and bearing her young on her wings (Deut. 32:11); under whose wings you have come to take refuge, said to Ruth (Ruth 2:12); hide me in the shadow of your wings (Ps. 17:8; cf. 36:7; 57:1; 91:4).

But a hen is not an eagle, and the difference matters. A hen has no talons and cannot fight. What she has is a body and a pair of wings, and the way a hen saves her chicks in a fire is by spreading them and staying where she is — and farmers have found them afterwards, burnt through, with the chicks alive underneath.

That is the image he chose for himself, in the week he set his face towards a city that was going to kill him.

And you were not willing.

Four words, and they are the whole tragedy. Every verb before them is his — I would have gathered. The willingness was entirely on one side and the refusal entirely on the other.

He does not say they were unable. He says they were not willing, which is worse, and it is the only thing standing between those chicks and those wings.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, your house is forsaken.

If your Bible reads left to you desolate, that is the longer form found in some manuscripts and in Matthew's parallel; the shorter reading here is very likely what Luke wrote, and the sense is not softened by it. If anything it is sharper.

Your house. Two words, and they are devastating.

It had never been their house. Solomon built it and God filled it, and it was called my house in every prophet — my house shall be called a house of prayer, which Jesus will say in that very building within a week (19:46). To hand it back to them with the possessive changed is to say that the owner has moved out.

And Israel had seen this before. Ezekiel watched the glory of God rise from the cherubim, move to the threshold, and go out of the city to the mountain on the east (Ezek. 10:18-19; 11:23) — and the temple stood for a few more years and was then flattened. A building God has left is not a temple. It is masonry.

And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.

The quotation is Psalm 118:26, the psalm sung by pilgrims arriving at the temple for the feasts, and the crowd will shout it over him within six chapters as he comes down the Mount of Olives (19:38).

So does that settle it? Some read the promise as fulfilled at the triumphal entry, and the words match exactly. But the entry is days away, not an era, and what happens after it does not look like a welcome. Others read it as pointing further on — to a day when the city that would not be gathered finally says it and means it, which is the hope Paul holds out when he writes that all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11:26).

It is better not to force a choice. What is certain is the shape of the sentence, and the shape is what matters.

It ends with until.

He has just pronounced the most terrible sentence in the Gospel over the city he was born to save, and he did not stop at the desolation. He put a door in the last line — and the words on the far side of it are not a demand for reparations or a list of terms. They are a welcome, which is the one thing that city never gave him.

The hen is still on the road, still walking towards Jerusalem, still saying how often would I have gathered you. And the sentence that ends her lament is not never. It is not until you are ready to say: blessed is he who comes.

13.text: <sup>1</sup> There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. <sup>2</sup> And he answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? <sup>3</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. <sup>4</sup> Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? <sup>5</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” <sup>6</sup> And he told this parable: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. <sup>7</sup> And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’ <sup>8</sup> And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. <sup>9</sup> Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’” <sup>10</sup> Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. <sup>11</sup> And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself. <sup>12</sup> When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your disability.” <sup>13</sup> And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God. <sup>14</sup> But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, “There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.” <sup>15</sup> Then the Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? <sup>16</sup> And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?” <sup>17</sup> As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him. <sup>18</sup> He said therefore, “What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? <sup>19</sup> It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.” <sup>20</sup> And again he said, “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? <sup>21</sup> It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.” <sup>22</sup> He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. <sup>23</sup> And someone said to him, “Lord, will those who are saved be few?” And he said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able. <sup>25</sup> When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ <sup>26</sup> Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ <sup>27</sup> But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’ <sup>28</sup> In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. <sup>29</sup> And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. <sup>30</sup> And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.” <sup>31</sup> At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, “Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.” <sup>32</sup> And he said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ <sup>33</sup> Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem. <sup>34</sup> O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>35</sup> Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

14.title: The Banquet, the Invitation, and the Cost
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is built around a dinner table — and it is one of the most dramatically productive dinner tables in the Gospels. Jesus is at a meal in the house of a prominent Pharisee, being watched carefully. A man with dropsy appears; Jesus heals him on the Sabbath and challenges the watching lawyers and Pharisees. He observes the guests scrambling for the best seats and tells a parable about table manners that is really about the kingdom's reversal of honour. He turns to the host and tells him who to invite to dinner — not the friends and family who will reciprocate, but the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, who cannot repay. And when a guest at the table says “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God,” Jesus responds with the parable of the great banquet — the most complete statement of grace and rejection in the Gospel.

The chapter's second movement (vv. 25–35) shifts from the dinner table to the crowd following Jesus on the road, and the tone shifts from parable to direct confrontation. “Whoever does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple.” Two parables of counting the cost — the tower-builder and the king going to war — press the same point. “Any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.” This is not the Christianity of added benefits; it is the Christianity of total claim. The banquet of grace and the cross of discipleship belong to the same Gospel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the Sabbath Jesus goes to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees — the third such invitation Luke records, and every one of them ends in confrontation. He kept going anyway.

“They were watching him carefully.” The verb is one used of keeping something under observation for a purpose; Luke uses it in Acts of men watching the gates day and night to kill Paul (Acts 9:24). It is not curiosity but surveillance. There is food on the table, a host at the head of it, and a set of guests whose real business is to collect evidence.

A man with dropsy is “before him.” The medical term is Luke's own — hydrōpikos, a word that appears nowhere else in the Greek Bible and belongs to the physicians' vocabulary. Dropsy is what would now be called oedema: fluid retention, the limbs and abdomen swelling, usually a symptom of failing organs. And the ancient world understood something about it we might miss — a man with dropsy is swollen with water and desperately thirsty, which made it the standing image in Greek moralists for insatiable greed: a man consumed by wanting the very thing that is killing him. Worth holding, in a chapter about people at a table who cannot stop wanting the best seat.

Note the staging, too. A man with a visible chronic condition does not turn up uninvited at a Pharisee's Sabbath table. Somebody put him there.

Jesus does not wait for the trap; he springs it himself, asking the question out loud before touching anybody — and framing it exactly as they would have framed it. Their silence is not puzzlement. They cannot say yes without undercutting their own position, and cannot say no with a swollen man standing in the room.

Then he heals him and sends him away, which is a mercy on its own: the man does not have to stand there for the argument that follows.

And the second question silences them completely — “a son or an ox” put in one sentence, as items in the same category, because that is where their practice puts them. They could not reply.
verseByVerse.theology:
The silence of the lawyers and Pharisees — both times — is the silence of people who know they have no answer and will not give the answer they do have. It is worth naming, because it is the commonest form cowardice takes among religious people: not denial, not opposition, but a careful and dignified silence held until the moment passes and the question can be treated as though it were never asked.

The argument is the same shape as the one in the previous chapter but sharpened in two ways. There, the animal was thirsty and being led to water; here something has fallen into a well and is drowning, and the word is immediately. This is an emergency, and nobody stands at the wellhead consulting a ruling.

The manuscripts vary slightly at v.5 and some read “a donkey or an ox,” which is the more expected pair and very likely why some copyists produced it. “Son or ox” is the harder reading and almost certainly what Luke wrote — and it is the one that does the work: if you would break the Sabbath for your child, and also for your livestock, on what grounds is a man with dropsy in a lower category than both?

They are beaten by their own practice, which is the only argument that cannot be got round. He has not quoted an obscure text or appealed to his own authority; he has described what every man in that room does on a Sabbath afternoon when something valuable falls down a hole.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus heals the man before making the argument. That is not bad pedagogy but the right order: the principle of Sabbath mercy is not established by syllogism and then applied — it is demonstrated in flesh and blood and then defended. The compassion leads the argument.

And there is a hard general truth in the second silence. Most people's real theology is not in what they say but in what they do without thinking, and the fastest way to expose a bad doctrine is very often to ask where its holder makes an exception for himself.

The two-tier system is the thing being dismantled: their own emergencies justify Sabbath flexibility, and somebody else's does not. That instinct did not die out in the first century. It is at work wherever a rule is applied rigorously to people at a distance and generously to oneself and one's own — and it is almost never noticed by the person doing it, because the exceptions feel like common sense.

Note also that Jesus sends the healed man away before the debate begins. He will not have a person used as an exhibit, even in an argument he is winning.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees.

He accepted the invitation. That is the first thing, and it is the third time Luke has recorded it (7:36; 11:37) — and every one of these dinners ends in confrontation. He kept going anyway.

A ruler of the Pharisees is a man of standing, perhaps a member of the Sanhedrin. This is a formal Sabbath meal, the best meal of the week, and Jesus is the guest of honour in the sense that he is the one everybody has come to see.

They were watching him carefully.

The verb is one used of watching for a purpose — the word for keeping something under observation, and in Luke's second volume it is used of a plot to kill Paul, watching the gates day and night (Acts 9:24). It is not curiosity. It is surveillance.

So the room is not what it appears. There is food on the table, a host at the head of it, and a set of guests whose real business is to collect evidence.

And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy.

Luke's behold is his usual signal to look, and the medical term is his own — hydrōpikos, a word that appears nowhere else in the Greek Bible and belongs to the physicians' vocabulary. Dropsy is what would now be called oedema: fluid retention, the limbs and abdomen swelling, usually a symptom of failing heart, liver or kidneys.

And the ancient world understood one thing about it that we might miss. A man with dropsy is swollen with water and desperately thirsty — the more fluid he retains, the more he craves. It was the standing image in Greek moralists for insatiable greed: a man consumed by wanting the very thing that is killing him.

Which is a detail worth holding, because the rest of this chapter is about people at a table who cannot stop wanting the best seat.

Note also the staging: before him, in a private house, at a formal dinner, on the Sabbath. A man with a visible chronic condition does not turn up uninvited at a Pharisee's Sabbath table. Somebody put him there.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, 'Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?' But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?

Luke says he responded, though nobody has said anything. He is answering what is in the room.

And notice who moves first. They have set the trap and are waiting for him to walk into it; he asks the question himself, out loud, before touching anybody. There is nothing to catch him at, because he has put the whole matter on the table in advance.

The question is also framed exactly as they would have framed it. Is it lawful? — the technical language of their own debates, addressed to the experts, inviting a ruling.

But they remained silent.

And here is the answer, and it is the loudest thing in the chapter.

They cannot say yes, because their whole position depends on saying no. And they cannot say no, because there is a swollen man standing in the room and everybody can see him.

So they say nothing — which is not neutrality. Silence is a decision, and this one has been taken in front of a suffering man. The most learned religious men in that district have been asked a straight question about mercy, and every one of them has calculated that answering would cost him something.

It is worth naming, because it is the commonest form that cowardice takes among religious people. Not denial. Not opposition. A careful, dignified silence, held until the moment passes and the question can be treated as though it were never asked.

Then he took him and healed him and sent him away.

Seven words in Greek, and each verb is worth a moment.

He took him — literally took hold of him, laid hands on him, which is contact with a diseased body at a Sabbath dinner in front of men obsessed with purity. He healed him. And he sent him away, which is a mercy on its own: the man does not have to stand in that room for the argument that is coming. Whatever he was brought there for, he is not going to be used for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?' And they could not reply to these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?

The argument is the same shape as the one in the previous chapter — from what they already do to what they will not allow — but it has been sharpened in two ways.

There, the animal was thirsty and being led to water. Here, something has fallen into a well and is drowning, and the word is immediately. This is not routine care. It is an emergency, and nobody stands at the wellhead consulting a ruling.

And the pairing is deliberately shocking: a son or an ox. He puts them in one sentence, as items in the same category — because that is where their practice puts them. A man will haul either one out without pausing to think about the day.

The manuscripts vary slightly here and some read a donkey or an ox, which is the more expected pair and is very likely why some copyists produced it. Son or ox is the harder reading and almost certainly what Luke wrote, and it is the one that does the work: if you would break the Sabbath for your child, and also for your livestock, on what grounds is a man with dropsy in a lower category than both?

And they could not reply to these things.

The second silence, and Luke reports it as an inability rather than a choice. The first time they remained silent; this time they could not reply.

They have been beaten by their own practice, which is the only argument that cannot be got round. He has not quoted an obscure text at them or appealed to his own authority. He has described what every man in that room does on a Sabbath afternoon when something valuable falls down a hole.

And there is a hard general truth in it. Most people's real theology is not in what they say but in what they do without thinking — and the fastest way to expose a bad doctrine is very often to ask where its holder makes an exception for himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Places of Honour; Inviting the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus has been watching the guests arrive. Seating at such a meal was not casual — guests reclined on couches around a U-shaped arrangement graded by proximity to the host, a visible ranking of the room that everybody could read at a glance. Choosing your couch was choosing your public estimate of yourself. These men have just come from a Sabbath service, and their first act on arrival was to work out how important they were.

The parable begins as pure social advice, and the scenario would have made everyone wince. Honour in that culture was public and finite, gained and lost in front of witnesses. Follow the mechanics of the humiliation: the man is not merely demoted but has to get up and walk the whole length of the room, because the only seat left is the last one. And “begin with shame” is exact — the shame is not a moment; it starts, and goes on all evening.

Then the reversal, which would be shrewd manoeuvring if it stopped there. What closes the trap is the last verse: “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” Both verbs are passive, which in Jewish speech is the reverent way of saying God will do it. This is not about how the evening goes; it is about who runs the seating arrangements of the universe.

Which is what makes false modesty useless rather than merely distasteful. A man who takes the low seat in order to be moved up has exalted himself, and the passive verb has already seen it.

Jesus then turns to the host — at the host's own table, having eaten his food. The four categories he names are the entire ordinary guest list, and the objection is stated plainly: “lest they also invite you in return.” Hospitality in that world ran on reciprocal obligation; an invitation created a debt discharged by a return invitation of matching quality. A dinner party was a transaction with a settlement date.

The alternative list is the exact opposite: people who create no obligation because they can discharge none. And the reason given is not that they are more deserving — it is that they “cannot repay you.” The inability is the qualification.
verseByVerse.theology:
“He who humbles himself will be exalted” appears repeatedly in Luke (14:11; 18:14; and in substance in the Magnificat). It is the law of the kingdom inverting the law of the world, and it is grounded eschatologically: “you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” The accounts are not settled in this life, but they are settled.

The parable cannot be obeyed as a technique. It can only be obeyed by somebody who has genuinely stopped competing — and there is exactly one thing that produces that, which is knowing what your actual standing is. The man who has understood where he stands before God is not being humble when he takes the low seat; he is being accurate. There is no lower place in that room than the one he already occupies before God, and he is at the table by invitation rather than merit.

Which is precisely why he is free. A person who is not defending a position cannot be demoted from it, and an evening at the bottom of the table costs him nothing.

And the promise on the other side is not a better seat at a dinner party. The one saying it is on his way to Jerusalem to take the lowest place there is, and Paul describes the outcome in the same two movements: “he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him” (Phil. 2:8-9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Read flatly, the instruction to the host bans Christmas dinner, and someone will read it flatly. Is a believer forbidden to have his own family round a table?

No — and the same chapter shows why. A dozen verses on, Jesus says a disciple must “hate” his father and mother (v.26), and everyone rightly understands that as the Semitic way of stating a comparison in absolute terms. The identical device is at work here. It is not never invite your friends but do not let your table be only that. Jesus himself ate with friends — at Levi's feast, in Martha's house, and at this very Pharisee's dinner while he says it.

So the practical question is not whether the family may come on Sunday. It is whether anyone else ever does. Put the two lists side by side and ask honestly which one your hospitality actually serves: the guests who will have you back, or the guests who cannot. Most of us have a table that runs entirely on exchange without ever having decided to make it so — and this is a command with a doorbell, not a principle to admire.

The host who invites only those who will invite him back has not given; he has traded. The host who invites those who cannot repay has given, and in doing so has imitated the God who invites sinners to his table knowing they have nothing to offer him. And note that the account is not cancelled but moved: what is on offer is a debt owed by God, payable at the resurrection, which is a far better security than a return invitation from a rich neighbour.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, 'When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor.

He has been watching them arrive.

The seating at such a meal was not casual. Guests reclined on couches around a U-shaped arrangement, and the positions were graded by proximity to the host — a visible ranking of the room that everybody present could read at a glance. Choosing your couch was choosing your public estimate of yourself.

So this is a room of men who have just come from a Sabbath service, at the house of a Pharisee, and their first act on arrival was to work out how important they were.

And Luke says Jesus noticed. He watched the whole performance from wherever he had been put.

Then he tells a parable, and it opens as pure social advice — the sort of thing a wise uncle might say.

When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him.

The scenario is entirely realistic and would have made everyone wince. Honour in that culture was public and finite; it was gained and lost in front of witnesses, and a man's standing was whatever the room said it was.

And he who invited you both will come and say to you, Give your place to this person, and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place.

Follow the mechanics of the humiliation, because Jesus has thought it through. The man is not merely demoted. He has to get up, in front of everybody, and walk the whole length of the room — because the only seat left is the last one. Every guest between the top and the bottom watches him go past.

And the phrase begin with shame is exact. The shame is not a moment; it starts, and it goes on for the rest of the evening while he sits where everyone can see he ended up.

That is what the grasping actually costs, and the parable has not yet said a word about God.

verseByVerse.quote: But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, Friend, move up higher.

The advice is exactly reversed, and if it stopped here it would be a piece of shrewd manoeuvring — take the bottom seat as a tactic, and enjoy being moved up in front of everybody.

Anyone who has read it that way has been outmanoeuvred by the parable, and the last verse is what closes the trap.

For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.

The two verbs are in the passive, and in Jewish speech that is the reverent way of saying God will do it. This is not about how the evening goes. It is a statement about who runs the seating arrangements of the universe.

Which is what makes false modesty useless here rather than merely distasteful. A man who takes the low seat in order to be moved up has exalted himself; the manoeuvre is the exaltation, and the passive verb has already seen it.

So the parable cannot be obeyed as a technique. It can only be obeyed by somebody who has genuinely stopped competing — and there is exactly one thing that produces that, which is knowing what your actual standing is.

And here is where the parable turns from advice into gospel. The man who has understood where he stands before God is not being humble when he takes the low seat. He is being accurate. There is no lower place in that room than the one he already occupies before God, and he is at the table by invitation and not by merit.

Which is precisely why he is free. A person who is not defending a position cannot be demoted from it, and an evening spent at the bottom of the table costs him nothing at all.

And the promise on the other side is not a better seat at a dinner party. The one saying it is on his way to Jerusalem to take the lowest place there is — and Paul will describe the outcome in the same two movements, humbling and exalting: he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him (Phil. 2:8-9).

verseByVerse.quote: He said also to the man who had invited him, 'When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said also to the man who had invited him.

Having dealt with the guests, he turns to the host — at the host's own table, having eaten his food. It is one of the least comfortable moments in the Gospels.

When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid.

The four categories are the entire ordinary guest list, and the objection is stated plainly: lest they also invite you in return.

That was not a hypothetical in that world. Hospitality ran on an understood system of reciprocal obligation; an invitation created a debt, and the debt was discharged by a return invitation of matching quality. A dinner party was a transaction with a settlement date.

But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you.

The four categories here are the exact opposite: people who create no obligation because they can discharge none. And the reason given is not that they are more deserving. It is precisely that they cannot repay you — the inability is the qualification.

Read flatly, though, this verse bans Christmas dinner, and someone will read it flatly. Is a believer actually forbidden to have his own family round a table?

No, and the same chapter tells you why. A dozen verses on, Jesus will say that a disciple must hate his father and mother (v. 26), and everyone rightly understands that as the Semitic way of stating a comparison in absolute terms. The identical device is at work here. It is not never invite your friends; it is do not let your table be only that. Jesus himself ate with friends — at Levi's feast, in Martha's house, and at this very Pharisee's dinner while he says it.

So the practical question is not whether the family may come on Sunday. It is whether anyone else ever does. Put the two lists side by side and ask honestly which one your hospitality actually serves. Most of us have a table that runs entirely on exchange without ever having decided to make it so.

For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.

Not you will not be repaid. The account is not cancelled; it is moved. And it is worth seeing what the host is being offered: a debt owed by God, payable at the resurrection — which is a far better security than a return invitation from a rich neighbour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Parable of the Great Banquet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A guest breaks the silence with something entirely correct: “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” The picture he invokes was the settled hope of Israel — the feast on the mountain, rich food for all peoples, death swallowed up (Isa. 25:6-8).

So why does Jesus answer with a parable about people who refuse an invitation? Listen to the sentence again. It is a beatitude in the third person and the future tense, and nobody in the room is implicated by it. Jesus has just told them to stop grasping for seats and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay them — both remarks about this table, tonight — and what comes back is a warm sentiment about a banquet in the age to come. It is the religious equivalent of saying what a wonderful idea in principle.

The parable changes the tense. And it turns on a custom: a formal banquet involved two invitations, the first well in advance so the host knew the numbers before he killed the animals, the second on the day to say it was ready. So these guests are not being asked whether they would like to attend. They accepted weeks ago, and the host has slaughtered on the strength of it.

“Come, for everything is now ready” is the gospel in five words. Not would you consider coming? The work is done, the cost has been met, and the only thing missing is the guests. And notice who carries it — not the host but a servant, sent on foot to men who outrank him, saying words that are not his own.

Then the excuses, and not one is disreputable. A field already bought; five yoke of oxen already bought; a new marriage. Property, work, family — every one a good thing, and not one a sin. Nobody says “I do not want to come.” They express regret, cite legitimate business, and stay at home.
