For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God. <sup>16</sup> “The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it. <sup>17</sup> But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void. <sup>18</sup> “Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery. <sup>19</sup> “There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. <sup>20</sup> And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, <sup>21</sup> who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores. <sup>22</sup> The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, <sup>23</sup> and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side. <sup>24</sup> And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ <sup>25</sup> But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish. <sup>26</sup> And besides all this, between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, in order that those who would pass from here to you may not be able, and none may cross from there to us.’ <sup>27</sup> And he said, ‘Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house— <sup>28</sup> for I have five brothers—so that he may warn them, lest they also come into this place of torment.’ <sup>29</sup> But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them.’ <sup>30</sup> And he said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent.’ <sup>31</sup> He said to him, ‘If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead.’”

17.title: Forgiveness, Faith, Gratitude, and the Coming Son of Man
17.overview:
Luke 17 gathers teachings that might appear loosely connected but share a common thread: the shape of life in the kingdom as it moves toward its final consummation. Disciples are warned about causing others to stumble, commanded to forgive repeatedly, confronted about the nature of faith, and then — after the extraordinary healing of ten lepers — taught about gratitude. The chapter then pivots to sustained teaching about the coming of the Son of Man: apocalyptic instruction that would be at home in the Olivet Discourse.

The healing of the ten lepers is one of the most poignant episodes in Luke, precisely because of what does not happen: nine healed men simply walk away. The one who returns is a Samaritan — an outsider — and his return becomes the occasion for Jesus to say something remarkable: “your faith has saved you.” The Greek is sesōken se — the same word used for salvation throughout Luke. The nine received physical healing; the one received something more.

The eschatological teaching (vv. 20–37) is deliberately disorienting. The kingdom does not come with observable signs (v. 20); it is already in your midst (v. 21). Yet the day of the Son of Man will come with lightning-like sudden visibility (v. 24). The tension is not a contradiction: the kingdom is already present in the person of Jesus, but its final manifestation remains future — and when it comes, it will be unmistakable, inescapable, and final.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Stumbling Blocks, Forgiveness, Faith, and Duty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Four short teachings, each pressing the disciples on a different part of their calling.

The stumbling-block saying uses skandalon — not primarily an enticement but the baited trigger-stick of an animal trap, the innocent-looking thing that brings the whole apparatus down. And the millstone Luke names is the great upper stone turned by a donkey, not the small hand-mill. Drowning carried a particular horror for a Jew who expected burial in his own ground, and it is offered as the preferable outcome.

The weight of the saying falls on the influential, because nobody trips a person who is not following them. The “little ones” include children and reach wider: the young in faith, the recently converted, anybody whose hold is not yet firm and who is watching somebody stronger to learn how this is done.

The forgiveness command opens with “pay attention to yourselves,” and the order governs everything after it — a man who has just examined himself rebukes differently from a man who has not. Seven times in one day is deliberately absurd, and it is meant to kill the arithmetic: anyone who apologises seven times before evening for the same thing is, by any ordinary judgement, not sincere, and Jesus takes that objection away by naming the number himself. The test is not whether the repentance convinces but whether forgiveness is a policy or a supply that runs out.

The apostles respond “Increase our faith!” — and note when. Not before a storm or a demon. They have been told to forgive, and they say they have not got enough of whatever it takes. The answer is not what they asked for: he tells them the quantity was never the issue.

Then the servant parable, which checks the pride that obedience produces. And note the condition: “when you have done all that you were commanded” — this is the sentence for the best possible day, with nothing outstanding. Even then there is no credit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The forgiveness teaching anticipates the Lord's Prayer — “forgive us our sins, as we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us” (11:4). This does not make forgiveness a condition of justification; it describes the effect of justification on a heart. Those forgiven much love much (7:47).

The mulberry saying needs a guard, because it has been lifted out of this paragraph and made into a promise that sufficient faith secures whatever is asked. On that reading the tree stays rooted because you did not believe hard enough — and the corollary follows at once about the tumour and the child. It cannot be got out of this text.

Start with where it sits: the apostles asked for help to forgive, and this is his answer about that. Then consider that Luke wrote the sequel — if this were a promise about relocating vegetation, Acts is where we would watch it claimed, and men who heal the lame and raise the dead never once move a tree. And Luke has already recorded the one prayer offered in perfect faith: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). Nobody will suggest the faith in Gethsemane was too small.

Achreioi — “unworthy” — means unprofitable, contributing no surplus. It does not mean worthless in God's sight; the parable is about ledgers, not affection. And it must be guarded from the opposite error, because the same Lord says he will gird himself and serve his watching servants (12:37) and set the faithful man over ten cities (19:17). There is no wage; there is a Master who pays anyway.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke tells us what to do when the brother repents and leaves the other case open. What if he never says “I repent”? That silence is where most real wounds live.

The answer begins with a distinction: forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act. Forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart — releasing the debt, refusing to nurse the injury. Jesus does this from the cross for men who had not repented and never would (23:34). Reconciliation is the restored relationship, and Jesus attaches it to “if he repents.” You can be commanded to forgive unilaterally; you cannot be commanded to reconcile unilaterally, because you do not hold both ends.

That protects both people. It frees the one who was wronged from having to pretend nothing happened, and from being bound to endless re-injury in the name of grace. And it keeps the one who did wrong from being written off, because he remains someone Christ came for. The gravest danger in a long unrepented offence is not that the other man stays hard. It is that you do.

And the servant parable has a reader for whom the whole scene will sting: anybody who has spent years serving in a church without acknowledgement, doing the work that is simply expected and eating after everybody else. Jesus is not telling such a person that this is all there is. He has already said that when the master comes he will gird himself and have them recline at table and serve them (12:37). Both pictures are his, and the second one is the ending.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come!

The word is skandala — and it is not primarily about enticement. A skandalon was the baited trigger-stick of an animal trap: the innocent-looking thing that brings the whole apparatus down. What is being described is not a tempting offer but a snare somebody has set.

And the first half is a flat acknowledgement of the world as it is. They are sure to come. Jesus does not promise a church in which nobody is ever tripped up, and a man who expects one will be disillusioned within a year.

But the inevitability changes nothing about the responsibility. Woe to the one through whom they come — and Luke's woe is the prophets' word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict.

It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea.

The image is deliberately extreme, and the detail matters. Luke's phrase is a millstone of the kind turned by a donkey — not the small hand-mill a woman used but the great upper stone of a village mill, a wheel of rock a man could not lift.

And drowning carried a particular horror for a Jew, who expected burial in his own ground. This is being described as the preferable outcome.

Than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin.

Who are the little ones? The phrase can cover children, and it certainly includes them. But in this context it reaches wider: the young in faith, the recently converted, the weak — anybody whose hold is not yet firm and who is watching somebody stronger to learn how this is done.

Which is where the weight of the saying falls, and it falls on the influential. Nobody trips a person who is not following them.

So this is a word for parents, and for anyone who teaches, leads, or is simply admired by a younger believer — and the terms of it are severe beyond anything else Jesus says about the consequences of a bad example. To ruin your own soul is a catastrophe. To be the trigger-stick under somebody else's is worse, and he measures it with a millstone.

verseByVerse.quote: Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pay attention to yourselves!

The imperative comes first and it governs everything after it. Before a word is said about rebuking anybody, the man doing the rebuking is told to look at himself.

If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him.

Three obligations, and the middle one is the least popular. The rebuke is not optional and it is not unkind; it is what love does when it sees somebody going wrong and would rather they did not arrive.

What makes it bearable is the order. A man who has just examined himself rebukes differently from a man who has not.

And if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, I repent, you must forgive him.

Seven times in one day is deliberately absurd, and it is meant to kill the arithmetic. Anyone who apologises seven times before evening for the same thing is, by any ordinary judgement, not sincere — and Jesus takes that objection away by naming the number himself.

The test is not whether the repentance convinces. It is whether forgiveness is a policy or a supply that runs out.

But Luke tells us what to do when the brother repents, and leaves the other case open. What if he never says I repent? The silence is worth pressing, because that is where most real wounds live.

The answer begins with a distinction Luke's own wording invites: forgiveness and reconciliation are not the same act. Forgiveness is what you do before God with your own heart — releasing the debt, refusing to nurse the injury, declining to make yourself the creditor. Jesus does this from the cross for men who had not repented and never would (23:34). Reconciliation is the restored relationship, and that takes two; Jesus attaches it to if he repents.

You can be commanded to forgive unilaterally. You cannot be commanded to reconcile unilaterally, because you do not hold both ends.

And that protects both people. It frees the one who was wronged from the cruelty of having to pretend nothing happened, and from being bound to endless re-injury in the name of grace. And it keeps the one who did wrong from being written off, because he remains someone Christ came for.

Hold the two together and the opening command does its work. The gravest danger in a long unrepented offence is not that the other man stays hard. It is that you do.

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles said to the Lord, 'Increase our faith!' And the Lord said, 'If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles said to the Lord, Increase our faith!

Note when they say it. Not before a storm, not facing a demon, not in front of a crowd of five thousand. They have just been told to forgive a brother seven times in a day, and their response is that they have not got enough of whatever it takes.

It is an honest request and a good one, and it is worth registering that they were right to be daunted.

If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, Be uprooted and planted in the sea, and it would obey you.

The answer is not what they asked for. They wanted more; he tells them the quantity was never the issue.

The mustard seed is the standard image of the negligible, and the mulberry — the black mulberry of Palestine — was proverbially deep-rooted and long-lived, said to stand for six hundred years. Uprooting one and planting it in the sea is doubly absurd: a tree that cannot be moved, put where nothing grows.

But the verse needs a guard, because it has been lifted out of this paragraph and turned into something else: a promise that sufficient faith secures whatever is asked. On that reading the tree stays rooted because you did not believe hard enough — and the corollary follows at once, that the tumour did not shrink and the child did not recover for the same reason. That has been preached to a great many people at the worst hour of their lives, and it cannot be got out of this text.

Start with where the saying sits. The apostles have not asked for power to work wonders. They have asked for help to forgive, and the mulberry tree is his answer about that. To pull it out and make it a lever for moving circumstances is to use a sentence about pardoning your brother as a technique for rearranging your life.

Then consider that Luke wrote the sequel. If this were a promise about relocating vegetation, Acts is where we would watch it claimed — and in the whole of that book, men who heal the lame and raise the dead never once move a tree. And Luke has already recorded the one prayer in history offered in perfect faith: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me (22:42). The cup was not removed, and nobody will suggest the faith in Gethsemane was too small.

What is promised is not that faith is a force whose output rises with its volume, but that its power lies in what it is attached to. What you already have, actually used, is enough for the seventh apology today.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, Come at once and recline at table?

The question expects the answer no, and every man listening would have given it without hesitation.

Picture the household. This is a small farm, not a great estate — a man with one servant, who does the ploughing and the shepherding, and who has been out all day. There is no second slave in the kitchen. When he comes in, the supper has not been made, because he is the one who makes it.

And recline at table is the posture of a guest at a formal meal. The suggestion is not that the master might let him sit down; it is that he might treat him as an honoured visitor in his own master's house.

Will he not rather say to him, Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink?

The arrangement is not cruel by the standards of that world and Jesus is not commending it as a model for employment. It is simply how a household ran, and everybody knew it.

Dress properly is literally gird yourself — tuck up the robe for work, the same phrase used of the servants waiting for their master in chapter 12.

And note the last clause, because it is easy to miss under the severity: and afterward you will eat and drink. The servant is not going hungry. He eats; he simply eats second.

Which is worth holding, because this parable is about to say something very hard about deserving, and it says it inside a picture where the servant is fed.

There is also a reader for whom the whole scene will sting, and it is worth saying now rather than at the end. Anybody who has spent years serving in a church without acknowledgement will recognise this household exactly — the work that is simply expected, the meal made after everybody else has eaten.

Jesus is not telling such a person that this is all there is. He has already said, in this same Gospel, that when the master comes he will gird himself and have them recline at table and serve them (12:37). Both pictures are his, and the second one is the ending.

verseByVerse.quote: Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded?

Again the answer is obvious and again it is no — not because thanks would be wrong, but because thanks are for something over and above. Nobody is owed gratitude for meeting the terms.

So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.

Note the condition attached: when you have done all that you were commanded. This is not addressed to a man who has failed. It is the sentence he is to say on the day he has done everything — the best possible day, with nothing outstanding.

And even then there is no credit. Not a small credit; none. Duty done is duty done.

The word translated unworthy is achreioi — literally useless, unprofitable, contributing no surplus. It does not mean worthless in God's sight; the parable is about ledgers, not affection. It means that at the end of the accounting there is nothing on the credit side that God did not first supply.

Which is why this parable exists where it does. Chapter 17 has just demanded three enormous things — do not trip the weak, forgive seven times a day, exercise the faith you have. A disciple who manages any of that will feel something rise in him, and what rises is the thought that God now owes him a little.

That thought is the target.

And it needs guarding from the opposite error, because this saying has been used to flatten people who were already flat. It does not mean God is indifferent to what his servants do, and Luke will not allow that reading. The same Lord says he will gird himself and serve his watching servants (12:37), and that the faithful man will be set over ten cities (19:17). He is generous past anything owed.

The two sit together without strain once the direction is right. There is no wage. There is a Master who pays anyway — and the whole point of the parable is that the second sentence is a gift and not an invoice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is in the border country where Jewish Galilee met Samaritan territory — a detail that will matter in six verses.

The ten stand at a distance because the law required it: a man with the disease lived outside the camp, in torn clothes, calling “unclean” as anyone approached (Lev. 13:45-46). “Leprosy” covered a range of skin conditions, but the social consequence was the same whatever the diagnosis — total exclusion from worship, family, work, and touch.

And ten of them are together, which tells its own story. Whatever each had been before, the disease had stripped it off and left them with the one thing they now had in common. Which is what makes verse 16 so striking: one of these ten is a Samaritan. Nine Jews and a Samaritan are living together outside a village, because the disease has done to their divisions what nothing else could.

“Master” is epistata, Luke's own word, used everywhere else in this Gospel by disciples. And they ask not for cleansing but for mercy, leaving the content of it to him.

He does not touch them and does not pronounce them clean. He gives them an errand that only makes sense afterwards — the inspection of Leviticus 14 is what you go for when the disease has gone. So ten men with visible leprosy are told to set off and be examined for its absence.

“And as they went they were cleansed.” Not before they went. There would have been a stretch of that road during which they had obeyed and nothing whatever had changed.

One turns back — and it is worth being clear that the other nine were obeying. Until a priest certified them they could not go home or touch their children. Nine men are hurrying towards the thing they have wanted for years, doing exactly what they were told. One of them stops.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story illustrates the difference between receiving a benefit from God and responding to God himself. All ten received cleansing; only one responded to the Giver. And the nine were not ingrates by worldly standards — their failure was not defiance but distraction. They moved from the gift to the system without pausing to return.

The Samaritan's outsider status is theologically loaded in Luke, who shows Samaritans in a positive light three times: the good Samaritan (10:33), this leper, and Samaria as the first step beyond Jerusalem in Acts (1:8; 8:5).

And the point is sharper than it first appears. The nine were going to the priests in Jerusalem — to the temple, the sacrifices, the machinery of a religion this man was excluded from. He could not have gone with them. So the outsider, who had no temple to report to and no certificate available to him, went to the only place open to him, and it turned out to be the right one.

“Foreigner” at v.18 is allogenēs, a word found only here in the New Testament — and it is the word carved on the stone barrier in the temple court warning Gentiles not to pass beyond on pain of death. That inscription has been dug up. Jesus uses of this man the word on the sign that kept him out, and the only man in the story fenced out of the temple is the only one who came back to God.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Your faith has made you well” translates sesōken se — the perfect of sōzō, the ordinary New Testament word for save. Luke has used the identical phrase to the woman weeping at his feet, who was forgiven (7:50), and to the woman who touched his garment (8:48).

Which answers the obvious difficulty: all ten were cleansed, so what is left for this man to receive? Ten men were cleansed of leprosy. One was saved. A man can receive a great deal from Christ and never arrive at Christ, and this is the clearest picture of it in the Gospels.

And notice what his faith actually consisted of, because it was not much. He shouted for mercy from a distance with nine other men, obeyed an instruction that made no sense, and when he saw what had happened, turned round and went back to the one who did it. There is no impressive spiritual content anywhere in his story.

The three questions at v.17 are among the few places where Jesus expresses something like disappointment at how he has been treated. He does not do it elsewhere for himself — not when a village will not house him, not when a Pharisee omits the courtesies at dinner.

And the nine are not villains but ordinary. Nobody in that group decided to be ungrateful. They received something enormous and moved straight to the next necessary thing, and the next, and by evening it was a fortnight ago. A family prays for a sick child and the child recovers; within weeks the thankfulness has given way to relief and resumed normal life. The story calls ordinary people to come back.

verseByVerse.quote: On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee.

Luke reminds us of the destination again, and gives us the geography — the border country, the strip where Jewish Galilee met Samaritan territory.

It is a detail that will matter in six verses. Border regions are where mixed populations live, and where the ordinary boundaries are thinner than they are further in.

And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance.

They are outside the village, which is where the law required them to be. Leviticus put a man with the disease outside the camp, in torn clothes, with his hair loose, calling unclean, unclean as anyone approached (Lev. 13:45-46).

Leprosy in that world covered a range of skin conditions, not only the disease that now bears the name. But the social consequence was the same whatever the diagnosis: total exclusion from worship, from family, from work, from touch.

And ten of them are together, which tells its own story. Whatever they had been before — farmer, father, householder — the disease had stripped it off and left them with the one thing they now had in common. This is a colony of the excluded, formed because there was nowhere else for any of them to go.

Which is what makes the next detail so striking, and Luke saves it for verse 16. One of these ten is a Samaritan.

A Jew and a Samaritan did not eat together, worship together or share a cup. But nine Jews and one Samaritan are living together outside a village, because the disease has done to their divisions what nothing else could.

It is a bleak observation and a true one. There are forms of suffering severe enough to dissolve hatreds that no argument would ever have touched — and it takes something like leprosy to do it.

They stood at a distance. That is the last thing said about them before they speak, and it is where every one of them had been standing for years.

verseByVerse.quote: and lifted up their voices, saying, 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.' When he saw them he said to them, 'Go and show yourselves to the priests.' And as they went they were cleansed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And lifted up their voices, saying, Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.

They shout, because they have to. The distance the law imposed is the reason the request is delivered at the top of ten voices.

Master is epistata — Luke's own word, used nowhere else in the New Testament, and everywhere else in this Gospel it is on the lips of disciples (5:5; 8:24; 9:33). These men are not disciples. They have picked up the word from somewhere and are using it correctly.

And note what they ask for: not cleansing but mercy. They do not specify the terms. They ask him to be merciful and leave the content of it to him.

When he saw them he said to them, Go and show yourselves to the priests.

He does not touch them, which he had done for the leper in chapter 5. He does not pronounce them clean. He gives them an errand.

And the errand only makes sense afterwards. Leviticus 14 lays down a detailed procedure for a man whose leprosy has healed: he presents himself to the priest, is examined, and after the offerings is certified clean and readmitted to the community. It is the inspection you go for when the disease has gone.

So ten men with visible leprosy are told to set off and be examined for its absence.

And as they went they were cleansed.

There it is, and the timing is the whole point. Not before they went. As they went.

Every one of them had to turn round and walk towards a priest while still covered in the disease, having been given nothing but a sentence. There would have been a stretch of that road — a hundred yards, half a mile — during which they had obeyed and nothing whatever had changed.

Which is a fair description of most of the Christian life, and it is why this detail is worth stopping at. The instruction is given first and the evidence arrives on the way. A man who waits to see the change before he starts walking will not see it, because the walking is where it happens.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice.

He is the only one who stops.

And it is worth being clear about what the other nine were doing, because they are usually described as ungrateful and it is not quite that simple. They were obeying. They had been told to go to the priests, and they went — and until a priest certified them they were not legally clean, could not go home, could not enter the synagogue, could not touch their children.

Nine men are hurrying towards the thing they have wanted for years, doing exactly what they were told.

One of them turns round.

Note also the loud voice. It is the same phrase Luke used of them in verse 13, shouting from a distance for mercy. The same volume, redirected.

And he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks.

Two things here, and the second is the theology of the passage.

He fell on his face, which is not the posture of gratitude but of worship. And he gives thanks to Jesus — while praising God with the same breath, in the same act.

He has not merely worked out that a benefit came from somewhere. He has worked out where.

Now he was a Samaritan.

Luke saves it for the end of the sentence, and it detonates the whole story.

The nine were going to the priests in Jerusalem — to the temple, to the sacrifices, to the machinery of a religion this man was excluded from. He could not have gone with them; the priest would not have received him.

So the outsider, who had no temple to report to and no certificate available to him, went to the only place that was open. And it turned out to be the right one.

Which is the story Luke keeps telling. The Samaritan on the Jericho road (10:33); Samaria as the first stop beyond Jerusalem in his second volume (Acts 1:8; 8:5). The man with the fewest religious options in the group is the one who ends up on his face in the right place.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus answered, 'Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus answered, Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine?

Three questions, and they are not rhetorical flourishes. Something is being registered.

It is worth noticing that this is one of the few places in the Gospels where Jesus expresses something like disappointment about how he has been treated. He does not do it for himself elsewhere — not when a village will not house him, not when a Pharisee omits the courtesies at dinner. Here he asks where the other nine are.

And the arithmetic is stated plainly: were not ten cleansed? Every one of them got what he asked for. The healing was not withheld from the ungrateful, and it is important to see that. All ten were cleansed before any of them had shown what he would do about it.

Where are the nine?

Down the road, doing what they were told, about to be certified, going home to their families. Not villains. Ordinary.

Which is what makes the question searching rather than merely sad. Nobody in that group made a decision to be ungrateful. They received something enormous and moved straight on to the next necessary thing, and the next, and by evening it was a fortnight ago.

Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?

The word is allogenēs — literally of another race. And it is a startling word to find here, because it appears in the New Testament only once, and it is the word that was carved on the stone barrier in the temple court warning Gentiles not to pass beyond on pain of death.

That inscription has been dug up. The word Jesus uses of this man is the word on the sign that kept him out.

He uses it, and the point is unmistakable. The only man in the story who was fenced out of the temple is the only one who came back to God.

And note that Jesus does not say the nine failed to be grateful. He says nobody was found to return. The failure named is a matter of direction: nine men were walking one way and one man turned round.

Which is worth having, because gratitude is usually discussed as a feeling and this passage will not let it be one. All ten were presumably delighted. Only one of them changed course.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him, Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.

One verse, and it gives the man something the other nine did not receive.

Start with the difficulty, because it is a real one. All ten were cleansed — Luke says so twice (vv. 14, 17). So what is left for this man to get?

The answer is in the verb. Made you well translates sesōken se — the perfect of sōzō, which is the ordinary New Testament word for save. Luke has used the identical phrase twice before, and both times about something more than a body: to the woman weeping at his feet, who was forgiven (7:50), and to the woman who touched his garment (8:48).

The word can mean physical healing and it can mean salvation, and Luke's usage here is deliberate. Ten men were cleansed of leprosy. One was saved.

Which is the whole point of the story, and it sharpens the question about the nine. They received a genuine, enormous, undeserved gift from Jesus of Nazareth and went home with it. There is no suggestion anywhere that it was taken back.

But a man can receive a great deal from Christ and never arrive at Christ, and this passage is the clearest picture of it in the Gospels.

Rise and go your way. He is not kept there. He is sent home like the others, with a certificate no priest issued and a body no priest examined.

And it is worth noticing what his faith actually consisted of, because it was not much. He shouted for mercy from a distance with nine other men. He obeyed an instruction that made no sense. And when he saw what had happened, he stopped, turned round, and went back to the one who did it.

That is all of it. There is no impressive spiritual content anywhere in this man's story.

Nine men were given their lives back and walked on. One came back to say thank you, and was told his faith had saved him — which means that turning round is a good deal more than a courtesy, and that the distance between the nine and the one is not gratitude. It is where each of them ended up standing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–37 — The Kingdom and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees ask when the kingdom is coming, and the question assumes a datable event that can be worked out by people currently standing outside it.

“Not coming in ways that can be observed” uses paratērēsis — a word belonging to two vocabularies at once: the physician watching a patient for symptoms, and the astronomer observing the heavens. It means surveillance for signs, which is precisely what men who study prophecy in order to date the end have always done.

“The kingdom of God is in the midst of you” has probably been misquoted more than any other line in Luke. The King James renders it “within you,” and that has been carried off to mean that the kingdom is an inner glow native to every human heart. The Greek entos can mean within, so the translation is not dishonest — what settles it is who he is addressing. He is answering the Pharisees, who will shortly hand him over to be killed. He is not telling them the kingdom is glowing inside their hearts; he is telling them it is standing in the room.

Turning to the disciples, he warns of days when they will long to see one ordinary day of his presence and will not. The longing is named and allowed — and then he deals with the danger it creates, because a man who badly wants Christ to appear is exactly the man who will travel to where somebody says he has. The lightning settles it: nobody has ever been told where the lightning was.

Then, dropped into the middle of it, verse 25: first he must suffer. The Son of Man who comes like lightning is the same man about to be spat at and hung up outside a city wall, and he will be that first.

The Noah and Lot examples select, out of everything available, the ordinary: eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting and building. Not one is a sin. On its last morning, Sodom was a town where people were putting in orchards.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tension between “the kingdom is in the midst of you” and “the days of the Son of Man are coming” is the foundation of the New Testament's already-not-yet. The kingdom has come in the person and work of Jesus; it has not yet come in fullness. Believers live in the overlap.

“Revealed” at v.30 is apokalyptetai, unveiled — which says something precise about what is coming. It is not that the Son of Man will arrive from elsewhere like a visitor; he will be uncovered, and the implication is that he is not absent now, merely unseen. The day does not change where he is; it changes what can be seen.

On the missing verse 36: your Bible may go straight from 35 to 37, or may print a verse 36 reading “two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left.” Nothing has been removed. The line is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts of Luke and appears to have been copied in from Matthew 24:40 by a scribe who noticed Luke had two examples where Matthew had three. Modern versions drop it to a footnote and keep the old numbering rather than renumber the chapter, which is why the gap is visible — honest bookkeeping, with the workings printed rather than tidied away.

On “taken”: popular retellings fix the picture so that the taken are caught up to safety. But two paragraphs earlier the examples were Noah and Lot, and in both it was the judgement that did the taking — the flood took them all away, and the fire fell on those who stayed in Sodom while Lot was left alive outside it.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Remember Lot's wife” is the shortest verse in Luke, and it does not need the story told. She had been brought out by the hand — the angels seized Lot and his wife and set them outside the city, “the LORD being merciful to him” (Gen. 19:16). She was rescued, physically, past the point of danger. And she looked back.

Her looking back was not curiosity. Everything she had was in that town — her house, her married daughters, the whole shape of a life. She was out of Sodom and Sodom was not out of her.

Which is worth taking personally rather than eschatologically. There is a kind of Christian who has genuinely left something behind and spends the rest of his life half-turned towards it: the career surrendered and still mourned, the old life renounced and remembered fondly. He is walking forward; he is not looking forward. And Jesus does not say “remember Sodom.” He says remember the woman who got out and did not get away.

“Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it” is a statement about how reality is constructed rather than a piece of moral advice, and everybody knows a version of it. The parent who holds a child too tightly loses him; the man who protects his reputation above everything is left with nothing but a reputation. The grip is what loses the thing.

And the disciples' “Where, Lord?” is our instinct exactly. They have just been told that two people in one bed will be separated for ever, and what they want is the geography. He answers with a proverb that tells them nothing useful about location, and the uselessness is the sermon.

verseByVerse.quote: Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, 'The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come.

The question assumes a great deal, and the assumptions are what Jesus answers. It assumes the kingdom is a future event with a date; that the date can be worked out; and that the people asking are not currently in any relation to it except waiting.

The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed.

The word is paratērēsis, and it belonged to two vocabularies at once: the physician's, for watching a patient for symptoms, and the astronomer's, for observing the heavens. It means surveillance for signs.

He is not saying the kingdom is invisible. He is saying it is not the kind of thing you detect by scanning for indicators — which is precisely what men who study prophecy in order to date the end have always done.

Nor will they say, Look, here it is! or There!

The pointing is the giveaway. Anything requiring a guide is not it.

For behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.

This verse deserves a note, because in its older wording it has probably been misquoted more than any other line in Luke. The King James renders it the kingdom of God is within you, and that sentence has been carried off to mean something Jesus never said: that the kingdom is an inner spiritual glow native to every human heart, that God's reign is simply the divinity we already carry, that religion is a journey inward needing no king outside us at all.

The Greek word entos can indeed mean within, so the translation is not dishonest. What settles it is who Jesus is talking to.

Look back at the first line. He is answering the Pharisees — the men who in a few chapters will hand him over to be killed. He is not telling them that the kingdom of God is glowing quietly inside their hearts.

He is telling them it is standing in the room.

In the midst of you is the reading the sentence demands, and it is a far sharper word than the one that usually replaces it. The kingdom is not a feeling located by looking inward. It is a Person they have so far managed to look straight past — and they are asking him when he is going to arrive.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the disciples, 'The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to the disciples.

The audience changes. What follows is not for the Pharisees but for the men who will still be here when he is not.

The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.

A tender sentence and a bleak one. There will be a time — and Luke's readers were living in it — when they will want one day back. Not the second coming; one of the days, singular, an ordinary day of walking about with him.

And they will not get it. He says so plainly rather than promising them a substitute.

Which is worth registering by anyone who has known a season of unusual nearness to God and now does not. The longing is not a fault, and it is not answered here with a technique for recovering the feeling. It is named, and allowed, and then he moves straight to what to do about the danger it creates.

And they will say to you, Look, there! or Look, here! Do not go out or follow them.

Because that is what longing makes a person vulnerable to. A man who badly wants Christ to appear is exactly the man who will get in a car and drive to where somebody says he has.

The instruction is blunt and it is doubled: do not go out, and do not follow. Not weigh the claim carefully. Do not go.

For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.

And there is the test, and it is beautifully simple.

Nobody has ever been told where the lightning was. Nobody has ever had to travel to see it, or been let in on it by a teacher with special knowledge, or missed it because he was facing the wrong way. It fills the sky from one horizon to the other, and everybody in the country sees it at once.

So the rule is: anything that has to be pointed out is not it. Every claim that Christ has returned quietly, or secretly, or to a particular place, or to a particular group, is refuted by one sentence about weather — and the refutation was issued in advance, by him, precisely so that his people would not spend the centuries chasing rumours.

verseByVerse.quote: But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.

One sentence, dropped into the middle of a discourse about the end, and it changes the shape of everything around it.

First. Before the lightning, before the day, before any of it — this.

And there is the must again, dei, the divine necessity that has run through this Gospel since a boy in the temple said I must be in my Father's house (2:49). The suffering is not a setback on the way to the glory. It is on the schedule.

Suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.

Note who does the rejecting. Not Rome, though Rome will drive the nails. This generation — the people he is standing among, including the Pharisees he was answering four verses ago and the crowds who have followed him from Galilee.

Luke has recorded the prediction twice already (9:22; 9:44), and both times the disciples failed to take it in. Here it arrives without warning, in the middle of a different subject, and moves on without elaboration.

Why put it here at all?

Because the disciples have just been told about a day of unmistakable, sky-filling glory, and a man can build a very attractive religion out of that alone. Jesus will not let the second coming be detached from the first.

The Son of Man who comes like lightning is the same man who is going to be spat at, flogged, and hung up outside a city wall — and he is going to be that first. Any expectation of his return that skips the cross has the wrong person coming back.

And there is a word here for the way Christians think about the future generally. It is possible to be genuinely thrilled by prophecy and entirely unmoved by Calvary — to find the trumpet stirring and the crown of thorns merely sad. That is a taste, not a theology, and this verse is placed exactly where it is to correct it.

The road to the day of the Son of Man runs through Jerusalem, and he was walking it while he said this.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man.

The first of two examples, and the thing to notice is what he does not say about Noah's generation.

Genesis is not gentle about them: the earth was corrupt and filled with violence, and every intention of the thoughts of their hearts was only evil continually (Gen. 6:5, 11). Jesus could have made that the point. He does not.

They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage.

Four activities, and not one of them is a sin. Eating, drinking, arranging weddings. This is ordinary life in a village, and it is the picture of a world that is not doing anything unusual at all.

Which is the warning, and it is quite different from the one people expect. The danger is not that the world will become monstrous and everybody will see it coming. The danger is that it will look exactly like this.

Until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.

Two clauses, and the order is the point. The ark had been under construction for years, in public, by a man who preached while he built (2 Pet. 2:5). Everybody knew. And then one day Noah went inside — and the day he went in was the day it came.

Note the phrase destroyed them all. Luke does not soften it, and he will use the identical phrase about Sodom two verses later.

And it is worth saying plainly what the parallel implies about warning. Noah's generation was not short of it. They had a preacher, and a boat going up in their own neighbourhood, and decades to think about it — and they went on eating and drinking, not because they had considered the evidence and rejected it, but because life was going on and it always had.

That is the exact position of the modern world with respect to the return of Christ, and it is why the illustration is here. Nobody in Noah's village decided to drown. They simply had a normal week, and then another one, until the last one.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot.

The second example, and Jesus adds it because the first could be dismissed. Noah's flood was a unique event at the dawn of history; Sodom was a town, in living memory of the patriarchs, in country his hearers could have walked to.

They were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building.

Six activities this time, and again not one is wicked. Two of them — planting and building — are the most hopeful things a person can do, because both are investments in a future.

And that is what makes the list so bleak. On its last morning, Sodom was a town where people were putting in orchards and laying foundations.

It is worth registering how differently Jesus handles Sodom from the way it is usually handled. The city is a byword for a particular wickedness, and Genesis records it. He never mentions it. What he selects, out of everything available, is the property market and the planting season.

But on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all.

The same structure as Noah, and the same hinge: the rescue of the righteous man and the arrival of the judgement are the same day. Genesis is explicit that the angels could do nothing until Lot was out — escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there (Gen. 19:22).

So will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.

And there is the application, and one word in it is worth stopping at. Revealed — apokalyptetai, unveiled.

Which says something precise about what is coming. It is not that the Son of Man will arrive from somewhere else, like a visitor. He will be uncovered — and the implication is that he is not absent now, merely unseen.

The day does not change where he is. It changes what can be seen. And the reason the world will be caught eating and drinking is not that a stranger turned up unannounced, but that the one who was there all along stopped being invisible.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away.

The picture is exact for a Palestinian village. Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair; people slept, dried grain and sat in the cool up there. So a man on the roof can get to the street without entering the house at all — which is what makes the instruction possible and what makes it cost something.

He must leave with what he is wearing.

And likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back.

Not even for the cloak he took off at the end of the row. The urgency is total, and the thing being forbidden is not sin but retrieval.

Remember Lot's wife.

Three words, and it is the shortest verse in Luke's Gospel.

He does not tell the story; he does not need to. She had been brought out by the hand — the angels seized Lot and his wife and daughters and set them outside the city, the LORD being merciful to him (Gen. 19:16). She was rescued, physically, past the point of danger.

And she looked back, and became a pillar of salt (Gen. 19:26).

What is worth pressing is what her looking back actually was, because it sounds like a small thing punished enormously. It was not curiosity. Everything she had was in that town — her house, her married daughters, the whole shape of a life. To turn round was to have her heart still in it.

She was out of Sodom and Sodom was not out of her.

Which is the warning to a disciple, and it is worth taking personally rather than eschatologically. There is a kind of Christian who has genuinely left something behind and spends the rest of his life half-turned towards it — the career surrendered and still mourned, the relationship broken off and still visited in the imagination, the old life renounced and remembered fondly.

He is walking forward. He is not looking forward.

And Jesus does not say remember Sodom. He says remember the woman who got out and did not get away.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.

He has said this before, at Caesarea Philippi (9:24), and it is worth noticing where it is repeated. There it followed the first passion prediction and the call to take up a cross daily. Here it follows a man on a roof being told to leave his possessions and a woman being remembered for looking back.

The principle is the same; the application has moved from a lifetime to a moment.

Seeks to preserve is peripoiēsasthai — to acquire for oneself, to secure as one's own possession. And that verb is the link with the two verses before it. The man on the roof who goes back for his goods is trying to preserve; so is Lot's wife.

What they are trying to keep hold of is not merely property. It is the arrangement — the shape of a life that has been built and is now being taken away.

And the sentence says the attempt is self-defeating in the strictest sense. Not that it is wrong, or greedy, or short-sighted. That it does not work. The grip is what loses the thing.

Which is a statement about how reality is constructed, not a piece of moral advice, and it applies well outside the day of the Son of Man. Everybody knows a version of it. The parent who holds a child too tightly loses him; the person who cannot bear to be disliked ends up with no friendships of any weight; the man who protects his reputation above everything is eventually left with nothing but a reputation.

But whoever loses his life will keep it.

Note the two verbs on this side: loses and keeps — literally will give it life, will make it alive.

So the alternative is not a heroic sacrifice with nothing on the other side. It is the only route by which anything survives at all. The man who lets go is not choosing loss over gain; he is choosing the one grip that does not crush what it holds.

And the whole of it is settled by who said it. He is on the road to Jerusalem, and he is about to demonstrate both halves in the same week.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.' And they said to him, 'Where, Lord?' He said to them, 'Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left.

Before the saying itself, a note about the numbering, because a reader comparing Bibles will find one missing. Your version may go straight from verse 35 to verse 37; another may print a verse 36 reading two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left.

Nothing has been removed. The line is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts of Luke and appears to have been copied in from the parallel in Matthew 24:40 by a scribe who noticed Luke had two examples where Matthew had three. Modern versions drop it to a footnote and keep the old numbering rather than renumber the whole chapter — which is why the gap is visible. It is a small piece of honest bookkeeping, and it is worth knowing that the workings are printed rather than tidied away.

Now the saying. Two in one bed — a household at night; two women grinding together — the small hand-mill worked by two women sitting opposite each other at dawn. The nearest possible proximity in both cases, and identical circumstances.

And one of each pair is taken.

A word on taken, because most readers arrive at this verse already certain which they would rather be. Popular retellings have fixed the picture: the taken are caught up to safety and the left are abandoned to disaster. That reading belongs to a particular scheme of the end times held sincerely by many Christians, and nothing here needs to be unkind about it.

But notice what Jesus has just been talking about. Two paragraphs earlier the examples were Noah and Lot — and in both, it was the judgement that did the taking. The flood took them all away (Matt. 24:39); the fire fell on those who stayed in Sodom while Lot was left alive outside it. If the Lord's own illustrations set the sense of the word, then to be taken here is to be swept off, and to be left is to be spared.

And they said to him, Where, Lord?

And there it is — the disciples' instinct, and ours. They have just been told that two people in one bed will be separated for ever, and what they want to know is the geography.

Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.

He answers with a proverb that tells them nothing useful about location, and the uselessness is the sermon. It means only this: when the thing is ready, the gathering happens, and nobody has to be told where.

The question is not which group you would prefer. It is whether the day, arriving in the middle of an ordinary night, would find you facing the right direction.

17.text: <sup>1</sup> And he said to his disciples, “Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! <sup>2</sup> It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin. <sup>3</sup> Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, <sup>4</sup> and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.” <sup>5</sup> The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you. <sup>7</sup> “Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? <sup>8</sup> Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’? <sup>9</sup> Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? <sup>10</sup> So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’” <sup>11</sup> On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. <sup>12</sup> And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance <sup>13</sup> and lifted up their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” <sup>14</sup> When he saw them he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went they were cleansed. <sup>15</sup> Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; <sup>16</sup> and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan. <sup>17</sup> Then Jesus answered, “Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? <sup>18</sup> Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, “Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.” <sup>20</sup> Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, “The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, <sup>21</sup> nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to the disciples, “The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. <sup>23</sup> And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. <sup>24</sup> For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day. <sup>25</sup> But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. <sup>26</sup> Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. <sup>27</sup> They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. <sup>28</sup> Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, <sup>29</sup> but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— <sup>30</sup> so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. <sup>31</sup> On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. <sup>32</sup> Remember Lot's wife. <sup>33</sup> Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it. <sup>34</sup> I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. <sup>35</sup> There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.” <sup>37</sup> And they said to him, “Where, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.”

18.title: Prayer, Humility, Children, Wealth, and Sight
18.overview:
Luke 18 is constructed around a series of contrasts: persistent widow versus unjust judge; Pharisee versus tax collector; those who would keep children from Jesus versus Jesus who receives them; a rich young ruler who goes away sorrowful versus disciples who have left everything; blind Bartimaeus who cries out versus those who rebuke his cry. In each pair, the unexpected person receives what they need — and the principle is always the same: those who come to God with empty hands receive; those who come convinced they already have what is required leave empty.

Luke tells us explicitly why Jesus told the opening parables. The widow-and-judge parable is told to show that “they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (v. 1). The Pharisee-and-tax-collector parable addresses “those who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt” (v. 9). Together they define authentic prayer: persistent, humble, directed entirely toward a God who can do what we cannot.

The final section (vv. 31–43) contains the third passion prediction — which the disciples cannot understand — and closes with blind Bartimaeus, a man who cannot see physically but sees Jesus with perfect spiritual clarity: “Son of David, have mercy on me.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Persistent Widow and the Unjust Judge
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke tells us the point before the story starts — something he rarely does — which suggests he was not prepared to risk it being missed. And the two halves of the purpose are the same thing from two sides: “always to pray” and “not lose heart,” where the second word means to grow weary, to give out. The alternative to persistent prayer is not some other spiritual activity. It is quitting.

Note where it sits. The previous paragraph closed with a discourse about a day that comes without warning after a long wait. This parable is what to do in the meantime.

The judge is described comprehensively: he neither feared God nor respected man, which is the whole of the Old Testament's requirement for the office (cf. 2 Chr. 19:6-7). He is not corrupt — a bribe would be a lever, and a lever would work. He simply does not care, and Luke says so twice, once as narrator and once in the man's own mouth, so nobody can call it a hostile characterisation.

The widow is the other end of the scale. Without husband, father or male relative she had no standing in a court at all, no money for a lawyer and no influence. And the law was emphatic about her: God “executes justice for the fatherless and the widow” (Deut. 10:18), and cursed is the man who perverts it (Deut. 27:19). The one case this judge is most obliged to hear is the one he is refusing.

What she asks for is not charity but a verdict — “give me justice,” ekdikēson me, vindicate me. And the verb the judge uses for what she is doing to him is from the boxing ring: hypōpiazē, to strike under the eye. He is not worn down by sympathy or shamed into it. He is being hit, repeatedly, in the same place.

So justice is done in that city for the worst possible reason, by a man who cared nothing about it, because one powerless woman would not go away. Which is the setup for the argument, and the argument runs by contrast: if even that produces justice, consider who you are actually dealing with.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer is not a mechanism for overcoming divine reluctance. The unjust judge is the contrast, not the model — this is an argument from the lesser to the greater, and every term in v.7 is set against him. He had no fear of God; this is God. The widow was a stranger; these are “his elect.” She was a nuisance at a door; they “cry to him day and night,” which is the language of the Psalms and of a people in exile.

And Jesus raises the delay himself rather than pretending it is not there. The parable assumes a widow who has been coming a long time. What is denied is not the delay but its meaning: the widow's problem was that her judge did not care, and that was the only reason for her wait. Whatever the reason for yours, it is not that one — because the one you are asking chose you.

“Speedily” does not promise a quick answer. It means without dawdling — that when God moves he does not drag his feet, and that nothing is being held up by reluctance at his end. And notice what the elect are crying for: not relief but justice, the setting right of all things, which arrives in full at the coming of the Son of Man named in the very next line. Some prayers are answered in this life; every prayer of God's people is answered at that day, and none of them a minute late.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable ends with a question, and it is the reverse of the one everybody arrives with. We come asking whether God will keep faith with us; he settles that flatly and moves on. What he asks is whether he will find faith in us — and he leaves it open, which is more unsettling than any answer would have been.

The “nevertheless” is doing the work. Justice is certain; the perseverance of the people waiting for it is not. Which is exactly the danger the parable was told to address: the risk is not an unanswering God but a widow who stops coming.

So if you are still praying after eleven years and have concluded that the long silence is evidence of being ignored, read the last line again. The thing he says he will be looking for when he comes is the very thing you are doing.

And there is a word here for the man whose prayer life has quietly collapsed — who prays in a crisis but finds sustained daily prayer pointless, since God knows what he needs anyway. The purpose of persistent prayer is not to overcome divine ignorance. It is to keep the heart oriented toward the right Source, and to sustain the posture of a person who genuinely believes help is coming from outside himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. He said, 'In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart.

Luke does something here he rarely does: he tells us the point before the story starts. Usually a parable is left to do its own work; this one comes with the moral attached at the front, which suggests he was not prepared to risk it being missed.

And the two halves of the purpose are worth holding together, because they are the same thing described from two sides. Always to pray and not lose heart — the word for losing heart means to grow weary, to give out, to become a coward.

Which tells you that the alternative to persistent prayer is not some other spiritual activity. It is quitting. Nobody stops praying because they have found something better to do with the time.

Note also where this sits. The previous paragraph closed with two people in one bed and the disciples asking where, Lord? — a discourse about a day that will come without warning after a long wait. This parable is what to do in the meantime.

In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man.

The description is devastating and it is comprehensive. The whole of the Old Testament's requirement for a judge is contained in two things: he must fear God, and he must have some regard for the people in front of him. Jehoshaphat's charge to the judges of Judah says exactly this — consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD… let the fear of the LORD be upon you (2 Chr. 19:6-7).

This man has neither. He is not a corrupt judge who can be bribed; that would be a lever, and a bribe would work. He simply does not care, in either direction, and Luke says so twice — once here and once in the man's own mouth at verse 4, so nobody can suggest it is a hostile characterisation.

He is the worst judge imaginable, and that is the point of him. He is in the story to be the opposite of somebody.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there was a widow in that city.

The other end of the scale, and the pairing is deliberate.

A widow in that world was the standard biblical shorthand for defencelessness. She had no husband to represent her, and unless a son or a brother-in-law took up her case she had no standing in a court at all — women did not ordinarily give testimony. She had no money for a lawyer and no influence to bring.

And the law was emphatic about her: God executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deut. 10:18), and cursed is the man who perverts it (Deut. 27:19). The prophets return to it constantly. So the one case this judge is most obliged to hear is the one he is refusing.

Who kept coming to him and saying, Give me justice against my adversary.

The tense is continuous — she kept coming. And what she asks for is not charity or leniency. Give me justice — ekdikēson me, vindicate me, settle my case. She believes she is in the right, and she is asking for a verdict rather than a favour.

For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself.

Luke takes us inside his head, and the man is entirely candid there. He repeats the narrator's assessment of himself word for word — though I neither fear God nor respect man — which is a rare thing in Scripture and slightly chilling. He knows exactly what he is and it does not trouble him.

Yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.

The verb is hypōpiazē, and it is a word from the boxing ring: to strike under the eye, to give somebody a black eye. Paul uses it of disciplining his own body (1 Cor. 9:27).

So the judge is not moved. He is not worn down by sympathy, or shamed, or persuaded. He is being hit, repeatedly, in the same place — and he gives her the verdict to make it stop.

Justice is done in that city for the worst possible reason, by a man who cared nothing about it, because one powerless woman would not go away.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said, 'Hear what the unrighteous judge says. And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear what the unrighteous judge says.

Jesus tells them to listen to the villain — which is the instruction that unlocks the parable, and it is worth saying plainly what it does and does not mean.

This is an argument from the lesser to the greater, and such arguments work by contrast, not comparison. God is not the unjust judge; he is his opposite in every particular. The parable does not say God is reluctant, so keep pestering him. It says: if even that produces justice, consider who you are actually dealing with.

And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night?

Every term is set against the judge.

He had no fear of God; this is God. The widow was a stranger to him; these are his elect — his chosen, the people he has bound himself to. She was a nuisance at his door; they cry to him day and night, which is the language of Psalms and of a people in exile.

And the verb for their crying is a strong one. This is not the recitation of a list. It is the sound people make when something is badly wrong and they know who to shout at.

Will he delay long over them?

The question is put to be answered, and it is worth noticing that Jesus raises the delay himself. He does not pretend it is not there. The parable assumes a widow who has been coming for a long time and elect who are crying day and night — which is to say, the waiting is written into the story.

What is being denied is not the delay but its meaning.

The widow's problem was that her judge did not care. That was the reason for her wait, and it was the only reason. Jesus is telling people whose prayers have gone unanswered for years that whatever the reason for their wait, it is not that one — because the one they are asking chose them.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily.

And there is the word that snags on real life.

Speedily — and the person reading this has perhaps prayed for the same thing for eleven years. A marriage. A son who will not come home. A body that does not heal.

Luke told us at the top of the chapter who this parable is for: people in danger of losing heart. So it is worth being honest about what the promise says and does not say.

It does not promise a quick answer. The phrase means without delay in the sense of without dawdling — that when God moves he does not drag his feet, and that nothing is being held up by reluctance at his end.

And notice what the elect in the parable are actually crying for. Not relief; justice — the setting right of all things, which is precisely what arrives at the coming of the Son of Man named in the very next line. Some prayers are answered in this life. Every prayer of God's people is answered at that day, and none of them a minute late.

Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?

The parable ends with a question, and it is the reverse of the one everybody arrives with.

We come to a passage like this asking whether God will keep faith with us. He settles that flatly and moves on. What he asks is whether he will find faith in us — and he leaves it open, which is more unsettling than any answer would have been.

The nevertheless is doing the work. Justice is certain; the perseverance of the people waiting for it is not.

Which is exactly the danger the parable was told to address. The risk here is not an unanswering God. It is a widow who stops coming.

So if you are still praying after eleven years, and have concluded that the long silence is evidence of being ignored — read the last line again. The thing he says he will be looking for when he comes is the very thing you are doing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke names the target before the story begins, and the two clauses belong together as cause and effect. “Trusted in themselves that they were righteous” places confidence in something that can be inspected — and a righteousness that has to be maintained needs a scale, and a scale needs other people on it. The contempt is not an unfortunate trait attached to an otherwise sound position; it is generated by the position.

Note too that Luke does not say “to the Pharisees.” He says “to some who” — a description rather than a party, which leaves the door open for anybody to walk through.
