And look at the numbers, because they are not arbitrary. Half is far beyond anything the law required. And fourfold is the penalty for the aggravated case — a stolen ox slaughtered or sold (Ex. 22:1); ordinary restitution was the sum plus a fifth (Lev. 6:5). He sentences himself at the highest rate on the books.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Today salvation has come to this house.

Today — the fourth of Luke's great todays, and they form a spine through the Gospel: unto you is born this day a Saviour (2:11); today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (4:21); this one; and, from a cross, today you will be with me in Paradise (23:43).

And note what is said to have arrived. Not you have been forgiven, though he has. Salvation has come — and it came up the road that morning and is currently sitting at the table.

To this house. Not merely to Zacchaeus. Whatever else that means, the household is included in the reckoning — the wife, the children, the servants, all of whom had been living on the proceeds and are now living in a house where half of it has just been given away.

Since he also is a son of Abraham.

Which is a deliberate provocation, because it is precisely what the grumblers would have denied. In the popular reckoning a tax collector had forfeited his place; he was a traitor living off his own people, and some rabbinic rulings treated his repentance as practically impossible, since he could never trace everyone he had defrauded.

Jesus hands him the title back. And Luke has done this once before, six chapters earlier, for a bent woman nobody had helped in eighteen years — a daughter of Abraham (13:16). It is the same move, and it is aimed at the same people.

For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.

Here is the sentence that gathers up the whole Gospel, and Luke has been building to it for eighteen chapters.

It answers the grumbling in verse 7 completely. They objected that he had gone in to a sinner's house; he replies that this is the errand. Not a regrettable necessity, not an exception made for a promising case — the stated purpose of the coming.

And the verbs are the shepherd's from chapter 15: to seek, and to save. There is a search going on. It has been going on the whole time, and it is why he was walking through Jericho at all.

Zacchaeus climbed a tree to get a look at somebody who had come to that town looking for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–27 — The Parable of the Ten Minas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke tells us exactly why the parable is given, and there are two reasons: they were near Jerusalem, and they supposed the kingdom was about to appear immediately. Seventeen miles from the city, at Passover, behind a man who raises the dead — every expectation they had was about to be fulfilled, and they were sure of it.

So everything in the parable is arranged to insert a delay where they expected a coronation: a departure, a long absence, an accounting on the return. And the shape is strange as a picture of the Messiah and exactly right — the King does not receive his kingdom in Jerusalem but in a far country, and comes back. Which is precisely what Luke's second volume describes (Acts 1:9-11).

Ten servants, ten minas — one each. Worth registering, because Matthew's cousin-parable of the talents distributes different amounts according to ability (Matt. 25:15). Where the sums differ, the story is partly about capacity; where they are identical, the only variable left is what each man did. And a mina was about three months' wages — modest, and that is the point.

The subplot of the rebel citizens is borrowed from living memory. In 4 BC Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship confirmed, and a delegation of fifty Jews followed to argue against it (Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1). They failed; he came back with power and dealt with them. Jericho of all towns would have felt it — Archelaus rebuilt it and had a palace there.

The first two servants are rewarded proportionately and without comparison. The third produces the mina intact, wrapped in a soudarion, and explains that he was afraid — and his accusation is turned against him. If the master really were what he says, the sensible course would have been the bank.

And the parable ends with the enemies. It is the hardest sentence in Luke.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable teaches two related truths. The kingdom has a “not yet”: the King goes away and returns, and faithful servants must live faithfully in the in-between. And stewardship in the in-between is not optional maintenance — “engage in business” is a commercial verb, and it is not “look after this.”

“Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little” is worth weighing for the disproportion. The master calls the mina — everything the servant had for the whole absence — a trifle, and gives ten cities in return. The exchange rate is absurd, and meant to be.

And notice what the reward is: more responsibility, on an enormously larger scale. Not rest, and not a payment. Which says something about heaven that cuts against the popular picture, since Scripture's images run the other way — “his servants will worship him… and they will reign for ever and ever” (Rev. 22:3-5).

“To everyone who has, more will be given” is not a celebration of the rich getting richer. It is a description of how entrusted things behave: capacity grows by use and atrophies without it. And note the last clause carefully — “from the one who has not.” The third servant was still holding the mina when that was said. In the master's reckoning a coin wrapped in a cloth for a whole absence is not a possession but an absence dressed up as one.

A reader with Matthew open should also know this is not the parable of the talents, though the two are cousins. Matthew's setting asks what you did with what you were given. Luke's, told in sight of Jerusalem, asks that and one thing more — whether you wanted the King at all.
verseByVerse.examples:
The third servant's fear is not reverence, though it wears the same clothes. Reverence produces obedience; this produced nothing. He was not too frightened to disobey — he was too frightened to act, which is a different thing entirely, and he had been calling it caution for the whole of the absence.

And his accusation is untrue, as the parable has already shown. This is a master who handed money to ten men with no supervision and no conditions, and who has just given a servant ten cities for a mina. The servant constructed a master he could justify doing nothing about.

The word “wicked” lands where a reader might not expect it. He has not stolen the money or wasted it or run off with it. He is called wicked for burying it — and there is a category of failure here that comfortable religion rarely counts as sin at all. Nothing bad was done; that is the whole defence, and it is exactly what is condemned. A life that has carefully avoided doing anything wrong has not on that account done what it was left here to do.

Verse 27 should not be hurried past. Two things keep it in place. These are words spoken by a character inside a parable, borrowed wholesale from a tyrant's homecoming, and not one command in this parable is addressed to the servants about the citizens; their whole task is to trade. And the horror of the image is the point rather than an embarrassment — Jesus is drawing a picture of what it is to refuse a king who is coming back anyway, and the tears of vv. 41-44 are fourteen verses off. A judgement described in terms this stark, by a man crying about it, is not bloodlust. It is the last warning of someone who would give anything to be heard.

verseByVerse.quote: As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. He said therefore, 'A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable.

Luke, unusually, tells us exactly why — and there are two reasons.

Because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately.

Seventeen miles from the city, at Passover, with a man who raises the dead at the head of the procession and a crowd shouting about a blind man. Every expectation they had was about to be fulfilled, and they were sure of it.

They were also wrong about the timing in a way that would nearly destroy them within the week.

So the parable is corrective, and everything in it is arranged to insert a delay where they were expecting an immediate coronation: a departure, a long absence, an accounting on the return.

A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.

And there is the shape of it. Before there is a kingdom there is a journey, and the throne is granted somewhere else.

It is worth registering how strange that is as a picture of the Messiah, and how exactly it fits. The King does not receive his kingdom in Jerusalem. He receives it in a far country and comes back — which is, as Luke's second volume will describe it, precisely what happened: a man taken up out of their sight, seated at the right hand of God, and a promise that he will come in the same way (Acts 1:9-11).

The disciples wanted the crown on Friday. What they were going to get was a crucifixion, an ascension, and a wait of unspecified length with work to do in it.

Which is where every Christian since has been standing. The kingdom is real, the King has been enthroned, and he is not here — and the whole question of the Christian life is what a man does with the interval.

And it is worth noticing that Jesus is correcting an error of timing, not of hope. He does not tell them the kingdom is a spiritual metaphor, or that they have misunderstood what a king is. He tells them it is further off than they think and that there is work to do meanwhile.

Both halves of that have been lost in turn by the church. A Christianity that expects nothing has stopped believing there is a return; a Christianity that expects it next Tuesday has generally stopped trading.

verseByVerse.quote: Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, Engage in business until I come.

Three details, and each is deliberate.

Ten servants, and ten minas — one each. This is worth registering, because Matthew's cousin-parable of the talents distributes different amounts to different men, according to ability (Matt. 25:15). Here everybody gets exactly the same.

Which changes what the parable is measuring. Where the sums differ, the story is partly about capacity. Where they are identical, the only variable left is what each man did.

A mina was a hundred denarii — about three months' wages for a labourer. Not a fortune, and that too is the point. He does not hand over the estate. He gives each man a modest, manageable sum and goes away.

Engage in business until I come.

The verb is a commercial one — trade with it, put it to work. It is not look after this. And the instruction contains its own deadline: until I come, which is both a promise that he will and a statement that the trading has an end date.

So the servants are left with three things: a sum of money, an instruction to risk it, and a return that is certain but unscheduled.

And that is the situation of the church, stated in a sentence. Every believer has been given something — and the parable's insistence that the amounts were identical is a rebuke to the very common conviction that one has been given nothing worth trading. Ten men, ten minas, no exceptions.

What was not given is instructions. He does not tell them what business to engage in, or set targets, or explain how he will assess them. He gives them the money and goes, and the freedom is real — which means the timid servant's failure in a few verses' time is not a failure to follow orders. It is a failure to believe that the freedom was genuinely given.

There is a particular comfort in the smallness of the sum, and it is easily missed. A mina is not a fortune, and the men receiving it are servants — they are not being handed the estate to run.

Which means that whatever a Christian has been given to trade with, the parable has already described it accurately: modest, ordinary, and entirely adequate for the purpose. Nobody in this story is under-resourced, and nobody is asked to produce something out of nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, We do not want this man to reign over us.

A second plot enters the parable, and it has nothing to do with the servants and their money.

The detail is not invented, and Jesus's hearers would have known it instantly. In 4 BC, on the death of Herod the Great, his son Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship confirmed by Caesar — and a delegation of fifty Jews followed him there to argue that he should not be given it (Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1). They failed. He came back with power, and he dealt with those who had opposed him.

Jesus is telling this parable on the road up to Jerusalem, within living memory of the event, in a country that had watched it happen. And Jericho of all places would have felt it: Archelaus rebuilt the town and had a palace there.

Which sharpens what he is doing with it. He is walking towards the city that is about to say exactly this about him — we will not have this man to reign over us — and he says it out loud, in a shape they cannot miss, days before they prove it true.

Note also the wording of the objection. It is not this man is unfit or we prefer another. It is we do not want this man to reign over us. The issue is not his credentials but his rule, and that has always been the issue.

When he returned, having received the kingdom.

Their delegation failed. That is the first thing the verse says, and it is said without comment: the objection was lodged, considered, and overruled somewhere far away, and the kingdom was granted anyway.

He ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.

And the first thing he does on arriving with a kingdom is not to deal with the rebels. It is to send for his own servants and ask what they did with what he left them.

verseByVerse.quote: The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.

Note whose mina it is. Not I have made ten — your mina has made ten. The servant reports a result without claiming it, and there is no trace of a man presenting his own achievement.

The return is extraordinary. A thousand per cent, on three months' wages, in an unspecified but evidently long absence. Whatever he did, he did it well.

Well done, good servant!

Two words in Greek, and they are the first thing the returning king says to anybody in the parable. Before any assessment of the estate, before the rebels are dealt with, the man who traded faithfully hears his master say good.

Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.

And now the disproportion, which is the whole point of the verse.

A very little. That is the master's description of the mina — three months' wages, and everything the servant had to work with for the entire absence. He calls it a trifle.

Set that against what is given in return: authority over ten cities. Not ten minas, not a hundred. Cities, with people in them, in the kingdom he has just been granted.

The exchange rate is absurd, and it is meant to be. Whatever any Christian is trading with in this life — and it may look and feel like very little indeed — the parable insists on calling it small precisely in order to make the reward look impossible.

And notice what the reward actually is. Not rest, and not a payment. It is more responsibility, on an enormously larger scale. The faithful servant's prize is a bigger job in the King's administration.

Which says something about heaven that is worth having, because the popular picture is largely of rest. Scripture's images run the other way: his servants will worship him… and they will reign for ever and ever (Rev. 22:3-5). Whatever the life to come is, it is not retirement, and the training for it is going on now, in something the King calls very little.

verseByVerse.quote: And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the second came, saying, Lord, your mina has made five minas. And he said to him, And you are to be over five cities.

Two verses, and it would be easy to read them as a repetition. They are not, and what they add is one of the kindest things in the parable.

The second man has produced exactly half what the first produced. Same starting sum, same length of absence, same instruction — and half the result.

And there is no rebuke of any kind. Not a word about why he did not do better, no comparison with his colleague, no suggestion that five is disappointing.

What he gets is five cities: a reward proportioned exactly to the return, and every bit as real.

Which is worth sitting with by anyone who has ever measured his own Christian usefulness against somebody else's and gone quiet. There is a man in this parable who did half as well as the man standing next to him, and the King's response is to put him over five cities.

It should be said, though, that the master's reply to the second man is noticeably shorter. He gets the reward and not the commendation — no well done is recorded. Some readers press that; it is probably better not to. Luke is compressing, as he does everywhere, and the parable's contrast is not between the ten and the five. It is between both of them and the man with the handkerchief.

What the two together establish is the principle: the King rewards what was actually done, at the rate it was done, without grading on a curve.

And the arithmetic has one further implication that the third servant is about to discover. Five minas earned five cities. One mina, kept safe and returned intact, earns nothing at all — because nothing at all is what it produced.

There is one more thing in these two verses, and it is easy to walk past because so little happens in them. The second servant came. He had a smaller result than the man in front of him and he came anyway, and said out loud in front of the whole court exactly what he had produced.

That takes something. And it is the opposite of what the third servant will do in the next verse, which is to arrive with an explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then another came, saying, Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief.

He has it. That is the first thing, and it is what he thinks will save him. Nothing has been lost, nothing spent, nothing risked. He can put the coin on the table exactly as he received it.

The handkerchief is a soudarion — a cloth for wiping the face, and the same word used of the cloth over the face of Lazarus in the tomb (John 11:44). He wrapped the money in a rag and put it somewhere.

And note the difference from the others. They reported what the mina had made. He reports where he put it.

For I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.

Now the reason, and he offers it as an explanation. It is in fact an accusation.

Severe is austēros — the root of the English austere, used of unripe fruit and of a man with no give in him. And the two charges that follow describe a profiteer: someone who collects where he has not invested and harvests fields he never planted.

So this servant's defence is that his master is grasping and unfair, and that his own inactivity was a rational response.

Two things about that are worth naming, because the type is common and rarely recognises itself.

The first is that his fear is not reverence, though it wears the same clothes. Reverence produces obedience; this produced nothing. He was not too frightened to disobey. He was too frightened to act, which is a different thing entirely, and he has been calling it caution for the whole of the master's absence.

The second is that the accusation is untrue, and the parable has already shown it. This is a master who handed out money to ten men with no supervision and no conditions, and who has just given a servant ten cities for a mina. Whatever he is, he is not a man who takes what he did not deposit.

The servant has constructed a master he could justify doing nothing about.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant!

The master does not argue the description. He does not say I am not severe. He takes the servant's own account of him and turns it round.

You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow?

The Greek can be read as a statement or a question, and either way the logic is the same: very well — suppose I am exactly what you say.

Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?

And there is the trap closing.

Banking existed and paid interest; the money-changers took deposits, and there was nothing exotic about it. It required no skill, no judgement, and no courage. A man could walk in, hand the mina over, and walk out.

So the servant's own premise convicts him. If the master really were a hard man who reaped where he had not sown, the sensible response would have been to make certain he got something. The one course of action his stated fear cannot possibly justify is doing absolutely nothing.

Which exposes the fear as a cover story. He did not act on his belief about the master, because it was never the reason. It was the excuse he had ready.

And the word wicked lands where a reader might not expect it. He has not stolen the money, or wasted it, or run off with it. He is called wicked for burying it — and there is a category of failure here that comfortable religion very rarely counts as sin at all.

Nothing bad was done. That is the whole defence, and it is exactly what is being condemned. The servant was not asked to avoid loss. He was asked to trade, and he did not, and a life that has carefully avoided doing anything wrong has not on that account done what it was left here to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.

The bystanders object — Lord, he has ten minas! — which is the natural response and the one most readers share. Why give more to the man who already has most?

I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.

The principle sounds harsh until it is read as what it is: not a rule about distributing rewards, but a description of how entrusted things actually behave.

The saying has appeared before in this Gospel, attached to hearing (8:18), and the mechanism is the same. Capacity grows by use. A man who trades finds he can trade more, because the trading itself made him a better trader. And a man who buries what he was given loses even the ability to use it — not by confiscation but by atrophy.

Every musician, every craftsman, every preacher knows this without being taught it. Nothing is more perishable than an unexercised gift.

And notice the last clause carefully: from the one who has not. The third servant was still holding the mina when that was said. In the master's reckoning a coin wrapped in a cloth for the whole of an absence is not a possession at all — it is an absence dressed up as one. He has nothing, because he has done nothing with it, and the removal of the coin is simply the paperwork catching up.

There is a hard word in this for a certain kind of Christian caution, and it is worth stating plainly. The instinct to protect — to hold what one has been given, to take no risk with it, to be able to produce it intact at the end — feels like faithfulness and is its opposite.

The mina was never in danger of being lost. It was in danger of doing nothing, and that is the only danger the parable takes seriously.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.

It is the hardest sentence in Luke, and it should not be hurried past. Readers recoil, and some have quoted the line as though Jesus were commanding violence against opponents.

Two things keep it in its place.

First, these are words spoken by a character inside a parable, not an instruction issued to disciples. The king in the story is doing what such kings did, and the picture has been borrowed wholesale from Archelaus, whose reprisals after Rome confirmed him were remembered with horror. Nobody in that crowd would have heard it as a policy for them to carry out. Not one command in this parable is addressed to the servants about the citizens; their whole task, from first to last, is to trade with what they were given.

Second, the horror of the image is the point rather than an embarrassment to be explained away. Jesus is drawing a picture of what it is to refuse a king who is coming back anyway — and he is doing it while on the road to weep over the city that is refusing him. The tears of vv. 41-44 are fourteen verses off. Both belong to the same person on the same afternoon.

A judgement described in terms this stark, by a man who is crying about it, is not bloodlust. It is the last warning of someone who would give anything to be heard.

And there is a structural point that a reader with Matthew open should have. This is not the parable of the talents (Matt. 25:14-30), though the two are cousins. There the sums are enormous and unequal and there are no rebel citizens; here every servant gets the same modest mina and the throne itself is contested.

Jesus taught constantly and on the road, and a teacher reworks his material for the moment he is in. Matthew's setting asks what you did with what you were given. Luke's, told in sight of Jerusalem within days of the crowd shouting for his execution, asks that and one thing more — whether you wanted the King at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Triumphal Entry and Jesus Weeping over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He goes on ahead, leading — and “going up” is exact: Jericho lies 800 feet below sea level, Jerusalem 2,500 above, so the seventeen miles climb over three thousand feet through desert.

The Mount of Olives is not incidental scenery. Zechariah had said the LORD's feet would stand on it (Zech. 14:4), and from that ridge a king approaching Jerusalem first sees the city laid out below.

The instructions about the colt are startlingly specific, and Luke will not settle whether this is prior arrangement or foreknowledge. What it establishes is that nothing about the next hour is improvised. And “on which no one has ever yet sat” is not about comfort: an animal never worked was the requirement for sacred use — the cart that carried the ark (1 Sam. 6:7), the red heifer (Num. 19:2).

He has walked everywhere for three years. On the one occasion he rides, he sends for a specific animal, and the animal is the prophecy: “humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zech. 9:9). A king entering a capital rode a horse, and a horse was the animal of war.

The cloaks on the road are a coronation gesture, not enthusiasm — when Jehu was proclaimed king the officers put their garments under him on the steps and blew the trumpet (2 Kgs. 9:13). And a cloak was a poor man's blanket and often his most valuable possession, so protected in law that a creditor could not keep one overnight (Ex. 22:26-27).

Luke alone specifies who is shouting: “the whole multitude of his disciples.” And the reason is backward-looking — “for all the mighty works that they had seen.”

Then, at the point on the descent where the whole city comes into view at once, he weeps aloud.
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples' shout alters Psalm 118:26. The psalm reads “blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD” — the greeting pilgrims received at the festivals. They insert one word: “blessed is the King who comes.” That is not a liturgical greeting any more but a public claim, at Passover, in earshot of Jerusalem — which is exactly why the Pharisees object. And it fulfils what Jesus said at 13:35: they would not see him again until they said it.

“Peace in heaven and glory in the highest” closes a circle Luke opened in chapter 2. The angels sang “glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace” (2:14); the disciples sing it back with the terms reversed. Which is exact, and not sentimental. There will be no peace on earth this week — there will be a mob, a trial, a scourging and an execution. What is settled in heaven is another matter, and it is being accomplished by the very week that is about to look like total defeat.

“If these were silent, the very stones would cry out” has roots in Habakkuk, where the stone cries out from the wall against injustice (Hab. 2:11) — stones as witnesses that cannot be silenced. And there is a bitter appropriateness in the choice: he is looking at magnificent stonework, and within four verses will say not one of those stones will be left on another.

The prophecy of vv.43-44 was fulfilled with precision. In AD 70 Titus built a wall of circumvallation right round the city — some four and a half miles, thrown up in three days — to stop anyone getting out or supplies getting in. Josephus, who was there, describes it. The temple was burned and then dismantled, and the great platform stones were levered off the walls into the street below, where they are still lying.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke's verb for the weeping is not the quiet one. Greek has two words: one for silent tears, used of Jesus at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35), and this one — eklausen, to wail aloud, the word used of the mourners at Jairus's house (8:52) and of Peter after the cock crowed (22:62). So the sound coming from the middle of that procession is a man sobbing audibly, and the singing does not appear to have stopped.

And the sentence he speaks breaks off unfinished in Greek — an exclamation that starts and does not complete, exactly as a sentence does when the person speaking cannot finish it. “Even you” is emphatic and heartbreaking: of all the cities on earth, this one, whose name means foundation of peace, did not know the things that make for peace.

A pastor preaching this every Palm Sunday finds it tempting to stop at the Hosannas. The passage insists on including the tears. Palm Sunday is not unambiguously triumphant; it is triumphant and heartbroken at once.

“Visitation” is episkopē — God coming to see about his people, the word Zechariah used in the Gospel's first chapter: “he has visited and redeemed his people” (1:68). The visitation happened. That is what makes the sentence unbearable. And the word cuts both ways, because a visitation is an inspection as well as a rescue: the same coming that saves those who know it for what it is condemns those who do not — not by a change in God, but because there is nothing else left when the visit has been made and refused.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, saying, 'Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.

Went on ahead — in front of them, leading. Nobody is dragging him up that road.

And going up is geographically exact as well as customary: Jericho lies about 800 feet below sea level and Jerusalem some 2,500 feet above it, so the seventeen miles are a climb of over three thousand feet through desert.

When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples.

The Mount of Olives is not incidental scenery. Zechariah had prophesied that the LORD would come and his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zech. 14:4), and it was from that hill that a king approaching Jerusalem would first see the city and the temple laid out below him.

Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat.

The instructions are startlingly specific — the village, the animal, its condition, and what to say if challenged. Luke does not tell us whether this is prior arrangement or foreknowledge, and the text will not settle it. What it does establish is that nothing about the next hour is improvised.

And on which no one has ever yet sat is not a note about comfort. An animal never worked was the requirement for sacred use — the cart that carried the ark was drawn by cows that had never been yoked (1 Sam. 6:7), and the red heifer had to be one on which a yoke has never come (Num. 19:2). This colt is being set apart.

If anyone asks you, Why are you untying it? you shall say this: The Lord has need of it.

Which is either a password arranged in advance or a claim of extraordinary boldness, and either way it is the only explanation offered.

Note also what he is choosing. A king entering a capital rode a horse; a horse was the animal of war. Zechariah had described the alternative: Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey (Zech. 9:9).

He has walked everywhere for three years. On the one occasion he rides, he sends for a specific animal, and the animal is the prophecy.

verseByVerse.quote: So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, 'Why are you untying the colt?' And they said, 'The Lord has need of it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them.

Luke is careful to record it, and the phrasing is deliberate: just as he had told them. Every detail checked out.

That verification matters more than it looks. The disciples have been told a great deal in recent chapters that they did not understand and could not test — that he must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise. Here is a small prediction they could walk into a village and check within twenty minutes, and it was exact.

And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, Why are you untying the colt?

So the challenge came, precisely as he said it would — and the fact that Luke bothers to record it tells us he thought the fulfilment worth pointing at.

Note the word owners, plural. This is somebody's animal, and they are standing right there, watching two strangers untie it.

And they said, The Lord has need of it.

Five words, and the owners let it go.

What are we to make of that? The most likely explanation is the simplest: Jesus was known in that area — Bethany was Martha and Mary's village, and he had been staying there — and an arrangement had been made, or the phrase was recognised.

But do not lose what the sentence says while explaining how it worked. The Lord has need of it. The one through whom every colt in Judea was made, who owns the cattle on a thousand hills, sends two men to ask for the loan of a donkey.

He came into the world in a borrowed stable, rode into his capital on a borrowed animal, ate his last meal in a borrowed room, and was buried in a borrowed grave. He owned nothing, and everything he used was lent to him by people who did not know what they were lending it for.

Which is worth registering by anyone who has ever wondered whether what they have is of any use to God. The answer this passage gives is that he asks for ordinary things, from ordinary people, at short notice, and that the only reason ever given is that he needs them.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it.

The cloaks go on first, over the animal's back, because there is no saddle. And then they set Jesus on it — the disciples lift him up.

It is a small domestic detail and it is the last quiet moment before everything becomes public.

And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.

Now the gesture changes meaning entirely, because this one has a precedent that every Jew would have recognised.

When Jehu was proclaimed king in the north, the officers took off every man his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and blew the trumpet and proclaimed, Jehu is king (2 Kgs. 9:13). Cloaks under the feet of a man is not enthusiasm. It is a coronation.

And consider what a cloak was to a poor Galilean. It was his outer garment, his blanket at night, and often the most valuable thing he owned — so valuable that the law forbade a creditor to keep one overnight in pledge, for that is his only covering (Ex. 22:26-27).

They are laying the most expensive things they possess in the dust of a road so that a donkey can walk over them.

Which is a fair picture of worship, and it is worth noticing what makes it worship rather than waste. Nothing is achieved by putting a coat under a colt. The road was passable; the animal was not troubled by stones. The gesture is pure declaration — a way of saying, with the only material available, this man is the King and nothing I own is too good to be walked on by him.

Nobody in that procession got anything back except a dirty cloak.

And there is a further thing in the gesture that only shows up on the way back down. Within the week, other men will take his clothes off him and gamble for them at the foot of a cross (23:34).

On the road into the city his own people threw down everything they had so that he could pass over it. On the road out, the last garment he owned was taken from him and divided up by strangers.

Of everyone in that procession, the only one who fully understood where it was going was the man on the donkey.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was drawing near — already on the way down the Mount of Olives — the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice.

Luke fixes the exact spot, and anyone who has stood there will know why.

The road from Bethany crosses the shoulder of the Mount of Olives, and at a particular point on the descent the whole city comes into view at once — the Kidron valley below, the wall opposite, and the temple platform filling the eye, its stonework and gold catching the light. It is one of the great sights of the ancient world and it arrives suddenly.

That is where the shouting starts.

And note who is shouting. The whole multitude of his disciples — Luke is specific, and he is the only evangelist who is. Matthew and Mark have the crowds; Luke says it was his own followers. Whatever the pilgrim crowd made of it, this is not a spontaneous public demonstration. It is the people who have been with him.

For all the mighty works that they had seen.

And there is the reason, and it is worth pausing on because it is entirely backward-looking. They are not praising him for what they expect on Friday. They are praising God for what they have already watched him do — and they have watched a great deal.

Luke's readers can supply the list, because they have just read it. A dead girl sitting up. A legion evicted. Five loaves and twelve baskets. A leper who came back. A blind man at the gate of that very morning's town, still with them in the procession and presumably shouting louder than anybody.

These men have three years of evidence and they are using it.

Which is the only honest ground for praise there has ever been. Not a mood, and not an expectation of what God is about to do next. A memory of what he has actually done, recited out loud — and it is available on the days when nothing whatever is happening.

They were wrong about the week ahead. They were not wrong about him, and the reasons they gave were sound.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!

The line is Psalm 118:26, and it was one of the best-known sentences in Israel's worship. Psalm 118 closed the Hallel, sung at the great festivals, and pilgrims arriving at Jerusalem were greeted with those exact words by the priests. Every person on that road had said it a hundred times.

But they have altered it, and the alteration is the whole point. The psalm reads blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. Luke's disciples insert one word: blessed is the King who comes.

That is not a liturgical greeting any more. It is a claim about the man on the donkey, made in public, at Passover, in earshot of Jerusalem — and it is precisely why the Pharisees will object in the next verse.

Note also that this is the sentence Jesus himself said they would not see him again until they said (13:35). The condition he named is being fulfilled on the road, six chapters later, by his own disciples.

Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!

And here Luke closes a circle he opened in his second chapter.

Over a field outside Bethlehem the angels had sung glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased (2:14). Now human voices sing it back — with the terms reversed. The angels said peace on earth; the disciples say peace in heaven.

Which is exact, and it is not sentimental. There will be no peace on earth this week. There will be a mob, a trial, a scourging and an execution, and the man they are singing about will be dead inside five days.

What is settled in heaven is another matter. The reconciliation is being accomplished, and it is being accomplished by the very week that is about to look like total defeat.

So the song is right and the singers do not know how right. They think they are welcoming a king to a coronation. They are walking beside him to an altar, singing the anthem of a peace that will be made in blood on Friday afternoon — and it will hold for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, rebuke your disciples.' He answered, 'I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, Teacher, rebuke your disciples.

It is the last time the Pharisees appear in Luke's Gospel, and their final recorded words are a request to stop the worship.

Their concern may have been genuine. A messianic acclamation at Passover, with Roman troops reinforced in the Antonia fortress overlooking the temple and a governor in town precisely because festivals produced riots, was a dangerous thing to be shouting. Men had died for less. It is entirely possible that some of them were trying to prevent a massacre.

But notice the address: Teacher. They will not use the word his disciples have just used. The disciples said King; the Pharisees say Teacher — and the whole dispute is contained in the gap between those two nouns.

And notice what they ask for. Not that he deny the claim. Rebuke your disciples — silence them. It is enough for their purposes if nobody says it out loud.

He answered, I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.

The refusal is absolute and the reason is not tactical.

He does not say the disciples are entitled to their opinion, or that he cannot control a crowd. He says that if these voices stop, the created order will take over — which is a claim that the praise is not optional, and not generated by enthusiasm, but owed.

The image has roots. Habakkuk, denouncing a man who builds his house by injustice, says the stone will cry out from the wall (Hab. 2:11) — stones as witnesses that cannot be silenced.

And there is a bitter appropriateness in the choice, three verses before he weeps. He is looking at a city of magnificent stonework, and within four verses he will say that not one of those stones will be left on another (v. 44).

The stones will cry out. In forty years' time they will be lying in a heap in the valley, and they will be saying something after all.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying, 'Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it.

The shouting is still going on. He is on a donkey, surrounded by people singing that he is the King, at the summit of the only public acclaim he ever received — and he is crying.

Luke's verb is not the quiet one. There are two words in Greek for weeping: one for silent tears, used of Jesus at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35), and this one — eklausen, which means to wail aloud. It is the word used of the mourners at Jairus's house (8:52) and of Peter going out after the cock crowed (22:62).

So the sound coming from the middle of that procession is a man sobbing audibly, and the singing does not appear to have stopped.

This is the second time Luke records him weeping over this city; the first was the lament of 13:34, the hen and the chicks. He has been carrying this the whole way.

Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace!

The sentence breaks off. In Greek it is unfinished — an exclamation that starts and does not complete, exactly as a sentence does when the person speaking cannot finish it.

Even you. The pronoun is emphatic and it is heartbreaking. Of all the cities on earth, this one. The city of David, the place of the temple, the address to which every prophet was sent.

The things that make for peace — and the name of the city means foundation of peace. Jerusalem, of all places, did not know the things that make for peace.

But now they are hidden from your eyes.

And there is the tragedy stated exactly. Not they were never offered. Hidden — now, at this point, after everything.

He is weeping because he can see what is coming and it is too late to stop it, and because it did not have to be this way. Whatever else is true about the God of the Bible, he is not indifferent to the ruin of people who would not have him. He goes to the cross for them with his face wet.

verseByVerse.quote: For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side.

The prophecy is specific in a way that is worth reading slowly, because within one generation every clause of it happened.

In AD 70, Titus besieged Jerusalem. When the defenders held out and the siege dragged on, he built exactly what this verse describes — a wall of circumvallation right round the city, some four and a half miles of it, thrown up in three days, to stop anyone getting out or supplies getting in. Josephus, who was there, describes it in detail. The famine inside was appalling.

And tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you.

The verb can mean to dash to the ground, and it is used in the Greek Old Testament of infants killed in a captured city (Ps. 137:9; Hos. 13:16). The horror is not softened.

And they will not leave one stone upon another in you.

The temple was burned and then dismantled. The great platform stones were levered off the walls and pushed into the street below, and they are still lying there — visible today, piled at the foot of the southern wall where they fell, with the paving cracked under them.

He said it three verses after saying the stones would cry out.

Because you did not know the time of your visitation.

Here is the cause, and it is the only one given.

Visitation is episkopē — God coming to see about his people, the word Zechariah used in his song at the beginning of this Gospel: blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people (1:68).

The visitation happened. That is what makes the sentence unbearable. God came to Jerusalem, on a donkey, weeping, and the city did not recognise the day.

And that word episkopē cuts both ways in Scripture, because a visitation is an inspection as well as a rescue. The same coming that saves the people who know it for what it is condemns the people who do not — not by a change in God, but because there is nothing else left when the visit has been made and refused.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–48 — The Cleansing of the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's account is the briefest of the four — one clause for the action, no overturned tables, no whip of cords. He is not interested in the drama. He gives the words.

The selling was in the Court of the Gentiles, the great outer platform, and it was not in itself illegitimate: pilgrims from a distance needed sacrificial animals, and needed foreign coinage changed into the Tyrian shekel required for the temple tax. Somebody had to provide both. What had happened was that the provision had taken over the place — and the place it had taken over was the one part of the temple where a non-Jew could come and pray.

The two quotations are not equally weighted. The first is Isaiah 56:7, and the full verse matters: “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.” That is the promise the Court of the Gentiles existed to fulfil, and the cattle market was standing on it.

The second is Jeremiah 7:11, and it is a bomb. Jeremiah's temple sermon was preached at the gate of the first temple to people who believed the building guaranteed their safety — “the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD” — while cheating and oppressing outside it. It ended by announcing that God would do to that house what he did to Shiloh, which was to destroy it. So Jesus, four verses after prophesying that not one stone will be left on another, quotes the sermon that announced the destruction of the previous temple.

And note the exact charge. Not “you have made it a market.” A den of robbers is not where robbery happens; it is where robbers retreat to feel safe afterwards.

Then he stays. Having cleared the court he takes up residence in it, teaching daily — which is the behaviour of an owner, not a protester.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cleansing is a prophetic act, not a reform. Jesus is not trying to improve the temple's efficiency; he is enacting in symbol what he has just prophesied in words. The combination of texts is deliberate: Isaiah 56:7 describes the eschatological temple as a house of prayer for all nations, and Jeremiah 7:11 the corrupt pre-exilic temple. You were called to be one; you have become the other.

“A den of robbers” names a use religion has never stopped being put to — a system that people use to feel secure while their lives are indefensible. That is what Jeremiah's hearers were doing with the first temple, and it is the charge here.

The closing two verses describe the strangest week in history in a single sentence. The most powerful men in Jerusalem want a man dead and cannot touch him — not because he is hiding but because he is standing in the most public place in the city, in daylight, every day, surrounded by crowds who will not leave. Luke's phrase is worth having: the people were “hanging on his words,” literally hanging out of themselves, suspended from him.

What finally breaks the deadlock is not a change in the crowd but a man on the inside who offers to hand him over quietly, away from the people (22:6). Which settles something about how this ends. The authorities did not overpower him, and Luke says so plainly.
verseByVerse.examples:
A church becomes known primarily for its events, its café, its networking and its programmes — all good things in themselves, which have gradually crowded out sustained corporate prayer. The cleansing is not a template for expelling coffee shops from church lobbies; it is a question every community of faith must ask about its primary purpose and what has displaced it.

And the specific displacement here is worth naming, because it was not frivolous. Everything in that court served the sacrificial system. The animals were for worship; the money-changing existed so that the temple tax could be paid in the right coin. This was religion crowding out prayer, not entertainment crowding out religion — which is much harder to see from the inside and a great deal more common.

It also matters where it happened. Of all the spaces on that platform, the trade had colonised the only one open to Gentiles — so the practical effect of a thoroughly religious arrangement was that the people furthest from God found the door blocked by the machinery of worship.

That is a question worth putting to any congregation. Not whether the activity is legitimate, but whether a stranger walking in could find room to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, saying to them, 'It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold.

Luke's account is the briefest of the four — one clause for the action, and no mention of overturned tables or a whip of cords. He is not interested in the drama. He gives the words.

The selling was in the Court of the Gentiles, the great outer platform, and it was not in itself illegitimate. Pilgrims arriving from a distance needed sacrificial animals, and needed to change foreign coinage into the Tyrian shekel required for the temple tax. Somebody had to provide both.

What had happened was that the provision had taken over the place, and the place it had taken over was the one part of the temple where a non-Jew could come and pray.

It is written, My house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers.

Two quotations, and the second is much sharper than the first.

The first is Isaiah 56:7, and Luke's readers should hear what the verse actually says in full: my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples. That is the promise the Court of the Gentiles existed to fulfil, and the cattle market was standing on it.

The second is Jeremiah 7:11, and it is a bomb. Jeremiah's temple sermon was preached at the gate of the first temple to people who believed the building guaranteed their safety — the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD — while cheating and oppressing outside it. And it ended with the announcement that God would do to that house what he did to Shiloh, which was to destroy it.

So Jesus, four verses after prophesying that not one stone will be left on another, quotes the sermon that announced the destruction of the previous temple.

And note the exact charge. Not you have made it a market. A den of robbers is not where robbery happens; it is where robbers retreat to feel safe afterwards. The accusation is that the temple has become a hiding place — a religious system that people use to feel secure while their lives are indefensible.

Which is a use religion has never stopped being put to.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he was teaching daily in the temple.

Having driven out the sellers, he stays — and the imperfect tense means it went on. This is not a raid. He cleared the court and then took up residence in it, teaching every day for the rest of the week.

That is the behaviour of an owner, not a protester. He has just called it my house.

The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him.

Three groups, and between them they are the entire leadership of the nation — the temple establishment, the legal experts, and the leading laymen. Luke names them together, and the verb is continuous: they kept on seeking.

Note that the object is not to answer him or to discredit him. To destroy him. The decision has been taken; only the method is outstanding.

But they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.

And here is the strangest week in history, described in one sentence.

The most powerful men in Jerusalem want a man dead and cannot touch him — not because he is hiding, but because he is standing in the most public place in the city, in daylight, every day, surrounded by crowds who will not leave.

The phrase Luke chooses is worth having: the people were hanging on his words — literally hanging out of themselves, suspended from him, the picture of a crowd leaning in.

So for several days the two things run alongside each other. He teaches; they plot; nothing can be done. And what finally breaks the deadlock is not a change in the crowd but a man on the inside who offers to hand him over quietly, away from the people (22:6).

Which is worth noticing as the chapter closes, because it settles something about how this ends. The authorities did not overpower him. They could not, and Luke says so plainly.

He walked into that city on a colt he had sent for, cleared the temple, and taught in it daily under the eyes of men who wanted him dead and could do nothing about it — until the hour came that he had been walking towards since chapter nine, and he let them have him.

19.text: <sup>1</sup> He entered Jericho and was passing through. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich. <sup>3</sup> And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. <sup>4</sup> So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way. <sup>5</sup> And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” <sup>6</sup> So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully. <sup>7</sup> And when they saw it, they all grumbled, “He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.” <sup>8</sup> And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” <sup>9</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. <sup>10</sup> For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” <sup>11</sup> As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. <sup>12</sup> He said therefore, “A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return. <sup>13</sup> Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’ <sup>14</sup> But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ <sup>15</sup> When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business. <sup>16</sup> The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ <sup>17</sup> And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ <sup>18</sup> And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’ <sup>20</sup> Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; <sup>21</sup> for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’ <sup>22</sup> He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? <sup>23</sup> Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’ <sup>24</sup> And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ <sup>25</sup> And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ <sup>26</sup> ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>27</sup> But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’” <sup>28</sup> And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. <sup>29</sup> When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, <sup>30</sup> saying, “Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. <sup>31</sup> If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’” <sup>32</sup> So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. <sup>33</sup> And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?” <sup>34</sup> And they said, “The Lord has need of it.” <sup>35</sup> And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. <sup>36</sup> And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road. <sup>37</sup> As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen, <sup>38</sup> saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” <sup>39</sup> And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.” <sup>40</sup> He answered, “I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.” <sup>41</sup> And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. <sup>43</sup> For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side <sup>44</sup> and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.” <sup>45</sup> And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, <sup>46</sup> saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>47</sup> And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, <sup>48</sup> but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.

20.title: Authority, Parables, and Traps in the Temple
20.overview:
Luke 20 records a sustained series of confrontations between Jesus and the religious authorities in the temple precincts during what we call Holy Week. Three major challenges are mounted: the question of authority (by what right does Jesus act?), the parable of the wicked tenants (Jesus's own counter-attack in story form), and a series of trick questions — the tribute to Caesar, the Sadducees' resurrection riddle, and the question about David's son. Each challenge is designed to trap Jesus; each is turned back on its questioners.

The chapter is a masterclass in Jesus's handling of religious and political hostility. He does not evade, capitulate, or compromise. He answers each question in a way that exposes the questioner's bad faith, defends the truth, and advances his own mission. The parable of the wicked tenants is the most sustained theological statement: it is a compressed history of Israel's relationship with God, a prophecy of Jesus's rejection and death, and an announcement of the judgment that will fall on those who reject the cornerstone.

The chapter closes with Jesus warning about the scribes — those who love the long robes and the best seats and the deferential greetings, who devour widows' houses and for a pretence make long prayers. The contrast with the genuine piety of the widow in 21:1–4 is deliberate and damning.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chief priests, scribes, and elders approach Jesus while he is teaching in the temple and ask a two-part question: by what authority is he doing these things, and who gave him this authority? The “things” refer to both the temple cleansing (ch. 19) and his daily teaching. The challenge is not a genuine inquiry — it is a trap. If Jesus claims divine authority, they can charge him with blasphemy; if he claims human authority, they can dismiss him as self-appointed.

Jesus's counter-question is a masterstroke: was John's baptism from heaven or from man? This forces them into a dilemma they cannot escape. If they say from heaven, Jesus will ask why they did not believe him — and John had explicitly pointed to Jesus as the Coming One. If they say from man, the crowd will turn on them, for the people regard John as a prophet. They cannot answer honestly; they retreat into “we do not know.” Jesus then refuses to answer their question: “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.” The answer has already been given — by John, by the voice at the baptism, by the deeds themselves. Their refusal to face John's witness is their refusal to face the answer.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus's authority is not a merely administrative question; it is the central question of the Gospels. By what right does he cleanse the temple? By what right does he teach and heal and forgive sins? The answer the religious authorities are trying to avoid is: divine right — the right of the Son sent by the Father. Their counter-question strategy is itself an answer: those who cannot acknowledge John's prophetic authority cannot acknowledge the one John announced. Unwillingness to acknowledge the truth is not an epistemic failure but a moral and spiritual one.
verseByVerse.examples: A university student challenges a campus minister: “By what authority do you claim Jesus is the only way?” The question sounds like an intellectual inquiry, but the minister notices that every answer he gives is followed by a new objection rather than genuine engagement. This passage is instructive: there are moments when the right response is not another argument but a question that surfaces the real issue — what do you do with the testimony that has already been given?

verseByVerse.quote: One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up and said to him, 'Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.' He answered them, 'I also will ask you a question. Tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?'
verseByVerse.commentary: The question of authority is the first of four controversies that the religious authorities bring to Jesus in the temple. They are not seeking information; they are building a case. If he claims divine authority, he can be charged with blasphemy; if he claims human authority, his credentials can be challenged. Jesus's counter-question about John's baptism is not evasion — it is exposure. He is forcing them to make a public decision about John that will reveal the quality of their own judgment and the honesty of their inquiry. The authority question and the John question are connected: both ask about the source of a prophetic ministry that challenged the religious establishment.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, 'If we say, "From heaven," he will say, "Why did you not believe him?" But if we say, "From man," all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.' So they answered that they did not know where it came from. And Jesus said to them, 'Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Their deliberation is public — they discuss it with one another, presumably in earshot — and it is entirely calculated: which answer protects us? Not: which answer is true? They are not reasoning toward truth; they are managing a political situation. The result is the public admission of ignorance — we do not know — which is not ignorance but dishonesty. They know what they think about John; they are not willing to say it. Jesus's refusal to answer is not pettiness; it is a recognition that his interlocutors are not engaged in genuine inquiry. Questions asked in bad faith do not earn honest answers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus tells this parable to the people while the religious authorities are listening. It is simultaneously transparent and devastating — so transparent that at the end “the scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them” (v. 19). The parable is drawn from Isaiah 5:1–7, where the “vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” — the echo would have been immediately recognisable to any educated Jewish listener.

A man plants a vineyard, lets it out to tenants, and goes to another country. At harvest he sends servants to receive his portion; they are beaten and sent away empty-handed. He sends another; he too is beaten and treated shamefully. He sends a third; he too is wounded and thrown out. Finally he sends his beloved son, saying “Perhaps they will respect him.” The tenants, seeing the heir, say: “Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.” They throw him out of the vineyard and kill him. The question: what will the owner do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others.

Jesus then quotes Psalm 118:22: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” And he adds the application: everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces; it will crush anyone on whom it falls. The parable maps precisely onto the history of Israel (the prophets as servants), the cross (the son killed outside the vineyard — cf. Heb. 13:12), the judgment of AD 70 (the vineyard given to others), and the resurrection (the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone).
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable is one of the most explicit statements in Luke of Jesus's divine sonship and the doctrine of substitutionary judgment. The son is sent as a final and climactic envoy — not merely one more servant in a long series but the heir, the beloved son, whose rejection is categorically different from the rejection of the prophets. The owner's hope that “perhaps they will respect him” is not ignorance of the outcome (God is omniscient) but the expression of genuine relational intention: the Father sends the Son with genuine saving purpose, not as a trap.

Psalm 118:22 (cited also in Acts 4:11; 1 Pet. 2:7) is the cornerstone text for early Christian understanding of the resurrection as reversal: the stone rejected in the building process becomes the very foundation. The image of crushing (v. 18 — drawn from Dan. 2:44–45) adds eschatological weight: the rejected cornerstone will ultimately be the stone of judgment for those who have rejected him.
verseByVerse.examples: A church member who grew up in the faith has gradually become merely a religious consumer — attending worship when convenient, treating the church as a service provider, contributing little. The parable of the wicked tenants is not only about the chief priests of first-century Jerusalem. It is about the chronic human tendency to receive the benefits of God's provision while withholding the fruit that belongs to him. The vineyard was not given to the tenants to keep; it was entrusted to them to cultivate and return. Every gift of grace is entrusted, not owned.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to tell the people this parable: 'A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed. And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The vineyard is Israel — the image from Isaiah 5 that every listener would recognise. The owner is God; the tenants are Israel's religious leaders; the servants are the prophets. The pattern of sending, rejection, and violence is the pattern of Israel's history with the prophets compressed into a parable. The escalation — beaten, beaten and shamed, wounded and cast out — mirrors the escalating hostility toward God's messengers throughout the Old Testament. The owner's repeated sending despite repeated rejection is the patience of God applied to the history of the covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Then the owner of the vineyard said, "What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him." But when the tenants saw him, they said to one another, "This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may ours." And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.' When they heard this, they said, 'Surely not!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sending of the beloved son (ton huion mou ton agapēton — the same words as the voice at the baptism and the Transfiguration) is the final, supreme act of the owner's generosity. The tenants' reasoning — let us kill him so that the inheritance may be ours — is the logic of sinful self-assertion: if the heir is removed, the tenants become owners. They throw the son out of the vineyard before killing him — outside the walls, as Jesus will be killed outside Jerusalem (Heb. 13:12). The parable is transparent, and the crowd's horrified response — surely not! — is the response of people who can see what it means and do not want to believe it is true of them.

One phrase in the owner's mouth should not be hurried past, because it puzzles thoughtful readers and has been pressed into service to prove something it does not prove. He sends the son saying, perhaps they will respect him. Does that mean God did not know? Was heaven hoping for an outcome it could not foresee, and disappointed on Good Friday? Some have read it exactly so. But the same Scripture that records this parable also says the Son was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23), and Jesus has already told his disciples three times, in detail, precisely how this would end. He is not guessing. He is telling a story against the men in front of him, and the perhaps is spoken from the owner's side of it — the language of a genuine appeal, not a report of God's ignorance. The point of the word is not what God did not know but what the tenants cannot claim: that the offer was real, that every possible envoy was sent, that the last one was the owner's own beloved son, and that their rejection of him was therefore without a shred of excuse. God knew exactly what they would do, and sent the Son anyway — which is not the story of a father caught out, but of a love that kept knocking at a door it knew would not open, so that no one could ever say the door was never knocked upon.

verseByVerse.quote: But he looked directly at them and said, 'What then is this that is written: "The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone"? Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.' The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary: The citation from Psalm 118:22 — the same psalm sung at the Triumphal Entry — reframes the rejection: the stone the builders discarded is the one on which the whole building rests. The rejected son is also the cornerstone. God's purposes are not derailed by the killing of the son; they are accomplished through it. The stone image has two edges: it is foundation for those who build on it and judgment for those who stumble against it or are crushed by it.
